“But, mamma, when we have already asked her!—Besides, she is a lady,” said Cherry.

“I can’t say that I think Mrs. Butler Cornbury would wish to meet her,” said Mrs. Tappitt.

“Mrs. Butler Cornbury’s father is their particular friend,” said Martha. “Mrs. Ray always goes to Mr. Comfort’s parties.”

===Chinese===
“妈妈，这话太没道理了，”彻丽说。“他要是喜欢她，在这儿找不着，别处也找得着。”

“我的宝贝，你不该说我讲的话没道理，”塔皮特太太说。

“可是，妈妈，我们已经邀请过她了呀！——再说，她是位小姐，”彻丽说。

“要我说，巴特勒·康伯里太太未必愿意见她，”塔皮特太太说。

“巴特勒·康伯里太太的父亲是她们家的至交，”玛莎说。“雷太太向来回回都去康福特先生（Mr. Comfort）的聚会。”

===Original===
In this way the matter was discussed, and at last Cherry’s eagerness and Martha’s sense of justice carried the day. The envelope which Cherry had addressed was brought into use, and the note to Rachel was deposited in the post with all those other notes, the destination of which was too far to be reached by the brewery boy without detrimental interference with the brewery work. We will continue our story by following the note which was delivered by the Cawston postman at Bragg’s End about seven o’clock on the Tuesday morning. It was delivered into Rachel’s own hand, and read by her as she stood by the kitchen dresser before either her mother or Mrs. Prime had come down from their rooms. There still was sadness and gloom at Bragg’s End. During all the Monday there had been no comfort in the house, and Rachel had continued to share her mother’s bedroom. At intervals, when Rachel had been away, much had been said between Mrs. Ray and Mrs. Prime; but no conclusion had been reached; no line of conduct had received their joint adhesion; and the threat remained that Mrs. Prime would leave the cottage. Mrs. Ray, while listening to her elder daughter’s words, still continued to fear that evil spirits were hovering around them; but yet she would not consent to order Rachel to become a devout attendant at the Dorcas meetings. Monday had not been a Dorcas day, and therefore it had been very dull and very tedious.

Rachel stood a while with the note in her hand, fearing that the contest must be brought on again and fought out to an end before she could send her answer to it. She had told her mother that she was to be invited, and Mrs. Ray had lacked the courage at the moment which would have been necessary for an absolute and immediate rejection of the proposition. If Mrs. Prime had not been with them in the house, Rachel little doubted but that she might have gone to the party. If Mrs. Prime had not been there, Rachel, as she was now gradually becoming aware, might have had her own way almost in everything. Without the support which Mrs. Prime gave her, Mrs. Ray would have gradually slid down from that stern code of morals which she had been induced to adopt by the teaching of those around her, and would have entered upon a new school of teaching under Rachel’s tutelage. But Mrs. Prime was still there, and Rachel herself was not inclined to fight, if fighting could be avoided. So she put the note into her pocket, and neither answered it or spoke of it till Mrs. Prime had started on her after-dinner walk into Baslehurst. Then she brought it forth and read it to her mother. “I suppose I ought to answer it by the post this evening, mamma?”

“Oh, dear, this evening! that’s very short.”

===Chinese===
事情便这样议论开来，末了，彻丽的热心肠和玛莎的公道心占了上风。彻丽写好地址的那个信封派上了用场，给雷切尔的请柬同其余那些请柬一道交进了邮局——那些人家住得太远，酿酒厂的小伙计送不到，硬要送就会妨害酿酒厂的正活。下面，我们且跟着那张请柬继续讲我们的故事：礼拜二早晨七点钟光景，考斯顿（Cawston）的邮差把它送到了布拉格斯恩德。它交到雷切尔本人手上，她站在厨房碗柜边就读了——那时她母亲和普赖姆太太（Mrs. Prime）都还没从楼上下来。布拉格斯恩德照旧愁云惨雾。整个礼拜一，屋里没有一丝宽慰，雷切尔也仍旧同母亲合住一间卧室。趁雷切尔不在跟前的时候，雷太太（Mrs. Ray）和普赖姆太太之间断断续续说过许多话；但没有谈出结果；没有任何一条行事的准绳得到两人共同的归附；普赖姆太太要搬出村舍的狠话依旧悬在那里。雷太太听着大女儿的话语，心里仍旧害怕有恶灵在她们四近盘旋；可她终究不肯吩咐雷切尔去做多卡斯缝纫会（Dorcas meetings）的虔诚信众。礼拜一不是多卡斯会的日子，因此那一天过得沉闷至极、百无聊赖。

雷切尔捏着请柬站了片刻，心里犯愁：这场仗怕是又要摆开阵势，而且非见个高低不可，她才回得了这份帖子。她早同母亲说过自己要被邀请，而雷太太当时缺乏那种当机立断、即刻断然回绝这件事所必需的勇气。倘若屋里没有普赖姆太太同她们在一处，雷切尔几乎毫不怀疑，她本可以去赴会的。倘若普赖姆太太不在，雷切尔——她此刻已渐渐醒悟——本可以几乎事事都由着自己的性子来。没有了普赖姆太太给她撑腰，雷太太早就会从那套严苛的道德章程上渐渐滑落下来——那章程原是她被身边人的教导劝着才接受下来的——转而投入一门新的教诲，拜雷切尔为师，受她教导。可普赖姆太太还在，而雷切尔自己呢，只要仗能不打，也无意开战。于是她把请柬揣进口袋，既不回复，也不提起，直到普赖姆太太动身去巴斯尔赫斯特做她饭后的散步。这时她才把帖子掏出来，念给母亲听。“我想我今晚就该把回帖交邮吧，妈妈？”

“哎呀，天哪，今晚！这也太急了。”

===Original===
“It can be put off till tomorrow if there’s any good in putting it off,” said Rachel. Mrs. Ray seemed to think that there might be good in putting it off, or rather that there would be harm in doing it at once.

“Do you particularly want to go, my dear?” Mrs. Ray said, after a pause.

“Yes, mamma; I should like to go.” Then Mrs. Ray uttered a little sound which betokened uneasiness, and was again silent for a while.

“I can’t understand why you want to go to this place—so particularly. You never used to care about such things. You know your sister won’t like it, and I’m not at all sure that you ought to go.”

===Chinese===
“要是拖一拖有什么好处，拖到明天也行，”雷切尔说。雷太太似乎觉得拖一拖或许有好处，毋宁说，她觉得立刻回帖会招来坏处。

“你特别想去吗，我的宝贝？”雷太太停了停才说。

“想，妈妈；我愿意去。”于是雷太太发出一声小小的声响，透着不安，接着又沉默了半晌。

“我不明白你怎么偏偏想去那个地方——这样地非去不可。你从来不在乎这类事的呀。你知道你姐姐不会喜欢，而我也实在拿不准你该不该去。”

===Original===
“I’ll tell you why I wish it particularly, only—”

“Well, my dear.”

“I don’t know whether I can make you understand just what I mean.”

“If you tell me, I shall understand, I suppose.”

Rachel considered her words for a moment or two before she spoke, and then she endeavoured to explain herself. “It isn’t that I care for this party especially, mamma, though I own that, after what the girls have said, I should like to be there; but I feel—”

===Chinese===
“我可以告诉你我为什么特别想去，只不过——”

“说吧，我的宝贝。”

“我不知道能不能让你正好明白我的意思。”

“你既然说出来，我想我总能明白吧。”

雷切尔把措辞在心里斟酌了一两分钟才开口，接着便竭力把自己剖白清楚。“倒不是说我对这个聚会有多上心，妈妈，虽然我承认，姑娘们既已这么说过，我是愿意到场的；可我觉得——”

===Original===
“You feel what, my dear?”

“It is this, mamma. Dolly and I do not agree about these things, and I don’t intend to let her manage me just in the way she thinks right.”

“Oh, Rachel!”

“Well, mamma, would you wish it? If you could tell me that you really think it wrong to go to parties, I would give them up. Indeed it wouldn’t be very much to give up, for I don’t often get the chance. But you don’t say so. You only say that I had better not go, because Dolly doesn’t like it. Now, I won’t be ruled by her. Don’t look at me in that way, mamma. Is it right that I should be?”

===Chinese===
“觉得什么，我的宝贝？”

“是这样的，妈妈。多莉（Dolly）和我在这类事情上合不来，我不打算让她照着她自以为对的那一套来管我。”

“哎呀，雷切尔！”

“那么，妈妈，你愿意这样吗？倘若你能对我说，你当真认为赴聚会是罪过，我就从此不去了。说实在的，舍弃这个也算不了什么，因为我本就难得有这样的机会。可你不这么说。你只是说我最好别去，因为多莉不喜欢。如今我可不受她的辖制了。妈妈，别那样瞧着我。难道我就该受她的辖制吗？”

===Original===
“You have heard what she says about going away.”

“I shall be very sorry if she goes, and I hope she won’t; but I can’t think that her threatening you in that way ought to make any difference. And—I’ll tell you more; I do particularly wish to go to Mrs. Tappitt’s, because of all that Dolly has said about—about Mr. Rowan. I wish to show her and you that I am not afraid to meet him. Why should I be afraid of anyone?”

“You should be afraid of doing wrong.”

“Yes; and if it were wrong to meet any other young man I ought not to go; but there is nothing specially wrong in my meeting him. She has said very unkind things about it, and I intend that she shall know that I will not notice them.” As Rachel spoke Mrs. Ray looked up at her, and was surprised by the expression of unrelenting purpose which she saw there. There had come over her face that motion in her eyes and that arching of her brows which Mrs. Ray had seen before, but which hitherto she had hardly construed into their true meaning. Now she was beginning to construe these signs aright, and to understand that there would be difficulty in managing her little family.

===Chinese===
“她那些要搬走的话，你是听见了的。”

“她要真走了，我心里会非常难过，我也不希望她走；可我不认为她那样威胁你，我们就该因此让步。还有——我索性再告诉你一层；我确实是特别想去塔皮特太太家的，就因为多莉说了那么多——关于罗恩先生的话。我要让她、也让你看看，我同他见面并不害怕。我为什么要怕什么人呢？”

“你该怕的是做错事。”

“不错；倘若同别的年轻男人见面是错事，我就不该去；可我同他见面，并没有什么特别的错处。她为这事说了许多刻薄话，我就要让她知道，这些话我概不理会。”雷切尔说这些话的时候，雷太太抬头望着她，被她脸上那股决不回头的决绝神情吓了一跳。她脸上现出那种眼神的流转、那种眉梢的扬挑——雷太太从前见过，却始终没把它们解到真处。如今她开始把这些征兆解对了，也明白了：要管住她这个小小的家，怕是不容易了。

===Original===
The conversation ended in an undertaking on Rachel’s part that she would not answer the note till the following day. “Of course that means,” said Rachel, “that I am to answer it just as Dolly thinks fit.” But she repented of these words as soon as they were spoken, and repented of them almost in ashes when her mother declared, with tears in her eyes, that it was not her intention to be guided by Dorothea in this matter. “You ought not to say such things as that, Rachel,” she said. “No, mamma, I ought not; for there is no one so good as you are; and if you’ll say that you think I ought not to go, I’ll write to Cherry, and explain it to her at once. I don’t care a bit about the party—as far as the party is concerned.” But Mrs. Ray would not now pronounce any injunction on the matter. She had made up her mind as to what she would do. She would call upon Mr. Comfort at the parsonage, explain the whole thing to him, and be guided altogether by his counsel.

Not a word was said in the cottage about the invitation when Mrs. Prime came back in the evening, nor was a word said on the following morning. Mrs. Ray had declared her intention of going up to the parsonage, and neither of her daughters had asked her why she was going. Rachel had no need to ask, for she well understood her mother’s purpose. As to Mrs. Prime, she was in these days black and full of gloom, asking but few questions, watching the progress of events with the eyes of an evil-singing prophetess, but keeping back her words till the moment should come in which she would be driven by her inner impulses to speak them forth with terrible strength. When the breakfast was over, Mrs. Ray took her bonnet and started forth to the parsonage.

I do not know that a widow, circumstanced as was Mrs. Ray, could do better than go to her clergyman for advice, but nevertheless, when she got to Mr. Comfort’s gate she felt that the task of explaining her purpose would not be without difficulty. It would be necessary to tell everything; how Rachel had become suddenly an object of interest to Mr. Luke Rowan, how Dorothea suspected terrible things, and how Rachel was anxious for the world’s vanities. The more she thought over it, the more sure she felt that Mr. Comfort would put an embargo upon the party. It seemed but yesterday that he had been telling her, with all his pulpit unction, that the pleasures of this world should never be allowed to creep near the heart. With doubting feet and doubting heart she walked up to the parsonage door, and almost immediately found herself in the presence of her husband’s old friend.

===Chinese===
这场谈话收场时，雷切尔应承下来，回帖要等到第二天再写。“这当然就是说，”雷切尔道，“回帖怎么写，全凭多莉觉得怎么合适了。”话一出口她就后悔了；而等母亲噙着眼泪声明，她并无在此事上听多萝西娅（Dorothea）摆布的意思，雷切尔更是悔得几乎要披麻蒙灰。“你不该说这样的话，雷切尔，”她说。“是不该，妈妈，我不该；因为再没有谁像你这样好了；只要你肯说你认为我不该去，我就给彻丽写信，立刻跟她说明白。那个聚会我一点儿也不在乎——单就聚会本身而言。”可雷太太这时却不肯就此发出任何禁令。她已打定了主意，知道自己要怎么做：她要上牧师府去拜访康福特先生，把事情原原本本讲给他听，一切全听他的指点。

傍晚普赖姆太太回来，村舍里对那份请柬只字未提；第二天早晨，也只字未提。雷太太已声明要上牧师府去，两个女儿都没有问她去做什么。雷切尔无须问，她把母亲的用意看得一清二楚。至于普赖姆太太，她这些天满面寒霜、郁气沉沉，问得极少，只以一双唱凶歌的女先知的眼睛注视着事态的进展，却把话按住不说，静候那一刻的来临——到那时，内心的冲动会逼着她以可怕的力道把话倾吐出来。早饭一过，雷太太便戴上软帽，动身往牧师府去了。

我不知道，一个像雷太太这样境况的寡妇，除去向她的牧师求教之外还能有更好的做法；尽管如此，走到康福特先生家大门的时候，她还是觉得，要讲明白自己的来意，绝非易事。一切都得说出来：雷切尔如何突然之间成了卢克·罗恩先生青眼相加的对象，多萝西娅如何疑心着可怕的事，雷切尔又如何一心惦着尘世的浮华。这事她越想，越确信康福特先生一定会给这个聚会下禁令。仿佛就在昨天，他还满口讲坛上那股油润劲儿对她说，此世的欢娱万万不可容它挨近心头。她步履犹疑、心头犹疑地走到牧师府门前，几乎立刻便见到了她亡夫的旧友。

===Original===
Whatever faults there might be in Mr. Comfort’s character, he was at any rate good-natured and patient. That he was sincere, too, no one who knew him well had ever doubted—sincere, that is, as far as his intentions went. When he endeavoured to teach his flock that they should despise money, he thought that he despised it himself. When he told the little children that this world should be as nothing to them, he did not remember that he himself enjoyed keenly the good things of this world. If he had a fault it was perhaps this—that he was a hard man at a bargain. He liked to have all his temporalities, and make them go as far as they could be stretched. There was the less excuse for this, seeing that his children were well, and even richly, settled in life, and that his wife, should she ever be left a widow, would have ample provision for her few remaining years. He had given his daughter a considerable fortune, without which perhaps the Cornbury Grange people would not have welcomed her so kindly as they had done, and now, as he was still growing rich, it was supposed that he would leave her more.

He listened to Mrs. Ray with the greatest attention, having first begged her to recruit her strength with a glass of wine. As she continued to tell her story he interrupted her from time to time with good-natured little words, and then, when she had done, he asked after Luke Rowan’s worldly means. “The young man has got something, I suppose,” said he.

“Got something!” repeated Mrs. Ray, not exactly catching his meaning.

“He has some share in the brewery, hasn’t he?”

“I believe he has, or is to have. So Rachel told me.”

===Chinese===
康福特先生的品性里纵有种种毛病，至少他脾气温厚，有耐心。至于说他为人诚恳，凡深知他的人也从不怀疑——所谓诚恳，是就他的本心而言。当他劝导他的羊群应当轻视钱财时，他自以为他自己是轻视钱财的。当他告诉小孩子们，此世于他们应当形同无物时，他并不记得他自己正津津有味地受用着此世的美好事物。他若有一桩毛病，或许便是这一桩：谈起价钱来，他是个寸步不让的硬手。凡属他的世俗进项，他一样也舍不得放手，还要把它们抻到极处。这一点愈发情无可原，因为他的儿女们安顿得都好，甚至极为殷实，而他的太太，万一守了寡，余下不多的岁月也会有充足的供养。他给女儿的嫁妆很是可观；若没有这份财产，康伯里庄园（Cornbury Grange）那家人或许不会像后来那样亲切地接纳她；如今他还在日益富起来，人们料想他留给她的还会更多。

他先请雷太太喝杯酒，补一补力气，然后便全神贯注地听她讲述。她絮絮地讲着，他不时插进一两句和善的小话；等她讲完，他便问起卢克·罗恩的世俗家产。“这个年轻人手头是有些资财的吧，”他说。

“有些资财！”雷太太跟着重复了一遍，没太抓住他的意思。

“他在那家酿酒厂里是有股份的，是不是？”

“我相信是有的，或者将会有的。雷切尔是这么对我说的。”

===Original===
“Yes—yes; I’ve heard of him before. If Tappitt doesn’t take him into the concern he’ll have to give him a very serious bit of money. There’s no doubt about the young man having means. Well, Mrs. Ray, I don’t suppose Rachel could do better than take him.”

“Take him!”

“Yes—why not? Between you and me, Rachel is growing into a very handsome girl—a very handsome girl indeed. I’d no idea she’d be so tall, and carry herself so well.”

“Oh, Mr. Comfort, good looks are very dangerous for a young woman.”

===Chinese===
“是——是的；这人我从前就听说过。塔皮特先生若不让他入伙，就得给他一笔很可观的钱。这年轻人有家底，那是确凿无疑的。这样吧，雷太太，我看雷切尔嫁给他，再好不过了。”

“嫁给他！”

“是啊——为什么不呢？咱们关起门来说，雷切尔出落得越来越标致了——实在是很标致。我没料到她长这么高了，站坐行走又这么有仪态。”

“哎呀，康福特先生，好容貌对一个年轻女人来说是很危险的。”

===Original===
“Well, yes; indeed they are. But still, you know, handsome girls very often do very well; and if this young man fancies Miss Rachel—”

“But, Mr. Comfort, there hasn’t been anything of that. I don’t suppose he has ever thought of it, and I’m sure she hasn’t.”

“But young people get to think of it. I shouldn’t be disposed to prevent their coming together in a proper sort of way. I don’t like night walkings in churchyards, certainly, but I really think that was only an accident.”

“I’m sure Rachel didn’t mean it.”

“I’m quite sure she didn’t mean anything improper. And as for him, if he admires her, it was natural enough that he should go after her. If you ask my advice, Mrs. Ray, I should just tell her to be cautious, but I shouldn’t be especially careful to separate them. Marriage is the happiest condition for a young woman, and for a young man, too. And how are young people to get married if they are not allowed to see each other?”

===Chinese===
“呃，是啊；的确危险。不过你知道，标致的姑娘往往结局很好；这个年轻人要是看上了雷切尔小姐——”

“可是，康福特先生，根本没有这回事呀。我想他从没想过这个，而且我敢说她也没想过。”

“可年轻人慢慢就会想到这上头的。只要来路正派，我不打算拦着他们往来。教堂墓地里的夜间散步我自然不喜欢，可我确实觉得，那一回不过是场意外。”

“我敢说雷切尔不是故意的。”

“我很肯定她没有半点不规矩的心思。至于他呢，他既仰慕她，追着去见她，原也在情理之中。你若问我有什么高见，雷太太，我就教她谨慎些便是，但我不至于费心去把他们拆开。婚姻是年轻女人最幸福的境况，对年轻男人也是如此。不许年轻人见面，他们又怎么结婚呢？”

===Original===
“And about the party, Mr. Comfort?”

“Oh, let her go; there’ll be no harm. And I’ll tell you what, Mrs. Ray; my daughter, Mrs. Cornbury, is going from here, and she shall pick her up and bring her home. It’s always well for a young girl to go with a married woman.” Then Mrs. Ray did take her glass of sherry, and walked back to Bragg’s End, wondering a good deal, and not altogether at ease in her mind as to that great question—what line of moral conduct might best befit a devout Christian.

Something also had been said at the interview about Mrs. Prime. Mrs. Ray had intimated that Mrs. Prime would separate herself from her mother and her sister unless her views were allowed to prevail in this question regarding the young man from the brewery. But Mr. Comfort, in what few words he had said on this part of the subject, had shown no consideration whatever for Mrs. Prime. “Then she’ll behave very wickedly,” he had said. “But I’m afraid Mrs. Prime has learned to think too much of her own opinion lately. If that’s what she has got by going to Mr. Prong she had better have remained in her own parish.” After that, nothing more was said about Mrs. Prime.

===Chinese===
“那这个聚会呢，康福特先生？”

“哦，让她去吧，碍不了事。还有，我告诉你怎么办，雷太太；我女儿康伯里太太就要打我这里动身去，就叫她捎上雷切尔，再把她送回家。年轻姑娘有位已婚的太太同行，总是妥当些。”于是雷太太这才把她那杯雪利酒喝了，动身走回布拉格斯恩德，一路上满腹诧异，而一想到那个大问题——虔诚信奉基督的人，究竟行在哪条道德路线上才最相宜——她的心里总不能全然安适。

这次会面里，也谈到几句普赖姆太太。雷太太暗示说，除非在这桩事关酿酒厂那个年轻男人的问题上依了普赖姆太太的见解，否则她是要同母亲和妹妹分开过的。可康福特先生在这部分话题上仅有的那几句话里，对普赖姆太太没有丝毫体恤。“那她的行为可就太邪恶了，”他说。“不过我怕普赖姆太太近来学会了把自己的意见看得太重。她去投普朗先生（Mr. Prong），若落得的就是这个，那她还不如留在自己堂区的好。”这之后，普赖姆太太便再没有被提起。

===Original===
“Oh, let her go; there’ll be no harm.” That had been Mr. Comfort’s dictum about the evening party. Such as it was, Mrs. Ray felt herself bound to be guided by it. She had told Rachel that she would ask the clergyman’s advice, and take it, whatever it might be. Nevertheless she did not find herself to be easy as she walked home. Mr. Comfort’s latter teachings tended to upset all the convictions of her life. According to his teaching, as uttered in the sanctum of his own study, young men were not to be regarded as ravening wolves. And that meeting in the churchyard, which had utterly overwhelmed Dorothea by the weight of its iniquity, and which even to her had been very terrible, was a mere nothing;—a venial accident on Rachel’s part, and the most natural proceeding in the world on the part of Luke Rowan! That it was natural enough for a wolf Mrs. Ray could understand; but she was now told that the lamb might go out and meet the wolf without any danger! And then those questions about Rowan’s share in the brewery, and Mr. Comfort’s ready assertion that the young wolf—man or wolf, as the case might be—was well to do in the world! In fact Mrs. Ray’s interview with her clergyman had not gone exactly as she had expected, and she was bewildered; and the path into evil—if it was a path into evil—was made so easy and pleasant! Mrs. Ray had already considered the difficult question of Rachel’s journey to the party, and journey home again; but provision was now made for all that in a way that was indeed very comfortable, but which might make Rachel very vain. She was to be ushered into Mrs. Tappitt’s drawing-room under the wing of the most august lady of the neighbourhood. After that, for the remaining half-hour of her walk home, Mrs. Ray gave her mind up to the consideration of what dress Rachel should wear.

When Mrs. Ray reached her own gate, Rachel was in the garden waiting for her. “Well, mamma?” she said. “Is Dorothea at home?” Mrs. Ray asked; and on being informed that Dorothea was at work within, she desired Rachel to follow her up to her bedroom. When there she told her budget of news—not stinting her child of the gratification which it was sure to give. She said nothing about Luke Rowan and his means, keeping that portion of Mr. Comfort’s recommendation to herself; but she declared it out as a fact, that Rachel was to accept the invitation, and to be carried to the party by Mrs. Butler Cornbury. “Oh, mamma! Dear mamma!” said Rachel, who was leaning against the side of the bed. Then she gave a long sigh, and a bright colour came over her face—almost as though she were blushing. But she said no more at the moment, but allowed her mind to run off and revel in its own thoughts. She had indeed longed to go to this party, though she had taught herself to believe that she could bear being told that she was not to go without disappointment. “And now we must let Dorothea know,” said Mrs. Ray. “Yes—we must let her know,” said Rachel; but her mind was away, straying, I fear, under the churchyard elms with Luke Rowan, and looking at the arm amidst the clouds. He had said that it was stretched out as though to take her; and she had never shaken off from her imagination the idea that it was his arm on which she had been bidden to look—the arm which had afterwards held her when she strove to go.

It was teatime before courage was mustered for telling the facts to Mrs. Prime. Mrs. Prime, after dinner, had gone into Baslehurst; but the meeting at Miss Pucker’s had not been a regular full gathering, and Mrs. Prime had come back to tea. There was no hot toast, and no clotted cream. It may appear selfish on the part of Mrs. Ray and Rachel that they should have kept such good things for their only little private banquets, but, in truth, such delicacies did not suit Mrs. Prime. Nice things aggravated her spirits and made her fretful. She liked the tea to be stringy and bitter, and she liked the bread to be stale;—as she preferred also that her weeds should be battered and old. She was approaching that stage of discipline at which ashes become pleasant eating, and sackcloth is grateful to the skin. The self-indulgences of the saints in this respect often exceed anything that is done by the sinners.

“哦，让她去吧，碍不了事。”这便是康福特先生对这个晚间聚会下的裁断。裁断虽只有这么一句，雷太太却觉得自己有责任遵行。她跟雷切尔说过，她要去请教牧师，而且无论牧师怎么说，她都照办。可是在走回家的路上，她并不觉得心里踏实。康福特先生后一段的教导，几乎把她一辈子的信念都掀翻了。照他在自己书房圣所里所说的话，年轻男人是不必当作残暴的豺狼看待的。还有教堂墓地边那一次相会——它压在多萝西娅身上的罪孽之重，直把她整个人都压垮了，连雷太太自己也觉得万分可怕——如今竟算不得什么；在雷切尔一方，是无伤大雅的意外；在卢克·罗恩一方，更是天底下最自然的行止！狼的行止自然，这层道理雷太太明白；可如今人家告诉她：羊羔尽管走出去会那匹狼，毫无危险！还有那些关于罗恩在酿酒厂股份的盘问，还有康福特先生一口断定那匹小狼——是人还是狼，且看情形——在世上处境优渥！说实在的，雷太太同她的牧师这番会面，进行得同她预想的全不一样，她给搅糊涂了；而那条通向邪恶的路——倘若那真是通向邪恶的路——竟铺排得这样平顺、这样叫人舒坦！雷切尔怎么去聚会、又怎么回家，这个难题雷太太原先已经想过；如今这一切都有了安排，安排得确实非常妥帖，只是或许会把雷切尔惯得很虚荣。她将由左近最有威仪的一位太太护送着，被引进塔皮特太太的客厅。此后，在回家的剩下半个钟头里，雷太太把心思全放在了盘算雷切尔该穿哪件衣裳上。

雷太太走到自家院门时，雷切尔正在园子里等她。“怎么样，妈妈？”她说。“多萝西娅在家吗？”雷太太问；听说多萝西娅正在屋里做活，她便让雷切尔跟她上楼，到自己卧室去。到了那里，她把带来的一包新闻抖搂出来——这消息必定带来的快活，她一分也不曾让自家孩子短少。卢克·罗恩和他的家底，她只字未提，把康福特先生指点中的那一节留给了自己；但她把一件事当作定局宣告出来：雷切尔要接受邀请，由巴特勒·康伯里太太送去赴会。“哦，妈妈！亲爱的妈妈！”雷切尔说，人斜倚在床沿上。随后她长长叹了一口气，脸上涌起一片明亮的红晕——简直像是害臊了。但这会儿她再没有说什么，只由着自己的心思跑开了，在种种念头里纵情遨游。她心里实在渴望去赴这个聚会，虽然她一向教导自己相信，即便人家说她去不成，她也能受得住，不觉得失望。“眼下咱们得让多萝西娅知道了，”雷太太说。“是啊——得让她知道，”雷切尔说；可她的心早已飞走了，恐怕正伴着卢克·罗恩，在教堂墓地的榆树下流连，仰望着云中的那条手臂。他说过，那条手臂伸张出来，仿佛要来接她；打那以后，她的想象里始终驱不散那个念头：吩咐她凝望的，正是他那条手臂——就是后来她挣着要走时，揽住她的那条手臂。

一直挨到喝茶时分，才鼓起勇气把实情对普赖姆太太说明。普赖姆太太饭后去了巴斯尔赫斯特；但帕克小姐（Miss Pucker）那里的聚会并非正式的全员大会，普赖姆太太便回来用茶。桌上没有热吐司，也没有凝脂奶油。雷太太和雷切尔把这样的好东西只留给她们娘儿俩小小的私下盛宴，看起来或许自私；但说真的，这类精细吃食本不合普赖姆太太的脾胃。可口的东西会激起她的火气，叫她烦躁。她喜欢茶泡得又酽又苦，喜欢面包放得又干又陈——正如同她乐意自己的丧服也穿得破旧磨损一般。她正一步步走向那样的苦修阶段：到了那地步，灰烬吃起来也香甜，粗麻衣贴在皮肉上也舒适。单在这一桩上，圣徒们的自我放纵，往往就胜过罪人们所作的一切。

“Oh, very well,” said Mrs. Prime. “Of course, mamma, you must judge for yourself.”

“Yes, my dear, I must; or rather, as I didn’t wish to trust my own judgment, I went to Mr. Comfort for advice. He says that he sees no harm in Rachel going to this party.”

“Party! what party?” almost screamed Mrs. Prime. Mrs. Ray had forgotten that nothing had as yet been said to Dorothea about the invitation.

“Mrs. Tappitt is going to give a party at the brewery,” said Rachel, in her very softest voice, “and she has asked me.”

“And you are going? You mean to let her go?” Mrs. Prime had asked two questions, and she received two answers. “Yes,” said Rachel; “I suppose I shall go, as mamma says so.” “Mr. Comfort says there is no harm in it,” said Mrs. Ray; “and Mrs. Butler Cornbury is to come from the parsonage to take her up.” All question as to Dorcas discipline to be inflicted daily upon Rachel on account of that sin of which she had been guilty in standing under the elms with a young man was utterly lost in this terrible proposition! Instead of being sent to Miss Pucker in her oldest merino dress, Rachel was to be decked in muslin and finery, and sent out to a dancing party at which this young man was to be the hero! It was altogether too much for Dorothea Prime. She slowly wiped the crumbs from off her dingy crape, and with creaking noise pushed back her chair. “Mother,” she said, “I couldn’t have believed it! I could not have believed it!” Then she withdrew to her own chamber.

Mrs. Ray was much afflicted; but not the less did Rachel look out for the returning postman, on his road into Baslehurst, that she might send her little note to Mrs. Tappitt, signifying her acceptance of that lady’s kind invitation.

## VI Preparations for Mrs. Tappitt’s Party / VI 塔皮特太太聚会的筹备

===Original===
I am disposed to think that Mrs. Butler Cornbury did Mrs. Tappitt an injury when she with so much ready good nature accepted the invitation for the party, and that Mrs. Tappitt was aware of this before the night of the party arrived. She was put on her mettle in a way that was disagreeable to her, and forced into an amount of submissive supplication to Mr. Tappitt for funds, which was vexatious to her spirit. Mrs. Tappitt was a good wife, who never ran her husband into debt, and kept nothing secret from him in the management of her household—nothing at least which it behoved him to know. But she understood the privileges of her position, and could it have been possible for her to have carried through this party without extra household moneys, or without any violent departure from her usual customs of life, she could have snubbed her husband’s objections comfortably, and have put him into the background for the occasion without any inconvenience to herself or power of remonstrance from him. But when Mrs. Butler Cornbury had been gracious, and when the fiddles and horn had become a fact to be accomplished, when Mrs. Rowan and Mary began to loom large on her imagination and a regular supper was projected, then Mrs. Tappitt felt the necessity of superior aid, and found herself called upon to reconcile her lord.

And this work was the more difficult and the more disagreeable to her feelings because she had already pooh-poohed her husband when he asked a question about the party. “Just a few friends got together by the girls,” she had said. “Leave it all to them, my dear. It’s not very often they see anybody at home.”

“I believe I see my friends as often as most people in Baslehurst,” Mr. Tappitt had replied indignantly, “and I suppose my friends are their friends.” So there had been a little soreness which made the lady’s submission the more disagreeable to her.
===Chinese===
我倒倾向于认为，巴特勒·康伯里太太那口应承了聚会的邀请，答应得那样爽快热心，实在是害了塔皮特太太；而聚会之夜未到，塔皮特太太自己心里已有了数。她被将了一军，逼得打起精神，那滋味好不受用；还不得不低声下气向塔皮特先生讨经费，讨到那份上，实在有伤她的心气。塔皮特太太是位贤妻，从不拖丈夫负债，料理家务也从不背着他藏半点私——至少从不瞒他那些他理应知道的事。可她也明白自己身份里的种种特权：倘若这台聚会不添一分额外家用、也不大张旗鼓破一破平日的生计规矩便能办下来，她尽可以从从容容把丈夫的异议驳回去，把他撂到后台，自己毫无不便，他也无从申辩。可是，巴特勒·康伯里太太既已赏脸，几把提琴和一支号已成了非兑现不可的事实，罗恩太太（Mrs. Rowan）和玛丽（Mary）又开始在她想象中日益显赫，一场像样的夜宴也已排上日程——到这地步，塔皮特太太便觉得非有高一级的援手不可，发觉自己只得去求老爷息怒修好。

而这桩差事之所以格外难办、格外伤她的心，是因为先前丈夫问起聚会时，她曾把他的话轻轻浮浮地搪塞过去。“不过是姑娘们邀了几个朋友聚聚，”她当时说，“全都交给她们去办吧，我亲爱的。她们在家难得见着什么人呢。”

“我相信，我见朋友的次数不比巴斯尔赫斯特随便哪个人少，”塔皮特先生愤愤然答道，“况且我想，我的朋友也就是她们的朋友。”于是两人心里存下了一点小疙瘩，这使得太太后来那番低头服软，愈发叫她自己难以下咽。

“You need not tell her so, my dear; and he’s not coming. I suppose you like your girls to hold their heads up in the place; and if they show that they’ve respectable people with them at home, respectable people will be glad to notice them.”

“Respectable! If our girls are to be made respectable by giving grand dances, I’d rather not have them respectable. How much is the whole thing to cost?”

===Original===
“Well, very little, T.; not much more than one of your Christmas dinner-parties. There’ll be just the music, and the lights, and a bit of something to eat. What people drink at such times comes to nothing—just a little negus and lemonade. We might possibly have a bottle or two of champagne at the supper-table, for the look of the thing.”

“Champagne!” exclaimed the brewer. He had never yet incurred the cost of a bottle of champagne within his own house, though he thought nothing of it at public dinners. The idea was too much for him; and Mrs. Tappitt, feeling how the ground lay, gave that up—at any rate for the present. She gave up the champagne; but in abandoning that, she obtained the marital sanction, a quasi sanction which he was too honourable as a husband afterwards to repudiate, for the music and the eatables. Mrs. Tappitt knew that she had done well, and prepared for his dinner that day a beefsteak pie, made with her own hands. Tappitt was not altogether a dull man, and understood these little signs. “Ah,” said he, “I wonder how much that pie is to cost me?”

“Oh, T., how can you say such things! As if you didn’t have beefsteak pie as often as it’s good for you.” The pie, however, had its effect, as also did the exceeding “boilishness” of the water which was brought in for his gin-toddy that night; and it was known throughout the establishment that papa was in a good humour, and that mamma had been very clever.
===Chinese===
“哦，没多少的，T.；比你哪一回圣诞宴客多不了一点。无非是乐师，灯烛，再备一点点吃的。这种场合大家喝下的实在有限——不过一点尼格斯热酒（negus）和柠檬水罢了。夜宴桌上兴许上一两瓶香槟，装点装点门面。”

“香槟！”酿酒商失声叫道。他自己家里至今还没破费过一瓶香槟，虽则在公宴上喝起来他全不放在心上。这个念头叫他实在受不住；塔皮特太太看准了风往哪边吹，便把这一项让了——至少暂时让了。香槟是让掉了，可让掉香槟，她却换来了丈夫对乐师和吃食的恩准——一道半正式的恩准，他这个当丈夫的极重体面，日后断不肯亲口翻悔。塔皮特太太知道自己这一手干得漂亮，当天便亲手做了一只牛排饼给他当晚饭。塔皮特并不全然是笨人，这类小小的征候他都懂。“啊，”他说，“我倒想知道，这饼要我破费多少？”

“哎哟，T.，看你说的！倒好像你不是只要对身体有益便顿顿有牛排饼吃似的。”然而那只饼毕竟起了作用，那天夜里为他的金酒托迪送进来的水，那份“滚沸劲儿”也格外到家；于是全家上下都知道，爸爸脾气正好，妈妈手段高明。

===Original===
“The girls must have had new dresses anyway before the month was out,” Mrs. Tappitt said to her husband the next morning before he had left the conjugal chamber.

“Do you mean to say that they’re to have gowns made on purpose for this party?” said the brewer; and it seemed by the tone of his voice that the hot gin and water had lost its kindly effects.

“My dear, they must be dressed, you know. I’m sure no girls in Baslehurst cost less in the way of finery. In the ordinary way they’d have had new frocks almost immediately.”

“Bother!” Mr. Tappitt was shaving just at this moment, and dashed aside his razor for a moment to utter this one word. He intended to signify how perfectly well he was aware that a muslin frock prepared for an evening party would not fill the place of a substantial morning dress.
===Chinese===
“反正不出这个月，姑娘们横竖也该添新衣裳了，”第二天早上，塔皮特太太趁丈夫还没出夫妻卧房，便对他说。

“你是说，她们还要专为这台聚会做新裙子？”酿酒商说；听那腔调，仿佛昨夜那杯热金酒糖水的温柔功效已烟消云散。

“我亲爱的，姑娘们总得有个打扮呀，这你明白。我敢说巴斯尔赫斯特没有哪家的姑娘在穿戴上的花费比我们家更省。按平常的日子，她们差不多也马上就该添新连衣裙了。”

“麻烦！”塔皮特先生这会儿正在刮脸，把剃刀一偏，吐出这一个词来。他这意思是再明白不过：为晚会备下的平纹细布连衣裙，顶替不了一件经穿的家常日装。

===Original===
“Well, my dear, I’m sure the girls ain’t unreasonable; nor am I. Five-and-thirty shillings apiece for them would do it all. And I shan’t want anything myself this year in September.” Now Mr. Tappitt, who was a man of sentiment, always gave his wife some costly article of raiment on the 1st of September, calling her his partridge and his bird—for on that day they had been married. Mrs. Tappitt had frequently offered to intromit the ceremony when calling upon his generosity for other purposes, but the September gift had always been forthcoming.

“Will thirty-five shillings apiece do it?” said he, turning round with his face all covered with lather. Then again he went to work with his razor just under his right ear.

“Well, yes; I think it will. Two pounds each for the three shall do it anyway.”

Mr. Tappitt gave a little jump at this increased demand for fifteen shillings, and not being in a good position for jumping, encountered an unpleasant accident, and uttered a somewhat vehement exclamation. “There,” said he, “now I’ve cut myself, and it’s your fault. Oh dear; oh dear! When I cut myself there it never stops. It’s no good doing that, Margaret; it only makes it worse. There; now you’ve got the soap and blood all down inside my shirt.”
===Chinese===
“好啦，我亲爱的，我知道姑娘们不是不讲道理的人；我也不。她们每人三十五先令便全办下来了。再说今年九月我自己什么也不要。”原来塔皮特先生是个多情种子，每年九月一日总要送妻子一件值钱的衣饰，管她叫他的鹧鸪、他的鸟儿——因为那一天正是他们结缡的日子。塔皮特太太为旁的用处来求他慷慨解囊时，屡屡主动提出把这道礼数免了；可那份九月之礼却从未短少过。

“每人三十五先令就够了？”他说，转过脸来，满脸皂沫。说罢又拿起剃刀，在右耳底下干起活来。

“呃，是啊；我想够了。三个人每人两镑，横竖总够了。”

十五先令的加码让塔皮特先生猛地一跳，而跳的时候他的姿势原不凑手，便遭了一场不痛快的小祸，嗓子里迸出一声相当激烈的惊叫。“瞧瞧，”他说，“这下割着我了，都怪你。哎呀，哎呀！那地方一割开就没个停。你别弄了，玛格丽特（Margaret），越弄越糟。瞧瞧，皂沫带血，全淌进我衬衫里头了。”

===Original===
Mrs. Tappitt on this occasion was subjected to some trouble, for the wound on Mr. Tappitt’s cheekbone declined to be stanched at once; but she gained her object, and got the dresses for her daughters. It was not taken by them as a drawback on their happiness that they had to make the dresses themselves, for they were accustomed to such work; but this necessity joined to all other preparations for the party made them very busy. Till twelve at night on three evenings they sat with their smart new things in their laps and their needles in their hands; but they did not begrudge this, as Mrs. Butler Cornbury was coming to the brewery. They were very anxious to get the heavy part of the work done before the Rowans should arrive, doubting whether they would become sufficiently intimate with Mary to tell her all their little domestic secrets, and do their work in the presence of their new friend during the first day of her sojourn in the house. So they toiled like slaves on the Wednesday and Thursday in order that they might walk about like ladies on the Friday and Saturday.

But the list of their guests gave them more trouble than aught else. Whom should they get to meet Mrs. Butler Cornbury? At one time Mrs. Tappitt had proposed to word certain of her invitations with a special view to this end. Had her idea been carried out people who might not otherwise have come were to be tempted by a notification that they were especially asked to meet Mrs. Butler Cornbury. But Martha had said that this she thought would not do for a dance. “People do do it, my dear,” Mrs. Tappitt had pleaded.

“Not for dancing, mamma,” said Martha. “Besides, she would be sure to hear of it, and perhaps she might not like it.”

“Well, I don’t know,” said Mrs. Tappitt. “It would show that we appreciated her kindness.” The plan, however, was abandoned.
===Chinese===
这一回塔皮特太太着实费了些手脚，因为塔皮特先生颧骨上的伤口一时竟不肯止血；可她终究如愿以偿，为女儿们争得了裙子。裙子得亲手来做，她们并不把这当作乐事上的减损，因为这类的活计她们做惯了；只是这桩活计连同聚会的其他种种筹备，把她们弄得忙碌非常。有三个晚上，她们坐着做到夜里十二点，漂亮的新衣裳摊在膝头，针在手里；可这份辛苦她们并不吝惜，因为巴特勒·康伯里太太就要驾临酿酒厂了。她们一心盼着在罗恩家母女到来之前把重活干完，心里直嘀咕：同玛丽未必就能熟络到那种地步，头一天便把自家那些小秘密全数讲给她听，还当着新朋友的面做针线。于是礼拜三、礼拜四两天，她们像奴隶般苦干，为的是礼拜五、礼拜六两天能像贵妇人般悠游。

可是宾客名单比什么都更叫她们费神。请谁来陪巴特勒·康伯里太太呢？有一个时候，塔皮特太太曾打算在某些请帖的措辞上特别为此做点文章。倘若她的主意得以实行，有些本来未必肯来的人，便会因请帖上注明是专诚请他们来会巴特勒·康伯里太太而动了心。但玛莎说，她以为这对一场舞会不相宜。“人家确有这样办的，我亲爱的，”塔皮特太太央告道。

“办舞会可不兴这样，妈妈，”玛莎说。“再说，她准会听说的，说不定她还不乐意呢。”

“呃，这我说不好，”塔皮特太太说。“这正显得我们领她的情嘛。”不过这计划终究作罢了。

===Original===
Of the Baslehurst folk there were so few that were fitted to meet Mrs. Butler Cornbury! There was old Miss Harford, the rector’s daughter. She was fit to meet anybody in the county, and, as she was good-natured, might probably come. But she was an old maid, and was never very bright in her attire. “Perhaps Captain Gordon’s lady would come,” Mrs. Tappitt suggested. But at this proposition all the girls shook their heads. Captain Gordon had lately taken a villa close to Baslehurst, but had shown himself averse to any intercourse with the townspeople. Mrs. Tappitt had called on his “lady,” and the call had not even been returned, a card having been sent by post in an envelope.

“It would be no good, mamma,” said Martha, “and she would only make us uncomfortable if she did come.”

“She is always awfully stuck up in church,” said Augusta.

“And her nose is red at the end,” said Cherry.

Therefore no invitation was sent to Captain Gordon’s house.
===Chinese===
巴斯尔赫斯特镇上的人，配得上会一会巴特勒·康伯里太太的何其少！有年迈的哈福德小姐（Miss Harford），教区长的女儿。她同全郡什么人相会都配得过，人又和善，多半肯来。可她是位老小姐，穿戴从来不见鲜亮。“戈登上尉（Captain Gordon）的那位太太兴许肯来，”塔皮特太太出主意道。可这话一出口，几位姑娘一齐摇头。戈登上尉新近在巴斯尔赫斯特近旁置了一座别墅，却露出一副不愿与镇民往来的样子。塔皮特太太曾登门拜会他的“太太”，那回拜访竟连回拜都没有，只从邮局寄来一只信封，封里一张名片。

“请了也没用，妈妈，”玛莎说，“再说她真来了，也只会叫我们局促不安。”

“她在教堂里总是傲气得不得了，”奥古斯塔说。

“还有她鼻子尖儿是红的，”彻丽说。

于是戈登上尉府上便没有下帖。

===Original===
“If we could only get the Fawcetts,” said Augusta. The Fawcetts were a large family living in the centre of Baslehurst, in which there were four daughters, all noted for dancing, and noted also for being the merriest, nicest, and most popular girls in Devonshire. There was a fat good-natured mother, and a thin good-natured father who had once been a banker at Exeter. Everybody desired to know the Fawcetts, and they were the especial favourites of Mrs. Butler Cornbury. But then Mrs. Fawcett did not visit Mrs. Tappitt. The girls and the mothers had a bowing acquaintance, and were always very gracious to each other. Old Fawcett and old Tappitt saw each other in town daily, and knew each other as well as they knew the cross in the butter-market; but none of the two families ever went into each other’s houses. It had been tacitly admitted among them that the Fawcetts were above the Tappitts, and so the matter had rested. But now, if anything could be done? “Mrs. Butler Cornbury is all very well, of course,” said Augusta, “but it would be so nice for Mary Rowan to see the Miss Fawcetts dancing here.”

Martha shook her head, but at last she did write a note in the mother’s name. “My girls are having a little dance, to welcome a friend from London, and they would feel so much obliged if your young ladies would come. Mrs. Butler Cornbury has been kind enough to say that she would join us, etc., etc., etc.” Mrs. Tappitt and Augusta were in a seventh heaven of happiness when Mrs. Fawcett wrote to say that three of her girls would be delighted to accept the invitation; and even the discreet Martha and the less ambitious Cherry were well pleased.

“I declare I think we’ve been very fortunate,” said Mrs. Tappitt.

“Only the Miss Fawcetts will get all the best partners,” said Cherry.

“I’m not so sure of that,” said Augusta, holding up her head.

But there had been yet another trouble. It was difficult for them to get people proper to meet Mrs. Butler Cornbury; but what must they do as to those people who must come and who were by no means proper to meet her? There were the Griggses for instance, who lived out of town in a wonderfully red brick house, the family of a retired Baslehurst grocer. They had been asked before Mrs. Cornbury’s call had been made, or, I fear, their chance of coming to the party would have been small. There was one young Griggs, a man very terrible in his vulgarity, loud, rampant, conspicuous with villainous jewellery, and odious with the worst abominations of perfumery. He was loathsome even to the Tappitt girls; but then the Griggses and the Tappitts had known each other for half a century, and among their ordinary acquaintances Adolphus Griggs might have been endured. But what should they do when he asked to be introduced to Josceline Fawcett? Of all men he was the most unconscious of his own defects. He had once shown some symptoms of admiration for Cherry, by whom he was hated with an intensity of dislike that had amounted to a passion. She had begged that he might be omitted from the list; but Mrs. Tappitt had been afraid of angering their father.
===Chinese===
“要是能把福西特一家（the Fawcetts）请来就好了，”奥古斯塔说。福西特一家住在巴斯尔赫斯特镇中心，人口众多，家里有四位小姐，个个以舞艺著称，也个个以全德文郡最快活、最可亲、最得人缘的姑娘著称。有一位胖胖的、和和气气的母亲，一位瘦瘦的、和和气气的父亲——他从前在埃克塞特做过银行家。人人都巴望结识福西特家，而她们又是巴特勒·康伯里太太的特别宠儿。可话又要说回来，福西特太太不登塔皮特家的门。姑娘们和两位太太彼此只有点头之交，见面倒总是客客气气。老福西特同老塔皮特天天在镇上照面，彼此熟得就像熟识黄油市场那座十字碑一般；只是两家谁也没进过谁家的门。两家心照不宣地认下了一条：福西特家高过塔皮特家——事情便这样搁下了。可如今，倘若能想点办法呢？“巴特勒·康伯里太太自然是谁也比不了的，”奥古斯塔说，“可要是能让玛丽·罗恩看看福西特家小姐们在我们这儿跳舞，那该多好。”

玛莎直摇头，可末了到底还是以母亲的名义写了张短简。“我的女儿们准备办一次小小的舞会，欢迎一位从伦敦来的朋友；倘若府上的小姐们肯赏光，她们将感激不尽。巴特勒·康伯里太太已蒙她俯允，说要来同我们相聚，等等，等等，等等。”等到福西特太太回信说她家三位小姐乐意接受邀请，塔皮特太太和奥古斯塔简直乐得如同登上了第七重天；就连素来谨慎的玛莎和志向不那么远的彻丽，也都满心欢喜。

“我说句心里话，咱们运气真算不错，”塔皮特太太说。

“只怕福西特家小姐们要把最好的舞伴全抢了去，”彻丽说。

“那可不一定，”奥古斯塔说，把头昂了起来。

可麻烦还有一宗。要凑几个配同巴特勒·康伯里太太见面的人已然不易；而那些非来不可、却又万万配不上同她见面的人，又该如何处置？譬如格里格斯一家（the Griggses），住在城外一幢红砖大宅里，红得出奇，那是巴斯尔赫斯特一位歇业杂货商的家眷。请帖是康伯里太太登门之前就发出去的——要不然，我怕他们想来赴会的机会可就渺茫了。格里格斯家有这么一位少爷，俗气得叫人心惊，嗓门洪亮，不可一世，一身恶俗的珠宝招摇刺眼，喷的香水又是里头最不堪的腻人货色。连塔皮特家的姑娘们都嫌他可憎；可话虽如此，格里格斯家和塔皮特家相交已有半个世纪，在寻常熟人的圈子里，阿道弗斯·格里格斯（Adolphus Griggs）原也忍得下。可他倘若开口要人介绍他同乔斯琳·福西特（Josceline Fawcett）认识，那可怎么办？普天之下数他最看不见自己的短处。他从前曾对彻丽露出几分爱慕的苗头，彻丽恨他恨得入骨，那股嫌恶之烈，简直成了一种激情。她曾央求把他从名单上勾掉；但塔皮特太太怕惹恼了她们的父亲。

===Original===
The Rules also would be much in the way. Old Joshua Rule was a maltster, living in Cawston, and his wife and daughter had been asked before the accession of the Butler Cornbury dignity. Old Rule had supplied the brewery with malt almost ever since it had been a brewery; and no more harmless people than Mrs. Rule and her daughter existed in the neighbourhood;—but they were close neighbours of the Comforts, of Mrs. Cornbury’s father and mother, and Mr. Comfort would have as soon asked his sexton to dine with him as the Rules. The Rules never expected such a thing, and therefore lived on very good terms with the clergyman. “I’m afraid she won’t like meeting Mrs. Rule,” Augusta had said to her mother; and then the mother had shaken her head.

Early in the week, before Rachel had accepted the invitation, Cherry had written to her friend. “Of course you’ll come,” Cherry had said; “and as you may have some difficulty in getting here and home again, I’ll ask old Mrs. Rule to call for you. I know she’ll have a place in the fly, and she’s very good-natured.” In answer to this Rachel had written a separate note to Cherry, telling her friend in the least boastful words which she could use that provision had been already made for her coming and going. “Mamma was up at Mr. Comfort’s yesterday,” Rachel wrote, “and he was so kind as to say that Mrs. Butler Cornbury would take me and bring me back. I am very much obliged to you all the same, and to Mrs. Rule.”

“What do you think?” said Cherry, who had received her note in the midst of one of the family conferences; “Augusta said that Mrs. Butler Cornbury would not like to meet Rachel Ray; but she is going to bring her in her own carriage.”
===Chinese===
鲁尔家（the Rules）也是一重躲不开的麻烦。老乔舒亚·鲁尔（Joshua Rule）是个制麦芽的，住在考斯顿，他的妻女是在巴特勒·康伯里太太那桩尊荣加临之前就请下了的。老鲁尔给酿酒厂供麦芽，几乎打这厂子成了酿酒厂那天起就没有断过；左近再也找不出比鲁尔太太（Mrs. Rule）和她女儿更无害的人家——可偏偏他们是康福特家的近邻，也就是康伯里太太爹娘的近邻；康福特先生若是请鲁尔家来同席用饭，那同请他那位教堂司事来吃饭是一般无二的事。鲁尔家压根儿没指望过那种事，所以同这位牧师一向相处得极好。“我怕她不愿意见鲁尔太太，”奥古斯塔对母亲说过；母亲听了直摇头。

那个礼拜早些时候，雷切尔还没应下邀请，彻丽已先给她的朋友去了信。“你当然要来的，”彻丽信里说；“你来去路上也许不便，我叫老鲁尔太太顺路来接你。我知道她那辆单马轻便马车上总有个空座，她人又顶和气。”对此雷切尔另写了一张短简回复彻丽，用她找得出的最不夸口的字眼告诉朋友：她来去的事早有安排了。“妈妈昨天上康福特先生家去了，”雷切尔写道，“承他好意说，巴特勒·康伯里太太会接我去，再送我回来。虽然这样，我一样感激你们大家，也感激鲁尔太太。”

“你们猜怎么着？”彻丽说；那张短简送到时，恰值家里一次家庭会议开到半截；“奥古斯塔说巴特勒·康伯里太太不愿意见雷切尔·雷；可人家现在要用自己的马车接她来了。”

===Original===
“I never said anything of the kind,” said Augusta.

“Oh, but you did, Augusta; or mamma did, or somebody. How nice for Rachel to be chaperoned by Mrs. Butler Cornbury!”

“I wonder what she’ll wear,” said Mrs. Tappitt, who had on that morning achieved her victory over the wounded brewer in the matter of the three dresses.

On the Friday morning Mrs. Rowan came with her daughter, Luke having met them at Exeter on the Thursday. Mrs. Rowan was a somewhat stately lady, slow in her movements and careful in her speech, so that the girls were at first very glad that they had valiantly worked up their finery before her coming. But Mary was by no means stately; she was younger than them, very willing to be pleased, with pleasant round eager eyes, and a kindly voice. Before she had been three hours in the house Cherry had claimed Mary for her own, had told her all about the party, all about the dresses, all about Mrs. Butler Cornbury and the Miss Fawcetts, and a word or two also about Rachel Ray. “I can tell you somebody that’s almost in love with her.” “You don’t mean Luke?” said Mary. “Yes, but I do,” said Cherry; “but of course I’m only in fun.” On the Saturday Mary was hard at work herself assisting in the decoration of the drawing-room, and before the all-important Tuesday came even Mrs. Rowan and Mrs. Tappitt were confidential. Mrs. Rowan perceived at once that Mrs. Tappitt was provincial—as she told her son, but she was a good motherly woman, and on the whole, Mrs. Rowan condescended to be gracious to her.

At Bragg’s End the preparations for the party required almost as much thought as did those at the brewery, and involved perhaps deeper care. It may be remembered that Mrs. Prime, when her ears were first astounded by that unexpected revelation, wiped the crumbs from out of her lap and walked off, wounded in spirit, to her own room. On that evening Rachel saw no more of her sister. Mrs. Ray went up to her daughter’s bedroom, but stayed there only a minute or two. “What does she say?” asked Rachel, almost in a whisper. “She is very unhappy. She says that unless I can be made to think better of this she must leave the cottage. I told her what Mr. Comfort says, but she only sneers at Mr. Comfort. I’m sure I’m endeavouring to do the best I can.”

“It wouldn’t do, mamma, to say that she should manage everything, otherwise I’m sure I’d give up the party.”

“No, my dear; I don’t want you to do that—not after what Mr. Comfort says.” Mrs. Ray had in truth gone to the clergyman feeling sure that he would have given his word against the party, and that, so strengthened, she could have taken a course that would have been offensive to neither of her daughters. She had expected, too, that she would have returned home armed with such clerical thunders against the young man as would have quieted Rachel and have satisfied Dorothea. But in all this she had been—I may hardly say disappointed—but dismayed and bewildered by advice the very opposite to that which she had expected. It was perplexing, but she seemed to be aware that she had no alternative now, but to fight the battle on Rachel’s side. She had cut herself off from all anchorage except that given by Mr. Comfort, and therefore it behoved her to cling to that with absolute tenacity. Rachel must go to the party, even though Dorothea should carry out her threat. On that night nothing more was said about Dorothea, and Mrs. Ray allowed herself to be gradually drawn into a mild discussion about Rachel’s dress.

“妈妈，总不能说什么事都归她管呀，要不然，说实话，我这聚会宁可不去。”

===Original===
But there was nearly a week left to them of this sort of life. Early on the following morning Mrs. Prime left the cottage, saying that she should dine with Miss Pucker, and betook herself at once to a small house in a back street of the town, behind the new church, in which lived Mr. Prong. Have I as yet said that Mr. Prong was a bachelor? Such was the fact; and there were not wanting those in Baslehurst who declared that he would amend the fault by marrying Mrs. Prime. But this rumour, if it ever reached her, had no effect upon her. The world would be nothing to her if she were to be debarred by the wickedness of loose tongues from visiting the clergyman of her choice. She went, therefore, in her present difficulty to Mr. Prong.

Mr. Samuel Prong was a little man, over thirty, with scanty, light-brown hair, with a small, rather upturned nose, with eyes by no means deficient in light and expression, but with a mean mouth. His forehead was good, and had it not been for his mouth his face would have been expressive of intellect and of some firmness. But there was about his lips an assumption of character and dignity which his countenance and body generally failed to maintain; and there was a something in the carriage of his head and in the occasional projection of his chin, which was intended to add to his dignity, but which did, I think, only make the failure more palpable. He was a devout, good man; not self-indulgent; perhaps not more self-ambitious than it becomes a man to be; sincere, hardworking, sufficiently intelligent, true in most things to the instincts of his calling—but deficient in one vital qualification for a clergyman of the Church of England; he was not a gentleman. May I not call it a necessary qualification for a clergyman of any church? He was not a gentleman. I do not mean to say that he was a thief or a liar; nor do I mean hereby to complain that he picked his teeth with his fork and misplaced his *h*’s. I am by no means prepared to define what I do mean—thinking, however, that most men and most women will understand me. Nor do I speak of this deficiency in his clerical aptitudes as being injurious to him simply—or even chiefly—among folk who are themselves gentle; but that his efficiency for clerical purposes was marred altogether, among high and low, by his misfortune in this respect. It is not the owner of a good coat that sees and admires its beauty. It is not even they who have good coats themselves who recognize the article on the back of another. They who have not good coats themselves have the keenest eyes for the coats of their better-clad neighbours. As it is with coats, so it is with that which we call gentility. It is caught at a word, it is seen at a glance, it is appreciated unconsciously at a touch by those who have none of it themselves. It is the greatest of all aids to the doctor, the lawyer, the member of Parliament—though in that position a man may perhaps prosper without it—and to the statesman; but to the clergyman it is a vital necessity. Now Mr. Prong was not a gentleman.

不过这样的日子，她们还得过上将近一个礼拜。第二天一早，普赖姆太太便离开村舍，说是去帕克小姐家吃饭，随即径直往镇后街一所小屋去了——新教堂后面，普朗先生就住在那里。普朗先生是位单身汉，这话我说过没有？事实如此；巴斯尔赫斯特不乏有人宣称，他将来娶了普赖姆太太，正好把这个缺憾补上。但这桩流言，即便传进她耳朵，对她也不生半分影响。倘若因为饶舌之徒的歹毒，她便不得登门拜访自己择定的牧师，那这个世界于她还有什么意义。因此她遇着当下的难处，便去找普朗先生。

塞缪尔·普朗先生是个小个子男人，三十出头，头发浅褐而稀疏，鼻子小巧而微微上翘，眼睛绝不缺乏光彩与神气，唯独一张嘴生得寒碜。他额头生得好，若不是那张嘴碍事，他的脸本会显出智力与几分坚毅来。可他嘴唇上总摆着一副人格与尊严的架势，而他的面色、他的整个身形却撑不起这副架势；还有他摆头的姿势、时不时往前伸一伸下巴的做派，本想给自己添些威严，可我看，反倒只把那份不像添得更扎眼了。他是个虔诚的好人；不放纵自己；好胜之心或许也没有超出一个人本分的分寸；诚恳，勤勉，智力够用，在多数事情上忠于他那一行的本能——唯独在英国国教牧师一条性命交关的资格上有所欠缺：他不是个绅士。这资格，我难道不能称之为任何教会的牧师都必不可少么？他不是个绅士。我并不是说他做贼，也不是说他撒谎；我也不是要数落他拿叉子剔牙，或是把 h 音念得颠三倒四。我那意思究竟是什么，我断不敢贸然界说——不过我想，大多数男男女女自会明白。我之所以提他牧师资质里的这一缺陷，也不是说它单单——甚或主要——在上流人中间于他有损；而是说，无论高门还是寒户，他那点不幸都把他牧师职分的效验整个儿毁了。好衣裳的主人，并不就是看见它、赏识别样好衣裳的人。甚至自己有好衣裳的人，也未必认得清别人背上的那一件。自己没有好衣裳的人，眼光才最毒，专会打量那些穿得比他们好的邻居的衣裳。衣裳如此，我们所谓的斯文气派也如此。自己身上没有它的人，从一个字里便把它捉住，一瞥之下便把它看见，一触之间便不自觉地掂出它的分量。对医生、律师、议会议员——尽管坐在这个位置上的人没有它兴许也发得了达——对政治家，它都是顶大的助力；可对牧师，它是性命交关的必需。而普朗先生，恰恰不是个绅士。

===Original===
Mrs. Prime told her tale to Mr. Prong, as Mrs. Ray had told hers to Mr. Comfort. It need not be told again here. I fear that she made the most of her sister’s imprudence, but she did not do so with intentional injustice. She declared her conviction that Rachel might still be made to go in a straight course, if only she could be guided by a hand sufficiently strict and armed with absolute power. Then she went on to tell Mr. Prong how Mrs. Ray had gone off to Mr. Comfort, as she herself had now come to him. It was hard—was it not?—for poor Rachel that the story of her few minutes’ whispering under the elm tree should thus be bruited about among the ecclesiastical councillors of the locality. Mr. Prong sat with patient face and with mild demeanour while the simple story of Rachel’s conduct was being told; but when to this was added the iniquity of Mr. Comfort’s advice, the mouth assumed the would-be grandeur, the chin came out, and to anyone less infatuated than Mrs. Prime it would have been apparent that the purse was not made of silk, but that a coarser material had come to hand in the manufacture.

“What shall the sheep do,” said Mr. Prong, “when the shepherd slumbers in the folds?” Then he shook his head and puckered up his mouth.

“Ah!” said Mrs. Prime; “it is well for the sheep that there are still left a few who do not run from their work, even in the heat of the noonday sun.”

Mr. Prong closed his eyes and bowed his head, and then reassumed that peculiarly disagreeable look about his mouth by which he thought to assert his dignity, intending thereby to signify that he would willingly reject the compliment as unnecessary, were he not forced to accept it as being true. He knew himself to be a shepherd who did not fear the noonday heat; but he was wrong in this—that he suspected all other shepherds of stinting their work. It appeared to him that no sheep could nibble his grass in wholesome content, unless some shepherd were at work at him constantly with his crook. It was for the shepherd, as he thought, to know what tufts of grass were rank, and in what spots the herbage might be bitten down to the bare ground. A shepherd who would allow his flock to feed at large under his eye, merely watching his fences and folding his ewes and lambs at night, was a truant who feared the noonday sun. Such a one had Mr. Comfort become, and therefore Mr. Prong despised him in his heart. All sheep will not endure such ardent shepherding as that practised by Mr. Prong, and therefore he was driven to seek out for himself a peculiar flock. These to him were the elect of Baslehurst, and of his elect, Mrs. Prime was the most elect. Now this fault is not uncommon among young ardent clergymen.

普赖姆太太把她的状子讲给普朗先生听，一如雷太太把她的讲给康福特先生听。这里不必再说一遍了。我怕她把妹妹的轻率极尽渲染，倒不是存心不公。她声言自己深信，雷切尔仍可以被引上正路，只要执辔的手足够严厉，又握有绝对的权柄。接着她又说下去，讲雷太太如何去了康福特先生那里，正如她自己如今来到他这里。可怜的雷切尔，她榆树底下那几分钟的喁喁私语，竟这样传遍了本地的诸位教会参议之口——岂不叫人难堪？普朗先生听着雷切尔行止的这桩简单情由时，端坐着，一脸耐心，举止平和；可等到添上康福特先生那番主意的罪愆，那张嘴便摆出自命威严的架势，下巴也支了出来；在凡不像普赖姆太太那样被迷了心窍的人眼里，这本是一望而知的：那只撅成的“钱袋”并非绸缎所制，下料的材质粗陋得多。

“牧人若在羊圈里打盹，”普朗先生说，“羊儿们可怎么办呢？”说罢他摇了摇头，把嘴瘪了又瘪。

“唉！”普赖姆太太说；“羊儿们有福了，世上还剩下几位不躲活的，正午的暑热再毒，也照旧当工。”

普朗先生闭上眼睛，垂下头颅，随后又恢复了嘴边那副格外惹人厌的神气——他素来仗它撑持尊严——意在表示：这番恭维，倘若不是因其属实而叫人不得不领，他原乐于当作多余的客套辞谢掉的。他自知是个不惧正午暑热的牧人；可在这一点上他错了——他疑心所有的别家牧人都在偷工减料。在他看来，羊儿若能安安然然地啃草，必得常有牧人执着曲柄杖不停地管着它才行。哪几丛草长野了，哪几处草地可以啃到见土，这些照他想都该由牧人心里有数。一个牧人若任他的羊群在自己眼皮底下随意吃草，自己只看着栅栏，夜里把母羊羊羔圈一圈，那便是个躲正午日头的旷工之徒。康福特先生恰恰成了这样的人，因此普朗先生打心底里看不起他。不是所有的羊都受得住普朗先生这般火热的牧羊之道，于是他只得替自己另觅一群特选的羊。这群羊在他眼里便是巴斯尔赫斯特的选民，而在他的选民之中，普赖姆太太又是选民中的选民。何况这类毛病，在年轻而热忱的牧师中间原不算少见。

===Original===
I will not repeat the conversation that took place between the two, because they used holy words and spoke on holy subjects. In doing so they were both sincere, and not, as regarded their language, fairly subject to ridicule. In their judgment I think they were defective. He sustained Mrs. Prime in her resolution to quit the cottage unless she could induce her mother to put a stop to that great iniquity of the brewery. “The Tappitts,” he said, “were worldly people—very worldly people; utterly unfit to be the associates of the sister of his friend. As to the ‘young man,’ he thought that nothing further should be said at present, but that Rachel should be closely watched—very closely watched.” Mrs. Prime asked him to call upon her mother and explain his views, but he declined to do this. “He would have been most willing—so willing! but he could not force himself where he would be unwelcome!” Mrs. Prime was, if necessary, to quit the cottage and take up her temporary residence with Miss Pucker; but Mr. Prong was inclined to think, knowing something of Mrs. Ray’s customary softness of character, that if Mrs. Prime were firm, things would not be driven to such a pass as that. Mrs. Prime said that she would be firm, and she looked as though she intended to keep her word.

Mr. Prong’s manner as he bade adieu to his favourite sheep was certainly of a nature to justify that rumour to which allusion has been made. He pressed Mrs. Prime’s hand very closely, and invoked a blessing on her head in a warm whisper. But such signs among such people do not bear the meaning which they have in the outer world. These people are demonstrative and unctuous—whereas the outer world is reticent and dry. They are perhaps too free with their love, but the fault is better than that other fault of no love at all. Mr. Prong was a little free with his love, but Mrs. Prime took it all in good part, and answered him with an equal fervour. “If I can help you, dear friend,”—and he still held her hand in his—“come to me always. You never can come too often.”

“You can help me, and I will come, always,” she said, returning his pressure with mutual warmth. But there was no touch of earthly affection in her pressure; and if there was any in his at its close, there had, at any rate, been none at its commencement.

两人之间的那番谈话，我不在这里复述了，因为他们用的都是圣洁的字眼，谈的都是圣洁的题目。这两人如此言谈，都是出于至诚，单就语言而论，也不该拿来公然取笑。至于他们的判断，我以为是有毛病的。他支持普赖姆太太的决意：除非能劝动她母亲止住酿酒厂那桩滔天大罪，否则便离开村舍。“塔皮特家那起子人，”他说，“是属世的人——属世得很的人；要他们同他那位朋友的妹妹为伍，万万不相宜。至于那个‘年轻男人’，目下不必多说，只须把雷切尔严加看管——严严地看管。”普赖姆太太请他到她母亲府上把他的意见讲明，他不肯。“他本是最甘愿的——多甘愿啊！可是人家不欢迎的地方，他总不能硬闯进去！”普赖姆太太必要之时便离开村舍，暂且住到帕克小姐家去；不过普朗先生深知雷太太平素性情之软，倾向于认为：普赖姆太太只要咬定不放，事情断不至于逼到那一步。普赖姆太太说她一定咬定不放，看她的神气，也像是打算言而有信。

普朗先生同他那头心爱的羊儿道别的神情，确实足以坐实前文提到的那桩流言。他把普赖姆太太的手紧紧一握，又用一阵热乎乎的耳语为她祝祷求福。不过在这样的人们中间，这类表示并不带着它在尘俗世界里的那种含义。这一路人表情外露、言带膏油——而尘俗世界却讷于表情、干干巴巴。他们爱得或许太随便，可这个毛病总比压根儿无爱的那个毛病好些。普朗先生的爱是稍稍随便了些，但普赖姆太太全不以为忤，往好处领受，也以同等的火热回敬他。“我若能帮得上你，亲爱的朋友，”——他仍然把她的手握在自己手里——“你随时来找我。你来得再勤也不嫌多。”

“你帮得上我的，我也一定来，永远来，”她说，回握时同样火热。可她这一握里没有一丝尘世的情意；至于他临了那一握里有没有，至少开头是断然没有的。

===Original===
While Mrs. Prime was thus employed, Rachel and her mother became warm upon the subject of the dress, and when the younger widow returned home to the cottage, the elder widow was actually engaged in Baslehurst on the purchase of trappings and vanities. Her little hoard was opened, and some pretty piece of muslin was purchased by aid of which, with the needful ribbons, Rachel might be made, not fit, indeed, for Mrs. Butler Cornbury’s carriage—no such august fitness was at all contemplated by herself—but nice and tidy, so that her presence need not be a disgrace. And it was pretty to see how Mrs. Ray revelled in these little gauds for her daughter now that the barrier of her religious awe was broken down, and that the waters of the world had made their way in upon her. She still had a feeling that she was being drowned, but she confessed that such drowning was very pleasant. She almost felt that such drowning was good for her. At any rate it had been ordered by Mr. Comfort, and if things went astray Mr. Comfort must bear the blame. When the bright muslin was laid out on the counter before her, she looked at it with a pleased eye and touched it with a willing hand. She held the ribbon against the muslin, leaning her head on one side, and enjoyed herself. Now and again she would turn her face upon Rachel’s figure, and she would almost indulge a wish that this young man might like her child in the new dress. Ah!—that was surely wicked. But if so, how wicked are most mothers in this Christian land!

The morning had gone very comfortably with them during Dorothea’s absence. Mrs. Prime had hardly taken her departure before a note came from Mrs. Butler Cornbury, confirming Mr. Comfort’s offer as to the carriage. “Oh, papa, what have you done?”—she had said when her father first told her. “Now I must stay there all the night, for of course she’ll want to go on to the last dance!” But, like her father, she was good-natured, and therefore, though she would hardly have chosen the task, she resolved, when her first groans were over, to do it well. She wrote a kind note, saying how happy she should be, naming her hour—and saying that Rachel should name the hour for her return.

“It will be very nice,” said Rachel, rejoicing more than she should have done in thinking of the comfortable grandeur of Mrs. Butler Cornbury’s carriage.
===Chinese===
普赖姆太太在外头忙她的这一摊，家里的雷切尔同母亲也已在衣裳的事情上谈得热火朝天；年轻的寡妇回到村舍时，年长的寡妇竟已在巴斯尔赫斯特采办装饰与浮华之物了。她那点私房开了封，买了一块上好的细布，配上必需的缎带，雷切尔便可拾掇得——虽则远够不上配巴特勒·康伯里太太的马车，那样庄严的够格，她本人连想都不曾想过——却也齐整受看，出场不致丢人。眼看雷太太为女儿在这些小小的华彩之物里陶然自乐——宗教畏怖的堤坝既已掘开，尘世的洪水漫上她身来——这景象着实可爱。她还有点觉得自己正在灭顶，可她招认，这样的灭顶实在惬意。她几乎觉得这样的灭顶于她有益。无论如何，这是康福特先生下的令，倘若事情走了岔，也自有康福特先生领罪。亮闪闪的细布在柜台上摊开在她面前，她满眼欢喜地看着，满心情愿地伸手抚摩。她把缎带比在细布上，头歪向一边，自家受用。时不时地，她的目光会转到雷切尔的身影上去，几乎纵容起一桩心愿来：但愿那个年轻男人会喜欢她的孩子穿上这身新衣裳。啊！——这自然是罪过。可倘若这是罪过，那这片基督徒的土地上，大多数做母亲的又何其罪孽深重！

多萝西娅不在家的那一个上午，她们过得舒舒服服。普赖姆太太前脚刚出门，巴特勒·康伯里太太的一张短简后脚就到，把康福特先生那桩马车的许诺坐实了。“哦，爸爸，您这是干的好事！”——父亲头一回告诉她的时候，她是这么说的。“这下我非得在那儿泡一整夜不可，她当然要跳到最后一支舞才肯走！”不过她同她父亲一样好性儿，因此，虽然这差事她原不会自己挑上，头一阵哀叹过后，她便打定主意要办得漂漂亮亮。她回了一封言辞亲切的短简，说她何等高兴，报了来接的时辰——又说要雷切尔自己定送她回来的时辰。

“那可太好了，”雷切尔说；一想到巴特勒·康伯里太太那辆马车舒服气派的场面，她欢喜得越了分寸。

===Original===
“And are you determined?” Mrs. Prime asked her mother that evening.

“It is too late to go back now, Dorothea,” said Mrs. Ray, almost crying.

“Then I cannot remain in the house,” said Dorothea. “I shall go to Miss Pucker’s—but not till that morning; so that if you think better of it, all may be prevented yet.”

But Mrs. Ray would not think better of it, and it was thus that the preparations were made for Mrs. Tappitt’s—ball. The word “party” had now been dropped by common consent throughout Baslehurst.
===Chinese===
“那么你拿定主意了？”当天晚上，普赖姆太太问她的母亲。

“如今要回头，已经来不及了，多萝西娅，”雷太太说，几乎要哭出来。

“那么我就不能在这个家里待下去了，”多萝西娅说。“我搬到帕克小姐家去住——不过要等到那天早上才搬；这样，倘若你们把主意想转来了，一切还来得及拦住。”

可雷太太终究没有把主意想转来。就这样，为塔皮特太太的——舞会——所做的一切筹备，停当了。“聚会”这个字眼，如今已蒙公议一致，在全巴斯尔赫斯特弃置不用了。

## VII An Account of Mrs. Tappitt’s Ball—Commenced / VII 塔皮特太太的舞会记（上）

===Original===

Mrs. Butler Cornbury was a very pretty woman. She possessed that peculiar prettiness which is so often seen in England, and which is rarely seen anywhere else. She was bright, well-featured, with speaking lustrous eyes, with perfect complexion, and full bust, with head of glorious shape and figure like a Juno;—and yet with all her beauty she had ever about her an air of homeliness which made the sweetness of her womanhood almost more attractive than the loveliness of her personal charms. I have seen in Italy and in America women perhaps as beautiful as any that I have seen in England, but in neither country does it seem that such beauty is intended for domestic use. In Italy the beauty is soft, and of the flesh. In America it is hard, and of the mind. Here it is of the heart, I think, and as such is the happiest of the three. I do not say that Mrs. Butler Cornbury was a woman of very strong feeling; but her strongest feelings were home feelings. She was going to Mrs. Tappitt’s party because it might serve her husband’s purposes; she was going to burden herself with Rachel Ray because her father had asked her; and her greatest ambition was to improve the worldly position of the squires of Cornbury Grange. She was already calculating whether it might not some day be brought about that her little Butler should sit in Parliament for his county.

===Chinese===

巴特勒·康伯里太太（Mrs. Butler Cornbury）是位非常标致的女人。她具有那种在英格兰随处可见、在别处却难得一见的特异的美。她明媚鲜亮，五官端正，一双眼睛流光溢彩、顾盼含情，肤色完美无瑕，胸脯丰盈，头型俊美，体态宛如神后朱诺（Juno）；然而纵有这满身的美，她身上始终萦绕着一股居家度日的家常气韵，这气韵让她为妻为母的温柔甜美，几乎比她容貌身段本身的可爱更加动人。我在意大利、在美国都见过也许不逊于英格兰任何美人的女子，但在那两个国家，这样的美似乎都不是预备给居家过日子用的。意大利的美柔软，是肉感的美。美国的美坚硬，是心智的美。而这里的美，我想，是心灵的美，三者之中，也数它最有福分。我并不是说巴特勒·康伯里太太是个感情格外炽烈的女人；只是她最深的感情，是室家之情。她去赴塔皮特太太（Mrs. Tappitt）的聚会，是因为这可能于丈夫的图谋有用；她肯带上雷切尔·雷（Rachel Ray），给自己添这份累赘，是因为父亲开了口；而她最大的抱负，是抬举康伯里庄园（Cornbury Grange）乡绅一门的世俗地位。她心里已经在盘算，有朝一日能否设法让她的小巴特勒为本郡在议会里占一个席位。

===Original===

At nine o’clock exactly on that much to be remembered Tuesday the Cornbury carriage stopped at the gate of the cottage at Bragg’s End, and Rachel, ready dressed, blushing, nervous, but yet happy, came out, and mounting on to the step was almost fearful to take her share of the seat. “Make yourself comfortable, my dear,” said Mrs. Cornbury, “you can’t crush me. Or rather I always make myself crushable on such occasions as this. I suppose we are going to have a great crowd?” Rachel merely said that she didn’t know. She supposed there would be a good many persons. Then she tried to thank Mrs. Cornbury for being so good to her, and of course broke down. “I’m delighted—quite delighted,” said Mrs. Cornbury. “It’s so good of you to come with me. Now that I don’t dance myself, there’s nothing I like so much as taking out girls that do.”

“And don’t you dance at all?”

“I stand up for a quadrille sometimes. When a woman has five children I don’t think she ought to do more than that.”

“Oh, I shall not do more than that, Mrs. Cornbury.”

“You mean to say you won’t waltz?”

===Chinese===

在那个值得永远铭记的星期二，九点整，康伯里家的马车停在了布拉格斯恩德（Bragg’s End）村舍的大门口。雷切尔早已穿戴齐整，红着脸，心里发慌，却又满心欢喜地走了出来，踏上马车踏板时，几乎不敢去占她自己那一半座位。“放宽心坐吧，我亲爱的，”康伯里太太说，“你压不坏我。或者说，逢着这样的场合，我一向把自己弄得经得起压。我想今晚人一定很多吧？”雷切尔只说她不知道。她猜人少不了。接着她想谢谢康伯里太太待她这么好，自然是一开口就语塞了。“我高兴着呢——实在高兴，”康伯里太太说，“你能陪我来真是太好了。如今我自己不跳舞了，顶顶称心的事，就是带爱跳舞的姑娘们出门。”

“那么您就一点儿也不跳了吗？”

“有时候我还会站到场子里跳一场四对舞（quadrille）。一个女人有了五个孩子，我看就不该再多跳了。”

“哦，我也不会跳多的，康伯里太太。”

“你是说你不想跳华尔兹（waltz）？”

===Original===

“Mamma never said anything about it, but I’m sure she would not like it. Besides—”

“Well—”

“I don’t think I know how. I did learn once, when I was very little; but I’ve forgotten.”

“It will soon come again to you if you like to try. I was very fond of waltzing before I was married.” And this was the daughter of Mr. Comfort, the clergyman who preached with such strenuous eloquence against worldly vanities! Even Rachel was a little puzzled, and was almost afraid that her head was sinking beneath the waters.

===Chinese===

“妈妈倒没说过什么，可我敢说她准不乐意。再说——”

“嗯——”

“我想我不会跳。很小的时候学过一回，可全忘了。”

“只要你乐意试试，很快就能想起来。我出嫁以前可爱跳华尔兹了。”而这一位，正是康福特先生（Mr. Comfort）的女儿——那位在讲坛上以何等激切的雄辩痛斥尘世虚华的牧师！连雷切尔都有点儿犯糊涂，几乎害怕自己的脑袋正在往水面底下沉。

===Original===

There was a great fuss made when Mrs. Butler Cornbury’s carriage drove up to the brewery door, and Rachel almost felt that she could have made her way up to the drawing-room more comfortably under Mrs. Rule’s mild protection. All the servants seemed to rush at her, and when she found herself in the hall and was conducted into some inner room, she was not allowed to shake herself into shape without the aid of a maidservant. Mrs. Cornbury—who took everything as a matter of course and was ready in a minute—had turned the maid over to the young lady with a kind idea that the young lady’s toilet was more important than that of the married woman. Rachel was losing her head and knew that she was doing so. When she was again taken into the hall she hardly remembered where she was, and when Mrs. Cornbury took her by the arm and began to walk upstairs with her, her strongest feeling was a wish that she was at home again. On the first landing—for the dancing-room was upstairs—they encountered Mr. Tappitt, conspicuous in a blue satin waistcoat; and on the second landing they found Mrs. Tappitt, magnificent in a green Irish poplin. “Oh, Mrs. Cornbury, we are so delighted. The Miss Fawcetts are here; they are just come. How kind of you to bring Rachel Ray. How do you do, Rachel?” Then Mrs. Cornbury moved easily on into the drawing-room, and Rachel still found herself carried with her. She was half afraid that she ought to have slunk away from her magnificent chaperon as soon as she was conveyed safely within the house, and that she was encroaching as she thus went on; but still she could not find the moment in which to take herself off. In the drawing-room—the room from which the carpets had been taken—they were at once encountered by the Tappitt girls, with whom the Fawcett girls on the present occasion were so intermingled that Rachel hardly knew who was who. Mrs. Butler Cornbury was soon surrounded, and a clatter of words went on. Rachel was in the middle of the fray, and some voices were addressed also to her; but her presence of mind was gone, and she never could remember what she said on the occasion.

There had already been a dance—the commencing operation of the night’s work—a thin quadrille, in which the early comers had taken part without much animation, and to which they had been driven up unwillingly. At its close the Fawcett girls had come in, as had now Mrs. Cornbury, so that it may be said that the evening was beginning again. What had been as yet done was but the tuning of the fiddles before the commencement of the opera. No one likes to be in at the tuning, but there are those who never are able to avoid this annoyance. As it was, Rachel, under Mrs. Cornbury’s care, had been brought upon the scene just at the right moment. As soon as the great clatter had ceased, she found herself taken by the hand by Cherry, and led a little on one side. “You must have a card, you know,” said Cherry handing her a ticket on which was printed the dances as they were to succeed each other. “That first one is over. Such a dull thing. I danced with Adolphus Griggs, just because I couldn’t escape him for one quadrille.” Rachel took the card, but never having seen such a thing before did not in the least understand its object. “As you get engaged for the dances you must put down their names in this way, you see,”—and Cherry showed her card, which already bore the designations of several cavaliers, scrawled in hieroglyphics which were intelligible to herself. “Haven’t you got a pencil? Well, you can come to me. I have one hanging here, you know.” Rachel was beginning to understand, and to think that she should not have very much need for the pencil, when Mrs. Cornbury returned to her, bringing a young man in her wake. “I want to introduce my cousin to you, Walter Cornbury,” said she. Mrs. Cornbury was a woman who knew her duty as a chaperon, and who would not neglect it. “He waltzes delightfully,” said Mrs. Cornbury, whispering, “and you needn’t be afraid of being a little astray with him at first. He always does what I tell him.” Then the introduction was made; but Rachel had no opportunity of repeating her fears, or of saying again that she thought she had better not waltz. What to say to Mr. Walter Cornbury she hardly knew; but before she had really said anything he had pricked her down for two dances—for the first waltz, which was just going to begin, and some not long future quadrille. “She is very pretty,” Mrs. Butler Cornbury had said to her cousin, “and I want to be kind to her.” “I’ll take her in hand and pull her through,” said Walter. “What a tribe of people they’ve got here, haven’t they?” “Yes, and you must dance with them all. Every time you stand up may be as good as a vote.” “Oh,” said Walter, “I’m not particular;—I’ll dance as long as they keep the house open.” Then he went back to Rachel, who had already been at work with Cherry’s pencil.

===Chinese===

巴特勒·康伯里太太的马车驰到酿酒厂大门口时，那阵张罗真是热闹非凡，雷切尔几乎觉得，要是在鲁尔太太（Mrs. Rule）温和的护送下自己走上客厅，倒还要自在些。仆人们仿佛一齐朝她扑了上来；等她发觉自己已进了门厅，又被领进某间里屋，若没有一名侍女帮忙，她竟连抖一抖衣裳、定一定神都不得获准。康伯里太太——她把一切都视作理所当然，一分钟便可就绪——把侍女让给了这位小姐，好心地认为小姐的梳妆总比结过婚的女人更要紧。雷切尔已经晕头转向，而且自己也知道晕了头。当她再被领回门厅时，她几乎记不起身在何处；当康伯里太太挽起她的胳膊、携她一道上楼时，她心头最强烈的感觉，便是巴不得此刻人在家里。第一处楼梯平台——舞厅设在楼上——她们遇见了塔皮特先生（Mr. Tappitt），一件蓝缎背心好不惹眼；第二处平台上，立着塔皮特太太，一身绿色爱尔兰波纹绸，雍容华贵。“哎呀，康伯里太太，我们真是高兴极了。福西特家小姐们（the Miss Fawcetts）到了，刚进门。您把雷切尔·雷带来了，多好心啊。你好啊，雷切尔？”于是康伯里太太从容不迫地径直进了客厅，雷切尔发觉自己还是被她携带着一路跟了进去。她心中七上八下，觉得自己本该在平安进了宅子以后，就悄悄从她那位气派十足的女伴（chaperon）身边溜开，如今这样一路走过去，未免有些僭越；可她始终找不出抽身而退的时机。客厅里——地毯已经撤走的那间——塔皮特家小姐们立刻迎上来，今晚福西特家姑娘们同她们掺在一处，雷切尔简直分不清谁是谁。巴特勒·康伯里太太很快被围住，一片叽叽喳喳，说个不停。雷切尔就在这场混战的中央，也有几句是对她说的；可她的镇定早已飞到九霄云外，那天她说了一些什么，后来怎么也记不起来了。

在此之前已经跳过一场舞——今夜正戏开锣前的头一道工序：一场稀稀拉拉的四对舞，先到的客人无精打采地应付了一阵，原本还是被硬拉进场的。舞一散，福西特家姑娘们进了门，康伯里太太也随之而到，因此可以说，晚会这才重新开始。此前的一切，不过是歌剧开演之前小提琴的调弦罢了。谁也不愿意赶上调弦的当口，可偏偏总有人躲不开这份罪。所幸雷切尔在康伯里太太的照拂之下，恰好在最合适的时辰被送到了场上。那一阵喧哗刚一停歇，她就发觉彻丽（Cherry）拉住了她的手，把她领到稍稍偏一边的地方。“你总得有一张节目单呀，你知道的，”彻丽说着递给她一张卡片，上面印着今晚依次进行的各场舞。“头一场已经跳完了。闷死了。我跟阿道弗斯·格里格斯（Adolphus Griggs）跳的，只因为他那一场四对舞我实在躲不开。”雷切尔接过卡片，可她从前从没见过这种东西，全然不明白它做什么用。“人家跟你约定了哪场舞，你就得把名字照这样子记下来，你瞧，”——彻丽把自己的卡片给她看，那上面已经记下好几位男伴的名号，鬼画符似的涂着，唯有她自己认得。“你没带铅笔吗？那就上我这儿来。我有一支挂在这儿呢，你知道的。”雷切尔刚有点明白过来，正想着自己多半用不着这支铅笔，康伯里太太已经回到她跟前，身后跟着一个年轻男人。“我想把我表弟介绍给你——沃尔特·康伯里（Walter Cornbury），”她说。康伯里太太是位深知女伴职责的女人，决不肯怠慢这份职分。“他华尔兹跳得可好了，”康伯里太太悄声说，“起头跟他跳得乱一点儿也别怕。我叫他做什么他都做的。”于是引见便成了礼；可雷切尔来不及再说一遍她的胆怯，也来不及再说一遍她觉得还是不跳华尔兹的好。对沃尔特·康伯里先生该说些什么，她心里一点数也没有；可还没等她真正开口，他已经在节目单上把她勾定了两场——一场是马上就要开始的头一场华尔兹，另一场是不久以后不知哪一场的四对舞。“她长得很俊，”巴特勒·康伯里太太对表弟说，“我想待她好些。”“我来带她入门，保她顺顺当当跳下来，”沃尔特说，“这儿的人可真多呀，是不是？”“是啊，你可得个个都陪到。你每站起身一场，说不定就顶得上一张选票。”“哦，”沃尔特说，“我不挑拣；房子不关门，我就一直跳。”说完他回到雷切尔身边——雷切尔这会儿已经拿着彻丽的铅笔使上了。

===Original===

“If there isn’t Rachel Ray going to waltz with Walter Cornbury,” said Augusta to her mother. Augusta had just refused the odious Griggs, and was about to stand up with a clerk in the brewery, who was almost as odious.

“It’s because she came in the carriage,” said Mrs. Tappitt; “but I don’t think she can waltz.” Then she hurried off to welcome other comers.

Rachel had hardly been left alone for a minute, and had been so much bewildered by the lights and crowd and strangeness of everything around her, that she had been unable to turn her thoughts to the one subject on which during the last week her mind had rested constantly. She had not even looked round the room for Luke Rowan. She had just seen Mary Rowan in the crowd, but had not spoken to her. She had only known her from the manner in which Cherry Tappitt had spoken to her, and it must be explained that Rachel had not seen young Rowan since that parting under the elm-trees. Indeed, since then she had seen none of the Tappitt family. Her mother had said no word to her, cautioning her that she had better not seek them in her evening walks; but she had felt herself debarred from going into Baslehurst by all that her sister had said, and in avoiding Luke Rowan she had avoided the whole party from the brewery.

===Chinese===

“瞧瞧，雷切尔·雷要跟沃尔特·康伯里跳华尔兹了，”奥古斯塔（Augusta）对她母亲说。奥古斯塔刚回绝了那个讨人嫌的格里格斯，正要同一个酿酒厂的职员站到场上去——那职员也差不多一样讨人嫌。

“那是因为她坐马车来的，”塔皮特太太说，“不过我看她不见得会跳华尔兹。”说完便匆匆迎别的客人去了。

雷切尔几乎没有一分钟独处的空闲；灯火、人群、周遭种种陌生的一切，早已把她搅得神魂颠倒，她根本没法把心思转到那个她整整一个星期里时刻萦怀的话题上去。她甚至连卢克·罗恩（Luke Rowan）都没朝屋里找过一眼。她方才在人群中瞥见了玛丽·罗恩（Mary Rowan），却没有同她说话。她只是从彻丽·塔皮特同她搭话的样子认出了她。这里必须交代一句：自榆树下的那次分别之后，雷切尔再没见过小罗恩。说实在的，打那以后，塔皮特家的人她一个也没见过。她母亲倒是一个字也没有提过，没嘱咐她晚间散步时最好别去找他们；可姐姐说过的那一番话，把她去巴斯尔赫斯特（Baslehurst）的路堵得死死的；她躲着卢克·罗恩，也就把酿酒厂那一伙人全躲开了。

===Original===

Now the room was partially cleared, the non-dancers being pressed back into a border round the walls, and the music began. Rachel, with her heart in her mouth, was claimed by her partner, and was carried forward towards the ground for dancing, tacitly assenting to her fate because she lacked words in which to explain to Mr. Cornbury how very much she would have preferred to be left in obscurity behind the wall of crinoline.

“Pray wait a minute or two,” said she, almost panting.

“Oh, certainly. There’s no hurry, only we’ll stand where we can get our place when we like it. You need not be a bit afraid of going on with me. Patty has told me all about it, and we’ll make it right in a brace of turns.” There was something very good-natured in his voice, and she almost felt that she could ask him to let her sit down.

“I don’t think I can,” she said.

“Oh yes; come, we’ll try!” Then he took her by the waist, and away they went. Twice round the room he took her, very gently, as he thought; but her head had gone from her instantly in a whirl of amazement! Of her feet and their movements she had known nothing; though she had followed the music with fair accuracy, she had done so unconsciously, and when he allowed her to stop she did not know which way she had been going, or at which end of the room she stood. And yet she had liked it, and felt some little triumph as a conviction came upon her that she had not conspicuously disgraced herself.

===Chinese===

这时屋子腾出了一部分，不跳舞的人被挤退到沿墙一圈，乐声起了。雷切尔心都提到了嗓子眼，被舞伴认领了去，朝舞池给带了过去；她听凭命运安排，默默顺从，只因为她找不出言语，向康伯里先生说明她其实多么情愿缩在裙撑之墙的后面、不为人见。

“求您稍等一两分钟，”她说，几乎喘不上气来。

“哦，当然。不着急，只是咱们得站在待会儿随时能占到位子的地方。跟我跳，你一点儿也别怕。帕蒂（Patty）把底细全告诉我了，转上两圈就顺了。”他的嗓音里有一股厚道劲儿，她几乎觉得可以开口求他让她坐下歇一歇。

“我想我不行的，”她说。

“哦，行的；来，咱们试试！”说着他搂住她的腰，两人便旋转起来。他带她在屋里转了两圈，自以为极尽轻柔；可她的神志当即在一片惊愕的眩晕里飞走了！自己那双脚、脚下的步子，她一概浑然不知；虽说她跟音乐跟得相当准，却是下意识跟上的，等他容她停下时，她不知道自己方才朝哪个方向转，也不知自己站在屋子的哪一头。然而她是喜欢的；当一种确信临到心头——她没有当众大出其丑——她感到几分小小的得意。

===Original===

“That’s charming,” said he. She essayed to speak a word in answer, but her want of breath did not as yet permit it.

“Charming!” he went on. “The music’s perhaps a little slow, but we’ll hurry them up presently.” Slow! It seemed to her that she had been carried round in a vortex, of which the rapidity, though pleasant, had been almost frightful. “Come; we’ll have another start,” said he; and she was carried away again before she had spoken a word. “I’d no idea that girl could waltz,” said Mrs. Tappitt to old Mrs. Rule. “I don’t think her mother would like it if she saw it,” said Mrs. Rule. “And what would Mrs. Prime say?” said Mrs. Tappitt. However the ice was broken, and Rachel, when she was given to understand that that dance was done, felt herself to be aware that the world of waltzing was open to her, at any rate for that night. Was it very wicked? She had her doubts. If anybody had suggested to her, before Mrs. Cornbury’s carriage had called for her, that she would waltz on that evening, she would have repudiated the idea almost with horror. How easy is the path down the shores of the Avernus! but then—was she going down the shores of the Avernus?

She was still walking through the crowd, leaning on her partner’s arm, and answering his good-natured questions almost in monosyllables, when she was gently touched on the arm by a fan, and on turning found herself confronted by Luke Rowan and his sister. “I’ve been trying to get at you so long,” said he, making some sort of half apology to Cornbury, “and haven’t been able; though once I very nearly danced you down without your knowing it.”

“We’re so much obliged to you for letting us escape,” said Cornbury; “are we not, Miss Ray?”

“We carried heavy metal, I can tell you,” said Rowan. “But I must introduce you to my sister. Where on earth have you been for these ten days?” Then the introduction was made, and young Cornbury, finding that his partner was in the hands of another lady, slipped away.

===Chinese===

“真叫人愉快，”他说。她想答一句话，可气息不济，一时还说不出来。

“愉快！”他又说，“乐子也许慢了点儿，回头咱们催他们快些。”还慢！在她感觉里，自己分明是在一个漩涡里给带着打转，那飞旋的速度虽说畅快，却几乎叫人害怕。“来，咱们再来一开场，”他说；她还没来得及吐一个字，又给旋走了。“想不到那丫头华尔兹跳得挺好，”塔皮特太太对老鲁尔太太说。“她母亲要是瞧见了，我看未必高兴，”鲁尔太太说。“那普赖姆太太（Mrs. Prime）又会怎么说呢？”塔皮特太太说。不管怎样，坚冰总算是打破了；当雷切尔被告知那场舞跳完了的时候，她发觉自己心里明白：华尔兹的天地已经向她敞开——至少今晚是敞开了。这很罪过吗？她心里犯着嘀咕。倘若在康伯里太太的马车来接她之前，有人对她讲，她今晚会跳华尔兹，她几乎会怀着惊骇把这念头驳回去。通向阿佛纳斯湖（Avernus，古罗马传说中的冥府入口）湖畔的路，何其好走！——可是话说回来，她这是在沿着阿佛纳斯湖畔往下走吗？

她还挽着舞伴的胳膊在人群里穿行，几乎全用一个字一个字，应付着他那些好性儿的问话，忽然有人用扇子在她胳膊上轻轻碰了一下；她一转身，卢克·罗恩和他妹妹正站在跟前。“我寻你好半天了，”他说，朝康伯里半是告罪地点了点头，“就是近不了身；不过有一回，我差一点儿就把你卷着跳了，你自己还不知道呢。”

“多谢你高抬贵手，放我们逃了过去，”康伯里说，“是不是，雷小姐？”

“你们两位可都是重量级人物，我跟你说，”罗恩说，“不过我得把你介绍给我妹妹。这十天你究竟上哪儿去了？”于是引见便成了礼；小康伯里见自己的舞伴已经落到另一位小姐手里，便悄然溜开了。

===Original===

“I have heard a great deal about you, Miss Ray,” said Mary Rowan.

“Have you? I don’t know who should say much about me.” The words sounded uncivil, but she did not know what words to choose.

“Oh, from Cherry especially;—and—and from my brother.”

“I’m very glad to make your acquaintance,” said Rachel.

“He told me that you would have been sure to come and walk with us, and we have all been saying that you had disappeared.”

“I have been kept at home,” said Rachel, who could not help remembering all the words of the churchyard interview, and feeling them down to her finger nails. He must have known why she had not again joined the girls from the brewery in their walks. Or had he forgotten that he had called her Rachel, and held her fast by the hand? Perhaps he did these things so often to other girls that he thought nothing of them!

===Chinese===

“久闻雷小姐的大名了，”玛丽·罗恩说。

“是吗？我不知道谁会说我多少话。”这话听着失礼，可她不知道该拣什么话说。

“哦，彻丽说得顶多；——还有——还有我哥哥。”

“认识你我很高兴，”雷切尔说。

“他跟我说，你一定会来同我们一道散步的；我们都念叨说，你失踪了。”

“我一直待在家里，”雷切尔说。教堂墓地那次相会的每一句话，她不由自主地全都记得，而且一路铭感到了指甲尖。她后来为什么没有再同酿酒厂那几位姑娘一道散步，他必定是知道的。要不，难道他忘了自己曾唤她作雷切尔，曾紧紧攥住她的手？也许他对别的姑娘这类事做得太多了，压根儿不放在心上！

===Original===

“You have been keeping yourself up for the ball,” said Rowan. “Precious people are right to make themselves scarce. And now what vacancies have you got for me?”

“Vacancies!” said Rachel.

“You don’t mean to say you’ve got none. Look here, I’ve kept all these on purpose for you, although twenty girls have begged me to dispose of them in their favour.”

“Oh, Luke, how can you tell such fibs?” said his sister.

===Chinese===

“你这是在养精蓄锐，预备舞会呢，”罗恩说。“贵重人物难得露面，这没有错。好啦，你给我留了哪几场空位？”

“空位！”雷切尔说。

“你该不会说你一个空位都没留吧。你瞧，这些场子我全是特意给你留的，虽然有二十个姑娘求我把空位让给她们。”

“哎，卢克，你怎么能这样扯瞎话？”他妹妹说。

===Original===

“Well;—here they are,” and he showed his card.

“I’m not engaged to anybody,” said Rachel; “except for one quadrille to Mr. Cornbury—that gentleman who just went away.”

“Then you’ve no excuse for not filling up my vacancies—kept on purpose for you, mind.” And immediately her name was put down for she knew not what dances.
