Then he took her card and scrawled his own name on it in various places. She knew that she was weak to let him thus have his way in everything; but he was strong and she could not hinder him.

===Chinese===

“呃；——喏，都在这儿，”他把自己的节目单亮了出来。

“我谁都没有约，”雷切尔说，“只除了一场四对舞约了康伯里先生——就是刚走开的那位先生。”

“那你就没有借口，不把我那些空位填上了——记住，是特意给你留的。”话音未落，她的名字已经给记到了她自己也不知哪几场舞上。接着他拿过她的节目单，在好几个地方龙飞凤舞地写上了自己的名字。她心里明白，任他这样事事摆布，是她软弱；可他强，她拦不住。

===Original===

She was soon left with Mary Rowan, as Luke went off to fulfil the first of his numerous engagements. “Do you like my brother?” said she. “But of course I don’t mean you to answer that question. We all think him so very clever.”

“I’m sure he is very clever.”

“A great deal too clever to be a brewer. But you mustn’t say that I said so. I wanted him to go into the army.”

“I shouldn’t at all like that for my brother—if I had one.”

===Chinese===

卢克赶去赴他一大串约会的头一场，雷切尔很快便同玛丽·罗恩留在了原处。“你喜欢我哥哥吗？”她说。“当然，我不是要你回答这个问题。我们都觉得他聪明极了。”

“他确实聪明极了，这我相信。”

“他太聪明了，当酿酒匠实在屈才。可你千万别说是我讲的。我本想让他去从军。”

“要我兄弟去干那个，我可一点儿也不乐意——假如我有兄弟的话。”

===Original===

“And what would you like?”

“Oh, I don’t know. I never had a brother;—perhaps to be a clergyman.”

“Yes; that would be very nice; but Luke would never be a clergyman. He was going to be an attorney, but he didn’t like that at all. He says there’s a great deal of poetry in brewing beer, but of course he’s only quizzing us. Oh, here’s my partner. I do so hope I shall see you very often while I’m at Baslehurst.” Then Rachel was alone, but Mrs. Tappitt came up to her in a minute. “My dear,” said she, “Mr. Griggs desires the honour of your hand for a quadrille.” And thus Rachel found herself standing up with the odious Mr. Griggs. “I do so pity you,” said Cherry, coming behind her for a moment. “Remember, you need not do it more than once. I don’t mean to do it again.”

===Chinese===

“那你愿意让他做什么呢？”

“哦，我不知道。我从没有过兄弟；——也许，当个牧师吧。”

“是啊；那再好不过了；可卢克绝当不成牧师。他本来要去当律师的，可他一点儿也不喜欢那一行。他说酿啤酒里有满满的诗意，当然，那不过是拿我们打趣罢了。哟，我的舞伴来了。我在巴斯尔赫斯特的这段日子，真盼着常见到你。”于是雷切尔独自留下了；可不到一分钟，塔皮特太太便凑上前来。“我亲爱的，”她说，“格里格斯先生想请你赏光，跳一场四对舞。”就这样，雷切尔发觉自己同那位讨人嫌的格里格斯先生对面站到了场上。“我实在替你难受，”彻丽在她背后闪了一下，说道。“记住，跳一回就够了。我可是再不打算跳第二回了。”

===Original===

After that she was allowed to sit still while a polka was being performed. Mrs. Cornbury came to her saying a word or two; but she did not stay with her long, so that Rachel could think about Luke Rowan, and try to make up her mind as to what words she should say to him. She furtively looked down upon her card and found that he had written his own name to five dances, ending with Sir Roger de Coverley at the close of the evening. It was quite impossible that she should dance five dances with him, so she thought that she would mark out two with her nail. The very next was one of them, and during that she would explain to him what she had done. The whole thing loomed large in her thoughts and made her feel anxious. She would have been unhappy if he had not come to her at all, and now she was unhappy because he had thrust himself upon her so violently—or if not unhappy, she was at any rate uneasy. And what should she say about the elm-trees? Nothing, unless he spoke to her about them. She fancied that he would say something about the arm in the cloud, and if so, she must endeavour to make him understand that—that—that—. She did not know how to fix her thoughts. Would it be possible to make him understand that he ought not to have called her Rachel?

While she was thinking of all this Mr. Tappitt came and sat beside her. “Very pretty; isn’t it?” said he. “Very pretty indeed, I call it.”

“Oh yes, very pretty. I had no idea it would be so nice.” To Mr. Tappitt in his blue waistcoat she could speak without hesitation. Ah me! It is the young men who receive all the reverence that the world has to pay;—all the reverence that is worth receiving. When a man is turned forty and has become fat, anybody can speak to him without awe!

“Yes, it is nice,” said Mr. Tappitt, who, however, was not quite easy in his mind. He had been into the supper room, and had found the waiter handling long-necked bottles, arranging them in rows, apparently by the dozen. “What’s that?” said he, sharply. “The champagne, sir! there should have been ice, sir, but I suppose they forgot it.” Where had Mrs. T. procured all that wine? It was very plain to him that she had got the better of him by some deceit. He would smile, and smile, and smile during the evening; but he would have it out with Mrs. Tappitt before he would allow that lady to have any rest. He lingered in the room, pretending that he was overlooking the arrangements, but in truth he was counting the bottles. After all there was but a dozen. He knew that at Griggs’s they sold it for sixty shillings. “Three pounds!” he said to himself. “Three pounds more; dear, dear!”

“Yes, it is nice!” he said to Rachel. “Mind you get a glass of champagne when you go in to supper. By the by, shall I get a partner for you? Here, Buckett, come and dance the next dance with Miss Ray.” Buckett was the clerk in the brewery. Rachel had nothing to say for herself; so Buckett’s name was put down on the card, though she would rather not have danced with Buckett. A week or two ago, before she had been taken up into Mrs. Cornbury’s carriage, or had waltzed with Mrs. Cornbury’s cousin, or had looked at the setting sun with Luke Rowan, she would have been sufficiently contented to dance with Mr. Buckett—if in those days she had ever dreamed of dancing with anyone. Then Mrs. Cornbury came to her again, bringing other cavaliers, and Rachel’s card began to be filled. “The quadrille before supper you dance with me,” said Walter Cornbury. “That’s settled, you know.” Oh, what a new world it was, and so different from the Dorcas meetings at Miss Pucker’s rooms!

===Chinese===

这以后，跳波尔卡舞（polka）的时候，她获准安安静静坐着。康伯里太太过来同她说了一两句话，却没有久留，好教雷切尔得空去想卢克·罗恩，打定主意该对他说些什么话。她偷偷低头看自己的节目单，发现他把名字写给了五场舞，末一场是晚会收尾的罗杰·德·科弗利爵士舞（Sir Roger de Coverley）。同他跳五场舞是万万不行的，于是她想，要用指甲划掉两场。紧接着的一场正是其中之一，就在那一场里，她要向他说明自己做了什么。整桩事情在她心里越想越大，搅得她心神不宁。他倘若压根儿不来找她，她会难受；如今他这样不由分说地扑上来，她也难受——就算说不上难受，至少心里七上八下。榆树那件事，她该说什么呢？什么都不说，除非他自己提起。她猜想他会说说云中那条胳膊的事；倘若果真如此，她必须设法让他明白——明白——明白——。她不知道该怎么把心思拴住。有没有可能让他明白，他本不该唤她作雷切尔？

她正想着这一切，塔皮特先生走过来，在她身旁坐下。“很好看，是不是？”他说，“要我说，实在好看得很。”

“哦，是啊，好看极了。我没想到会这么有意思。”对着穿蓝背心的塔皮特先生，她说话一点儿也不磕绊。唉！这世上要付出的敬畏，全让年轻人得了去；——一切值得受领的敬畏。一个男人过了四十、发了福，谁都可以毫无怯意地同他攀谈了！

“是啊，就是有意思，”塔皮特先生说；然而他心里并不十分安稳。他方才到夜宵间去了一趟，撞见侍者正摆弄一排长颈瓶子，看那样子，是按一打一打往行列里码。“这是什么？”他厉声问道。“是香槟，先生！本该备冰的，先生，想必是他们忘了。”塔皮特太太这些酒是从哪儿弄来的？他心里明镜似的：她是耍了什么花招赢了他。今晚他自会笑，笑，再笑；可不等这位太太得到安宁，他必得同她把账算个明白。他在那间屋里磨磨蹭蹭，装作查验布置，其实是在数瓶子。数来数去，统共一打。他知道在格里格斯那儿，这酒卖六十先令。“三镑！”他自忖道，“又多掏三镑；心疼啊，心疼！”

“是啊，就是有意思！”他对雷切尔说，“进去吃夜宵的时候，记着弄一杯香槟喝。对了，要不要我给你找个舞伴？来，巴克特（Buckett），过来同雷小姐跳下一场。”巴克特是酿酒厂的职员。雷切尔自己连一句囫囵话也说不出来，于是巴克特的名字便记上了卡片，尽管她宁可不同巴克特跳。搁在一两个星期以前——那时她还没坐上康伯里太太的马车，还没同康伯里太太的表弟跳过华尔兹，也还没同卢克·罗恩一道看落日——她若能同巴克特先生跳一场，本该心满意足——假如那些日子里她做梦想到过同什么人跳舞的话。随后康伯里太太又来了，身后还带着别的男伴，雷切尔的节目单便渐渐写满了。“夜宵前那场四对舞你跟我跳，”沃尔特·康伯里说，“就这么定了，你知道的。”啊，这是一个多么崭新的世界，同帕克小姐（Miss Pucker）屋里那些多卡斯缝纫会何其不同！

===Original===

Then came the moment of the evening which, of all the moments, was the most trying to her. Luke Rowan came to claim her hand for the next quadrille. She had already spoken to him—or rather he to her; but that had been in the presence of a third person, when, of course, nothing could be said about the sunset and the clouds—nothing about that promise of friendship. But now she would have to stand again with him in solitude—a solitude of another kind—in a solitude which was authorized, during which he might whisper what words he pleased to her, and from which she could not even run away. It had been thought to be a great sin on her part to have remained a moment with him by the stile; but now she was to stand up with him beneath the glare of the lights, dressed in her best, on purpose that he might whisper to her what words he pleased. But she was sure—she thought that she was sure, that he would utter no words so sweet, so full of meaning, as those in which he bade her watch the arm in the clouds.

Till the first figure was over for them he hardly spoke to her. “Tell me,” said he then, “why has nobody seen you since Saturday week last?”

“I have been at home.”

“Ah; but tell me the truth. Remember what we said as we parted—about being friends. One tells one’s friend the real truth. But I suppose you do not remember what we said?”

“I don’t think I said anything, Mr. Rowan.”

“Did you not? Then I must have been dreaming. I thought you promised me your friendship.” He paused for her answer, but she said nothing. She could not declare to him that she would not be his friend. “But you have not told me yet why it was that you remained at home. Come;—answer me a fair question fairly. Had I offended you?” Again she paused and made him no reply. It seemed to her that the room was going round her, and that the music made her dizzy. If she told him that he had not offended her would she not thereby justify him in having called her Rachel?

===Chinese===

于是，晚会里顶叫她难熬的一刻到来了。卢克·罗恩过来，要认领下一场四对舞。她已经同他说过话了——毋宁说是他同她说话；可那是在第三个人在场的时候，当然，落日也好，云彩也好，什么都说不上，那句关于友谊的许诺更是一个字也提不得。可现在，她得再同他单独站到一处了——另一种性质的独处——一种名正言顺的独处：这期间，他爱向她低语什么就低语什么，而她连逃都逃不开。那天在梯磴旁同他多待了片刻，已被认定是她的一桩大罪；可如今，她却要穿上最好的衣裳，在明晃晃的灯光底下同他站到场中，为的就是让他可以爱向她低语什么就低语什么。不过她有把握——她以为自己有把握：他说不出像他嘱她仰望云中那条胳膊时那样甜、那样满含深意的话来了。

头一个舞式跳完之前，他几乎没同她说话。“告诉我，”随后他开口了，“上上个星期六以来，怎么谁也没见过你？”

“我一直在家。”

“啊；可你得对我说真话。记得我们分别时说的话吗——说要做朋友的。人对自己的朋友是说真话的。不过，我猜你大概不记得我们说过什么了？”

“我想我没说过什么吧，罗恩先生。”

“没说过？那一定是我做梦了。我记得你是应许过我做朋友的。”他停下来等她回答，她却一言不发。她不能向他声明她不肯做他的朋友。“可你还没有告诉我，你为什么一直待在家里。来；——老老实实回答我一句光明正大的问话。我得罪过你没有？”她又一次沉默，没有给他回答。她只觉得整个屋子围着她打转，乐声搅得她头晕。倘若她说他没有得罪她，岂不等于认可他唤她雷切尔唤得有理？

===Original===

“Then I did offend you?” said he.

“Oh, Mr. Rowan—never mind now; you must go on with the figure,” and thus for a moment she was saved from her difficulty. When he had done his work of dancing, she began hers, and as she placed both her hands in his to make the final turn, she flattered herself that he would not go back to the subject.

Nor did he while the quadrille lasted. As they continued to dance he said very little to her, and before the last figure was over she had almost settled down to enjoyment. He merely spoke a word or two about Mrs. Cornbury’s dress, and another word about the singular arrangement of Mr. Griggs’ jewellery, at which word she almost laughed outright, and then a third word laudatory of the Tappitt girls. “As for Cherry,” said he, “I’m quite in love with her for her pure good-nature and hearty manners; and of all living female human beings Martha is the most honest and just.”

“Oh! I’ll tell her that,” said Rachel. “She will so like it.”

“No, you mustn’t. You mustn’t repeat any of the things I tell you in confidence.” That word confidence again silenced her, and nothing more was said till he had offered her his arm at the end of the dance.

===Chinese===

“这么说，我当真得罪你了？”他说。

“哦，罗恩先生——这会儿别提了；你该接着跳舞式了。”这样，她暂时从窘境里脱了身。他跳完了他那份舞步，她便开始跳她那份；当她把双手放进他手里做最后一个回旋时，她私心宽慰，以为他不会再回到那个话头上来了。

那场四对舞跳完之前，他果然没有再提。两人继续跳舞的时候，他同她说的话很少，最后一个舞式还没跳完，她已差不多定下心来，渐入乐境。他不过评了一两句康伯里太太的衣裳，又评了一句格里格斯先生首饰佩挂的别致——听到这一句，她差点儿笑出声来——末了又赞了第三句，夸塔皮特家小姐们。“至于彻丽，”他说，“她那样纯然的好性儿、那样爽朗的做派，我简直爱上她了；而天底下活着的女人里，数玛莎（Martha）最诚实、最公正。”

“哦！这话我一定讲给她听，”雷切尔说，“她听了会高兴坏了。”

“不，这可不行。我私下对你说的话，一句也不许传出去。”私下二字一出，又把她镇住了；直到舞终他伸臂来扶，两人再没说一句话。

===Original===

“Come away and have some negus on the stairs,” he said. “The reason I like these sort of parties is, that one is allowed to go into such queer places. You see that little room with the door open. That’s where Mr. Tappitt keeps his old boots and the whip with which he drives his grey horse. There are four men playing cards there now, and one is seated on the end of an upturned portmanteau.”

“And where are the old boots?”

“Packed away on the top of Mrs. Tappitt’s bed. I helped to put them there. Some are stuck under the grate because there are no fires now. Look here; there’s a seat in the window.” Then he placed her in the enclosure of an old window on the staircase landing, and brought her lemonade, and when she had drunk it he sat down beside her.

“Hadn’t we better go back to the dancing?”

“They won’t begin for a few minutes. They’re only tuning up again. You should always escape from the hot air for a moment or two. Besides, you must answer me that question. Did I offend you?”

===Chinese===

“走，上楼梯口喝点尼格斯热酒（negus，掺糖的热葡萄酒）去，”他说。“我喜欢这类聚会，就为了这个：可以随便钻进那些古古怪怪的屋子去。瞧那扇门开着的小屋。那是塔皮特先生搁旧靴子的地方，还有他赶灰马用的鞭子。这会儿有四个人在里头打牌，有一个坐在翻扣过来的大旅行箱头上。”

“那旧靴子搁在哪儿呢？”

“都包好了，搁在塔皮特太太床铺顶上。还是我帮着搁上去的。有几双塞在壁炉栅底下，如今不生火了嘛。你瞧，窗子这儿有个座儿。”说着他把她安顿在楼梯平台那扇老窗的窗龛里，给她取来柠檬水；她喝完，他就在她身旁坐下了。

“咱们是不是最好回去跳舞？”

“几分钟里开不了场。还不是又在那儿调弦。满屋的热气，人总该出来透一口气的。再说，你得回答我那个问题。我得罪过你没有？”

===Original===

“Please don’t talk of it. Please don’t. It’s all over now.”

“Ah, but it is not all over. I knew you were angry with me because—shall I say why?”

“No, Mr. Rowan, don’t say anything about it.”

“At any rate, I may think that you have forgiven me. But what if I offend in the same way again? What if I ask permission to do it, so that it may be no offence? Only think; if I am to live here in Baslehurst all my life, is it not reasonable that I should wish you to be my friend? Are you going to separate yourself from Cherry Tappitt because you are afraid of me?”

“Oh, no.”

“But is not that what you have done during the last week, Miss Ray;—if it must be Miss Ray?” Then he paused, but still she said nothing. “Rachel is such a pretty name.”

===Chinese===

“求你别提这个了。求你别提。如今都过去了。”

“唉，可这没有过去。我知道你为什么生我的气——要我说是为什么吗？”

“别，罗恩先生，这事儿你一个字也别提。”

“至少，我可以认为你已经饶恕我了。可倘若我照原样再犯一回呢？倘若我讨一个许可，让这事算不得冒犯呢？你想想；我若是要一辈子住在巴斯尔赫斯特，我巴望你做我的朋友，难道不合情理吗？难道因为怕我，你就要同彻丽·塔皮特断绝来往？”

“哦，不。”

“可这上个星期，你不正是这么干的吗，雷小姐；——如果非得叫雷小姐的话？”说到这里他停了停，她依旧一言不发。“雷切尔这名字多好看。”

===Original===

“Oh, I think it so ugly.”

“It’s the prettiest name in the Bible, and the name most fit for poetic use. Who does not remember Rachel weeping for her children?”

“That’s the idea, and not the name. Ruth is twice prettier, and Mary the sweetest of all.”

“I never knew anybody before called Rachel,” said he.

“And I never knew anybody called Luke.”

===Chinese===

“哦，我觉得这名字难看死了。”

“这是《圣经》里最美的名字，也是最有诗意的名字。谁不记得为儿女哀哭的拉结（Rachel）？”

“那说的是典故，又不是名字。路得（Ruth）比它好看一倍，马利亚（Mary）才是一切名字里最甜的。”

“我从前从没认识过叫雷切尔的人，”他说。

“我也从没认识过叫卢克的人。”

===Original===

“That’s a coincidence, is it not?—a coincidence that ought to make us friends. I may call you Rachel then?”

“Oh, no; please don’t. What would people think?”

“Perhaps they would think the truth,” said he. “Perhaps they would imagine that I called you so because I liked you. But perhaps they might think also that you let me do so because you liked me. People do make such mistakes.”

===Chinese===

“这就叫巧合，不是吗？——一桩合该让我们做朋友的巧合。那么，我可以叫你雷切尔了？”

“哦，不；请你别这样。人家会怎么想呢？”

“也许人家想的正是实情，”他说。“也许他们会以为，我这样叫你，是因为我喜欢你。可也许他们还会想，你容我这样叫，是因为你喜欢我。人这种错，倒是当真常犯的。”

===Original===

At this moment up came to them, with flushed face, Mr. Buckett. “I have been looking for you everywhere,” said he to Rachel. “It’s nearly over now.”

“I am so sorry,” said Rachel, “but I quite forgot.”

“So I presume,” said Mr. Buckett angrily, but at the same time he gave his arm to Rachel and led her away. The fag end of some waltz remained, and he might get a turn with her. People in his hearing had spoken of her as the belle of the room, and he did not like to lose his chance. “Oh, Mr. Rowan,” said Rachel, looking back as she was being led away. “I must speak one word to Mr. Rowan.” Then she separated herself, and returning a step or two almost whispered to her late partner—“You have put me down for ever so many dances. You must scratch out two or three of them.”

===Chinese===

正在这当口，巴克特先生红涨着脸来到他们跟前。“我到处找你，”他对雷切尔说，“这会儿都快跳完了。”

“实在对不起，”雷切尔说，“可我全给忘了。”

“想必如此，”巴克特先生怒冲冲地说，可他同时还是伸臂挽了雷切尔，把她带走了。某支华尔兹还剩一个尾巴，他没准还能捞着同她转上一圈。方才有人在他听得见的地方，称她是全场的花魁，他不愿错失这个良机。“哦，罗恩先生，”雷切尔让人带着走，回过头来说，“我得跟罗恩先生说一句话。”于是她抽身出来，退回一两步，几乎贴着耳朵，对方才的舞伴低声说——“你给我记了那么多场舞。你得划掉两三场。”

===Original===

“Not one,” said he. “An engagement is an engagement.”

“Oh, but I really can’t.”

“Of course I cannot make you, but I will scratch out nothing—and forget nothing.”

Then she rejoined Mr. Buckett, and was told by him that young Rowan was not liked in the brewery at all. “We think him conceited, you know. He pretends to know more than anybody else.”

===Chinese===

“一场也不划，”他说，“约定就是约定。”

“哦，可我真的不行。”

“我当然强迫不了你，可我什么也不划——也什么不忘。”

随后她回到巴克特先生身边，听他数落说，小罗恩在酿酒厂里一点儿也不招人待见。“我们都觉得他自大，你知道的。他装出一副比谁都懂的架子。”

## VIII An Account of Mrs. Tappitt’s Ball—Concluded / VIII 塔皮特太太的舞会记——终篇

===Original===

It came to be voted by public acclamation that Rachel Ray was the belle of the evening. I think this was brought about quite as much by Mrs. Butler Cornbury’s powerful influence as by Rachel’s beauty. Mrs. Butler Cornbury having begun the work of chaperon carried it on heartily, and talked her young friend up to the top of the tree. Long before supper her card was quite full, but filled in a manner that was not comfortable to herself—for she knew that she had made mistakes. As to those spaces on which the letter *R* was written, she kept them very sacred. She was quite resolved that she would not stand up with him on all those occasions—that she would omit at any rate two; but she would accept no one else for those two dances, not choosing to select any special period for throwing him over. She endeavoured to explain this when she waltzed with him, shortly before supper; but her explanation did not come easy, and she wanted all her attention for the immediate work she had in hand. “If you’d only give yourself to it a little more eagerly,” he said, “you’d waltz beautifully.”
“I shall never do it well,” she answered. “I don’t suppose I shall ever try again.”
“But you like it?”
“Oh yes; I like it excessively. But one can’t do everything that one likes.”
“No; I can’t. You won’t let me do what I like.”
“Don’t talk in that way, Mr. Rowan. If you do you’ll destroy all my pleasure. You should let me enjoy it while it lasts.” In this way she was becoming intimate with him.

===Chinese===

众望所归，全场一致公认：雷切尔·雷（Rachel Ray）是当晚的花魁。依我看，这份荣光一半固然出自雷切尔的姿色，另一半却也是巴特勒·康伯里太太（Mrs. Butler Cornbury）神通广大的影响所造就。巴特勒·康伯里太太既然开头发起了做女伴的差事，便满腔热忱地担当到底，把她的年轻朋友捧到了头顶上。离夜宴还早，她的节目卡已经填得满满当当，只是填得她自己心里不大熨帖——因为她知道自己出了差错。凡是写了字母 *R* 的那些空格，她都供得十分神圣。她打定了主意，那些场合同他决不场场都跳——至少要空下两场；可那两场她也不肯让别人顶上，因为她不愿意特意图出个专门甩开他的时点。夜宴前不久同他跳华尔兹的时候，她竭力想把这一层意思解释清楚；只是解释得并不顺当，眼前手头的正经事又要占去她全部的心神。“你只要再投入一点，”他说，“你的华尔兹会跳得美极了。”
“我永远也跳不好这个，”她答道，“我想我往后也不会再试了。”
“可是你喜欢跳吧？”
“哦，喜欢；喜欢得不得了。可人总不能样样喜欢的事都做呀。”
“是呀，不能。你就不肯让我做我喜欢的事。”
“别这么说话，罗恩先生（Mr. Rowan）。你这样会把我的兴头全毁掉的。趁它还没过去，你该让我好好快活快活。”她就这样同他渐渐熟稔起来。

===Original===

“How very nicely your house does for a dance,” said Mrs. Cornbury to Mrs. Tappitt.
“Oh dear—I don’t think so. Our rooms are so small. But it’s very kind of you to say so. Indeed, I never can be sufficiently obliged—”
“By the by,” said Mrs. Cornbury, “what a nice girl Rachel Ray has grown.”
“Yes, indeed,” said Mrs. Tappitt.
“And dances so well! I’d no idea of it. The young men seem rather taken with her. Don’t you think so?”
“I declare I think they are. I always fancy that is rather a misfortune to a young girl—particularly when it must mean nothing, as of course it can’t with poor Rachel.”

===Chinese===

“你这房子办起舞会来多合适啊，”康伯里太太对塔皮特太太（Mrs. Tappitt）说。
“哎呀——我可不这么想。我们的屋子太小了。不过您肯这么说是心眼儿好。说真的，我是千恩万谢也谢不尽——”
“顺便说一句，”康伯里太太说，“雷切尔·雷这丫头出落得多标致啊。”
“可不是嘛，”塔皮特太太说。
“舞又跳得那么好！我真没想到。年轻小伙子们好像都叫她迷住了。你不觉得吗？”
“说真的，我看也是。我一向觉得这对年轻姑娘反倒是桩不幸——尤其是在这必定当不得真的时候，可怜的雷切尔自然是当不得真的。”

===Original===

“I don’t see that at all.”
“Her mother, you know, Mrs. Cornbury;—they are not in the way of seeing any company. It was so kind of you to bring her here, and really she does look very nice. My girls are very good-natured to her. I only hope her head won’t be turned. Here’s Mr. Tappitt. You must go down Mrs. Cornbury, and eat a little bit of supper.” Then Mr. Tappitt in his blue waistcoat led Mrs. Cornbury away.
“I am a very bad hand at supper,” said the lady.
“You must take just one glass of champagne,” said the gentleman. Now that the wine was there, Mr. Tappitt appreciated the importance of the occasion.

===Chinese===

“这话我可一点也不懂。”
“她那位母亲，您是知道的，康伯里太太；——她们娘儿俩平素见不着什么客人。难得您好心把她带来，说真的，她今晚确实漂亮得很。我家几个姑娘待她够好的了。我只盼她的头别给捧晕了。塔皮特先生（Mr. Tappitt）来了。您可得下楼去了，康伯里太太，去用一点夜宴。”于是塔皮特先生穿着他那件蓝马甲，把康伯里太太引走了。
“我这个人是不大会在夜宴上受用的，”这位太太说。
“那您至少得喝上一杯香槟，”这位先生说。既然酒已经摆在了那里，塔皮特先生自然掂量得出这个场面的分量。

===Original===

For the last dance before supper—or that which was intended to be the last—Rachel had by long agreement been the partner of Walter Cornbury. But now that it was over, the majority of the performers could not go into the supper-room because of the crowd. Young Cornbury therefore proposed that they should loiter about till their time came. He was very well inclined for such loitering with Rachel.
“You’re flirting with that girl, Master Walter,” said Mrs. Cornbury.
“I suppose that’s what she came for,” said the cousin.
“By no means, and she’s under my care; therefore I beg you’ll talk no nonsense to her.”
Walter Cornbury probably did talk a little nonsense to her, but it was very innocent nonsense. Most of such flirtations if they were done out loud would be very innocent. Young men are not nearly so pointed in their compliments as their elders, and generally confine themselves to remarks of which neither mothers nor grandmothers could disapprove if they heard them. The romance lies rather in the thoughts than in the words of those concerned. Walter Cornbury believed that he was flirting and felt himself to be happy, but he had uttered nothing warmer to Rachel than a hope that he might meet her at the next Torquay ball.

===Chinese===

夜宴前的最后一场舞——或者说本该是最后的那一场——雷切尔早在许久之前便约定了做沃尔特·康伯里（Walter Cornbury）的舞伴。可这一场跳完，跳舞的人大半却挤不进夜宴厅去，人实在太多了。于是小康伯里提议，大家先四处闲步溜达，等着轮到自己。同雷切尔一道这样闲步溜达，他正是求之不得。
“你在同那姑娘调情呢，沃尔特少爷，”康伯里太太说。
“我看她来就是为了这个呗，”那位堂弟说。
“万万没有的事，再说她归我照管；所以我请你一句浑话也别同她讲。”
沃尔特·康伯里多半也确实同她说了一点浑话，不过那是十分清白的浑话。这类调情若是高声说出来，多半都是非常清白的。年轻小伙子说恭维话，远不像年长的人那么露骨，一般只说些让母亲们乃至祖母们听了也挑不出错的话头。涉事各人心里的罗曼司，远比嘴上的多。沃尔特·康伯里自信是在调情，也自觉快活；可他对雷切尔说过的最热乎的话，也不过是盼着下一场托基（Torquay）舞会上能再见到她。

===Original===

“I never go to public balls,” said Rachel.
“But why not, Miss Ray?” said Walter.
“I never went to a dance of any description before this.”
“But now that you’ve begun of course you’ll go on.” Mr. Cornbury’s flirtation never reached a higher pitch than that.
When he had got as far as that Luke Rowan played him a trick—an inhospitable trick, seeing that he, Rowan, was in some sort at home, and that the people about him were bound to obey him. He desired the musicians to strike up again while the elders were eating their supper—and then claimed Rachel’s hand, so that he might have the pleasure of serving her with cold chicken and champagne.

===Chinese===

“我从来不去公众舞会，”雷切尔说。
“那为什么呢，雷小姐？”沃尔特说。
“今晚以前，什么样儿的舞会我也没去过。”
“可您既然开了头，往后自然要接着跳喽。”康伯里先生（Mr. Cornbury）的调情，至多也就到此为止。
他刚说到这里，卢克·罗恩（Luke Rowan）便捉弄了他一下——一个不懂得待客之道的捉弄；要知道，罗恩自己好歹算是半个主人，他身边的人都得听他号令。趁长辈们正用着夜宴，他吩咐乐师们重新奏起乐来——随后便来讨雷切尔的手，好享受亲手服侍她吃冷鸡、喝香槟的乐趣。

===Original===

“Miss Ray is going into supper with me,” said Cornbury.
“But supper is not ready,” said Rowan, “and Miss Ray is engaged to dance with me.”
“Quite a mistake on your part,” said Cornbury.
“No mistake at all,” said Rowan.
“Indeed it is. Come, Miss Ray, we’ll take a turn down into the hall, and see if places are ready for us.” Cornbury rather despised Rowan, as being a brewer and mechanical; and probably he showed that he did so.

===Chinese===

“雷小姐要同我一道去用夜宴，”康伯里说。
“可夜宴还没备好呢，”罗恩说，“雷小姐还约了同我跳舞。”
“这您可弄错了，”康伯里说。
“一点也没弄错，”罗恩说。
“明明是弄错了。来吧，雷小姐，我们下楼去门厅转一圈，看看位子备好了没有。”康伯里颇为瞧不起罗恩，认为他不过是个酿酒匠，浑身机件气；而这番轻蔑，他八成也露在了脸上。

===Original===

“Places are not ready, so you need not trouble Miss Ray to go down as yet. But a couple is wanted for a quadrille, and therefore I’m sure she’ll stand up.”
“Come along, Rachel,” said Cherry. “We just want you. This will be the nicest of all, because we shall have room.”
Rachel had become unhappy seeing that the two men were in earnest. Had not Cherry spoken she would have remained with Mr. Cornbury, thinking that to be her safer conduct; but Cherry’s voice had overpowered her, and she gave her arm to young Rowan, moving away with slow, hesitating step.
“Of course Miss Ray will do as she pleases,” said Cornbury.
“Of course she will,” said Rowan.
“I am so sorry,” said Rachel, “but I was engaged, and it seems I am really wanted.” Walter Cornbury bowed very stiffly, and there was an end of his flirtation. “That’s the sort of thing that always happens when a fellow comes among this sort of people!” It was thus he consoled himself as he went down solitary to his supper.

===Chinese===

“位子还没备好，所以您眼下不必劳驾雷小姐下楼。不过四对舞正缺一对儿，所以我敢说她一定肯站起来。”
“来呀，雷切尔，”彻丽（Cherry）说，“我们就缺你一个。这场是顶好玩的，因为地方宽绰。”
眼见两位先生都动了真格，雷切尔心里发慌。要不是彻丽开了口，她会留在康伯里先生身边，觉得那样行事稳妥些；可彻丽的声音压倒了一切，她把手臂递给了年轻的罗恩，迈着迟疑的慢步挪开去了。
“雷小姐自然想怎样就怎样，”康伯里说。
“她当然想怎样就怎样，”罗恩说。
“实在对不起，”雷切尔说，“可我先前是约了人的，何况人家好像真的缺我不可。”沃尔特·康伯里僵直地一躬身，他那场调情就此告终。“一个人落到这号人中间，就准出这号事！”他孤零零地下楼去吃夜宴，一路便这么宽慰着自己。

===Original===

“That’s all right,” said Rowan; “now we’ve Cherry for our vis-à-vis, and after that we’ll go down to supper comfortably.”
“But I said I’d go with him.”
“You can’t now, for he has gone without you. What a brick Cherry is! Do you know what she said of you?”
“No; do tell me.”
“I won’t. It will make you vain.”

===Chinese===

“这样才好呢，”罗恩说；“这下对面是彻丽做我们的对舞（vis-à-vis），待会儿咱们再舒舒服服地下楼去吃夜宴。”
“可我说了要同他一道去的。”
“现在可去不成了，他没等你就走了。彻丽真是个顶好的人！你知道她说你什么来着？”
“不知道；快告诉我嘛。”
“偏不告诉你。说了你要骄傲的。”

===Original===

“Oh, dear no; but I want Cherry to like me, because I am so fond of her.”
“She says you’re by far—But I won’t tell you. I hate compliments, and that would look like one. Come, who’s forgetting the figure now? I shouldn’t wonder if young Cornbury went into the brewery and drowned himself in one of the vats.”
It was very nice—very nice indeed. This was her third dance with Luke Rowan, and she was beginning to think that the other two might perhaps come off without any marked impropriety on her part. She was a little unhappy about Mr. Cornbury—on his cousin’s account rather than on his own. Mrs. Cornbury had been so kind to her that she ought to have remained with Walter when he desired it. So she told herself;—but yet she liked being taken down to supper by Luke Rowan. She had one other cause of uneasiness. She constantly caught Mrs. Tappitt’s eye fixed upon herself, and whenever she did so Mrs. Tappitt’s eye seemed to look unkindly at her. She had also an instinctive feeling that Augusta did not regard her with favour, and that this disfavour arose from Mr. Rowan’s attentions. It was all very nice; but still she felt that there was danger around her, and sometimes she would pause a moment in her happiness, and almost tremble as she thought of things. She was dividing herself poles asunder from Mrs. Prime.
“And now we’ll go to supper,” said Rowan. “Come, Cherry; do you and Boyd go on first.” Boyd was a friend of Rowan’s. “Do you know, I’ve done such a clever trick. This is my second descent among the eatables. As I belong in a manner to the house I took down Miss Harford, and hovered about her for five minutes. Then I managed to lose myself in the crowd, and coming up here got the music up. The fellows were just going off. We’ve plenty of time now, because they’re in the kitchen eating and drinking. I contrived all that dodge that I might give you this glass of wine with my own hands.”

===Chinese===

“哦，不会的；我只是想让彻丽喜欢我，因为我太喜欢她了。”
“她说你是远远——罢了，我不告诉你。我顶讨厌恭维话，那听起来就像恭维了。来，如今倒是谁忘了舞步啊？我说小康伯里八成要扎进酿酒厂，一头淹死在哪只酒桶里呢。”
这真是快活——实在快活得很。这是她同卢克·罗恩跳的第三场舞，她开始盘算，剩下那两场或许也能顺顺当当地跳完，不至于显出她这方面有什么明显的失仪。她对康伯里先生有点过意不去——与其说是为他自己，不如说是为他堂嫂的缘故。康伯里太太待她那么好，沃尔特要她留下的时候，她本该留下才是。她心里是这么对自己说的；——可话虽如此，让卢克·罗恩陪着下楼去吃夜宴，她还是欢喜的。她另有一桩不安。她接二连三地撞见塔皮特太太的目光钉在自己身上，而每一回，那目光瞧着她的神气总像不怀好意。她还有种本能的预感：奥古斯塔（Augusta）对她并无好感，而这份恶感的根由，正是罗恩先生的殷勤。样样都很美；可她仍觉得四周有危险，有时会在快活当中猛地停一下，想起种种事情，几乎战栗起来。她同普赖姆太太（Mrs. Prime）之间，正裂开一道天南地北的鸿沟。
“现在咱们去吃夜宴吧，”罗恩说。“来，彻丽；你同博伊德（Boyd）先走一步。”博伊德是罗恩的朋友。“你们可知道，我刚使了个妙招。这已经是我第二回下去光顾吃食了。我好歹算这府上的人，便陪着哈福德小姐（Miss Harford）下去，在她身边周旋了五分钟。然后我设法在人群里脱了身，回到这楼上，叫乐师们奏起乐来。那伙人正要散场呢。现在咱们工夫宽裕得很，因为他们都在厨房里吃吃喝喝。我布下这一整套把戏，就为了能亲手端给你这杯酒。”

===Original===

“Oh, Mr. Rowan, it was very wrong!”
“And that’s my reward! I don’t care about its being wrong as long as it’s pleasant.”
“What shocking morality!”
“All is fair in—Well, never mind, you’ll own it is pleasant.”
“Oh, yes; it’s very pleasant.”
“Then I’m contented, and will leave the moral of it for Mr. Cornbury. I’ll tell you something further if you’ll let me.”

===Chinese===

“哦，罗恩先生，这可太不应该了！”
“这就是我的报答！只要快活，不该就不该吧，我不在乎。”
“好骇人听闻的道德观！”
“恋爱场上，一切都……罢了，别提这个，你总得承认这很快活。”
“哦，是呀；快活得很。”
“那我心满意足了，个中的道德教训就留给康伯里先生去讲吧。要是你肯听，我还有下文呢。”

===Original===

“Pray don’t tell me anything that you ought not.”
“I’ve done all I could to get up this party on purpose that we might have you here.”
“Nonsense.”
“But I have. I have cared about it just because it would enable me to say one word to you;—and now I’m afraid to say it.”
She was sitting there close to him, and she couldn’t go away. She couldn’t run as she had done from the stile. She couldn’t show any feeling of offence before all those who were around her; and yet—was it not her duty to do something to stop him? “Pray don’t say such things,” she whispered.

===Chinese===

“求你别讲那些你不该讲的话。”
“为了操办这场舞会，能尽的心力我都尽了，就是要把你请到这里来。”
“胡说。”
“可我确实上心。我这么经心，就因为它能让我对你说上一句话；——如今我倒不敢说了。”
她就坐在他紧旁边，脱不开身。她不能像那回在跨篱阶（stile）上那样一跑了之。当着周围这许多人，她不能露出半点受了冒犯的神气；可是——想法子拦住他，难道不正是她的本分吗？“求你别说了，”她悄声说。

===Original===

“I tell you that I’m afraid to say it. Here; give me some wine. You’ll take some more. No? Well; shall we go? I am afraid to say it.” They were now out in the hall, standing idly there, with their backs to another door. “I wonder what answer you would make me!”
“We had better go upstairs. Indeed we had.”
“Stop a moment, Miss Ray. Why is it that you are so unwilling even to stay a moment with me?”
“I’m not unwilling. Only we had better go now.”
“Do you remember when I held your arm at the stile?”
“No; I don’t remember anything about it. You ought not to have done it. Do you know, I think you are very cruel.” As she made the accusation, she looked down upon the floor, and spoke in a low, trembling voice that almost convinced him that she was in earnest.

===Chinese===

“我告诉你，我不敢说。喏，给我斟点酒。你也再来一点。不喝？那好；咱们走吗？我就是不敢说。”这会儿他们已经到了门厅里，百无聊赖地站在那儿，背对着另一扇门。“我倒想看看，你会怎么回答我！”
“我们还是上楼去吧。真的，还是上去的好。”
“等一下，雷小姐。为什么连同我多待片刻，你都不情愿？”
“我不是不情愿。只是我们现在最好还是走。”
“你还记得那回在跨篱阶上，我扶住你的胳膊吗？”
“不；那件事我什么都不记得了。你本不该那么做。你可知道，我觉得你狠心极了。”她说这句责备话时，眼睛望着地板，声音低低的、颤颤的，倒几乎让他信了她是当真的。

===Original===

“Cruel!” said he. “That’s hard too.”
“Or you wouldn’t prevent me enjoying myself while I am here, by saying things which you ought to know I don’t like.”
“I have hardly thought whether you would like what I say or not; but I know this; I would give anything in the world to make myself sure that you would ever look back upon this evening as a happy one.”
“I will if you’ll come upstairs, and—”
“And what?”
“And go on without—without seeming to mind me so much.”

===Chinese===

“狠心！”他说。“这话也够狠的。”
“要不然，你也不会挑那些你明知道我不爱听的话来说，叫我在这里痛快不成。”
“我说的话你爱听不爱听，我几乎没去想过；可这一点我知道：只消能保得你日后回想今晚，觉得它是一桩快活的夜晚，天底下随便什么我都舍得拿来换。”
“只要你肯上楼去，我就——”
“就怎么？”
“就照旧跳下去，别——别显得那么把我放在心上。”

===Original===

“Ah, but I do mind you. Rachel—no; you shall not go for a minute. Listen to me for one moment.” Then he tried to stand before her, but she was off from him, and ran upstairs by herself. What was it that he wished to say to her? She knew that she would have liked to have heard it;—nay, that she was longing to hear it. But she was startled and afraid of him, and as she gently crept in at the door of the dancing-room, she determined that she would tell Mrs. Cornbury that she was quite ready for the carriage. It was impossible that she should go through those other two dances with Luke Rowan; and as for her other engagements, they must be allowed to shift for themselves. One had been made early in the evening with Mr. Griggs. It would be a great thing to escape dancing with Mr. Griggs. She would ask Cherry to make her apologies to everybody. As she entered the room she felt ashamed of herself, and unable to take any place. She was oppressed by an idea that she ought not to be walking about without some gentleman with her, and that people would observe her. She was still very near the door when she perceived that Mr. Rowan was also coming in. She determined to avoid him if she could, feeling sure that she could not stop him in anything that he might say, while so many people would be close around them. And yet she felt almost disappointment when she heard his voice as he talked merrily with someone at the door. At that moment Mrs. Cornbury came up to her, walking across the room on purpose to join her.
“What, all alone! I thought your hand was promised for every dance up to five o’clock.”
“I believe I’m engaged to someone now, but I declare I don’t know who it is. I dare say he has forgotten.”
“Ah, yes; people do get confused a little just about this time. Will you come and sit down?”
“Thank you, I should like that. But, Mrs. Cornbury, when you’re ready to go away, I am—quite ready.”

===Chinese===

“唉，可我偏偏就把你放在心上。雷切尔——不行；你一分钟也不许走。听我说上一句。”说着他便想拦到她面前去，可她早已脱身，独自跑上了楼。他到底想对她说什么呢？她知道自己原是愿意听的；——不，她是渴望着听的。可她吓着了，怕他；待她轻轻溜进舞室的门，她拿定了主意：去告诉康伯里太太，说她已经随时可以备车回家了。剩下那两场舞，断乎不能再同卢克·罗恩跳；至于旁的几场邀约，也只好任它们自谋出路。其中一场是开席不久格里格斯先生（Mr. Griggs）定下的。能逃过同格里格斯先生跳舞，那可是天大的造化。她会请彻丽替她向众人一一致歉。进屋的时候，她又羞又窘，觉得哪儿都安身不得。一个念头压着她：身边没有位先生陪着，她不该在屋里走来走去，人家会盯着她看。她还离门不远，就察觉罗恩先生也进来了。她打定主意，能躲便躲；她心里有数，身边围的人这么多，他要说什么，她是一句也拦不住的。可听见他在门口同什么人谈笑风生，她心里竟又几乎生出一丝失望。恰在这时，康伯里太太穿过屋子，特地朝她走了过来。
“怎么，一个人待着！我记得你的每一场舞都约到五点钟了呢。”
“我好像这一场也约了人的，可说实话，我记不起是谁了。想必他早忘啦。”
“啊，是啊；到了这个时辰，人是容易有些糊涂的。过来坐下好不好？”
“谢谢，我正想坐呢。不过，康伯里太太，等您准备动身的时候，我——我随时都好。”

===Original===

“Go away! Why I thought you intended to dance at least for the next two hours.”
In answer to this, Rachel declared that she was tired. “And, Mrs. Cornbury, I want to avoid that man,” and she pointed out Mr. Griggs by a glance of her eye. “I think he’ll say I’m engaged to him for the next waltz, and—I don’t like him.”
“Poor man; he doesn’t look very nice, certainly; but if that’s all I’ll get you out of the scrape without running away.” Then Mr. Griggs came up, and, with a very low bow, struck out the point of his elbow towards Rachel, expecting her immediately to put her hand within it.
“I’m afraid, sir, you must excuse Miss Ray just at present. She’s too tired to dance immediately.”
Mr. Griggs looked at his card, then looked at Rachel, then looked at Mrs. Cornbury, and stood twiddling the bunch of little gilt playthings that hung from his chain. “That is too hard,” said he; “deuced hard.”
“I’m very sorry,” said Rachel.

===Chinese===

“动身！我原以为你至少还要跳上两个钟头呢。”
听了这话，雷切尔只说自己累了。“还有，康伯里太太，我想躲开那个人，”她拿眼风一指，指的是格里格斯先生。“下一场华尔兹他八成要说约的是我，而且——我不喜欢他。”
“可怜的人；他的模样自然说不上好看；可既然只是这么点事，我用不着逃走，也能替你脱身。”这时格里格斯先生走上前来，一躬到底，把胳膊肘朝雷切尔面前一伸，满以为她即刻就会把手搭进去。
“对不起，先生，眼下您得容雷小姐告个假。她累得狠了，一时半会儿跳不成。”
格里格斯先生瞧了瞧自己的节目卡，又瞧瞧雷切尔，再瞧瞧康伯里太太，杵在原地，捻弄着表链上垂着的一串镀金小玩意儿。“这就太狠了，”他说，“要命地狠。”
“我非常抱歉，”雷切尔说。

===Original===

“So shall I be—uncommon. Really, Mrs. Cornbury, I think a turn or two would do her good. Don’t you?”
“I can’t say I do. She says she would rather not, and of course you won’t press her.”
“I don’t see it in that light—I really don’t. A gentleman has his rights you know, Mrs. Cornbury. Miss Ray won’t deny—”
“Miss Ray will deny that she intends to stand up for this dance. And one of the rights of a gentleman is to take a lady at her word.”
“Really, Mrs. Cornbury, you are down upon one so hard.”
“Rachel,” said she, “would you mind coming across the room with me? There are seats on the sofa on the other side.” Then Mrs. Cornbury sailed across the floor, and Rachel crept after her more dismayed than ever. Mr. Griggs the while stood transfixed to his place, stroking his mustaches with his hand, and showing plainly by his countenance that he didn’t know what he ought to do next. “Well, that’s cool,” said he; “confounded cool!”

===Chinese===

“我也会抱歉的——抱歉得不得了。说真的，康伯里太太，依我看转上一两圈对她只有好处。您说是不是？”
“恕我不能苟同。她说了不愿意，您总不会强人所难。”
“我可不作如此想——实在不作如此想。先生自有先生的权利，您知道，康伯里太太。雷小姐总不至于否认——”
“雷小姐恰恰要否认：这一场舞，她无意奉陪。而先生的权利当中，有一条正是尊重女士亲口说出的话。”
“说真的，康伯里太太，您这一下把人钉得太狠了。”
“雷切尔，”她说，“劳驾同我到屋子那头去一趟好不好？那边的沙发上有座位。”于是康伯里太太仪态万方地飘过舞池，雷切尔比先前越发惶惶，跟在她身后挪了过去。格里格斯先生这会儿钉在原地，一只手捻着髭须，一脸明明白白地写着：下一步该怎么办，他全无主意。“哼，好大的架子，”他说，“见鬼地傲！”

===Original===

“Anything wrong, Griggs, my boy?” said a bank clerk, slapping him on the back.
“I call it very wrong; very wrong, indeed,” said Griggs; “but people do give themselves such airs! Miss Cherry, may I have the honour of waltzing with you?”
“Certainly not,” said Cherry, who was passing by. Then Mr. Griggs made his way back to the door.
Rachel felt that things were going wrong with her. It had so happened that she had parted on bad terms with three gentlemen. She had offended Mr. Cornbury and Mr. Griggs, and had done her best to make Mr. Rowan understand that he had offended her! She conceived that all the room would know of it, and that Mrs. Cornbury would become ashamed of her. That Mrs. Tappitt was already very angry with her she was quite sure. She wished she had not come to the ball, and began to think that perhaps her sister might be right. It almost seemed to herself that she had not known how to behave herself. For a short time she had been happy—very happy; but she feared that she had in some way committed herself during the moments of her happiness. “I hope you are not angry with me,” she said, “about Mr. Griggs?” appealing to her friend in a plaintive voice.
“Angry!—oh dear, no. Why should I be angry with you? I should be angry with that man, only I’m a person that never gets angry with anybody. You were quite right not to dance with him. Never be made to dance with any man you don’t like; and remember that a young lady should always have her own way in a ballroom. She doesn’t get much of it anywhere else; does she, my dear? And now I’ll go whenever you like it, but I’m not the least in a hurry. You’re the young lady, and you’re to have your own way. If you’re quite in earnest, I’ll get someone to order the carriage.”—Rachel said that she was quite in earnest, and then Walter was called. “So you’re going, are you?” said he. “Miss Ray has ill-treated me so dreadfully that I can’t express my regret.” “Ill-treated you, too, has she? Upon my word, my dear, you’ve shown yourself quite great upon the occasion. When I was a girl, there was nothing I liked so much as offending all my partners.” But Rachel was red with dismay, and wretched that such an accusation should be made against her. “Oh, Mrs. Cornbury, I didn’t mean to offend him! I’ll explain it all in the carriage. What will you think of me?” “Think, my dear?—why, I shall think that you are going to turn all the young men’s heads in Baslehurst. But I shall hear all about it from Walter tomorrow. He tells me of all his loves and all his disappointments.”

===Chinese===

“有什么不对劲吗，格里格斯，老弟？”一个银行职员拍着他的背说。
“依我看这事办得太不地道；实在不地道，”格里格斯说；“不过如今端架子的人可真不少！彻丽小姐，能赏脸同您跳一场华尔兹吗？”
“当然不赏，”正打旁边经过的彻丽说。于是格里格斯先生又一路挤回了门口。
雷切尔觉得事情到自己头上全不对劲了。事有凑巧，她竟同三位先生闹得不欢而散。她得罪了康伯里先生和格里格斯先生，又竭力想让罗恩先生明白：是他得罪了她！她估摸着满屋子的人都会知道，康伯里太太会为她丢脸。至于塔皮特太太已经对她老大不高兴，这一点她拿得十分准。她懊悔不该来赴这个舞会，开始想，兴许姐姐的话是对的。她自己几乎都觉得，她竟不懂得怎样规行矩步了。有那么一小会儿，她是快活的——非常快活；可她怕的是，正在那快活的时辰里，自己不知不觉已经失了分寸。“我希望您别生我的气，”她带着哀恳的声气向她的朋友说，“为了格里格斯先生的事？”
“生气！——哎呀，才不会呢。我干嘛要生你的气？要恼也是恼那个人，只可惜我这人从不对任何人动气。你不同他跳，做得对极了。千万别让任何你不喜欢的男人逼着你跳舞；要记住，在舞场上，年轻小姐永远该由着自己的性子来。出了舞场，她可就作不了多少主了；是不是呀，我亲爱的？好了，你想什么时候走，我就什么时候走，只是我一点也不急。你是小姐，自然该你做主。你若真定了主意，我就叫人去吩咐马车。”——雷切尔说她真定了主意，于是把沃尔特唤了过来。“怎么，这就走啦？”他说。“雷小姐把我欺负得好惨，叫我连这份歉意都没处表白去。”“把你也欺负啦？哎哟我的天，我亲爱的，这场面上你可真摆足了威风。我做姑娘的时候，天底下再没有比把舞伴们统统得罪一遍更叫我痛快的了。”雷切尔却窘得满脸通红，受了这样的冤枉，苦得不行。“哦，康伯里太太，我不是存心得罪他的！到车子里我全跟您解释。您会怎么看我呢？”“怎么看你，我亲爱的？——嗐，我就要看你把巴斯尔赫斯特（Baslehurst）的小伙子们一个个勾得神魂颠倒喽。不过明天沃尔特自会把底细讲给我听。他的每一段恋情、每一场失望，都从不瞒我。”

===Original===

While the carriage was being brought round, Rachel kept close to her chaperon; but every now and again her eyes, in spite of herself, would wander away to Mr. Rowan. Was he in any way affected by her leaving him, or was it all a joke to him? He was dancing now with Cherry Tappitt, and Rachel was sure that all of it was a joke. But it was a cruel joke—cruel because it exposed her to so much ill-natured remark. With him she would quarrel—quarrel really. She would let him know that he should not call her by her Christian name just when it suited him to do so, and then take himself off to play with others in the same way. She would tell Cherry, and make Cherry understand that all walks and visiting and friendly intercommunications must be abandoned because this young man would take advantage of her position to annoy her! He should be made to understand that she was not in his power! Then, as she thought of this, she caught his eye as he made a sudden stop in the dance close to her, and all her hard thoughts died away. Ah, dear, what was it that she wanted of him?
At that moment they got up to go away. Such a person as Mrs. Butler Cornbury could not, of course, escape without a parade of adieux. Mr. Tappitt was searched up from the little room in which the card-party held their meeting in order that he might hand the guest that had honoured him down to her carriage; and Mrs. Tappitt fluttered about, profuse in her acknowledgments for the favour done to them. “And we do so hope Mr. Cornbury will be successful,” she said, as she bade her last farewell. This was spoken close to Mr. Tappitt’s ear; and Mrs. Cornbury flattered herself that after that Mr. Tappitt’s vote would be secure. Mr. Tappitt said nothing about his vote, but handed the lady downstairs in solemn silence.
The Tappitt girls came and clustered about Rachel as she was going. “I can’t conceive why you are off so early,” said Martha. “No, indeed,” said Mrs. Tappitt; “only of course it would be very wrong to keep Mrs. Cornbury waiting when she has been so excessively kind to you.” “The naughty girl! It isn’t that at all,” said Cherry. “It’s she that is hurrying Mrs. Cornbury away.” “Good night,” said Augusta very coldly. “And Rachel,” said Cherry, “mind you come up tomorrow and talk it all over; we shall have so much to say.” Then Rachel turned to go, and found Luke Rowan at her elbow waiting to take her down. She had no alternative;—she must take his arm; and thus they walked downstairs into the hall together.

===Chinese===

马车绕过来之前，雷切尔紧紧挨着她的女伴；可她的眼睛由不得自己，时不时溜到罗恩先生那边去。她这一走，他心里到底有没有触动，还是这一切于他全不过玩笑？他这会儿正同彻丽·塔皮特跳舞，雷切尔断定这一切于他全是玩笑。可那是个残忍的玩笑——残忍就残忍在，把她推到了多少恶语的枪口前。她要同他吵——真真正正地吵。她要让他明白，不能由他高兴叫她教名就叫她教名，扭头又照这个路数跑去找别的姑娘厮混。她要告诉彻丽，让彻丽明白：散步、串门、一切亲亲热热的来往，往后统统作罢，因为这个年轻男人存心仗着他的位置来搅扰她！非得让他明白，她不是他捏在手心里的人！可就在她这么思量的当口，他的舞步恰恰一收，停在她近旁，同她的目光撞了个正着，她满腹的狠念霎时烟消云散。天哪，她到底想从他那里要什么呢？
这时她们起身要走。巴特勒·康伯里太太这样的人物，自然不能不打足告辞的排场就走。塔皮特先生让人从那间牌局聚会的小屋里搜寻了出来，好让他把这位赏光屈就的贵客一路搀送到马车跟前；塔皮特太太则在四下里张张罗罗，为他们受的这份抬举千恩万谢。“我们还这样巴望康伯里先生旗开得胜呢，”她末了告别时说。这话是贴着塔皮特先生的耳朵说的；康伯里太太暗自得意：经过这一番，塔皮特先生的那张选票算是十拿九稳了。塔皮特先生对选票只字不提，只在一派肃穆的沉默中，把这位太太送下了楼。
雷切尔正要动身，塔皮特家的姑娘们围拢上来。“我真想不出你怎么这么早就撤，”玛莎（Martha）说。“可不是，”塔皮特太太说；“只是当然喽，康伯里太太待你这样天大的好，可不能让她干等。”“这个鬼丫头！压根儿不是那么回事，”彻丽说。“是她自己在催康伯里太太走呢。”“晚安，”奥古斯塔冷冰冰地说。“还有啊，雷切尔，”彻丽说，“记着明天上楼来，咱们把这件事细聊一遍；要说的可多着呢。”雷切尔转身要走，却发觉卢克·罗恩已候在她臂弯旁，等着搀她下楼。她别无选择；——她只能挽住他的手臂；于是两人一道走下楼，进了门厅。

===Original===

“You’ll come up here tomorrow,” said he.
“No, no; tell Cherry that I shall not come.”
“Then I shall go to Bragg’s End. Will your mother let me call?”
“No, don’t come. Pray don’t.”
“I certainly shall;—certainly, certainly! What things have you got? Let me put your shawl on for you. If you do not come up to the girls, I shall certainly go down to you. Now, good night. Good night, Mrs. Cornbury.” And Luke, getting hold of Rachel’s reluctant hand, pressed it with all his warmth.
“I don’t want to ask indiscreet questions,” said Mrs. Cornbury; “but that young man seems rather smitten, I think.”

===Chinese===

“明天你会上这儿来的，”他说。
“不，不；告诉彻丽，我不会来的。”
“那我就上布拉格斯恩德（Bragg’s End）去。你母亲肯让我登门吗？”
“别，你别来。求你别来。”
“我一定要来；——一定，一定！你带了些什么？来，我替你把披肩披上。你若不肯上楼找那几位姑娘，我就一定下到你家去。好了，晚安。晚安，康伯里太太。”卢克攥住雷切尔不情愿的手，使出他全部的热乎劲儿紧紧一握。
“我不想问冒失的问题，”康伯里太太说；“不过依我看，那位年轻先生像是着了迷了呢。”

===Original===

“Oh, no,” said Rachel, not knowing what to say.
“But I say—oh, yes; a nice good-looking man he is too, and a gentleman, which is more than I can say for all of them there. What an escape you had of Mr. Griggs, my dear!”
“Yes, I had. But I was so sorry that you should have to speak to him.”
“Of course I spoke to him. I was there to fight your battles for you. That’s why married ladies go to balls. You were quite right not to dance with him. A girl should always avoid any intimacy with such men as that. It is not that he would have done you any harm; but they stand in the way of your satisfaction and contentment. Balls are given specially for young ladies; and it is my theory that they are to make themselves happy while they are there, and not sacrifice themselves to men whom they don’t wish to know. You can’t always refuse when you’re asked, but you can always get out of an engagement afterwards if you know what you’re about. That was my way when I was a girl.” And this was the daughter of Mr. Comfort, whose somewhat melancholy discourses against the world’s pleasures and vanities had so often filled Rachel’s bosom with awe!

===Chinese===

“哦，没有的事，”雷切尔说，全然不知道该说什么。
“可我说——哦，是的；他还是个漂亮的体面人，又是位绅士——后一条，今晚在场的那一伙里我可挑不出第二个。格里格斯先生那里，我亲爱的，你可真是逃过了一劫！”
“是啊，是逃过了一劫。只是让您亲自出面去同他交涉，我心里实在过意不去。”
“我去同他交涉，那还用说。我上这儿来，就是替你打这场仗的。太太们出嫁了还来赴舞会，图的就是这个。你不肯同他跳，做得对极了。这样的男人，姑娘家一律要避得远远的，半点亲近也不能有。倒不是他能把你怎么样；是这号人横在道儿上，碍着你称心遂意。舞会本来就是专为年轻小姐们办的；照我的理论，她们去了就该快快活活，而不是把自己牺牲给那些她们根本不认识的男人。人家来约，你未必回回都拒绝得了；可只要你肚里有数，事后总有法子把这场约退掉。我做姑娘的时候，向来就是这么办的。”——而这位，正是康福特先生（Mr. Comfort）的女儿！她父亲那些郁郁寡欢的训诫，一遍遍声讨尘世的欢愉与虚妄，曾经多少回叫雷切尔听得满心敬畏！

===Original===

Rachel sat silent, thinking of what had occurred at Mrs. Tappitt’s; and thinking also that she ought to make some little speech to her friend, thanking her for all that she had done. Ought she not also to apologise in some way for her own conduct? “What was that between you and my cousin Walter?” Mrs. Cornbury asked, after a few moments.
“I hope I wasn’t to blame,” said Rachel. “But—”
“But what? Of course you weren’t to blame;—unless it was in being run after by so many gentlemen at once.”
“He was going to take me down to supper—and it was so kind of him. And then while we were waiting because the room downstairs was full, there was another quadrille, and I was engaged to Mr. Rowan.”
“Ah, yes; I understand. And so Master Walter got thrown once. His wrath in such matters never lasts very long. Here we are at Bragg’s End. I’ve been so glad to have you with me; and I hope I may take you again with me somewhere before long. Remember me kindly to your mother. There she is at the door waiting for you.” Then Rachel jumped out of the carriage, and ran across the little gravel-path into the house.

===Chinese===

雷切尔默默坐着，想着塔皮特家这一晚的种种；一面又想，她总该向这位朋友说几句体己话，谢她为自己费的这一切心。自己举止不当的地方，是不是也该赔个不是？“你同我堂弟沃尔特，方才是怎么一回事？”康伯里太太隔了一会儿问道。
“我希望错不在我，”雷切尔说。“可是——”
“可是什么？错当然不在你；——除非说，同时被那么多先生追着，这也算个错处。”
“他正要带我下楼去吃夜宴——他心眼儿多好。后来我们等着，因为楼下的屋子挤满了人，这时又排起一场四对舞，而我是约了罗恩先生的。”
“啊，是了；我明白了。这么说，咱们沃尔特少爷也吃了回瘪。这种事上他的火气从来长不了。瞧，布拉格斯恩德到了。今晚有你做伴，我高兴极了；巴望不多久再带你出门走走。替我亲亲热热地问候你母亲。喏，她正在门口等你呢。”雷切尔跳下马车，沿着那条小砾石路一路飞跑进了屋。

===Original===

Mrs. Ray had been waiting up for her daughter, and had been listening eagerly for the wheels of the carriage. It was not yet two o’clock, and by ball-going people the hour of Rachel’s return would have been considered early; but to Mrs. Ray anything after midnight was very late. She was not, however, angry, or even vexed, but simply pleased that her girl had at last come back to her. “Oh, mamma, I’m afraid it has been very hard upon you, waiting for me!” said Rachel; “but I did come away as soon as I could.” Mrs. Ray declared that she had not found it all hard, and then—with a laudable curiosity, seeing how little she had known about balls—desired to have an immediate account of Rachel’s doings.
“And did you get anybody to dance with you?” asked the mother, feeling a mother’s ambition that her daughter should have been “respectit like the lave.”
“Oh, yes; plenty of people asked me to dance.”
“And did you find it come easy?”

===Chinese===

雷太太（Mrs. Ray）一直守着不睡等她女儿，耳朵急切地捕捉着马车的轮声。还不到两点钟；在常赴舞会的人看来，雷切尔这个时辰回家要算早的；可对雷太太来说，午夜一过，多晚都嫌太晚。不过她并没有恼，连一丝愠意也没有，只有单纯的欢喜：她的姑娘终于回到她身边了。“哦，妈妈，这样等着，只怕把您熬苦了！”雷切尔说；“可我一能脱身就脱身了。”雷太太连声说不苦不苦，随即——她对舞会实在知之甚少，这份好奇倒也值得嘉许——便急着要雷切尔立刻把今晚的行止一五一十讲来。
“那么，有人请你跳舞吗？”母亲问，怀着做母亲的那份心气：巴望她的女儿也曾“同旁人一样受到敬重”（respectit like the lave，苏格兰旧谣语，意谓与众人同受礼遇）。
“哦，有的；请我跳舞的人多着呢。”
“你跳起来觉得不难吗？”

===Original===

“Quite easy. I was frightened about the waltzing, at first.”
“Do you mean that you waltzed, Rachel?”
“Yes, mamma. Everybody did it. Mrs. Cornbury said she always waltzed when she was a girl; and as the things turned out I could not help myself. I began with her cousin. I didn’t mean to do it, but I got so ashamed of myself that I couldn’t refuse.”
Mrs. Ray still was not angry; but she was surprised, and perhaps a little dismayed. “And did you like it?”

===Chinese===

“一点也不难。只是起先还怕华尔兹呢。”
“你是说你跳了华尔兹，雷切尔？”
“跳了，妈妈。人人都跳的。康伯里太太说她做姑娘的时候向来跳华尔兹；而且事情到了那步田地，由不得我。头一场就是同她堂弟跳的。我本没打算跳，可臊得没奈何，怎么也推辞不出口了。”
雷太太倒也没恼，只是吃了一惊，或许还有几分惶惑。“那你觉得跳得高兴吗？”

===Original===

“Yes, mamma.”
“Were they all kind to you?”
“Yes, mamma.”
“You seem to have very little to say about it; but I suppose you’re tired.”
“I am tired, but it isn’t that. It seems that there is so much to think about. I’ll tell you everything tomorrow, when I get quiet again. Not that there is much to tell.”
“Then I’ll wish you good night, dear.”

===Chinese===

“高兴，妈妈。”
“人家都待你好吗？”
“都好，妈妈。”
“这桩事你怎么话这么少；想来你是累了。”
“我是累了，可不为这个。只觉得心里要想的事太多。明天等我静下来，什么都讲给您听。倒也不是有多少可讲的。”
“那我就道晚安啦，亲爱的。”

===Original===

“Good night, mamma. Mrs. Cornbury was so kind—you can have no idea how good-natured she is.”
“She always was a good creature.”
“If I’d been her sister she couldn’t have done more for me. I feel as though I were really quite fond of her. But she isn’t a bit like what I expected. She chooses to have her own way; but then she is so good-humoured! And when I got into any little trouble she—”
“Well, what else did she do; and what trouble had you?”
“I can’t quite describe what I mean. She seemed to make so much of me;—just as she might have done if I’d been some grand young lady down from London, or any, any;—you know what I mean.”
Mrs. Ray sat with her candle in her hand, receiving great comfort from the knowledge that her daughter had been “respectit.” She knew well what Rachel meant, and reflected, with perhaps a pardonable pride, that she herself had “come of decent people.” The Tappitts were higher than her in the world, and so were the Griggses. But she knew that her forbears had been gentlefolk, when there were, so to speak, no Griggses and no Tappitts in existence. It was pleasant to her to think that her daughter had been treated as a lady.

===Chinese===

“晚安，妈妈。康伯里太太真是好——她心肠多好，您根本想不到。”
“她这个人从来就是心眼好的。”
“哪怕我是她的亲妹妹，她待我也不过如此了。我简直觉得真心喜欢她。可她跟我先前想的半点都不一样。她做事由着自己的性子；可脾气又是那么好！我碰上一点小麻烦的时候，她就——”
“喏，她还做了什么？你又遇上什么麻烦了？”
“我说不清楚我的意思。她好像那么抬举我；——就像我是从伦敦下来的哪位阔气小姐似的，或者随便什么，随便什么；——您明白我的意思。”
雷太太手里擎着蜡烛坐着，得知女儿到底“受到了敬重”，心里受用得很。雷切尔的意思她全明白，还暗自得意——这份得意或许也怪不得她——想到自己原是“正经人家出身”。塔皮特家的世面比她高，格里格斯家的也比她高。可她知道，她的先辈是缙绅人家——那时候，不妨这么说，世上还没有什么格里格斯家，也没有什么塔皮特家呢。想到女儿被人当作大家闺秀一样相待，她心里美滋滋的。

===Original===

“And she did do me such a kindness. That horrid Mr. Griggs was going to dance with me, and she wouldn’t let him.”
“I don’t like that young man at all.”
“Poor Cherry! you should hear her talk of him! And she would have stayed ever so much longer if I had not pressed her to go; and then she has such a nice way of saying things.”
“She always had that, when she was quite a young girl.”
“I declare I feel that I quite love her. And there was such a grand supper. Champagne!”
“No!”

===Chinese===

“她还真帮了我一个大忙。那个讨厌的格里格斯先生正要同我跳舞，她愣是不让。”
“那个年轻人，我一点也不喜欢。”
“可怜的彻丽！您真该听听她说起他来！要不是我一再催她走，她还不知要待到几时呢；再说她说话的样子也那么叫人受用。”
“她还是个小姑娘的时候，就有这份本事了。”
“说实话，我觉得我真有点爱她了。还有那夜宴，好气派。香槟！”
“不会吧！”

===Original===

“I got some cold turkey. Mr. Rowan took me down to supper.” These last words were spoken very mildly, and Rachel, as she uttered them, did not dare to look into her mother’s face.
“Did you dance with him?”
“Yes, mamma, three times. I should have stayed later only I was engaged to dance with him twice more; and I didn’t choose to do so.”
“Was he—? Did he—?”
“Oh, mamma; I can’t tell you. I don’t know how to tell you. I wish you knew it all without my saying anything. He says he shall come here tomorrow if I don’t go up to the brewery; and I can’t possibly go there now, after that.”

===Chinese===

“我还吃到了冷火鸡。罗恩先生带我下去吃的夜宴。”末了这半句说得轻之又轻，雷切尔说出的时候，连母亲的脸都不敢望。
“你同他跳舞了吗？”
“跳了，妈妈，三场。我本来还能多待些时候，只因他还约了我两场，我不愿意再跳了。”
“他是不是——？他有没有——？”
“哦，妈妈；我说不出口。我不知道该怎么跟您说。真巴不得我什么也不说，您就全都明白。他说我明天若不上酿酒厂去，他就到这儿来；可出了今晚这些事，我是断乎不能上那儿去了。”

===Original===

“Did he say anything more than that, Rachel?”
“He calls me Rachel, and speaks—I can’t tell you how he speaks. If you think it wrong, mamma, I won’t ever see him again.”
Mrs. Ray didn’t know whether she ought to think it wrong or not. She was inclined to wish that it was right and to believe that it was wrong. A few minutes ago Rachel was unable to open her mouth, and was anxious to escape to bed; but, now that the ice was broken between her and her mother, they sat up for more than an hour talking about Luke Rowan.
“I wonder whether he will really come?” Rachel said to herself, as she laid her head upon her pillow—“and why does he want to come?”

===Chinese===

“除了这些，他还说什么了吗，雷切尔？”
“他叫我雷切尔，说话的样子——我没法跟您形容他说话的样子。妈妈，您若觉得不对，我往后再也不见他了。”
雷太太拿不定主意，不知这事究竟该当对，还是该当错。她心里巴望着它是对的，却又相信它是错的。几分钟以前，雷切尔还张不开嘴，一心只想逃上床去；可如今她同母亲之间的冰既然破开，母女俩竟又多坐了一个多钟头，讲的全是卢克·罗恩。
“他真的会来吗？”雷切尔把头搁上枕头，暗自寻思——“他又为什么要来呢？”

## IX Mr. Prong at Home / IX 普朗先生在家

===Original===
Mrs. Tappitt’s ball was celebrated on a Tuesday, and on the preceding Monday Mrs. Prime moved herself off, bag and baggage, to Miss Pucker’s lodgings. Miss Pucker had been elated with a dismal joy when the proposition was first made to her. “Oh, yes; it was very dreadful. She would do anything;—of course she would give up the front bedroom upstairs to Mrs. Prime, and get a stretcher for herself in the little room behind, which looked out on the tiles of Griggs’ sugar warehouse. She hadn’t thought such a thing would have been possible; she really had not. A ball! Mrs. Prime couldn’t help coming away;—of course not. And there would be plenty of room for all her boxes in the small room behind the shop. Mrs. Ray’s daughter go to a ball!” And then some threatening words were said as to the destiny of wicked people, which shall not be repeated here.

That flitting had been a very dismal affair. An old man out of Baslehurst had come for Mrs. Prime’s things with a donkey-cart, and the old man, assisted by the girl, had carried them out together. Rachel had remained secluded in her mother’s room. The two sisters had met at the same table at breakfast, but had not spoken over their tea and bread and butter. As Rachel was taking the cloth away Mrs. Prime had asked her solemnly whether she still persisted in bringing perdition upon herself and her mother. “You have no right to ask me such a question,” Rachel had answered, and taking herself upstairs had secluded herself till the old man with the donkey, followed by Mrs. Prime, had taken himself away from Bragg’s End. Mrs. Ray, as her eldest daughter was leaving her, stood at the door of her house with her handkerchief to her eyes. “It makes me very unhappy, Dorothea; so it does.” “And it makes me very unhappy, too, mother. Perhaps my sorrow in the matter is deeper than yours. But I must do my duty.” Then the two widows kissed each other with a cold unloving kiss, and Mrs. Prime had taken her departure from Bragg’s End Cottage. “It will make a great difference in the housekeeping,” Mrs. Ray said to Rachel, and then she went to work at her little accounts.

It was Dorcas-day at Miss Pucker’s, and as the work of the meeting began soon after Mrs. Prime had unpacked her boxes in the front bedroom and had made her little domestic arrangements with her friend, that first day passed by without much tedium. Mrs. Prime was used to Miss Pucker, and was not therefore grievously troubled by the ways and habits of that lady, much as they were unlike those to which she had been accustomed at Bragg’s End; but on the next morning, as she was sitting with her companion after breakfast, an idea did come into her head that Miss Pucker would not be a pleasant companion for life. She would talk incessantly of the wickednesses of the cottage, and ask repeated questions about Rachel and the young man. Mrs. Prime was undoubtedly very angry with her mother, and much shocked at her sister, but she did not relish the outspoken sympathy of her confidential friend. “He’ll never marry her, you know. He don’t think of such a thing,” said Miss Pucker over and over again. Mrs. Prime did not find this pleasant when spoken of her sister. “And the young men I’m told goes on anyhow, as they pleases at them dances,” said Miss Pucker, who in the warmth of her intimacy forgot some of those little restrictions in speech with which she had burdened herself when first striving to acquire the friendship of Mrs. Prime. Before dinner was over Mrs. Prime had made up her mind that she must soon move her staff again, and establish herself somewhere in solitude.

===Chinese===
塔皮特太太（Mrs. Tappitt）的舞会定在星期二举行；就在此前的星期一，普赖姆太太（Mrs. Prime）连人带行李，搬进了帕克小姐（Miss Pucker）的寓所。这桩提议头一回向帕克小姐提出来的时候，她心头涌起的是一种阴郁的狂喜。“哦，可不是嘛；这事太不像话了。让她做什么都行；——楼上前头的卧室自然让给普赖姆太太，她自己到后面那间小屋里支一张行军床，那屋子正对着格里格斯先生（Mr. Griggs）糖仓的瓦顶。她原以为这样的事断无可能；真的，断无可能。跳舞会！普赖姆太太不能不躲出来；——自然躲。铺子后面那间小屋放她的箱子，绰绰有余。雷太太（Mrs. Ray）的女儿竟去跳舞！”接着还说了些恶人下场如何的狠话，此处便不复述了。

那一场搬家，实在凄惶。巴斯尔赫斯特（Baslehurst）来了个老头儿，赶着一辆毛驴车来拉普赖姆太太的什物，老头儿帮着那小丫头，两下一齐把东西抬了出去。雷切尔（Rachel）一直躲在母亲房里，没有露面。姐妹俩早饭时同桌而坐，对着各自的茶和面包黄油，却一句话也没讲。雷切尔收拾桌布的时候，普赖姆太太神色凛然地问她，是否还执意要把自己和母亲一并拖进沉沦。“你没有权利问我这样的问题，”雷切尔答道，说罢便上楼把自己关了起来，直到那赶驴的老头儿——后头跟着普赖姆太太——离开了布拉格斯恩德（Bragg’s End）。大女儿动身的时候，雷太太站在自家门口，手绢按着眼睛。“这叫我心里难受得很，多萝西娅（Dorothea）；实在难受。”“我也难受，妈妈。这件事上，我的伤心也许比你还深。可我必须尽我的本分。”随后两个寡妇彼此亲了亲，那一吻又冷又无情，普赖姆太太便辞别了布拉格斯恩德村舍。“家里的开销可要大变样了，”雷太太对雷切尔说；说罢便低头做她那本小小的家用账去了。

那天正赶上帕克小姐家里多卡斯缝纫会（Dorcas meeting）做活的日子；普赖姆太太在前卧室里拆完箱子、同她这位朋友把家内种种小安排料理停当之后不久，聚会的活计便开始了，因此头一天过得还不算怎么煎熬。帕克小姐这个人，普赖姆太太原是处惯了的，所以尽管这位小姐的脾性习惯同她在布拉格斯恩德过惯的一切大相径庭，倒也不觉得怎么苦不堪言；可到了第二天早晨，早饭后她同这位同伴对坐着的时候，一个念头当真浮上了心头：帕克小姐这个人，若要终身作伴，怕是不宜。她没完没了地念叨村舍里的种种罪过，翻来覆去地打听雷切尔和那个年轻男人的事。普赖姆太太对母亲确实动了真怒，对妹妹确实震惊万分，可这位知交朋友那种直露露的同情，她实在消受不了。“他绝不会娶她的，你是知道的。他压根儿没往这上头想，”帕克小姐一遍又一遍地说。这话安在她妹妹身上，普赖姆太太听着并不入耳。“还有那些年轻男人，我听说呀，在那种舞会上可不管不顾，爱怎么着就怎么着呢，”帕克小姐说；她一亲热过了头，倒把当初为了攀结普赖姆太太的交情而给自己套上的那些说话的小忌讳，忘掉了几分。还没等到午饭吃完，普赖姆太太已经拿定主意：用不了多久，她还得再挪一次窝，另寻一处清静地方独居安身。

===Original===
After tea she took herself out for a walk, having managed to decline Miss Pucker’s attendance, and as she walked she thought of Mr. Prong. Would it not be well for her to go to him and ask his further advice? He would tell her in what way she had better live. He would tell her also whether it was impossible that she should ever return to the cottage, for already her heart was becoming somewhat more soft than was its wont. And as she walked she met Mr. Prong himself, intent on his pastoral business. “I was thinking of coming to you tomorrow,” she said, after their first salutation was over.

“Do,” said he; “do; come early—before the toil of the day’s work commences. I also am specially anxious to see you. Will nine be too early—or, if you have not concluded your morning meal by that time, half-past nine?”

Mrs. Prime assured him that her morning meal was always concluded before nine o’clock, and promised to be with him by that hour. Then as she slowly paced up the High Street to the Cawston Bridge and back again, she wondered within herself as to the matter on which Mr. Prong could specially want to see her. He might probably desire to claim her services for some woman’s work in his sheepfold. He should have them willingly, for she had begun to feel that she would sooner cooperate with Mr. Prong than with Miss Pucker. As she returned down the High Street, and came near to her own door, she saw the cause of all her family troubles standing at the entrance to Griggs’s wine-store. He was talking to the shopman within, and as she passed she frowned grimly beneath her widow’s bonnet. “Send them to the brewery at once,” said Luke Rowan to the man. “They are wanted this evening.”

“I understand,” said the man.

“And tell your fellow to take them round to the back door.”

“All right,” said the man, winking with one eye. He understood very well that young Rowan was ordering the champagne for Mrs. Tappitt’s supper, and that it was thought desirable that Mr. Tappitt shouldn’t see the bottles going into the house.

===Chinese===
茶后她独自出门散步，总算推掉了帕克小姐的随伴；走着走着，她想起了普朗先生（Mr. Prong）。去他那里再讨一讨主意，岂不是好？他会告诉她，往后的日子该怎么过才好。他还会告诉她，她究竟还有没有可能重回村舍——因为她这颗心，已经开始比往常软和了些。走着走着，她迎面遇上了普朗先生本人，正专心致志地忙他的牧养事务。头一遍见礼过后，她开口道：“我正想着明天到你那儿去呢。”

“来吧，”他说；“来吧；早点来——赶在一天的劳碌开始之前。我自己也正急切地盼着见你。九点钟太早吗？——或者，倘若到那时你还没用完晨餐，那就九点半？”

普赖姆太太向他保证，她的晨餐向来在九点钟以前用毕，并答应那个时辰准到。随后她沿着大街慢慢踱过去，到考斯顿桥（Cawston Bridge）又踱回来，心里暗暗琢磨：普朗先生会有什么事，要专门见她呢。多半是想在他那片羊圈里觅一项妇女的差事，要征用她的劳役吧。那劳役他尽可取用，她甘心情愿，因为她已开始觉得，同普朗先生共事，总好过同帕克小姐共事。她顺着大街往回走，快到自己门口的时候，看见那桩搅得她全家不宁的事端的祸首，正站在格里格斯先生酒库的门口。他在同铺子里的伙计说话；她走过时，在寡妇帽的帽檐底下狠狠地皱了皱眉。“马上把这些送到酿酒厂去，”卢克·罗恩（Luke Rowan）对那伙计说，“今晚就要用。”

“明白了。”伙计说。

“再叫你们那伙计把它们从后门绕进去。”

“好嘞。”伙计说着，挤了挤一只眼睛。他心里透亮得很：小罗恩这是在为塔皮特太太的夜宴订香槟呢，而且大家都觉得，顶好别让塔皮特先生（Mr. Tappitt）瞧见这些瓶子搬进家门。

===Original===
Miss Pucker possessed at any rate the virtue of being early, so that Mrs. Prime had no difficulty in concluding her “morning meal,” and being at Mr. Prong’s house punctually at nine o’clock. Mr. Prong, it seemed, had not been quite so steadfast to his purpose, for his teapot was still upon the table, together with the debris of a large dish of shrimps, the eating of small shellfish being an innocent enjoyment to which he was much addicted.

“Dear me; so it is; just nine. We’ll have these things away in a minute. Mrs. Mudge; Mrs. Mudge!” Whereupon Mrs. Mudge came forth, and between the three the table was soon cleared. “I wish you hadn’t caught me so late,” said Mr. Prong; “it looks as though I hadn’t been thinking of you.” Then he picked up the stray shell of a shrimp, and in order that he might get rid of it, put it into his mouth. Mrs. Prime said she hoped she didn’t trouble him, and that of course she didn’t expect him to be thinking about her particularly. Then Mr. Prong looked at her in a way that was very particular out of the corner of his eyes, and assured her that he had been thinking of her all night. After that Mrs. Prime sat down on a horsehair-seated chair, and Mr. Prong sat on another opposite to her, leaning back, with his eyes nearly closed, and his hands folded upon his lap.

“I don’t think Miss Pucker’s will quite do for me,” said Mrs. Prime, beginning her story first.

===Chinese===
好在帕克小姐至少占着一条早起的美德，因此普赖姆太太不费什么事便用完了她的“晨餐”，九点整准时到了普朗先生家里。普朗先生呢，看来对自己定下的章程却坚守得不那么彻底，因为茶壶还在桌上，旁边还摊着一大盘海虾的残骸——吃这种小小的贝壳水族，是他沉溺已久的一种无害的享受。

“哎呀，可不是；正九点。这些物件马上就撤。玛奇太太（Mrs. Mudge）；玛奇太太！”玛奇太太应声而出，三个人一齐动手，桌子很快便收拾干净了。“真不愿意让你撞见我拖到这么晚，”普朗先生说，“瞧着倒像我心里没有想着你似的。”说着他拾起一片零落的虾壳，为把它打发掉，送进了嘴里。普赖姆太太说她但愿没有搅扰他，又说她当然不曾指望他特别把她挂在心上。这时普朗先生从眼角里用一种十分特别的看法端详了她一眼，向她保证：他整夜都在想她。这之后，普赖姆太太在一把马鬃椅面的椅子上坐了，普朗先生在她对面另一把上坐了，身子朝后一靠，眼睛几乎阖上，双手交叠在膝头。

“我看帕克小姐家那地方，不大合我的意，”普赖姆太太说，抢先头一个把事情说了。

===Original===
“I never thought it would, my friend,” said Mr. Prong, with his eyes still nearly closed.

“She’s a very good woman—an excellent woman, and her heart is full of love and charity. But—”

“I quite understand it, my friend. She is not in all things the companion you desire.”

“I am not quite sure that I shall want any companion.”

“Ah!” sighed Mr. Prong, shaking his head, but still keeping his eyes closed.

===Chinese===
“我从来就没觉得它会合你的意，我的朋友，”普朗先生说，眼睛依旧几乎阖着。

“她是位很好的女人——一位极好的女人，她的心满盛着爱与仁慈。可是——”

“我完全明白，我的朋友。她在事事上头，都不是你所愿望的那种同伴。”

“我说不准自己究竟还要不要什么同伴。”

“唉！”普朗先生叹了一声，摇了摇头，眼睛却依旧阖着。

===Original===
“I think I would rather be alone, if I do not return to them at the cottage. I would fain return if only they—”

“If only they would return too. Yes! That would be a glorious end to the struggle you have made, if you can bring them back with you from following after the Evil One! But you cannot return to them now, if you are to countenance by your presence dancings and love-makings in the open air,”—why worse in the open air than in a close little parlour in a back street, Mr. Prong did not say—“and loud revellings, and the absence of all good works, and rebellion against the Spirit.” Mr. Prong was becoming energetic in his language, and at one time had raised himself in his chair, and opened his eyes. But he closed them at once, and again fell back. “No, my friend,” said he, “no. It must not be so. They must be rescued from the burning; but not so—not so.” After that for a minute or two they both sat still in silence.

“I think I shall get two small rooms for myself in one of the quiet streets, near the new church,” said she.

===Chinese===
“我想我宁可一个人过，倘若我不能回村舍去同她们团聚。我何尝不愿回去，只可惜她们——”

“只可惜她们也肯回头就好了。是啊！倘若你能带着她们一同回来，不再跟随那恶者，你这一番苦斗便有了何等荣耀的收场！可你现在不能回到她们那里去，倘若你在场便是给露天的跳舞、谈情说爱撑腰壮势，”——为什么露天就比背街上一间密不通风的小客厅更坏，普朗先生没有说——“还有喧闹的狂欢宴乐，还有一切善工的荒废，还有对圣灵的悖逆。”普朗先生的话渐渐铿锵起来，有一阵子竟在椅子上挺起了身子，睁开了眼睛。但他随即又阖上，重新靠了回去。“不，我的朋友，”他说，“不行。断不可以这样。她们必须从火中给抢救出来；但不是这样——不是这样。”这以后，有一两分钟，两个人都静坐着，一言不发。

“我想我会在某一条清静的街上，新堂近旁，给自己租两间小屋住，”她说。

===Original===
“Ah, yes, perhaps so—for a time.”

“Till I may be able to go back to mother. It’s a sad thing families being divided, Mr. Prong.”

“Yes, it is sad;—unless it tends to the doing of the Lord’s work.”

“But I hope;—I do hope, that all this may be changed. Rachel I know is obstinate, but mother means well, Mr. Prong. She means to do her duty, if only she had good teaching near her.”

“I hope she may, I hope she may. I trust that they may both be brought to see the true light. We will wrestle for them—you and me. We will wrestle for them—together. Mrs. Prime, my friend, if you are prepared to hear me with attention, I have a proposition to make which I think you will acknowledge to be one of importance.” Then suddenly he sat bolt upright, opened his eyes wide, and dressed his mouth with all the solemn dignity of which he was the master. “Are you prepared to listen to me, Mrs. Prime?”

===Chinese===
“啊，是的，或许可以——住一个时期。”

“住到我能回母亲身边去的时候。骨肉离散总是一件伤心事，普朗先生。”

“是啊，是伤心；——除非这离散有助于主的事工。”

“可是我盼望；——我实在盼望，这一切终有改变的一日。雷切尔我知道是倔强的，可母亲的本意是好的，普朗先生。她是想尽她的本分的，只要她身边有好的教导。”

“但愿她能，但愿她能。我信她们两个都能被领到真光跟前。我们要为她们苦苦角力——你和我。我们要为她们一同角力。普赖姆太太，我的朋友，倘若你准备好专心听我说话，我有一个提议要提出来，我想你会承认这是个要紧的提议。”说罢他霍地端端正正坐直了，睁大眼睛，端整起嘴脸，摆出他最拿手的全部庄严气派。“你准备好听我说了吗，普赖姆太太？”

===Original===
Mrs. Prime, who was somewhat astonished, said in a low voice that she was prepared to listen.

“Because I must beg you to hear me out. I shall fail altogether in reaching your intelligence—whatever effect I might possibly have upon your heart—unless you will hear me to the end.”

“I will hear you certainly, Mr. Prong.”

“Yes, my friend, for it will be necessary. If I could convey to your mind all that is now passing through my own, without any spoken word, how glad should I be! The words of men, when taken at the best, how weak they are! They often tell a tale quite different from that which the creature means who uses them. Every minister has felt that in addressing his flock from the pulpit. I feel it myself sadly, but I never felt it so sadly as I do now.”

Mrs. Prime did not quite understand him, but she assured him again that she would give his words her best attention, and that she would endeavour to gather from them no other meaning than that which seemed to be his. “Ah—seemed!” said he. “There is so much of seeming in this deceitful world. But you will believe this of me, that whatever I do, I do as tending to the strengthening of my hands in the ministry.” Mrs. Prime said that she would believe so much; and then as she looked into her companion’s face, she became aware that there was something of weakness displayed in that assuming mouth. She did not argue about it within her own mind, but the fact had in some way become revealed to her.

===Chinese===
普赖姆太太有些诧异，低声说她准备好听了。

“因为我必须求你听我把话说完。除非你肯听到末了，我便全然不能把话送进你的悟性里去——至于它在你心上可能起什么效用，倒在其次。”

“我一定听你说完，普朗先生。”

“是的，我的朋友，因为这是必要的。倘若不经一句出口的话，我就能把我心里此刻翻腾着的一切统统传到你心里，我该多么高兴！人的言语，就算挑最好的来用，又是何等软弱！它们所讲的故事，往往同用它们的那个人心里所想的，全然是两回事。每一位牧师从讲坛上向他的羊群讲道时，都体味过这一点。我自己就痛切地体味着，却从来没有像现在这样痛切过。”

普赖姆太太没有完全听懂他的意思，但她再次向他保证，她一定悉心留意他的话，而且会竭力只从他的话里领会那似乎是他本意的意思，不作别解。“啊——似乎！”他说，“这个诡诈的世界里，‘似乎’可太多了！可这一层你要信我：凡我所作的事，都是为了坚固我手中的圣工事工。”普赖姆太太说这一层她信；随后她望着这位同伴的脸，忽然觉察出，那张端着架子的嘴里透着几分虚弱。她并没有在心里就此论辩什么，可这个事实不知怎么已经被她看破了。

===Original===
“My friend,” said he—and as he spoke he drew his chair across the rug, so as to bring it very near to that on which Mrs. Prime was sitting—“our destinies in this world, yours and mine, are in many things alike. We are both alone. We both of us have our hands full of work, and of work which in many respects is the same. We are devoted to the same cause: is it not so?” Mrs. Prime, who had been told that she was to listen and not to speak, did not at first make any answer. But she was pressed by a repetition of the question. “Is it not so, Mrs. Prime?”

“I can never make my work equal to that of a minister of the Gospel,” said she.

“But you can share the work of such a minister. You understand me now. And let me assure you of this; that in making this proposition to you, I am not self-seeking. It is not my own worldly comfort and happiness to which I am chiefly looking.”

“Ah,” said Mrs. Prime, “I suppose not.” Perhaps there was in her voice the slightest touch of soreness.

“No;—not chiefly to that. I want assistance, confidential intercourse, sympathy, a congenial mind, support when I am like to faint, counsel when I am pressing on, aid when the toil is too heavy for me, a kind word when the day’s work is over. And you—do you not desire the same? Are we not alike in that, and would it not be well that we should come together?” Mr. Prong as he spoke had put out his hand, and rested it on the table with the palm upwards, as though expecting that she would put hers within it; and he had tilted his chair so as to bring his body closer to hers, and had dropped from his face his assumed look of dignity. He was quite in earnest, and being so had fallen away into his natural dispositions of body.

===Chinese===
“我的朋友，”他说——说话间他把椅子拽过地毯，挪得同普赖姆太太坐的那把十分挨近——“你我在这尘世上的命数，在许多事上是相像的。我们都是孤身。我们两个都是手里堆满了工作，而且在许多方面是同样的工作。我们献身于同一个事业：岂不是这样吗？”普赖姆太太既已被告知只许听、不许说，起初便没有作答。可对方把问题又追问了一遍。“岂不是这样吗，普赖姆太太？”

“我的工作，是永远赶不上福音牧师的工作的，”她说。

“可你能分享这样一位牧师的工作。你现在明白我的意思了。并且让我向你保证这一点：我向你提这个提议，并非出于自私自利。我所主要注目的，并不是我自己属世的安逸与幸福。”

“啊，”普赖姆太太说，“想必不会。”她的话音里，或许带着一丝最轻微不过的酸涩。

“不；——主要不是为了那个。我要的是扶助，是推心置腹的交谈，是同情，是一个意气相投的心智；是我快要软弱的时候有扶持，我奋力向前的时候有谋划，劳苦过于我所能担的时候有相助，一日的工做完的时候有温言一句。而你——难道你不盼望同样的东西？在这一点上我们岂不一样？我们走到一处，岂不是好事？”普朗先生说话间伸出了手，手心朝上搁在桌上，仿佛指望她会把自己的手放进去；他还把椅子翘起来，好让身子凑得更近些，脸上那副装出来的庄重神气也撂下了。他这番意思十分当真，而且正因为当真，他的身子便落回了天然生就的姿态。

===Original===
“I do not quite understand you,” said Mrs. Prime. She did however understand him perfectly, but thought it expedient that he should be required to speak a little further before she answered him. She wanted time also to arrange her reply. As yet she had not made up her mind whether she would say yes or no.

“Mrs. Prime, I am offering to make you my wife. I have said nothing of love, of that human affection which one of God’s creatures entertains for another;—not, I can assure you, because I do not feel it, but because I think that you and I should be governed in our conduct by a sense of duty, rather than by the poor creature-longings of the heart.”

“The heart is very deceitful,” said Mrs. Prime.

“That is true—very true; but my heart, in this matter, is not deceitful. I entertain for you all that deep love which a man should feel for her who is to be the wife of his bosom.”

“But Mr. Prong—”

===Chinese===
“我不太明白你的意思，”普赖姆太太说。其实她把他懂得再透彻不过了，只是觉得还是先逼他再往下说几句、自己再作回答，才是上策。她也需要时间来安排自己的答话。到目前为止，她还没有拿定主意，这声“是”或“否”究竟怎么说。

“普赖姆太太，我是在向你求婚，要你做我的妻子。我一句也没有提到爱情，没有提到上帝的一个造物对另一个造物所怀的那种人间情爱；——我可以向你保证，这并不是因为我心中无此情，而是因为我认为，你我在行事上应当受责任感的支配，而不应当受心里那些可怜的造物私欲的支配。”

“心是极其诡诈的，”普赖姆太太说。

“这话不错——极不错；可我这颗心，在这件事上并不诡诈。我怀着对你的那一种深爱，是男人对本该做他怀中妻子的女人应当怀着的那一种深爱。”

“可是普朗先生——”

===Original===
“Let me finish before you give me your answer. I have thought much of this, as you may believe; and by only one consideration have I been made to doubt the propriety of taking this step. People will say that I am marrying you for—for your money, in short. It is an insinuation which would give me much pain, but I have resolved within my own mind, that it is my duty to bear it. If my motives are pure,”—here he paused a moment for a word or two of encouragement, but received none—“and if the thing itself be good, I ought not to be deterred by any fear of what the wicked may say. Do you not agree with me in that?”

Mrs. Prime still did not answer. She felt that any word of assent, though given by her to a minor proposition, might be taken as involving some amount of assent towards the major proposition. Mr. Prong had enjoyed the advantage of thinking over his matrimonial prospects in undisturbed solitude, but she had as yet possessed no such advantage. As the idea had never before presented itself to her, she did not feel inclined to commit herself hastily.

“And as regards money,” he continued.

“Well,” said Mrs. Prime, looking down demurely upon the ground, for Mr. Prong had not at once gone on to say what were his ideas about money.

===Chinese===
“且让我说完，你再答我。这件事我已想得很多，你尽可以相信；使我疑心这一步走得不当的，只有一种考虑。人们会说，我娶你是为着——简单说吧，为着你的钱。这种影射会叫我痛心，可我心里已经拿定主意：忍受它，正是我的本分。倘若我的动机是纯洁的，”——他停了一停，本想讨一两句勉励的话，却一句也没讨着——“倘若这件事本身是善的，我就不该被恶人的闲话吓退。这一点你难道不同意我吗？”

普赖姆太太依旧不答。她心里明白，任何一句首肯的话，哪怕她只是应承了一个次要命题，也可能被当作对主要命题的某种认可。普朗先生享有在清静的独居中细细盘算他婚姻前景的好处，她却至今不曾享有过这样的好处。这念头以前从没有在她心里出现过，她也就不愿草率地把话许出去。

“至于钱嘛，”他接着说。

“嗯。”普赖姆太太说，端端正正地垂目望着地面，因为普朗先生没有接着就说他关于钱的见解。

===Original===
“And as regards money—need I hardly declare that my motives are pure and disinterested? I am aware that in worldly affairs you are at present better off than I am. My professional income from the pew-rents is about a hundred and thirty pounds a year.”—It must be admitted that it was very hard work. By this time Mr. Prong had withdrawn his hand from the table, finding that attempt to be hopeless, and had resettled his chair upon its four feet. He had commenced by requesting Mrs. Prime to hear him patiently, but he had probably not calculated that she would have listened with a patience so cruel and unrelenting. She did not even speak a word when he communicated to her the amount of his income. “That is what I receive here,” he continued, “and you are probably aware that I have no private means of my own.”

“I didn’t know,” said Mrs. Prime.

“No; none. But what then?”

“Oh, dear no.”

“Money is but dross. Who feels that more strongly than you do?”

===Chinese===
“至于钱——还用得着我多加申明，说我的动机纯洁无私吗？我知道，在属世的境况上，你眼下比我宽裕。我从座位租金上得来的职业进项，一年约莫一百三十镑。”——必须承认，这可是桩十分费力的活儿。到这时，普朗先生已把那只手从桌上收了回去，认出那番指望纯属无望，又让椅子的四条腿重新落了地。他起先请求普赖姆太太耐心听他讲，恐怕却不曾料到，她会用这样一副冷酷无情、毫不松劲的耐心来听。他向她通报自己进项的数目时，她竟连一个字也没说。“这就是我在此地的进项，”他接着说，“你多半也知道，我自己并没有什么私产。”

“这我倒不知道。”普赖姆太太说。

“没有；一点也没有。可那又怎么样呢？”

“哦，不碍的，哪儿的话。”

“钱财不过是粪土。这一点上，谁的感受比你更真切呢？”

===Original===
Mr. Prong in all that he was saying intended to be honest, and in asserting that money was dross, he believed that he spoke his true mind. He thought also that he was passing a just eulogium on Mrs. Prime, in declaring that she was of the same opinion. But he was not quite correct in this, either as regarded himself, or as regarded her. He did not covet money, but he valued it very highly; and as for Mrs. Prime, she had an almost unbounded satisfaction in her own independence. She had, after all, but two hundred a year, out of which she gave very much in charity. But this giving in charity was her luxury. Fine raiment and dainty food tempted her not at all; but nevertheless she was not free from temptations, and did not perhaps always resist them. To be mistress of her money, and to superintend the gifts, not only of herself but of others; to be great among the poor, and esteemed as a personage in her district—that was her ambition. When Mr. Prong told her that money in her sight was dross, she merely shook her head. Why was it that she wrote those terribly caustic notes to the agent in Exeter if her quarterly payments were ever late by a single week? “Defend me from a lone widow,” the agent used to say, “and especially if she’s evangelical.” Mrs. Prime delighted in the sight of the bit of paper which conveyed to her the possession of her periodical wealth. To her money certainly was not dross, and I doubt if it was truly so regarded by Mr. Prong himself.

“Any arrangements that you choose as to settlements or the like of that, could of course be made.” Mr. Prong when he began, or rather when he made up his mind to begin, had determined that he would use all his best power of language in pressing his suit; but the work had been so hard that his fine language had got itself lost in the struggle. I doubt whether this made much difference with Mrs. Prime; or it may be, that he had sustained the propriety of his words as long as such propriety was needful and salutary to his purpose. Had he spoken of the “like of that” at the opening of the negotiation, he might have shocked his hearer; but now she was too deeply engaged in solid serious considerations to care much for the words which were used. “A hundred and thirty from pew-rents,” she said to herself, as he endeavoured, unsuccessfully, to look under her bonnet into her face.

“I think I have said it all now,” he continued. “If you will trust yourself into my keeping I will endeavour, with God’s assistance, to do my duty by you. I have said but little personally of myself or of my feelings, hoping that it might be unnecessary.”

===Chinese===
普朗先生这一番话，本意是要老老实实；他断言钱财是粪土，也自以为说的是真心话。他还以为，宣布普赖姆太太同有此见，是给了她一篇公允的颂词。可这一点他并不很正确——无论就他自己而言，还是就她而言。他不贪钱，却把钱看得极重；至于普赖姆太太，她从自身的独立自主里得到一种近乎无边的满足。说到底，她不过一年两百镑，其中拿出去行善的着实不少。可这散财行善，正是她的奢侈。华服珍馐对她全无诱惑；然而她并非全无诱惑，而且也许并不总能抵挡。做自己钱财的女主人，督导施赠——不但督导自己的，也督导别人的；在穷人中间做大人物，在本地一带被尊为一位要人——这才是她的抱负。普朗先生对她说钱在她眼里不过是粪土时，她只是摇了摇头。倘若埃克塞特（Exeter）那位代理人把她的季度款项迟误了一个星期，她那一封封措辞刻毒得怕人的短简，又是写给谁看的呢？“老天保佑我别碰上孤零零的寡妇，”那位代理人常这么说，“尤其是福音派的寡妇。”那张把定期进项送到她手里的小纸片，普赖姆太太一看见就满心欢喜。对她来说，钱财断断不是粪土；至于普朗先生自己是否当真如此看待，我也很表怀疑。

“至于财产授定（settlements）或诸如此类的安排，自然都可以照你选定的办法去办。”普朗先生起初——毋宁说他拿定主意开口的时候——原已下定决心，要说尽他最漂亮的语言来推进他的求婚；可这桩差事实在辛苦，他的漂亮话竟在挣扎中丢掉了。我很怀疑这在普赖姆太太身上有多大效验；也可能，凡在他的目的还用得着体面、且体面对他还有益的时候，他一直把话撑在了体面上。倘若在谈判开场就说出“诸如此类的名堂”这样的话，他也许会把听的人吓一跳；可眼下她正陷在实实在在的郑重考量里，顾不上计较用的字眼儿。“座位租金，一年一百三十镑，”她心里自忖；这时他正竭力想从她软帽底下窥望她的脸，却没有成功。

“我想我已经把话都说尽了，”他接着说，“你若肯把你信托在我的看顾之下，我必竭力——仰赖上帝的帮助——向你尽我的本分。我极少说到我个人的情形或我个人的情感，指望着这或许是用不着的。”

===Original===
“Oh, quite so,” said she.

“I have spoken rather of those duties which we should undertake together in sweet companionship, if you will consent to—to—to be Mrs. Prong, in short.” Then he waited for an answer.

As she sat in her widow’s weeds, there was not, to the eye, the promise in her of much sweet companionship. Her old crape bonnet had been lugged and battered about—not out of all shape, as hats and bonnets are sometimes battered by young ladies, in which guise, if the young ladies themselves be pretty, the battered hats and bonnets are often more becoming than ever they were in their proper shapes—but so as closely to fit her head, and almost hide her face. Her dress was so made, and so put on, as to give to her the appearance of almost greater age than her mother’s. She had studied to divest herself of all outward show of sweet companionship; but perhaps she was not the less, on that account, gratified to find that she had not altogether succeeded.

===Chinese===
“哦，正是这样。”她说。

“我说的主要是那些本分——倘若你肯答应——答应——总而言之，答应做普朗太太——我们本该在甜蜜的相伴中一同承担的本分。”说罢他便等着回答。

她坐在那里，一身寡妇装裹，单从外表看，她身上可瞧不出多少甜蜜相伴的指望。她那顶旧绉纱软帽，早已拉扯得破旧不堪——还没有破到全然不成形状，不像年轻小姐们有时把帽子软帽糟蹋的那个样子；那样的形状，倘若小姐本人长得俏，破帽子破软帽反倒比端端正正的本来形状更加好看——她的帽子只是贴着她的头箍得紧紧的，几乎把脸都遮没了。她那身衣裳的裁法和穿法，叫她看去几乎比她母亲的年纪还大。她已经刻意把甜蜜相伴的一切外表从自己身上剥除干净了；可或许正因如此，她发现自己终究没能全然成功，心里反倒不见得不欢喜。

===Original===
“I have done with the world, and all the world’s vanities and cares,” she said, shaking her head.

“No one can have done with the world as long as there is work in it for him or her to do. The monks and nuns tried that, and you know what they came to.”

“But I am a widow.”
