“那我就说有，”雷太太说，“多萝西娅，你这样说你妹妹、这样揣想她，心眼儿也忒坏了。”

“哦，很好。我看我还是马上回巴斯尔赫斯特（Baslehurst）去的好。”

“这么说，就是心眼儿坏了。这样的争吵我可爱不了；可我非得替她说句话不可。我相信他是个很好的年轻男人，身上半点坏处也没有，他高兴几时上这儿来，这儿都欢迎。至于雷切尔，我相信她懂得照管自己，不差似你在她那个年纪的时候；只不过那时候，可怜的普赖姆先生已经来过又走掉了。至于说他没有正经心意，他上这儿来，恰恰就为着这份正经心意，而且专门是来求我点头的。我起先没敢应承他，是因为雷切尔上农场取奶油去了，我想总得先问过她本人；倘若这还不算光明正大、合乎体统，那真不知道什么才算；何况他自己还有一份营生，明天就能养活起一个妻子！再者，倘若一个年轻男人自觉喜欢上了一个姑娘，还不许他来讨个允许去见她，那依我看，年轻人到底该怎么成亲，我是真不知道了。”说完，雷太太坐下来，拉起围裙蒙住眼睛，放声大哭了一场。

===Original===
It was a most eloquent speech, and I cannot say which of her daughters was the most surprised by it. As to Rachel, it must be remembered that very much was communicated to her of which she had hitherto known nothing. Very much indeed, we may say, so much that it was of a nature to alter the whole tone and tenor of her life. This young man of whom she had thought so much, and of whom she had been so much in dread—fearing that her many thoughts of him were becoming dangerous—this young man who had interested her so warmly, had come out to Bragg’s End simply to get her mother’s leave to pay his court to her. And he had done this without saying a word to herself! There was something in this infinitely sweeter to her than would have been any number of pretty speeches from himself. She had hitherto been angry with him, though liking him well; she had been angry with though almost loving him. She had not known why it was so, but the cause had been this—that he had seemed in their intercourse together, to have been deficient in that respect which she had a right to claim. But now all that sin was washed away by such a deed as this. As the meaning of her mother’s words sank into her heart, and as she came to understand her mother’s declaration that Luke Rowan should be welcome to the cottage as her lover, her eyes became full of tears, and the spirit of her animosity against her sister was quenched by the waters of her happiness.

And Mrs. Prime was almost equally surprised, but was by no means equally delighted. Had the whole thing fallen out in a different way, she would probably have looked on a marriage with Luke Rowan as good and salutary for her sister. At any rate, seeing that the world is as it is, and that all men cannot be hardworking ministers of the Gospel, nor all women the wives of such or their assistants in godly ministrations, she would not have taken upon herself to oppose such a marriage. But as it was, she had resolved that Luke Rowan was a black sheep; that he was pitch, not to be touched without defilement; that he was, in short, a man to be regarded by religious people as anathema—a thing accursed; and of that idea she was not able to divest herself suddenly. Why had the young man walked about under the churchyard elms at night? Why, if he were not wicked and abandoned, did he wear that jaunty look—that look which was so worldly? And, moreover, he went to balls, and tempted others to do the like! In a word, he was a young man manifestly of that class which was esteemed by Mrs. Prime more dangerous than roaring lions. It was not possible that she should give up her opinion merely because this roaring lion had come out to her mother with a plausible story. Upon her at that moment fell the necessity of forming a judgment to which it would be necessary that she should hereafter abide. She must either at once give in her adherence to the Rowan alliance; or else, if she opposed it, she must be prepared to cling to that opposition. She was aware that some such decision was now required, and paused for a moment before she declared herself. But that moment only strengthened her verdict against Rachel’s lover. Could any serious young man have taken off his hat with the flippancy which had marked that action on his part? Would not any serious young man, properly intent on matrimonial prospects, have been subdued at such a moment to a more solemn deportment? Mrs. Prime’s verdict was still against him, and that verdict she proceeded to pronounce.

“Oh, very well; then of course I shall interfere no further. I shouldn’t have thought that Rachel’s seeing him twice, in such a way as that, too—hiding under the churchyard trees!”

===Chinese===
这一篇话真个是雄辩滔滔，两个女儿哪一个更吃惊，我可说不准。至于雷切尔，必须记住，这番话让她知道了许许多多她此前一无所知的事情。的确多得很——多得足以改变她整个生活的调子和走向。这个年轻男人，她想了那么多，又怕了那么久——生怕自己想他想得多了，会闹出危险——这个让她心头暖烘烘挂念着的年轻男人，原来专程到布拉格斯恩德来，只为求得她母亲允许，好向她求爱。而且这一切，他竟不曾向她自己吐露半个字！这件事的甜美，多少句漂亮话也抵不上。她先前一直生他的气，虽则满喜欢他；她生着他的气，虽说几乎已经是爱他了。她自己也不知道怎么会这样，缘由却在这一点上：在他们平日的来往中间，他似乎缺少她有权要求的那份敬重。可如今，这样一桩举动把那个过犯洗刷得干干净净。母亲话里的意思一层层沉进她心里，她渐渐听懂了母亲的宣言——卢克·罗恩作为她的恋人，这座村舍随时欢迎——她的眼睛便蓄满了泪水，她对姐姐的满腔怨愤，也叫幸福的流水浇熄了。

普赖姆太太也几乎同样吃惊，却断没有同样欢喜。倘若整件事换一副样子发生，她多半会把同卢克·罗恩结亲看作对妹妹有益而合宜的事。无论如何，既然世界就是如今这个样子，既然男人不可能个个都做勤奋的福音传道者，女人也不可能个个都嫁这样的人，或在敬虔的圣工上做他们的助手，她原不至于挺身出来反对这样一桩婚事。可事情既已如此，她早已认定卢克·罗恩是一只害群之马；认定他是沥青，一碰便染污；认定总而言之，在敬虔的人眼里，他就是个应当视同受咒逐之物的男人——一件可憎可诅的东西；而这个成见，她没法一下子撇开。这个年轻人夜里干吗在教堂墓地的榆树底下转悠？他若不是邪恶放荡，干吗偏是那副扬扬得意的小样儿——那么一副世俗气？况且他还去跳舞，还勾引别人也去！一句话，他分明属于那一类年轻人——照普赖姆太太的估价，这一类比吼叫的狮子还要危险。她断不能因为这只吼叫的狮子跑到她母亲跟前编了一套入耳的说辞，就放弃自己的看法。这会儿落在她肩上的，是必须形成一个判断，而且日后必须守着这个判断过日子。她要么立刻归附罗恩这门姻亲；要么反对它，而一旦反对，就必须准备把这反对坚持到底。她明白，眼下正需要这样一项决断，于是顿了一顿，才宣告自己的立场。可这一顿，反倒把她对雷切尔恋人的否定判决钉得更牢。哪个严肃的年轻男人，脱帽会脱出他那样一副轻浮相？哪个真正存心图谋婚娶的严肃年轻人，到了这种时刻，不该收敛心神、举止愈发庄重？普赖姆太太的判决依旧于他不利，当下她便把这判决宣读出来。

“哦，很好；那我自然不再过问了。我只是想不到，雷切尔同他见了两次面，还是那样一种见法——躲在墓地的树底下！”

===Original===
“I wasn’t hiding,” said Rachel, “and you’ve no business to say so.” Her tears, however, prevented her from fighting her own battle manfully, or with her usual courage.

“It looked very much like it, Rachel, at any rate. I should have thought that mother would have wished you to have known a great deal more about any young man before she encouraged you to regard him in that way, than you can possibly know of Mr. Rowan.”

“But how are they to know each other, Dorothea, if they mustn’t see one another?” said Mrs. Ray.

“I have no doubt he knows how to dance very cleverly. As Rachel is being taught to live now, that may perhaps be the chief thing necessary.”

===Chinese===
“我没躲，”雷切尔说，“你不该这么说。”可眼泪妨住了她，叫她没法像样地为自己一搏，拿不出平日那点勇气。

“至少，雷切尔，那看上去实在很像躲。我原以为，妈妈总愿意你把任何一个年轻男人都了解得多多的，然后才鼓励你那样看待他；而这个了解的程度，你对罗恩先生是无论如何谈不上的。”

“可是多萝西娅，他们要是见面都不许，又怎么互相了解呢？”雷太太说。

“我毫不怀疑，他的舞跳得很漂亮。照雷切尔如今受的这种教养，这也许就是顶要紧的一条了。”

===Original===
This blow did reach poor Mrs. Ray, who a week or two since would certainly have agreed with her elder daughter in thinking that dancing was sinful. Into this difficulty, however, she had been brought by Mr. Comfort’s advice. “But what else can she know of him?” continued Mrs. Prime. “He is able to maintain a wife you say—and is that all that is necessary to consider in the choice of a husband, or is that the chief thing? Oh, mother, you should think of your responsibility at such a time as this. It may be very pleasant for Rachel to have this young man as her lover, very pleasant while it lasts. But what—what—what?” Then Mrs. Prime was so much oppressed by the black weight of her own thoughts, that she was unable further to express them.

“I do think about it,” said Mrs. Ray. “I think about it more than anything else.”

“And have you concluded that in this way you can best secure Rachel’s welfare? Oh, mother!”

“He always goes to church on Sundays,” said Rachel. “I don’t know why you are to make him out so bad.” This she said with her eyes fixed upon her mother, for it seemed to her that her mother was almost about to yield.

===Chinese===
这一击确实扎中了可怜的雷太太；搁在一两个星期以前，她准会站在大女儿一边，认定跳舞是罪过。然而把她带进这道两难境地的，偏偏是康福特先生（Mr. Comfort）的忠告。“可除此之外，她还能知道他什么呢？”普赖姆太太接着说，“你说他能养活妻子——难道挑女婿只消考虑这一条？还是说，这就是顶要紧的一条？哦，妈妈，到了这样的时刻，你该想想你的责任。雷切尔有这个年轻男人做恋人，也许很快活；趁它还没完的时候，很快活。可是往后呢——往后——往后？”说到这里，普赖姆太太叫自己那些阴沉念头的千斤重量压住了，再也没法把话头续下去。

“我是在想的，”雷太太说，“我想这个，比想什么都多。”

“那你断定了，这样做最能保住雷切尔的幸福？哦，妈妈！”

“他星期天向来上教堂，”雷切尔说，“我不明白你为什么偏要把他编排得那么坏。”她说这话时两眼直盯着母亲，因为她看出母亲眼看着就要撑不住了。

===Original===
A good deal might be said in excuse for Mrs. Prime. She was not only acting for the best in accordance with her own lights, but the doctrine which she now preached was the doctrine which had been held by the inhabitants of the cottage at Bragg’s End. The fault, if fault there was, had been in the teaching under which had lived both Mrs. Prime and her mother. In their desire to live in accordance with that teaching, they had agreed to regard all the outer world, that is all the world except their world, as wicked and dangerous. They had never conceived that in forming this judgment they were deficient in charity; nor, indeed, were they conscious that they had formed any such judgment. In works of charity they had striven to be abundant, but had taken simply the Dorcas view of that virtue. The younger and more energetic woman had become sour in her temper under the regime of this life, while the elder and weaker had retained her own sweetness partly because of her weakness. But who can say that either of them were other than good women—good according to such lights as had been lit for their guidance? But now the younger was stanch to her old lessons while the elder was leaving them. The elder was leaving them, not by force of her own reason, but under the necessity of coming in contact with the world which was brought upon her by the vitality and instincts of her younger child. This difficulty she had sought to master, once and forever, by a reference to her clergyman. What had been the result of that reference the reader already knows.

“Mother,” said Mrs. Prime, very solemnly, “is this young man such a one as you would have chosen for Rachel’s husband six months ago?”

“I never wished to choose any man for her husband,” said Mrs. Ray. “I don’t think you ought to talk to me in that way, Dorothea.”

===Chinese===
替普赖姆太太辩解的话，原可以说上许多。她不只是按自己那点见识尽力而为；她此刻宣讲的教义，也正是布拉格斯恩德村舍里的住户向来奉行的教义。要说有过错——如果算过错的话——那过错在于普赖姆太太和她母亲一向所受的教导。她们一心要照那教导生活，便一商量定：凡外部世界——也就是她们那个世界以外的一切世界——都是邪恶而危险的。她们从来不曾想到，下这样的判断有亏仁爱；说实在的，她们也没意识到自己下过什么这样的判断。在慈善的善工上，她们曾勉力求其丰足，只是对这项美德，她们只取多卡斯会那一种看法。年轻些、精力旺些的那个女人，在这种生活的规制下脾性变得酸刻了；年长些、软弱些的那个，倒还保有自己的甜润，一部分恰恰因为她软弱。可谁又能说她们两个不是好女人呢——按着为指引她们而点亮的那些灯烛来说，是好的？只是如今，年轻的一个还死守着旧日的教训，年长的一个却正在离开它们。年长者离开那些教训，并非出于自己理智的力量，而是她那个年幼孩子的蓬勃生气与天性，逼得她不得不与外部世界打交道。这个难题，她本想求教于她的牧师，一劳永逸地解决掉。求教的结果如何，读者已经知道了。

“妈妈，”普赖姆太太板着极严肃的面孔说，“六个月以前，你会替雷切尔挑中这样一个人做丈夫吗？”

“我从没想过替她挑什么丈夫，”雷太太说，“多萝西娅，我不觉得你该这样同我说话。”

===Original===
“I don’t know in what other way to talk to you. I cannot be indifferent on such a subject as this. When you tell me, and that before Rachel herself, that you have given this young man leave to come and see her whenever he pleases.”

“I never said anything of the kind, Dorothea.”

“Did you not, mother? I am sure I understood you so.”

“I said he had come to ask leave, and that I should be glad to see him when he did come, but I didn’t say anything of having told him so. I didn’t tell him anything of the kind; did I, Rachel? But I know he will come, and I don’t see why he shouldn’t. And if he does, I can’t turn him out. He took his tea here quite like a steady young man. He drank three large cups; and if, as Rachel says, he always goes to church regularly, I don’t know why we are to judge him and say that he’s anything out of the way.”

===Chinese===
“我不知道还能怎么同你说。这样的事情，我没法不当一回事。你竟对我说出这样的话——还当着雷切尔本人的面——说你已经准了这个年轻男人，他高兴几时来见她，就几时来见她。”

“我从来没那么说过，多萝西娅。”

“没说过吗，妈妈？我分明是这样听懂的。”

“我说的是，他来讨过允许，等他当真来的时候我会乐意见他；可我没说过我已经答应他了。那种话我一个字也没对他讲过；对不对，雷切尔？不过我知道他会来的，我也看不出他为什么不该来。他要是来了，我总不能把人撵出去。他在这儿喝茶，十足像个稳重年轻人的样子。他喝了三大杯；再说，照雷切尔的说法，他一向按时上教堂，那我就不明白，我们凭什么还要评判他，说他有什么出格的地方。”

===Original===
“I have not judged him, mother.”

Then Rachel spoke out, and we may say that it was needful that she should do so. This offering of her heart had been discussed in her presence in a manner that had been very painful to her, though the persons discussing it had been her own mother and her own sister. But in truth she had been so much affected by what had been said, there had been so much in it that was first joyful and then painful to her, that she had not hitherto been able to repress her emotions so as to acquire the power of much speech. But she had struggled, and now so far succeeded as to be able to come to her mother’s support.

“I don’t know, mamma, why anybody should judge him yet; and as to what he has said to me, I’m sure no one has a right to judge him unkindly. Dolly has been very angry with me because she saw me speaking to him in the churchyard, and has said that I was—hiding.”

===Chinese===
“我没有评判他，妈妈。”

这时雷切尔开了口，我们可以说，她非开口不可。她这颗心的奉献之物，竟在她本人面前被人这般议论，叫她心里苦得很，尽管议论的人是她自己的母亲和自己的姐姐。说实在的，方才那些话给她触动太深，里头先叫她欢喜、继又叫她痛苦的东西太多，她一直没能把情绪压下去，聚起说许多话的力气。可她一直在挣扎，如今总算挣扎到了能来给母亲助阵的地步。

“妈妈，我不明白眼下有什么人就该评判他；至于他对我说过什么，我敢说谁也没有权利刻薄地评判他。多莉同我大发脾气，就因为她看见我在墓地里同他说话，还说我是在——躲。”

===Original===
“I meant that he was hiding.”

“Neither of us were hiding, and it was an unkind word, not like a sister. I have never had to hide from anybody. And as for—for—for liking Mr. Rowan after such words as that, I will not say anything about it to anybody, except to mamma. If he were to ask me to be—his wife, I don’t know what answer I should make—not yet. But I shall never listen to anyone while mamma lives, if she wishes me not.” Then she turned to her mother, and Mrs. Ray, who had before been driven to doubt by Mrs. Prime’s words, now again became strong in her resolution to cherish Rachel’s lover.

“I don’t believe she’ll ever do anything to make me think that I oughtn’t to have trusted her,” said Mrs. Ray, embracing Rachel and speaking with her own eyes full of tears.

===Chinese===
“我指的是他在躲。”

“我们俩谁也没躲，那是个刻薄字眼，不像姐姐说的。我从来用不着躲什么人。至于——至于——至于经过那样的话之后还喜不喜欢罗恩先生，这事我谁也不说，只说给妈妈听。他倘若真要开口求我——做他的妻子，我不知道自己会怎么回答——至少如今还不知道。可是只要妈妈在世一天，她不愿意，我就绝不听任何人的。”说罢她转向母亲；方才被普赖姆太太的话说得动摇起来的雷太太，此刻又坚定了疼爱雷切尔恋人的决心。

“我不信她会做出什么事来，叫我觉得自己原不该信她，”雷太太搂着雷切尔说，说话时自己也满眼是泪。

===Original===
It now seemed to Mrs. Prime that there was nothing left for her but to go. In her eagerness about her sister’s affairs, she had for a while forgotten her own; and now, as she again remembered the cause that had brought her on the present occasion to Bragg’s End, she felt that she must return without accomplishing her object. After having said so much in reprobation of her sister’s love-affair, it was hardly possible that she should tell the tale of her own. And yet her need was urgent. She had pledged herself to give Mr. Prong an answer on Friday, and she could hardly bring herself to accept that gentleman’s offer without first communicating with her mother on the subject. Any such communication at the present moment was quite out of the question.

“Perhaps it would be better that I should go and leave you,” she said. “If I can do no good, I certainly don’t want to do any harm. I wish that Rachel would have taken to what I think a better course of life.”

“Why, what have I done?” said Rachel, turning round sharply.

===Chinese===
到这地步，普赖姆太太觉得除了走，再没有别的路了。她方才只顾操心妹妹的事，一时间把自己的事忘了；如今重新想起此番来布拉格斯恩德的缘由，她感到自己这趟怕要白跑，目的达不成了。把妹妹的恋爱事情数落了这么多之后，再讲自己的那一段，几乎是不可能的事。可她的需要又是急迫的。她已经应下普朗先生，星期五给他答复；不经事先同母亲商量，她几乎下不了决心接受那位先生的求婚。而眼下这种时刻，什么商量都根本无从谈起。

“或许我走了、撇下你们更好，”她说，“我既然帮不上忙，自然也不想帮倒忙。只可惜雷切尔不肯走那条依我看更好的路子。”

“咦，我做什么了？”雷切尔猛地扭转身来。

===Original===
“I mean about the Dorcas meetings.”

“I don’t like the women there;—that’s why I haven’t gone.”

“I believe them to be good, praiseworthy, godly women. But it is useless to talk about that now. Good night, Rachel,” and she gave her hand coldly to her sister. “Good night, mother; I wish I could see you alone tomorrow.”

“Come here for your dinner,” said Mrs. Ray.

===Chinese===
“我说的是多卡斯缝纫会（Dorcas meetings）的事。”

“那儿那几个女人我不喜欢；——所以我才不去。”

“我相信她们都是善良、可嘉、敬虔的女人。可这话如今说也无用。晚安，雷切尔，”说着，她冷冷地把手伸给妹妹。“晚安，妈妈；但愿明天能同你单独见一面。”

“上这儿来吃饭吧，”雷太太说。

===Original===
“No;—but if you would come to me in the morning I should take it kindly.” This Mrs. Ray promised to do, and then Mrs. Prime walked back to Baslehurst.

Rachel, when her sister was gone, felt that there was much to be said between her and her mother. Mrs. Ray herself was so inconsequent in her mental workings, so shandy-pated if I may say so, that it did not occur to her that an entirely new view of Luke Rowan’s purposes had been exposed to Rachel during this visit of Mrs. Prime’s, or that anything had been said, which made a further explanation necessary. She had, as it were, authorized Rachel to regard Rowan as her lover, and yet was not aware that she had done so. But Rachel had remembered every word. She had resolved that she would permit herself to form no special intimacy with Luke Rowan without her mother’s leave; but she was also beginning to resolve that with her mother’s leave, such intimacy would be very pleasant. Of this she was quite sure within her own heart—that it should not be abandoned at her sister’s instigation.

“Mamma,” she said, “I did not know that he had spoken to you in that way.”

===Chinese===
“不；——不过你早上要是肯到我这儿来，我会领情的。”雷太太应承下来，普赖姆太太便步行回巴斯尔赫斯特去了。

姐姐走后，雷切尔觉得，她同母亲之间有许多话要说。雷太太自己心思的运转本是这般没个连贯——恕我斗胆说一句，一副“项狄式”的没头绪头脑——她压根儿没想到，普赖姆太太这一趟来访，已把卢克·罗恩心意的全新一面露给了雷切尔；也没想到有什么话已经出口，非再解释一番不可。可以说，她已授权雷切尔把罗恩当作恋人看待，自己却不知道已经这么做了。可雷切尔把每个字都记下了。她已拿定主意：没有母亲的许可，决不容自己同卢克·罗恩缔结什么特别的亲密；可她也渐渐拿定另一个主意：有了母亲的许可，这样的亲密将是非常甜美的。有一点她心里十分确定：这事决不能在姐姐的撺掇下半途扔掉。

“妈妈，”她说，“我不知道他曾那样同你提过。”

===Original===
“In what way, Rachel?” Mrs. Ray’s voice was not quite pleasant. Now that Mrs. Prime was gone, she would have been glad to have had the dangerous subject abandoned for a while.

“That he had asked you to let him come here, and that he had said that about me.”

“He did then—while you were away at Mrs. Sturt’s.”

“And what answer did you give him?”

===Chinese===
“怎么个提法，雷切尔？”雷太太的声气不太自在。普赖姆太太既已走掉，她正巴不得把这个危险话题搁开一会儿。

“说他求过你让他上这儿来，还说了那些关于我的话。”

“他是提过的——你上斯特特太太（Mrs. Sturt）家去的那一会儿。”

“那你给了他什么回答？”

===Original===
“I didn’t give him any answer. You came back, and I’m sure I was very glad that you did, for I shouldn’t have known what to say to him.”

“But what was it that he did say, mamma?—that is, if you don’t think it wrong to tell me.”

“I hardly know; but I don’t suppose it can be wrong, for no young man could have spoken nicer; and it made me happy to hear him—so it did, for the moment.”

“Oh, mamma, do tell me!” and Rachel kneeled down before her.

===Chinese===
“我什么回答也没给他。你就回来了；说真的，你回来我高兴得很，要不然我真不知道该同他说什么。”

“可他到底说了什么呀，妈妈？——就是说，你若不觉得告诉我是做错了的话。”

“我说不大上来；不过我想，这总归错不了，因为再没有哪个年轻男人能说得那么中听；听他那么说，我心里欢喜——真个欢喜，就在那一刻。”

“哦，妈妈，快告诉我吧！”雷切尔说着，在她面前跪了下去。

===Original===
“Well;—he said you were the nicest girl he had ever seen.”

“Did he, mamma?” And the girl clung closer to her mother as she heard the pleasant words.

“But I oughtn’t to tell you such nonsense as that; and then he said that he wanted to come out here and see you, and—and—and—; it is simply this, that he meant to ask you to be his sweetheart, if I would let him.”

“And what did you say, mamma?”

===Chinese===
“好；——他说你是他平生见过的顶标致的姑娘。”

“他真这么说，妈妈？”听着这句甜话，姑娘把母亲偎得更紧了。

“可这样的傻话，我本不该学给你听；后来他说，他想上这儿来见你，还——还——还——；说穿了就是这么回事：他要请你做他的心上人，只消我肯点头。”

“那你怎么说，妈妈？”

===Original===
“I couldn’t say anything because you came back.”

“But you told Dolly that you would be glad to see him whenever he might choose to come here.”

“Did I?”

“Yes; you said he was welcome to come whenever he pleased, and that you believed him to be a very good young man.”

===Chinese===
“我什么也没能说，因为你回来了。”

“可你对多莉说过，他几时高兴上这儿来，你都乐意见他。”

“我说过吗？”

“说过；你说他高兴几时来都欢迎，还说你信他是个很好的年轻男人。”

===Original===
“And so I do. Why should he be anything else?”

“I don’t say that he’s anything else; but, mamma—”

“Well, my dear.”

“What shall I say to him if he does ask me that question? He has called me by my name two or three times, and spoken to me as though he wanted me to like him. If he does say anything to me like that, what shall I answer?”

===Chinese===
“我如今也这么信。他又能是什么别的样子呢？”

“我没说他是什么别的样子；可是，妈妈——”

“怎么，我的乖。”

“他倘若当真问我那句话，我该对他怎么说？他已经两三回叫起我的名字来了，同我说话的那口气，就像巴望我喜欢他似的。他倘若真同我说出那样的话来，我怎么回答？”

===Original===
“If you think you don’t like him well enough, you must tell him so, of course.”

“Yes, of course I must.” Then Rachel was silent for a minute or two. She had not as yet received the full answer which she desired. In such an alternative as that which her mother had suggested, we may say that she would have known how to frame her answer to the young man without any advice from her mother. But there was another alternative as to which she thought it well that she should have her mother’s judgment and opinion. “But, mamma, I think I do like him,” said Rachel, burying her face.

“I’m sure I don’t wonder at it,” said Mrs. Ray, “for I like him very much. He has a way with him so much nicer than most of the young men now; and then, he’s very well off, which, after all, must count for something. A young woman should never fall in love with a man who can’t earn his bread, not if he was ever so religious or steady. And he’s very good-looking, too. Good looks are only skin-deep I know, and they won’t bring much comfort when sorrow comes; but I do own I love to look on a young fellow with a sonsy face and a quick lively step. Mr. Comfort seemed to think it would do very well if there was to be any such thing; and if he’s not able to tell, I’m sure I don’t know who ought to be. And nothing could be fairer than his coming out here and telling me first. There’s so many of them are sly; but there was nothing sly about that.”

In this way, with many more rambling words, with many kisses also, and with some tears, Rachel Ray received from her mother permission to regard Luke Rowan as her lover.

===Chinese===
“你倘若觉得喜欢他喜欢得还不够，那自然得这么告诉他。”

“是的，那自然得这么说。”随后雷切尔沉默了一两分钟。她想要的那句囫囵回答，还没有得到。像母亲方才提示的那种局面，可以说，不必母亲指点，她也知道该怎么给那年轻人措辞回话。可还有另一种局面，她觉得最好先听听母亲的判断和意见。“可是妈妈，我想我是喜欢他的，”雷切尔说着，把脸埋了起来。

“我一点儿也不奇怪，”雷太太说，“因为我就很喜欢他。他那派头，比眼下大多数年轻男人中看得多；再说，他家境又宽裕，这终究是要算数的。年轻姑娘决不该爱上一个挣不来面包的男人，哪怕他再敬虔再稳重也不行。还有，他相貌又好。我知道，好相貌不过一层皮，愁苦来的时候它带不来多少安慰；可我认账，我就是爱看一个小伙子脸膛红润喜人、脚步轻快利落。康福特先生好像也觉得，倘若真有那么一回事，倒也满好；他要是都看不准，我看天下就没人看得准了。再说，他先上这儿来对我说明白，天下再没有比这更光明正大的了。如今这班年轻人，鬼鬼祟祟的太多；这一桩里头，可半点鬼祟也没有。”

就这样，又是许多东拉西扯的话，又是无数亲吻，还添了几滴眼泪，雷切尔·雷从母亲手里得到了许可，可以把卢克·罗恩当作自己的恋人了。

## XIII Mr. Tappitt in His Countinghouse / XIII 塔皮特先生在账房

===Original===
Luke Rowan, when he left the cottage, walked quickly back across the green towards Baslehurst. He had sauntered out slowly on his road from the brewery to Bragg’s End, being in doubt as to what he would do when he reached his destination; but there was no longer room for doubt now; he had said that to Rachel’s mother which made any further doubt impossible, and he was resolved that he would ask Rachel to be his wife. He had spoken to Mrs. Ray of his intention in that respect as though he thought that such an offer on his part might probably be rejected, and in so speaking had at the time spoken the truth; but he was eager, sanguine, and self-confident by nature, and though he was by no means disposed to regard himself as a conquering hero by whom any young lady would only be too happy to find herself beloved, he did not at the present moment look forward to his future fate with despair. He walked quickly home along the dusty road, picturing to himself a happy prosperous future in Baslehurst, with Rachel as his wife, and the Tappitts living in some neighbouring villa on an income paid to old Tappitt by him out of the proceeds of the brewery. That was his present solution of the brewery difficulty. Tappitt was growing old, and it might be quite as well not only for himself, but for the cause of humanity in Devonshire, that he should pass the remainder of his life in that dignity which comfortable retirement from business affords. He did not desire Tappitt for a partner any more than Tappitt desired him. Nevertheless he was determined to brew beer, and was anxious to do so if possible on the spot where his great-uncle Bungall had commenced operations in that line.

It may be well to explain here that Rowan was not without good standing-ground in his dispute with Tappitt. Old Bungall’s will had somewhat confused matters, as it is in the nature of wills to do; but it had been Bungall’s desire that his full share in the brewery should go to his nephew after his widow’s death, should he on dying leave a widow. Now it had happened that he had left a widow, and that the widow had contrived to live longer than the nephew. She had drawn an income of five hundred a year from the concern, by agreement between her and her lawyer and Tappitt and his lawyer; and Tappitt, when the elder Rowan, Bungall’s nephew, died, had taught himself to believe that all the affairs of the brewery must now remain forever in his own hands, unless he himself might choose to make other provision. He knew that some property in the concern would pass away from him when the old lady died, but he had not acknowledged to himself that young Rowan would inherit from his father all the rights which old Rowan would have possessed had he lived. Luke’s father had gone into other walks of life, and had lived prosperously, leaving behind him money for his widow, and money also for his children; and Tappitt, when he found that there was a young man with a claim to a partnership in his business, had been not only much annoyed, but surprised also. He had been, as we have seen, persuaded to hold out the right hand of friendship, and the left hand of the partnership to the young man. He had thought that he might manage a young man from London who knew nothing of beer; and his wife had thought that the young man might probably like to take a wife as well as an income out of the concern; but, as we have seen, they had both been wrong in their hopes. Luke chose to manage the brewery instead of being managed; and had foolishly fallen in love with Rachel Ray instead of taking Augusta Tappitt to himself as he should have done.

There was much certainly of harshness and cruelty in that idea of an opposition brewery in Baslehurst to be established in enmity to Bungall and Tappitt, and to be so established with Bungall’s money, and by Bungall’s heir. But Luke, as he walked back to Baslehurst, thinking now of his beer and now of his love, declared to himself that he wanted only his own. Let Tappitt deal justly with him in that matter of the partnership, and he would deal even generously with Tappitt. The concern gave an income of some fifteen hundred pounds, out of which Mrs. Bungall, as taking no share of the responsibility or work, had been allowed to have a third. He was informed by his lawyer that he was entitled to claim one-half of the whole concern. If Tappitt would give in his adhesion to that villa arrangement, he should still have his thousand a year for life, and Mrs. Tappitt afterwards should have due provision, and the girls should have all that could fairly be claimed for them. Or, if the villa scheme could not be carried out quite at present, he, Rowan, would do two shares of the work, and allow Tappitt to take two shares of the pay; but then, in that case, he must be allowed scope for his improvements. Good beer should be brewed for the people of Baslehurst, and the eyes of Devonshire should be opened. Pondering over all this, and resolving that he would speak out his mind openly to Rachel on the morrow, Luke Rowan reached his inn.

===Chinese===
罗恩离开村舍后，快步穿过绿地，朝巴斯尔赫斯特走回去。来时他从酿酒厂一路信步慢行到布拉格斯恩德，心里正拿不定到了地方该做什么；如今却再没有迟疑的余地了；他已把那番话对雷切尔的母亲说出口，从此怀疑再无容身之地，他拿定主意要请雷切尔做他的妻子。他同雷太太谈起自己这番打算时，口气象是自觉这样一桩求婚多半会遭拒绝，说的时候也确是实情；但他天性热切、乐观、自信，虽然绝没有把自己看作常胜英雄的意思——仿佛哪位小姐得他垂爱便该喜出望外——此刻展望前程，却也并不绝望。他沿着尘土飞扬的大路快步往回走，一路给自己描画着巴斯尔赫斯特幸福兴旺的前景：雷切尔做他的妻子，塔皮特一家住到左近某幢小洋房里，靠他从酿酒厂收益中拨给老塔皮特的进项过活。这便是他眼下对酿酒厂难题的解法。塔皮特上了年纪，让他去安享脱身实业、舒适引退所给予人的那份体面，把余生这么打发了去，不但对他自己好，就是对德文郡的人道事业，多半也是桩好事。他不愿要塔皮特做合伙人，恰如塔皮特不愿要他。但他打定主意要酿啤酒，而且只要可能，就偏要在他的叔祖邦格尔当年开创这门营生的那块地方来酿。

在此不妨交代一句：罗恩在同塔皮特这场争执中，并非没有站得住脚的立足点。老邦格尔的遗嘱把事情搅得有些含混，遗嘱素来有此本性；但邦格尔的心愿是：他若身后留下寡妻，他在酿酒厂的全部股份，应于寡妻故去之后归他的侄儿。事有凑巧，他果然留下了一位寡妻，而这位寡妻又设法活得比侄儿长久。经她同她的律师、塔皮特同他的律师几方议定，她每年从这份产业中支取五百镑收益。及至老罗恩——邦格尔的那位侄儿——去世，塔皮特便让自己相信：从此以后，酿酒厂的一切事务必得永远握在他一人手中，除非他自己情愿另作安排。他知道老太太故去之后，产业中有若干权益会从他手里流走，却从不肯对自己承认：小罗恩将从他父亲名下继承老罗恩若活在世上所应有的全部权利。卢克的父亲后来转入了别的行当，日子过得兴旺，身后留给遗孀一笔钱财，也给儿女们留了钱财；塔皮特发现竟有个年轻人对他的买卖提出了合伙的权利要求，不但大为恼火，而且吃惊非小。我们已经看到，他被人劝动，向这年轻人伸出友谊的右手，和合伙的左手。他满以为，一个对啤酒一窍不通的伦敦小伙子，总归由他摆布；他老婆则满以为，这年轻人多半既乐意从这份产业里领一份进项，也乐意从这份产业里娶个老婆；然而我们已经看到，他们俩的指望全落了空。卢克偏要自己掌管酿酒厂，而不肯受人掌管；还傻乎乎地爱上了雷切尔·雷，而不曾像他分内该做的那样，把奥古斯塔·塔皮特娶到手上。

在巴斯尔赫斯特另开一家唱对台的酿酒厂，存心同邦格尔和塔皮特作对，而且用的是邦格尔的钱、出自邦格尔的继承人之手——这个主意里头，确实颇有些刻薄狠辣的成分。可卢克走回巴斯尔赫斯特的一路，一会儿想着他的啤酒，一会儿想着他的爱情，只对自己宣称：他要的不过是他自己名下的一份。只要塔皮特在合伙那件事上待他公正，他待塔皮特甚至可以慷慨。这份产业一年出一千五百镑上下的收益，邦格尔太太既不分担责任、又不出力做工，历来被让着分走其中三分之一。他的律师告诉他，他有权要求整份产业的一半。倘若塔皮特肯依从那幢小洋房的安排，他仍旧终身保有每年一千镑，日后塔皮特太太自当有妥帖的着落，几位小姐也尽可以拿到凡可为她们正当地要求的一切。或者，倘若那洋房的方案眼下还不能全然实行，他罗恩可以做两份的工，让塔皮特领两份的钱；只是那样的话，就必须容他施展他的种种改良。要为巴斯尔赫斯特的百姓酿出好啤酒，要让德文郡睁开眼睛。卢克·罗恩把这一切在心里盘算已定，又拿定主意明天要把心事向雷切尔和盘托出，说话间已到了他下榻的旅店。

===Original===
“There’s a lady, sir, upstairs, as wishes to speak to you,” said the waiter.

“A lady?”

“Quite elderly, sir,” said the waiter, intending to put an end to any excitement on Rowan’s part.

“It’s the gentleman’s own mother,” said the chambermaid, in a tone of reproof, “and she’s in number two sitting-room, private.” So Luke went to number two sitting-room, private, and there he found his mother waiting for him.

“This is very sad,” she said, when their first greetings were over.

“About old Tappitt? yes, it is; but what could I do, mother? He’s a stupid old man, and pigheaded. He would quarrel with me, so that I was obliged to leave the house. If you and Mary like to come into lodgings while you stay here, I can get rooms for you.”

===Chinese===
“楼上有一位女客，先生，说要同您说话，”侍者说。

“一位女客？”

“年纪相当大了，先生，”侍者说，存心要熄一熄罗恩心头的激动。

“是这位先生自己的母亲，”女侍带着数落的口气说，“在二号客厅里等着呢，单间。”于是卢克去了二号单间客厅，在那里见到母亲正等着他。

“这可真让人难过，”头一阵见面的寒暄过后，她说。

“是老塔皮特的事吧？是啊，是让人难过；可叫我有什么法子呢，妈妈？他是个又蠢又犟的老头儿。他非跟我吵不可，我只好离开那所房子。你同玛丽要是愿意在此小住期间另赁住处，我可以替你们租到房间。”

===Original===
But Mrs. Rowan explained that she herself did not wish to come to any absolute or immediate rupture with Mrs. Tappitt. Of course their visit would be shortened, but Mrs. Tappitt was disposed to be very civil, as were the girls. Then Mrs. Rowan suggested whether there might not be a reconciliation between Luke and the brewery family.

“But, mother, I have not quarrelled with the family.”

“It comes to the same thing, Luke; does it not? Don’t you think you could say something civil to Mr. Tappitt, so as to—to bring him round again? He’s older than you are, you know, Luke.”

Rowan perceived at once that his mother was ranging herself on the Tappitt side in the contest, and was therefore ready to fight with so much the more vigour. He was accustomed to yield to his mother in all little things, Mrs. Rowan being a woman who liked such yieldings; but for some time past he had held his own against her in all greater matters. Now and again, for an hour or so, she would show that she was vexed; but her admiration for him was so genuine, and her love so strong, that this vexation never endured, and Luke had been taught to think that his judgment was to be held supreme in all their joint concerns. “Yes, mother, he is older than I am; but I do not know that I can say anything particularly civil to him—that is, more civil than what I have said. The civility which he wants is the surrender of my rights. I can’t be so civil as that.”

===Chinese===
可罗恩太太解释说，她本人并不想同塔皮特太太闹到彻底破裂、立时翻脸的地步。做客的日子当然要缩短，但塔皮特太太尚且相当客气，几位小姐也是如此。随后罗恩太太便暗示：卢克同酿酒厂这一家人之间，是不是还可以言归于好。

“可是，妈妈，我并没有同这一家人吵翻呀。”

“那还不是一回事吗，卢克？你说是不是？你就不能对塔皮特先生说句客气话，好——好把他再劝转回来？他年纪比你大，你是知道的，卢克。”

罗恩立刻看出，在这场较量里，他母亲是把自己归到塔皮特一边去了，于是准备着斗争得格外来劲。琐事上他向来顺从母亲，罗恩太太是个喜欢人家这样顺从的女人；但一段时日以来，凡遇大事，他在她面前寸步不让。她偶尔也会恼上个小时把；可她对他的仰慕那么真，对他的爱那么深，恼意从来长久不了，卢克从小便被教得认定：凡他们母子共同的事务，一概以他的判断为至上。“是的，妈妈，他是比我年纪大；可我不知道还能对他说出什么格外客气的话来——我是说，比我已经说过的更客气的话。他要的那份客气，是要我交出自己的权利。那样的客气，我做不来。”

===Original===
“No, Luke, I should be the last to ask you to surrender any of your rights; you must be sure of that. But—oh, Luke, if what I hear is true I shall be so unhappy!”

“And what have you heard, mother?”

“I am afraid all this is not about the brewery altogether.”

“But it is about the brewery altogether;—about that and about nothing else to any smallest extent. I don’t at all know what you mean.”

“Luke, is there no young lady in the case?”

===Chinese===
“不，卢克，我断不会去求你交出自己的任何权利；这一点你只管放心。可是——哦，卢克，倘若我听来的话是真的，我可要伤心透了！”

“您都听见什么了，妈妈？”

“我怕这一切并不全是酿酒厂的事。”

“可它就全都出在酿酒厂上；——只出在它身上，别的丝毫不沾边。我全然不明白您是什么意思。”

“卢克，这里头就没有年轻小姐的事吗？”

===Original===
“Young lady! in what case;—in the case of my quarrel with old Tappitt;—whether he and I have had a difference about a young lady?”

“No, Luke; you know I don’t mean that.”

“But what do you mean, mother?”

“I’m afraid that you know too well. Is there not a young lady whom you’ve met at Mrs. Tappitt’s, and whom you—you pretend to admire?”

“And suppose there is—for the sake of the argument—what has that to do with my difference with Mr. Tappitt?” As Rowan asked this question some slight conception of the truth flashed across his mind; some faint idea came home to him of the connecting link between his admiration for Rachel Ray and Mr. Tappitt’s animosity.

===Chinese===
“年轻小姐！什么事里头；——在我同老塔皮特吵架这件事里头；——问他同我是不是为一位年轻小姐闹过别扭？”

“不，卢克；你知道我不是那个意思。”

“那您是什么意思，妈妈？”

“我怕你心里明白得很。你在塔皮特太太家不是结识了一位年轻小姐，你还——你还假装倾慕于她？”

“就算有这么一位——姑且这样假设——这同我同塔皮特先生的争执又有什么相干？”罗恩问出这句话的时候，一点真情的微光从他心头闪过；他隐隐约约头一回意识到，他对雷切尔·雷的爱慕同塔皮特先生的敌意之间，原有一环相扣。

===Original===
“But is it so, Luke?” asked the anxious mother. “I care much more about that than I do about all the brewery put together. Nothing would make me so wretched as to see you make a marriage that was beneath you.”

“I don’t think I shall ever make you wretched in that way.”

“And you tell me that there is nothing in this that I have heard;—nothing at all.”

“No, by heavens!—I tell you no such thing. I do not know what you may have heard. That you have heard falsehood and calumny I guess by your speaking of a marriage that would be beneath me. But, as you think it right to ask me, I will not deceive you by any subterfuge. It is my purpose to ask a girl here in Baslehurst to be my wife.”

“Then you have not asked her yet.”

===Chinese===
“可真是这样吗，卢克？”忧心的母亲问道。“比起整个酿酒厂加在一起，这事更叫我挂心。眼看你要结一门配不上你的亲事，天底下没有什么比这更叫我难受的了。”

“我想我不至于那样叫你难受。”

“那你是告诉我，我听来的这些话里头什么都没有；——一点儿也没有。”

“不，老天在上！——我可没那么说。我不知道您听来的是什么。您听来的是谰言和诽谤——您说出一门配不上我的亲事这种话，我就猜到了。不过，您既然认为该问我，我就不打半句遁词欺瞒您。我打算请巴斯尔赫斯特这儿的一位姑娘做我的妻子。”

“这么说，你还没有向她开口喽。”

===Original===
“You are cross-examining me very closely, mother. If I have not asked her I am bound to do so; not that any binding is necessary—for without being bound I certainly should do so.”

“And it is Miss Ray?”

“Yes, it is Miss Ray.”

“Oh, Luke, then indeed I shall be very wretched.”

“Why so, mother? Have you heard anything against her?”

===Chinese===
“您盘问得可真紧，妈妈。我倘若还没有开口，那我是一定要开的；倒不是非有这层约束不可——因为不加约束，我也断然要开的。”

“是雷小姐？”

“是的，是雷小姐。”

“哦，卢克，那我当真要难受极了。”

“为什么呢，妈妈？您听说了她的什么不是吗？”

===Original===
“Against her! well; I will not say that, for I do not wish to say anything against any young woman. But do you know who she is, Luke; and who her mother is? They are quite poor people.”

“And is that against them?”

“Not against their moral character certainly, but it is against them in considering the expediency of a connection with them. You would hardly wish to marry out of your own station. I am told that the mother lives in a little cottage, quite in a humble sphere, and that the sister—”

“I intend to marry neither the mother nor the sister; but Rachel Ray I do intend to marry—if she will have me. If I had been left to myself I should not have told you of this till I had found myself to be successful; as you have asked me I have not liked to deceive you. But, mother, do not speak against her if you can say nothing worse of her than that she is poor.”

===Chinese===
“说她的不是！这个嘛，我不说，因为我无意说任何年轻姑娘的不是。可你知道她是谁吗，卢克？她母亲又是谁？他们是相当穷苦的人家。”

“穷也算他们的一条不是吗？”

“论品德自然算不得不是，可是掂量同他们结亲是否相宜，这总归是一项不利。你总不见得愿意婚事越出自己的阶层吧。我听说那做母亲的住在一所小村舍里，境地十分寒微，还有那位姐姐——”

“做母亲的也好，做姐姐的也好，我都无意娶；雷切尔·雷我却是一定要娶的——只要她肯要我。若是随我自己，我原不会对你说起这些，除非事已办成；既是你问我，我便不愿骗你。可是，妈妈，你若说不出她比穷更坏的短处，就请不要说她的坏话。”

===Original===
“You misunderstand me, Luke.”

“I hope so. I do not like to think that that objection should be made by you.”

“Of course it is an objection, but it is not the one which I meant to make. There may be many a young lady whom it would be quite fitting that you should wish to marry even though she had not got a shilling. It would be much pleasanter of course that the lady should have something, though I should never think of making any serious objection about that. But what I should chiefly look to would be the young lady herself, and her position in life.”

“The young lady herself would certainly be the main thing,” said Luke.

===Chinese===
“你误会我了，卢克。”

“但愿如此。我不愿意想，这样的反对话会出自我母亲之口。”

“穷自然是一层障碍，但不是我预备提的那一条。许许多多年轻姑娘，哪怕身边没有一个先令，你想娶也尽可以名正言顺。姑娘手里有点财产，自然更好，可我从不打算拿这个正儿八经地反对什么。但我主要要看的是姑娘本人，和她置身其中的生活地位。”

“姑娘本人当然是最要紧的，”卢克说。

===Original===
“That’s what I say;—the young lady herself and her position in life. Have you made any inquiries?”

“Yes, I have;—and am almost ashamed of myself for doing so.”

“I have no doubt Mrs. Ray is very respectable, but the sort of people who are her friends are not your friends. Their most particular friends are the farmer’s family that lives near them.”

“How was it then that Mrs. Cornbury took her to the party?”

“Ah, yes; I can explain that. And Mrs. Tappitt has told me how sorry she is that people should have been deceived by what has occurred.” Luke Rowan’s brow grew black as Mrs. Tappitt’s name was mentioned, but he said nothing and his mother continued her speech. “Her girls have been very kind to Miss Ray, inviting her to walk with them and all that sort of thing, because of her being so much alone without any companions of her own.”

“Oh, that has been it, has it? I thought she had the farmer’s family out near where she lived.”

===Chinese===
“我就是这么说嘛；——姑娘本人，和她置身其中的生活地位。你打听过没有？”

“打听过；——而且几乎为自己打听这桩事害臊。”

“雷太太想必很可敬，这我不怀疑，可是她那些朋友那路人，可不是你的朋友。他们顶要好的朋友，就是住在他们近旁的那个农场主人家。”

“那康伯里太太怎么会带她去那次聚会呢？”

“啊，是啊；这个我能解释。塔皮特太太还同我说，出了这样的事，人家受了蒙蔽，她心里多么过意不去。”一提起塔皮特太太的名字，卢克·罗恩的眉头便阴沉下来，可他没作声，母亲继续说道。“她家几位小姐待雷小姐很好，请她同她们一道散步，诸如此类，只因她孤零零的，身边一个自家的同伴也没有。”

“哦，原来是这么回事，是不是？我还当有那个农场主家住在她左近呢。”

===Original===
“If you choose to listen to me, Luke, I shall be obliged to you, but if you take me up at every word in that way, of course I must leave you.” Then she paused, but as Luke said nothing she went on with her discourse. “It was in that way that she came to know the Miss Tappitts, and then one of them, the youngest I think, asked her to come to the party. It was very indiscreet; but Mrs. Tappitt did not like to go back from her daughter’s word, and so the girl was allowed to come.”

“And to make the blunder pass off easily, Mrs. Cornbury was induced to take her?”

“Mrs. Cornbury happened to be staying with her father, in whose parish they had lived for many years, and it certainly was very kind of her. But it has been an unfortunate mistake altogether. The poor girl has for a moment been lifted out of her proper sphere, and—as you must have seen yourself—hardly knew how to behave herself. It made Mrs. Tappitt very unhappy.”

===Chinese===
“你若肯听我说，卢克，我便领你的情；你若句句都这样同我抬杠，那我自然只好走开了。”说着她停了停，但卢克一言不发，她便接着她的宏论往下讲。“她就是这样结识塔皮特家小姐们的，后来她们里头的一位——我记得是最小的——请她来赴那次聚会。这事很不检点；可塔皮特太太不愿收回女儿说出口的话，便让那姑娘来了。”

“为了让这桩错举圆混过去，又请动了康伯里太太带她去？”

“康伯里太太恰好在她父亲那里小住——他们一家在他的堂区住了多年——她那样做，心肠自然是极好的。可这整个儿是一桩不幸的错举。那可怜的姑娘一时被捧出了她本来的位置，而且——你自己想必也看见了——简直不知道举手投足该是什么样子。这叫塔皮特太太难受极了。”

===Original===
This was more than Luke Rowan was able to bear. His anger was not against his own mother, but against the mistress of the brewery. It was manifest that she had been maligning Rachel, and instigating his mother to take up the cudgels against her. And he was vexed also that his mother had not perceived that Rachel held, or was entitled to hold, among women a much higher position than could be fairly accorded to Mrs. Tappitt. “I do not care one straw for Mrs. Tappitt’s unhappiness,” he said; “and as to Miss Ray’s conduct at her house, I do not think that there was anything in it that did not become her. I do not know what you mean, the least in the world; and I think you would have no such idea yourself, if Mrs. Tappitt had not put it into your head.”

“You should not speak in that way to your mother, Luke.”

“I must speak strongly when I am defending my wife—as I hope she will be. I never heard of anything in my life so little as this woman’s conduct! It is mean, paltry jealousy, and nothing else. You, as my mother, may think it better that I should not marry.”

===Chinese===
这话卢克·罗恩再忍不下去了。他的怒气不是冲着自己母亲，是冲着酿酒厂那位女主人。明摆着，她一直在败坏雷切尔的名声，还撺掇他母亲出头同雷切尔作对。他心里也恼，恼自己的母亲竟不曾看出：雷切尔在女人当中的地位，无论她已经实际居有的，还是她理当居有的，都远在塔皮特太太公平应得的那一等之上。“塔皮特太太难受不难受，我一个草芥也不在乎；”他说，“至于雷小姐在她府上的举止，我看没有一样有失她自己身份的地方。你的意思我一点儿也不懂；而且我相信，倘若不是塔皮特太太把这套念头塞进你脑子里，你自己决计不会有这样的想法。”

“你不该这样同你母亲说话，卢克。”

“我在回护我妻子的时候——我希望她将成为我的妻子——就不能不说得重。这个人行事之卑小，我生平闻所未闻！那不过是下流、卑贱的嫉妒，别的什么都不是。你作为我母亲，或许觉得我不结婚倒好。”

===Original===
“But, my dear, I want you to marry.”

“Then I will do as you want. Or you may think that I should find someone with money, or with grand friends, or with a better connection. It is natural that you should think like this. But why should she want to belittle a young girl like Rachel Ray—a girl that her own daughters call their friend? I’ll tell you why, mother. Because Rachel Ray was admired and they were not.”

“Is there anybody in Baslehurst that will say that she is your equal?”

“I am not disposed to ask anyone in Baslehurst just at present; and I would not advise anyone in Baslehurst to volunteer an opinion to me on the subject. I intend that she shall be my equal—my equal in every respect, if I can make her so. I shall certainly ask her to be my wife; and, mother, as my mind is positively made up on that point—as nothing on earth will alter me—I hope you will teach yourself to think kindly of her. I should be very unhappy if my house could not be your home when you may choose to make it so.”

===Chinese===
“可是，我亲爱的，我要你结婚呀。”

“那我就照你的意思办。再不，你或许觉得我该找个有钱的，或者有显赫朋友的，或者亲家门第更体面的。你这样想也是自然。可她何苦要贬低雷切尔·雷这样一个姑娘——一个连她亲女儿都认作朋友的姑娘？我告诉你为什么，妈妈。因为雷切尔·雷招人爱慕，而她们招不到。”

“巴斯尔赫斯特可有谁肯说她配得上你？”

“眼下我不打算去问巴斯尔赫斯特的什么人；也劝巴斯尔赫斯特的什么人，休要自告奋勇跑来对我发这一套议论。我的打算是让她做我的对等之人——各方面都对等，只要我做得到。我必定要请她做我的妻子；而且，妈妈，这一层我的心意已经断然拿定——天底下什么也改变不了我——我希望你学会善待她。往后你愿意的时候，我的家若不能作你的家，我会非常难过。”

===Original===
But Mrs. Rowan, much as she was accustomed to yield to her son, could not bring herself to yield in this matter—or, at least, not to yield with grace. She felt that the truth and wisdom all lay on her side in the argument, though she knew that she had lacked words in which to carry it on. She declared to herself that she was not at all inclined to despise anybody for living in a small cottage, or for being poor. She would have been delighted to be very civil to Mrs. Ray herself, and could have patronized Rachel quite as kindly, though perhaps not so graciously, as Mrs. Cornbury had done. But it was a different thing when her son came to think of making this young woman his wife! Old Mrs. Cornbury would have been very sorry to see either of her sons make such an alliance. When anything so serious as marriage was to be considered, it was only proper to remember that Mrs. Ray lived in a cottage, and that farmer Sturt was her friend and neighbour. But to all this prudence and wisdom Luke would not listen at all, and at last Mrs. Rowan left him in dudgeon. Foolish and hasty as he was, he could, as she felt, talk better than she could; and therefore she retreated, feeling that she had been worsted. “I have done my duty,” said she, going away. “I have warned you. Of course you are your own master and can do as you please.” Then she left him, refusing his escort, and in the last fading light of the long summer evening, made her way back to the brewery.

Luke’s first impulse was to start off instantly to the cottage, and settle the matter out of hand; but before he had taken up his hat for this purpose he remembered that he could not very well call at Bragg’s End on such a mission at eleven o’clock at night; so he threw himself back on the hotel sofa, and gave vent to his feelings against the Tappitt family. He would make them understand that they were not going to master him. He had come down there disposed to do them all manner of kindness—to the extent even of greatly improving their fortunes by improving the brewing business—and they had taken upon themselves to treat him as though he were a dependent. He did not tell himself that a plot had been made to catch him for one of the girls; but he accused them of jealousy, meanness, selfishness, and all those sins and abominations by which such a plot would be engendered. When, about an hour afterwards, he took himself off to bed, he was full of wrath, and determined to display his wrath early on the morrow. As he prayed for forgiveness on condition that he forgave others, his conscience troubled him; but he gulped it down, and went on with his angry feelings till sleep came upon him.

But in the morning some of this bitterness had worn away. His last resolve overnight had been to go to the brewery before breakfast, at which period of the day Mr. Tappitt was always to be found for half an hour in his countinghouse, and curtly tell the brewer that all further negotiations between them must be made by their respective lawyers; but as he was dressing, he reflected that Mr. Tappitt’s position was certainly one of difficulty, that amicable arrangements would still be best if amicable arrangements were possible, and that something was due to the man who had for so many years been his uncle’s partner. Mr. Tappitt, moreover, was not responsible for any of those evil things which had been said about Rachel by Mrs. Tappitt. Therefore, priding himself somewhat on his charity, he entered Mr. Tappitt’s office without the display of any anger on his face.

===Chinese===
可罗恩太太尽管素来百依百顺地让着儿子，这件事上却怎么也不能叫自己依从下来——至少，不能体体面面地依从。她觉得这场道理里，真理与明智全在自己一边，虽然她也知道自己辩起来词不达意。她对自己申明：她断断没有因为人家住小村舍、因为人家穷，就看不起谁的意思。雷太太本人她原乐意客客气气相待，雷切尔她也满可以抬举得同康伯里太太一样和气，只是兴许没有那样优雅。可轮到她儿子想着娶这个年轻女人做太太，那便是另一回事了！老康伯里太太（old Mrs. Cornbury）倘若看见自家两个儿子里哪一个结下这样一门姻亲，也会难过万分。凡是议到婚姻这样的大事，合该记着雷太太住的是村舍，农场主斯特特是她的朋友近邻，这才是正理。可这番审慎与明智，卢克压根儿听不进去，末了罗恩太太怏怏而去。他又蠢又急躁，可她感觉得到，论舌战他比她强；于是她退了这一阵，自觉败下风来。“我尽了本分，”她临走说道。“话也提醒到了。你自然是你自己的主子，爱怎样便怎样。”随后她离开了他，不肯让他相送，趁着漫长夏日傍晚最后那一点渐黯的余光，独自取道回酿酒厂去。

卢克头一个冲动是立刻动身去村舍，把事情当场了断；可还没及伸手拿帽子，他便想起夜里十一点钟为着这样一桩使命去敲布拉格斯恩德的门，总归不像话；于是他往旅店的沙发上一仰，把一腔对塔皮特家的怨气尽情倾泻出来。他要让他们明白：他们休想拿捏他。他到这镇上来，原存心要对他们行各样好处——甚至不惜改良酿造的营生，好叫他们的家业大大兴旺——他们倒竟敢拿他当个仰人鼻息的食客看待。他倒不曾对自己说，这家人设了圈套要捉他做自家姑娘的女婿；但他指责他们嫉妒、卑鄙、自私，指责他们犯下种种足以孕生这类圈套的罪愆与丑行。约莫一个钟头后，他自去就寝，满腔怒火，决意明晨一早便把怒火亮出来。他照着饶恕人的条件祷告求饶恕，良心这时搅得他不安；可他把这不安全咽了下去，带着满腔怒气，直到睡意压上来。

到了早晨，这股苦味已消磨掉几分。他昨夜最后的决意是：趁早饭前去酿酒厂——每天这个时辰，塔皮特先生总有半个钟头待在账房里——冷冷地丢一句话给这位酿酒商：往后他们之间一切交涉，各凭各的律师去办；可他穿衣裳的时候转念想道，塔皮特先生的处境确实作难，和平安排若属可能，和平安排终究最好；况且那人做了他叔祖多年的合伙人，总该得他几分情面。何况，雷切尔那些恶话出自塔皮特太太之口，账不能记到塔皮特先生头上。于是他多少为自己的宽厚自得，走进塔皮特先生的账房，脸上不带一丝怒气。

===Original===
The brewer was standing with his back to the empty fireplace, with his hands behind the tails of his coat, and his eyes fixed upon a letter which he had just read, and which lay open upon his desk. Rowan advanced with his hand out, and Tappitt, hesitating a little as he obeyed the summons, put out his own and just touched that of his visitor; then hastily he resumed his position, with his arm behind his coattail.

“I have come down,” said Rowan, “because I thought it might be well to have a little chat with you before breakfast.”

The letter which lay open on the desk was from Rowan’s lawyer in London, and contained that offer on Rowan’s part of a thousand a year and retirement, to which Luke still looked as the most comfortable termination of all their difficulties. Luke had almost forgotten that he had, ten days since, absolutely instructed his lawyer to make the offer; but there was the offer made, and lying on Tappitt’s table. Tappitt had been considering it for the last five minutes, and every additional moment had added to the enmity which he felt against Rowan. Rowan, at twenty-five, no doubt regarded Tappitt, who was nearer sixty than fifty, as a very old man; but men of fifty-five do not like to be so regarded, and are not anxious to be laid upon shelves by their juniors. And, moreover, where was Tappitt to find his security for the thousand a year—as he had not failed to remark to himself on his first glance over the lawyer’s letter. Buy him out, indeed, and lay him on one side! He hated Rowan with all his heart;—and his hatred was much more bitter in its nature than that which Rowan was capable of feeling for him. He remembered the champagne; he remembered the young man’s busy calling for things in his own house; he remembered the sneers against the beer, and the want of respect with which his experience in the craft had been treated. Buy him out! No; not as long as he had a five-pound note to spend, or a leg to stand upon. He was strong in his resolution now, and capable of strength, for Mrs. Tappitt was also on his side. Mrs. Rowan had not quite kept her secret as to what had transpired at the inn, and Mrs. Tappitt was certain that Rachel Ray had succeeded. When Tappitt declared that morning that he would fight it out to the last, Mrs. T. applauded his courage.

===Chinese===
那酿酒商背朝空壁炉立着，两手拢在衣裾后头，两眼盯住一封刚读完的信，信摊开着，搁在写字台上。罗恩伸着手走上前去，塔皮特应着这只招呼的手，迟疑了一下，把自己那只伸出来，只在来客的手上轻轻一碰；随即慌忙缩回原位，胳膊又藏到衣裾后头。

“我下来，”罗恩说，“是想趁早饭前同你略叙一谈，或许有些好处。”

摊在写字台上的那封信，是伦敦的罗恩律师写来的，里面装的正是罗恩那桩提议：每年一千镑、退出实业——卢克至今仍把这看作他们一切纠葛最安逸的了局。十天以前他确曾明白指示律师提出这份提议，这他几乎忘干净了；可提议就在这儿，躺在塔皮特的桌上。方才五分钟，塔皮特一直在掂量它，每多掂量一刻，他对罗恩的仇便添一分。罗恩二十五岁，自然把塔皮特——一个年近六十、离五十远去了的人——看作十足的老头儿；可五十五岁的男人不喜欢被人这样看，也不急于被晚辈搁上架子去。况且，每年一千镑的担保，叫塔皮特上哪儿寻去——律师的信他头一眼瞟过去，就不曾放过这一层。收买他，把他晾到一边去！他从心底恨罗恩；——这恨就其性质而论，远比罗恩所能对他怀的恨刻毒。他记得那香槟；记得这年轻人在他自己家里吆三喝四地支使人；记得人家讥诮他的啤酒，讥诮他这一行的老经验何等不受敬重。收买他！哼，只要他还有一张五镑钞票可花，还有一条腿立得住，休想。他此刻主意正硬，也硬得起来，因为塔皮特太太也站在他这一边。旅店里发生的那桩事，罗恩太太没怎么保得住密，塔皮特太太已经认定雷切尔·雷事竟成了。那天早晨塔皮特宣言要斗争到底，塔皮特太太直夸他有胆气。

===Original===
“Oh! a little chat, is it?” said Tappitt. “About this letter that I’ve just got, I suppose;” and he gave a contemptuous poke to the epistle with one of his hands.

“What letter?” asked Rowan.

“Come now, young man, don’t let us have any humbug and trickery, whatever we may do. If there’s anything I do hate, it’s deceit.”

All Rowan’s wrath returned upon him instantly, redoubled and trebled in its energy. “What do you mean, sir?” said he. “Who is trying to deceive anybody? How dare you speak to me in such language as that?”

“Now, look here, Mr. Rowan. This letter comes from your man in Craven Street, as of course you know very well. You have chosen to put our business in the hands of the lawyers, and in the hands of the lawyers it shall remain. I have been very wrong in attempting to have any dealings with you. I should have known what sort of a man you were before I let you put your foot in the concern. But I know enough of you now, and, if you please, you’ll keep yourself on the other side of those gates for the future. D’ye hear me? Unless you wish to be turned out by the men, don’t you put your feet inside the brewery premises any more.” And Tappitt’s face as he uttered these words was a face very unpleasant to behold.

===Chinese===
“哦！略叙一谈，是不是？”塔皮特说。“我猜，是要谈我刚收到的这封信吧；”说着，他伸出一只手，轻蔑地朝那封信戳了一记。

“什么信？”罗恩问。

“行了，年轻人，咱们不管怎么着，别来虚头滑脑、坑蒙拐骗那一套。要说这世上我恨什么，我最恨的就是骗。”

罗恩的怒火霎时整个儿涌了回来，威力一倍再加一倍。“您这是什么意思，先生？”他说。“谁想骗谁来着？您竟敢拿这种话对我讲？”

“好，你听着，罗恩先生。这封信出自你在克拉文街（Craven Street）的那位律师，这你自然一清二楚。你执意要把咱们的事交到律师们手里，那就让它在律师们手里搁着吧。我原先竟想同你有什么来往，实在大错特错。我本该在你把脚踏进这份产业之前，就认清你是个什么货色。如今你这个人，我算认清够了，对不住，往后劳驾你待在那几扇大门的外头。听见没有？除非你想叫工人们把你架出去，就再别把脚踏进酿酒厂的地界。”塔皮特说这些话时的那副面孔，叫人瞧着极不受用。

===Original===
Luke was so astounded that he could not bethink himself at the moment of the most becoming words in which to answer his enemy. His first idea had prompted him to repudiate all present knowledge of the lawyer’s letter, seeing that the lawyer’s letter had been the ground of that charge against him of deceit. But having been thus kicked out—kicked out as far as words could kick him, and threatened with personal violence should those words not be obeyed, he found himself unable to go back to the lawyer’s letter. “I should like to see any one of your men dare to touch me,” said he.

“You shall see it very soon if you don’t take yourself off,” said Tappitt. Luckily the men were gone to breakfast, and opportunity for violence was wanting.

Luke looked round, and then remembered that he and Tappitt were probably alone in the place. “Mr. Tappitt,” said he, “you’re a very foolish man.”

“I dare say,” said Tappitt; “very foolish not to give up my own bread, and my wife’s and children’s bread, to an adventurer like you.”

===Chinese===
卢克惊愕之至，一时竟想不起几句最得体的措辞来回敬他的仇敌。他头一个念头本是推说自己此刻全然不知那封律师的信，因为指控行骗，正是拿那封律师的信作由头。可他既已这样被踢了出来——就言辞所能踢人的限度被踢了出来，还以不遵便动武相威胁——他发觉自己再没法绕回那封律师的信上去。“你手下的工人，我倒想看看有哪一个敢碰我一碰，”他说。

“你不快滚，很快便让你见识见识，”塔皮特说。所幸工人们都吃早饭去了，动武的机会无从觅得。

卢克四下里看了看，这才记起这里多半只剩他同塔皮特两个人。“塔皮特先生，”他说，“你是个蠢透了的人。”

“也许吧，”塔皮特说；“蠢透了，竟不肯把我自己的面包、我老婆的和我儿女的面包，拱手让给你这样一个冒险家。”

===Original===
“I have endeavoured to treat you with kindness and also with honesty, and because you differ from me, as of course you have a right to do, you think it best to insult me with all the Billingsgate you can muster.”

“If you don’t go out of my countinghouse, young man, I’ll see if I can’t put you out myself;” and Tappitt, in spite of his fifty-five years, absolutely put his hand down upon the poker.

There is no personal encounter in which a young man is so sure to come by the worst as in that with a much older man. This is so surely the case that it ought to be considered cowardly in an old man to attack a young one. If an old man hit a young man over the head with a walking-stick, what can the young man do, except run away to avoid a second blow? Then the old man, if he be a wicked old man, as so many are, tells all his friends that he has licked the young man. Tappitt would certainly have acted in this way if the weapon in his hand had been a stick instead of a poker. But Tappitt, when he saw his own poker in his own hand, was afraid of it. If a woman attack a man with a knife, the man will be held to have fought fairly, though he shall have knocked her down in the encounter. And so also with an old man, if he take a poker instead of a stick, the world will refuse to him the advantage of his gray hairs. Some such an idea as this came upon Tappitt—by instinct, and thus, though he still held the poker, he refrained his hand.

===Chinese===
“我一向力求待你以厚道，也待你以诚实；只因为你的意见同我不合——你自然有权不合——你就觉得顶好的法子，是把你能搜罗来的比尔林斯盖特鱼市泼骂（Billingsgate）一齐拿来糟践我。”

“你不滚出我的账房，年轻人，我就试试自己能不能把你撵出去；”塔皮特说着，不顾自己已五十五岁，竟当真一把按住了拨火棍。

天下人与人之间的厮打，年轻人最没有胜算的一种，便是同老上许多的人交手。此理如此铁定，老年人向年轻人动手，理应算作怯懦才对。倘若一个老头用手杖照年轻人头上打去，年轻人除了逃开以避第二杖，还能怎样？随后那老头——倘若他是个坏老头，而坏老头又何其多——便去对他所有的相知夸说，他把那个年轻人教训了一顿。塔皮特手里那件家伙倘若是一根手杖而非拨火棍，他必定照此办理。可塔皮特一看见自家手里握着自家的拨火棍，倒怕起它来了。倘若一个女人持刀扑向男人，那男人哪怕当场把她打翻在地，世人也公认他打得公平。老年人亦复如此：他若抄起的是拨火棍而不是手杖，世人便不肯再让他占白发的便宜。诸如此类的一个念头凭本能涌上塔皮特心头，于是他虽仍握着拨火棍，那只手却按住不发了。

===Original===
“The man must be mad this morning,” said Rowan, standing firmly before him, with his two hands fixed upon his hips.

“Am I to send for the police?” said Tappitt.

“For a mad-doctor, I should think,” said Rowan. Then Tappitt turned round and rang a bell very violently. But as the bell was intended to summon some brewery servant who was now away at his breakfast, it produced no result.

“But I have no intention of staying here against your wish, Mr. Tappitt, whether you’re mad or only foolish. This matter must of course be settled by the lawyers now, and I shall not again come on to these premises unless I acquire a legal right to do so as the owner of them.” And then, having so spoken, Luke Rowan walked off.

Growling inwardly Tappitt deposited the poker within the upright fender, and thrusting his hands into his trousers pockets stood scowling at the door through which his enemy had gone. He knew that he had been wrong; he knew that he had been very foolish. He was a man who had made his way upwards through the world with fair success, and had walked his way not without prudence. He had not been a man of violence, or prone to an illicit use of pokers. He had never been in difficulty for an assault; and had on his conscience not even the blood of a bloody nose, or the crime of a blackened eye. He was hardworking and peaceable; had been churchwarden three times, and mayor of Baslehurst once. He was poor-law guardian and way-warden, and filled customarily the various offices of a steady good citizen. What had he to do with pokers, unless it were to extract heat from his coals? He was ashamed of himself as he stood scowling at the door. One fault he perhaps had; and of that fault he had been ruthlessly told by lips that should have been sealed forever on such a subject. He brewed bad beer; and by whom had this been thrown in his teeth? By Bungall’s nephew—by Bungall’s heir—by him who claimed to stand in Bungall’s shoes within that establishment! Who had taught him to brew beer—bad or good? Had it not been Bungall? And now, because in his old age he would not change these things, and ruin himself in a vain attempt to make some beverage that should look bright to the eye, he was to be turned out of his place by this chip from the Bungall block, this stave out of one of Bungall’s vats! “*Ruat coelum, fiat justitia*,” he said, as he walked forth to his own breakfast. He spoke to himself in other language, indeed, though the Roman’s sentiment was his own. “I’ll stand on my rights, though I have to go into the poorhouse.”

===Chinese===
“这家伙今儿早晨准是疯了，”罗恩说，稳稳地立在他面前，两手叉定在腰间。

“要不要我去喊警察？”塔皮特说。

“我看是喊疯人医生吧，”罗恩说。于是塔皮特转过身去，把铃扯得震天价响。可那铃原是唤酿酒厂一个仆役的，那仆役这会儿吃饭去了，铃声毫无结果。

“不过，塔皮特先生，无论你是疯了还是只是蠢，我都无意违拗你的意思赖在这里。此事如今自然得交律师们了断；除非我作为业主取得合法的权利，我不会再踏上这片地界。”说完这话，卢克·罗恩便扬长而去。

塔皮特腹中咕哝，把拨火棍插回竖立的炉围里，两手往裤袋一插，对着仇敌出去的那扇门横眉立目。他知道自己方才不对；知道自己蠢得很。他这个人一世往上爬，混得颇有成功，一路行走也并非全无谨慎。他从来不是逞凶动武的人，也不惯拿拨火棍干犯法的勾当。他从未因斗殴惹过官司；良心上连一桩打得人流鼻血的案底都没有，更不曾担过打青眼睛的罪名。他勤恳而爱好和平；做过三届教区委员，还当过一任巴斯尔赫斯特市长。他身兼济贫专员和道路督察，一个安分良民平日的各样职司，他一概照常充任。拨火棍同他什么相干——除非从煤里拨火？他立在那里对着门横眉立目，心里着实羞愧。他也许有一桩过错；而这一桩，曾有人毫不留情地当面数落过他——那两片嘴唇，原该在这桩事上永远封住的才对。他酿的啤酒不好；而这话是谁掷回他脸上来的？是邦格尔的侄儿——是邦格尔的继承人——是那个自命要在这份产业里顶邦格尔的缺的人！教他酿啤酒的——不管好啤酒坏啤酒——是谁？岂不是邦格尔？可如今，只因为他人到老境不肯改弦更张，不肯为试制一种看着清亮的饮料把自己家底糟蹋干净而落得徒劳无功，就要被这块从邦格尔木料上劈下来的碎木片、这根从邦格尔酒桶上拔下来的桶板，从他自己这个位置上撵出去！*Ruat coelum, fiat justitia*——纵使天崩地裂，正义必行——他一面走去吃自己的早饭，一面说道。当然，他对自己说的原是另一种语言，不过那位罗马人的豪情，正是他自己的豪情。“哪怕进济贫院，我也要守住我的权利。”

## XIV Luke Rowan Pays a Second Visit to Bragg’s End / XIV 卢克·罗恩再访布拉格斯恩德

===Original===
Early after breakfast on that morning—that morning on which Tappitt had for a moment thought of braining Luke Rowan with the poker—Mrs. Ray started from the cottage on her mission into Baslehurst. She was going to see her daughter, Mrs. Prime, at Miss Pucker’s lodgings, and felt sure that the object of her visit was to be a further discourse on the danger of admitting that wolf Rowan into the sheepfold at Bragg’s End. She would willingly have avoided the conference had she been able to do so, knowing well that Mrs. Prime would get the better of her in words when called upon to talk without having Rachel at her back. And indeed she was not happy in her mind. It had been conceded at the cottage as an understood thing that Rachel was to have this man as her lover; but what, if after all, the man didn’t mean to be a lover in the proper sense; and what, if so meaning, he should still turn out to be a lover of a bad sort—a worldly, good-for-nothing, rakish lover? “I wonder,” says the wicked man in the play, “I wonder any man alive would ever rear a daughter!” Mrs. Ray knew nothing of the play, and had she done so, she would not have repeated such a line. But the hardness of the task which Providence had allotted to her struck her very forcibly on this morning. Rachel was dearer to her than aught else in the world. For Rachel’s happiness she would have made any sacrifice. In Rachel’s presence, and sweet smile, and winning caresses was the chief delight of her existence. Nevertheless, in these days the possession of Rachel was hardly a blessing to her. The responsibility was so great; and, worse than that as regarded her own comfort, the doubts were so numerous; and then, they recurred over and over again, as often as they were settled!

“I’m sure I don’t know what she can have to say to me.” Mrs. Ray, as she spoke, was tying on her bonnet, and Rachel was standing close to her with her light summer shawl.

“It will be the old story, mamma, I’m afraid; my terrible iniquity and backslidings, because I went to the ball, and because I won’t go to Miss Pucker’s. She’ll want you to say that I shall go, or else be sent to bed without my supper.”
===Chinese===
那天早晨，早饭后没多久——就是塔皮特一时起念要拿拨火棍敲碎卢克·罗恩脑袋的那个早晨——雷太太便动身离了村舍，到巴斯尔赫斯特办她的差事去了。她要去帕克小姐的寓所看望女儿普赖姆太太，心里笃定，这趟拜访的名目，必然又是受一番训导，讲的是把罗恩那头狼引进布拉格斯恩德羊圈的危险。这场谈话她原愿意避开的，只要避得开；她心里明白，一旦没有雷切尔在背后撑腰，叫她开口同人对谈，普赖姆太太在言辞上总能占她的上风。何况她心里确实不踏实。村舍里早已默认了一件事：雷切尔要把这个男人当作情郎；可倘若这个人到头来根本无意做正经意义上的情郎呢？又倘若他倒真有此意，却终究显出是个不怎么样的情郎——一个世俗的、一无是处的、放荡轻佻的情郎呢？戏台上那个恶人说过：“我奇怪，我真奇怪，世上活着的人怎么还会养女儿！”雷太太没看过那出戏，即便看过，也不会去引这样一句。可这天早晨，上天派给她的这份苦差有多难当，她感受得格外真切。雷切尔是她的心肝，比世上什么都金贵。为了雷切尔的幸福，她什么牺牲都肯做。有雷切尔在眼前，有她甜甜的笑靥、讨人欢心的抚爱，便是她此生头一桩乐事。可是这些日子，身边有个雷切尔几乎算不得福气了。担子是这般沉重；而就她自己的安稳而论，更糟的是疑虑这般繁多；而且，疑虑刚一安顿下去，偏偏又一遍遍翻腾起来！

“我真不知道她能有什么话要对我讲。”雷太太说着，正系软帽，雷切尔披着轻薄的夏日披肩，紧挨在她身边站着。

“我怕又是老一套，妈妈；又是说我那些可怕的罪过和背道，因为我去了舞会，又因为我不肯去帕克小姐家。她要叫你说我必须去，不然就罚我不吃夜宴，早早上床。”

===Original===
“That’s nonsense, Rachel. Dorothea knows very well that I can’t make you go.” Mrs. Ray was wont to become mildly petulant when things went against her.

“But, mamma, you don’t want me to go?”

“I don’t suppose it’s about Miss Pucker at all. It’s about that other thing.”

“You mean Mr. Rowan.”

“Yes, my dear. I’m sure I don’t know what’s for the best. When she gets me to herself she does say such terrible things to me that it quite puts me in a heat to have to go to her. I don’t think anybody ought to say those sort of things to me except a clergyman, or a person’s parents, or a schoolmaster, or masters and mistresses, or suchlike.” Rachel thought so too—thought that at any rate a daughter should not so speak to such a mother as was her mother; but on that subject she said nothing.
===Chinese===
“胡说，雷切尔。多萝西娅很清楚，我没办法叫你去。”雷太太一遇事情不顺，照例要闹点小小的性子。

“可是，妈妈，你不想要我去吧？”

“我看根本不是为了帕克小姐。是为了另一件事。”

“你是说罗恩先生。”

“是啊，我亲爱的。我真不知道怎样才好。她一把我叫到没旁人的地方，就对我说那么些怕人的话，弄得我一想到要去见她，浑身就发燥。我看，除了牧师，或是人家的爹娘，或是学堂里的先生，或是东家、主妇，或是这一类人，谁也不该对我说那样的话。”雷切尔也是这么想——觉得无论如何，一个做女儿的，总不该对她母亲那样的一位母亲这样说话；只是这个话头她没有出口。

===Original===
“And I don’t like going to that Miss Pucker’s house,” continued Mrs. Ray. “I’m sure I don’t want her to come here. I wouldn’t go, only I said that I would.”

“I would go now, if I were you, mamma.”

“Of course I shall go; haven’t I got myself ready?”

“But I would not let her go on in that way.”

“That’s very easy said, Rachel; but how am I to help it? I can’t tell her to hold her tongue; and if I did, she wouldn’t. If I am to go I might as well start. I suppose there’s cold lamb enough for dinner?”
===Chinese===
“再说，我也不喜欢上帕克小姐家去，”雷太太接着说。“我自然也不愿意她上这儿来。要不是话已经说出了口，我才不去呢。”

“妈妈，我要是你，还是会去的。”

“我当然要去；我不是已经收拾好了吗？”

“可我不会容她那样说个没完。”

“雷切尔，这话说来容易，可叫我怎么拦呢？我总不能叫她闭嘴；就算说了，她也不会闭。反正要去，不如这就动身。午饭的冷羊肉够吃吧？”

===Original===
“Plenty, I should think.”

“And if I find poultry cheap, I can bring a chicken home in my basket, can’t I?” And so saying, with her mind full of various cares, Mrs. Ray walked off to Baslehurst.

“I wonder when he’ll come.” Rachel, as she said or thought these words, stood at the open door of the cottage looking after her mother as she made her way across the green. It was a delicious midsummer day, warm with the heat of the morning sun, but not yet oppressed with the full blaze of its noonday rays. The air was alive with the notes of birds, and the flowers were in their brightest beauty. “I wonder when he’ll come.” None of those doubts which so harassed her mother troubled her mind. Other doubts there were. Could it be possible that he would like her well enough to wish to make her his own? Could it be that anyone so bright, so prosperous in the world, so clever, so much above herself in all worldly advantages, should come and seek her as his wife—take her from their little cottage and lowly ways of life? When he had first said that he would come to Bragg’s End, she declared to herself that it would be well that he should see in how humble a way they lived. He would not call her Rachel after that, she said to herself; or, if he did, he should learn from her that she knew how to rebuke a man who dared to take advantage of the humility of her position. He had come, and he had not called her Rachel. He had come, and taking advantage of her momentary absence, had spoken of her behind her back as a lover speaks, and had told his love honestly to her mother. In Rachel’s view of the matter no lover could have carried himself with better decorum or with a sweeter grace; but because he had so done, she would not hold him to be bound to her. He had been carried away by his feelings too rapidly, and had not as yet known how poor and lowly they were. He should still have opened to him a clear path backwards. Then if the path backwards were not to his mind, then in that case—. I am not sure that Rachel ever declared to herself in plain terms what in such case would happen; but she stood at the door as though she was minded to stand there till he should appear upon the green.

“I wonder when he’ll come.” She had watched her mother’s figure disappear along the lane, and had plucked a flower or two to pieces before she returned within the house. He will not come till the evening, she determined—till the evening, when his day’s work in the brewery would be over. Then she thought of the quarrel between him and Tappitt, and wondered what it might be. She was quite sure that Tappitt was wrong, and thought of him at once as an obstinate, foolish, pigheaded old man. Yes; he would come to her, and she would take care to be provided in that article of cream which he pretended to love so well. She would not have to run away again. But how lucky on that previous evening had been that necessity, seeing that it had given opportunity for that great display of a lover’s excellence on Rowan’s part. Having settled all this in her mind, she went into the house, and was beginning to think of her household work, when she heard a man’s steps in the passage. She went at once out from the sitting-room, and encountered Luke Rowan at the door.
===Chinese===
“我想够有余的。”

“要是我碰上鸡鸭便宜，就能拎只鸡回来，好不好？”说着这话，雷太太带着满怀的种种操心，动身往巴斯尔赫斯特去了。

“不知道他什么时候来。”雷切尔嘴上念着，或是心里想着这句话，站在村舍敞开的门口，望着母亲穿绿地而去。这是个可爱的仲夏日，晨曦的暖气烘得人暖洋洋，却还没到日午光焰逼人的时辰。空气里满是鸟雀的啼啭，花儿开到了最明艳的时分。“不知道他什么时候来。”搅得她母亲心神不宁的那些疑虑，一样也没来搅她。她有的是别的疑虑。他会不会真心喜欢她，喜欢到要把她据为己有？像他这样出挑、这样在世上得意、这样聪明、样样世俗的长处都高过她一头的人，会不会当真来求她做妻子——把她从他们这所小村舍和寒微的生活路数里接走？他头一回说要到布拉格斯恩德来的时候，她就对自己说，让他看看他们过的是多么寒微的日子，倒是件好事。往后他就不会叫她雷切尔了，她这样对自己讲；就算还要叫，她也得让他知道，她懂得怎样斥责一个胆敢占她地位寒微的便宜的男人。他来了，却没有叫她雷切尔。他来了，趁她暂时不在跟前，用情郎的口吻背地里说起她，还老老实实向他母亲吐露了爱意。照雷切尔看这件事，天下再没有哪个情郎能比他举止更得体、风度更温雅的了；可正因为他做得这样好，她偏不肯就此认定他被拴在了自己身上。他是一时感情奔涌，来得太快，还没弄清他们的日子是何等清寒低微。她本该仍然给他留一条明明白白的退路。而倘若那条退路他不中意，那么一旦如此——雷切尔究竟有没有用明白的言辞对自己交代过，一旦如此会怎么样，我可说不准；只是她站在门口，一副打算一直站下去的架势，站到他出现在绿地上为止。

“不知道他什么时候来。”她望着母亲的身影顺着小巷消失了，又揪了一两朵花揉碎，才回到屋里。他到傍晚才会来，她断定——要到傍晚，等他酿酒厂一天的活儿忙完。于是她想起他和塔皮特的那场争吵，纳闷那究竟是怎么一回事。她断定错在塔皮特，一上来就把他想成一个顽固、愚蠢、死心眼的老头子。是的，他会来的，而她要记着备足那样东西——他口口声声顶顶喜欢的凝脂奶油。这回她用不着再逃开了。不过话说回来，前一晚那场不得不逃，又是何等的运气，正因为它才给了罗恩机会，把一个情郎的种种妙处那样大大地施展了一番。她心里把这一切盘算停当，走进屋去，正要开始想家务，忽听得过道里有男人的脚步声。她立刻从起居室出来，正撞见门口站着的卢克·罗恩。

Did she not know that Mrs. Ray’s absence would be esteemed by him as a great gain, and not a loss? Why did she thus falsely talk of his waiting a long time? Dogs fight with their teeth, and horses with their heels; swans with their wings, and cats with their claws;—so also do women use such weapons as nature has provided for them.

“I came specially to see you,” said he; “not but what I should be very glad to see your mother, too, if she comes back before I am gone. But I don’t suppose she will, for you won’t let me stay so long as that.”

He had come into the room, had put down his hat, and had got himself up to the window, so that his back was turned to her. “Rachel,” he said, turning round quickly, and speaking almost suddenly. I hope it will be understood that Rachel was quite a novice at this piece of work which she now had in hand. It must be the case that very many girls are not novices. A young lady who has rejected the first half-dozen suitors who have asked for her love, must probably feel herself mistress of the occasion when she rejects the seventh, and will not be quite astray when she accepts the eighth. There are, moreover, young ladies who, though they may have rejected and accepted none, have had so wide an advantage in society as to be able, when the moment comes, to have their wits about them. But Rachel had known nothing of what is called society, and had never before known either the trouble or the joy of being loved. So when the question was pressed upon her, she trembled, and felt that her breath was failing her. She had filled herself full of resolutions as to what she would do when this moment came—as to how she would behave and what words she would utter. But all that was gone from her now. She could only stand still and tremble. Of course he might call her Rachel;—might call her what he pleased. To him, with his wider experience, that now became manifest enough.

“You must give me leave for more than that, Rachel, if you would not send me away wretched. You must let me call you my own.” Then he moved round the table towards her; and as he moved, though she retreated from him, she did not retreat with a step as rapid as his own. “Rachel,”—and he put out his hand to her—“I want you to be my wife.” She allowed the tips of her fingers to turn themselves toward him, as though unable altogether to refuse the greeting which he offered her, but as she did so she turned away from him, and bent down her head. She had heard all she wanted to hear. Why did he not go away, and leave her to think of it? He had named to her the word so sacred between man and woman. He had said that he sought her for his wife. What need was there that he should stay longer?

He got her hand in his, and then passed his arm round her waist. “Say, love; say, Rachel;—shall it be so? Nay, but I will have an answer from you. You shall look it to me, if you will not speak it;” and he got his head round over her shoulder, as though to look into her eyes.
===Chinese===
我希望读者明白，雷切尔做眼下这桩活计，完全是个生手。想必有许多姑娘并不是生手。一位小姐若已回绝了头六个向她求爱的求婚者，到回绝第七个的时候，多半自觉对这般场面驾轻就熟，到接受第八个的时候，也不至于摸不着头脑。此外还有些小姐，虽则一个没回绝过、一个没接受过，却在社交场中历练得益处极大，等到那个时刻来临，也能应付裕如。可雷切尔全然不识所谓的社交，也从来没有尝过被人爱恋的烦恼或欢悦。所以当这个问题逼到她面前时，她发着抖，只觉得气息都要接不上了。她原把决心装得满满的：这个时刻来临时她要怎样做、要怎样举止、要说什么话。可如今这一切都抛到九霄云外去了。她只有站着发抖的份儿。他当然可以叫她雷切尔——爱叫什么就叫什么好了。这一点，凭他那更老到的阅历，如今已看得再明白不过。

“雷切尔，你若不想叫我伤心地走开，就得容我更进一层。你得让我叫你做我自己的人。”说着他绕过桌子朝她走去；他挪步的时候，她虽往后退，脚步却没有他挪得那样快。“雷切尔，”——他向她伸出手去——“我要你做我的妻子。”她任凭自己的指尖转向了他，仿佛要她全然拒绝他递过来的这份致意是做不到的，可就在这么做的时候，她扭过身去，垂下了头。她想听的话她都听到了。他怎么还不走开，留她一个人慢慢想？男女之间那句至重至圣的话，他已经说出了口。他说他要娶她为妻。他还留在这里做什么呢？

他把她的手握进自己的手里，随即一条手臂搂住了她的腰。“说呀，亲爱的；说呀，雷切尔；——行不行？不行的，我非要你一句话不可。你不肯说，就用眼神告诉我；”说着把头从她肩头绕过去，像要一直看进她的眼睛里。

===Original===
“Oh, Mr. Rowan; pray don’t;—pray don’t pull me.”

“But, dearest, say a word to me. You must say some word. Can you learn to love me, Rachel?”

Learn to love him! The lesson had come to her very easily. How was it possible, she had once thought, not to love him.

“Say a word to me,” said Rowan, still struggling to look into her face; “one word, and then I will let you go.”

“What word?”

“Say to me, ‘Dear Luke, I will be your wife.’ ”
===Chinese===
“哦，罗恩先生；求你别这样；——求你别拽我。”

“可是，最亲爱的，跟我说一句话吧。你总得说一句。你能学着爱我吗，雷切尔？”

学着爱他！这门功课她学来容易得很。她一度想过，不爱他怎么可能呢。

“跟我说一句话，”罗恩说，还挣扎着要看她的脸；“一句就行，说完我就放你走。”

“什么话？”

“对我说，‘亲爱的卢克，我愿意做你的妻子。’”

===Original===
She remained for a moment quite passive in his hands, trying to say it, but the words would not come. Of course she would be his wife. Why need he trouble her further?

“Nay, but, Rachel, you shall speak, or I will stay with you here till your mother comes, and she shall answer for you. If you had disliked me I think you would have said so.”

“I don’t dislike you,” she whispered.

“And do you love me?” She slightly bowed her head. “And you will be my wife?” Again she went through the same little piece of acting. “And I may call you Rachel now?” In answer to this question she shook herself free from his slackened grasp, and escaped away across the room.

“You cannot forbid me now. Come and sit down by me, for of course I have got much to say to you. Come and sit down, and indeed I will not trouble you again.”
===Chinese===
有那么一会儿，她全然被动地任他握着，想说那句话，话却说不出来。她横竖是要做他的妻子的。他还何必再搅扰她？

“不行，雷切尔，你一定得开口，不然我就待在这儿不走，等你妈妈回来，让她替你答。你若是不喜欢我，我想你早就会说了。”

“我不讨厌你，”她悄声说。

“那你爱我吗？”她微微点了点头。“那你愿意做我的妻子吗？”她又把那点小小的动作重演了一遍。“那如今我可以叫你雷切尔了吧？”回答这一问，她趁他手上一松，挣脱身子，飞快地逃到屋子那头去了。

“如今你可禁不住我叫了。来，挨着我坐下，我自然有许多话要对你说。来坐下吧，真的，我再不搅扰你了。”

===Original===
Then she went to him very slowly, and sat with him, leaving her hand in his, listening to his words, and feeling in her heart the full delight of having such a lover. Of the words that were then spoken, but very few came from her lips; he told her all his story of the brewery quarrel, and was very eloquent and droll in describing Tappitt as he brandished the poker.

“And was he going to hit you with it?” said Rachel, with all her eyes open.

“Well, he didn’t hit me,” said Luke; “but to look at him he seemed mad enough to do anything.” Then he told her how at the present moment he was living at the inn, and how it became necessary, from this unfortunate quarrel, that he should go at once to London. “But under no circumstances would I have gone,” said he, pressing her hand very closely, “without an answer from you.”

“But you ought not to think of anything like that when you are in such trouble.”

“Ought I not? Well, but I do, you see.” Then he explained to her that part of his project consisted in his marrying her out of hand—at once. He would go up to London for a week or two, and then, coming back, be married in the course of the next month.
===Chinese===
于是她慢慢地挪到他身边坐下，一只手留在他的手里，听他说话，心里满是拥有这样一个情郎的十足欢喜。那一席话，出自她口中的极少极少；他把酿酒厂争吵的前前后后讲给她听，讲到塔皮特挥舞拨火棍的那一段，形容得又伶俐又逗趣。

“那他当真要拿它打你？”雷切尔问道，眼睛睁得滚圆。

“哦，他没打着，”卢克说；“可瞧他那样子，简直疯了，什么事都干得出来。”接着他告诉她，他眼下住在客栈里，又因为这场倒霉的争吵，他不得不立刻动身去伦敦。“可无论如何，”他紧紧攥着她的手说，“得不到你一句话，我是怎么也不肯走的。”

“可你遭着这样的烦难，不该去想这样的事。”

“不该吗？可你瞧，我偏偏想。”于是他向她解释，他盘算里的一件事，就是把婚事立刻办了——马上。他去伦敦待上一两个星期，随后回来，下个月里就把婚结了。

===Original===
“Oh, Mr. Rowan, that would be impossible.”

“You must not call me Mr. Rowan, or I shall call you Miss Ray.”

“But indeed it would be impossible.”

“Why impossible?”

“Indeed it would. You can ask mamma;—or rather, you had better give over thinking of it. I haven’t had time yet even to make up my mind what you are like.”
===Chinese===
“哦，罗恩先生，那可办不到。”

“你不许叫我罗恩先生，不然我就叫你雷小姐。”

“可那实在是办不到的呀。”

“怎么就办不到？”

“实在是办不到。你可以去问妈妈；——不，倒不如说，你还是别再想这桩事了吧。我连你到底是个什么样的人，都还没来得及拿定主意呢。”

===Original===
“But you say that you love me.”

“So I do, but I suppose I ought not; for I’m sure I don’t know what you are like yet. It seems to me that you’re very fond of having your own way, sir;—and so you ought,” she added; “but really you can’t have your own way in that. Nobody ever heard of such a thing. Everybody would think we were mad.”

“I shouldn’t care one straw for that.”

“Ah, but I should—a great many straws.”
===Chinese===
“可你说了你爱我。”

“我是说了，可我想我不该说；因为我确实还不知道你是个什么样的人呢。我看你这人，先生，顶喜欢自行其是；——这也本该如此，”她又添上一句；“可这件事上，你实在由不得自己。这样的事谁也没听说过。人人都要当我们是疯了。”

“那个我半根草屑也不在乎。”

“啊，我可要在乎——要在乎好些草屑呢。”

===Original===
He sat there for two hours, telling her of all things appertaining to himself. He explained to her that, irrespective of the brewery, he had an income sufficient to support a wife—“though not enough to make her a fine lady like Mrs. Cornbury,” he said.

“If you can give me bread and cheese, it’s as much as I have a right to expect,” said Rachel.

“I have over four hundred a year,” said he: and Rachel, hearing it, thought that he could indeed support a wife. Why should a man with four hundred a year want to brew beer?

“But I have got nothing,” said Rachel; “not a farthing.”

“Of course not,” said Rowan; “it is my theory that unmarried girls never ought to have anything. If they have, they ought to be considered as provided for, and then they shouldn’t have husbands. And I rather think it would be better if men didn’t have anything either, so that they might be forced to earn their bread. Only they would want capital.”
===Chinese===
他在那儿一坐就是两个钟头，把自己的一切桩桩件件讲给她听。他向她解释，撇开酿酒厂不算，他有一份进项，足够养活一位太太——“虽说还不足以把她供成康伯里太太那样一位贵妇人，”他说。

“只要你给我面包和奶酪，就是我有权利指望的全部了，”雷切尔说。

“我一年有四百多镑进项，”他说。雷切尔听了，心想他确实养得起一位太太。一年有四百镑进项的男人，何苦还要去酿啤酒呢？

“可我什么也没有，”雷切尔说；“一个子儿也没有。”

“本来就不该有，”罗恩说；“我的理论是，没出嫁的姑娘压根就不该有什么财产。她们若有了，就该算作已经安顿妥当，那就不该再给她们配丈夫了。我倒还觉得，男人要也一无所有反倒更好，好逼着他们自己去挣面包。只是那样一来，他们又缺不得本钱。”

===Original===
Rachel listened to it all with the greatest content, and most unalloyed happiness. She did not quite understand him, but she gathered from his words that her own poverty was not a reproach in his eyes, and that he under no circumstances would have looked for a wife with a fortune. Her happiness was unalloyed at all she heard from him, till at last he spoke of his mother.

“And does she dislike me?” asked Rachel, with dismay.

“It isn’t that she dislikes you, but she’s staying with that Mrs. Tappitt, who is furious against me because—I suppose it’s because of this brewery row. But indeed I can’t understand it. A week ago I was at home there; now I daren’t show my nose in the house, and have been turned out of the brewery this morning with a poker.”

“I hope it’s nothing about me,” said Rachel.
===Chinese===
这一席话，雷切尔听得心满意足，喜乐再纯粹不过。他说的道理她不甚了然，但从他的话里她听出，她的清寒在他眼里并不是什么短处，而且无论情形如何，他都不会去找一个带着财产的太太。从他口里听来的种种，都叫她的幸福纯粹无杂，直到末了他提起他的母亲。

“那她讨厌我？”雷切尔问，心头一沉。

“倒不是她讨厌你，只是她住在塔皮特太太家里，那位太太对我恨得咬牙切齿，因为——我想就是因为酿酒厂这档子风波。可说实话，我实在想不通。一个星期前，我在那边还是个自家人；如今我在那所房子里连头都不敢露，今天早上还叫人拿着拨火棍从酿酒厂撵了出来。”

“但愿跟我没有关系，”雷切尔说。

===Original===
“How can it be about you?”

“Because I thought Mrs. Tappitt looked at the ball as though—. But I suppose it didn’t mean anything.”

“It ought to be a matter of perfect indifference whether it meant anything or not.”

“But how can it be so about your mother? If this is ever to lead to anything—”

“Lead to anything! What it will lead to is quite settled.”

“You know what I mean. But how could I become your wife if your mother did not wish it?”
===Chinese===
“怎么会跟你有关系？”

“因为我记得舞会那晚塔皮特太太瞧我的神气，好像——。可我想那没有什么意思吧。”

“它有意思是也罢，没意思是也罢，你本该全然不放在心上。”

“可那说的是你母亲，我怎么能不放在心上？倘若这事当真会有什么结果——”

“会有什么结果！会有什么结果，早已铁定了。”

“你明白我的意思。可你母亲若不愿意，我怎么做得成你的妻子？”

===Original===
“Look here, Rachel; that’s all very proper for a girl, I dare say. If your mother thought I was not fit to be your husband, I won’t say but what you ought to take her word in such a matter. But it isn’t so with a man. It will make me very unhappy if my mother cannot be friends with my wife; but no threats of hers to that effect would prevent me from marrying, nor should they have any effect upon you. I’m my own master, and from the nature of things I must look out for myself.”

This was all very grand and masterful on Rowan’s part, and might in theory be true; but there was that in it which made Rachel uneasy, and gave to her love its first shade of trouble. She could not be quite happy as Luke’s promised bride, if she knew that she would not be welcomed to that place by Luke’s mother. And then what right had she to think it probable that Luke’s mother would give her such a welcome? At that first meeting, however, she said but little herself on the subject. She had pledged to him her troth, and she would not attempt to go back from her pledge at the first appearance of a difficulty. She would talk to her own mother, and perhaps his mother might relent. But throughout it all there ran a feeling of dismay at the idea of marrying a man whose mother would not willingly receive her as a daughter!

“But you must go,” said she at last. “Indeed you must. I have things to do, if you have nothing.”

“I’m the idlest man in the world at the present moment. If you turn me out I can only go and sit at the inn.”

“Then you must go and sit at the inn. If you stay any longer mamma won’t have any dinner.”

“If that’s so, of course I’ll go. But I shall come back to tea.”
===Chinese===
“听我说，雷切尔；姑娘家这样想，我想是极应当的。你母亲若认为我不配做你的丈夫，在这类事上你该听她的话，这个我不否认。男人却不是这样。我母亲若不能同我妻子和睦相处，我自然万分难过；可她拿这个来吓唬我，休想叫我因此不娶，你也万不该因此动摇。我是自己的主人，照事物的本性，我必须为自己的前程打算。”
