罗恩这一番话，说得堂堂皇皇、独断专行，理论上或许站得住；可其中自有一层叫雷切尔不安的东西，给她的爱情投下了头一道阴影。她若知道卢克的母亲不会欢迎她坐上那个位子，做卢克聘定的新娘，她便无论如何快活不周全。何况她凭什么认定，卢克的母亲多半会给她这样的欢迎呢？不过这头一次谈话，她自己在这桩事上说得很少。她已把终身之誓许给了他，困难才一露头她便要从誓约上缩回来，这是她不肯做的。她会去同自己的母亲商量，他母亲或许也会心软。只是这一层一层想下来，始终贯着一股惊惶：一想到要嫁的男人，他的母亲不肯情愿把她当女儿接纳，她便暗暗心惊！

“可你该走了，”她末了说。“真的该走了。你没活儿，我可还有活儿呢。”

“这会儿我是天下头一号闲人。你把我撵走，我也只能去客栈里坐着。”

“那你就去客栈里坐着吧。你再待下去，妈妈就没午饭吃了。”

“既然如此，我当然走。可我吃茶的时候要回来的。”

===Original===
As Rachel gave no positive refusal to this proposition, Rowan took his departure on the understanding that he might return.

“Goodbye,” said he. “When I come this evening I shall expect you to walk with me.”

“Oh, I don’t know,” said she.

“Yes, you will; and we will see the sun set again, and you will not run from me this evening as though I were an ogre.” As he spoke he took her in his arms and held her, and kissed her before she had time to escape from him. “You’re mine altogether now,” said he, “and nothing can sever us. God bless you, Rachel!”

“Goodbye, Luke,” and then they parted.
===Chinese===
雷切尔对这个提议没有断然回绝，罗恩便告辞走了，讲好了他是可以回来的。

“再见，”他说。“今晚我来，可要你陪我散步。”

“哦，这我说不好，”她说。

“不，你会的；我们还要再看一回日落，今天晚上你可不会再从我身边逃开，把我当成什么吃人的妖怪了。”说着他把她搂进怀里抱住，没等她挣脱就吻了她。“你如今整个儿是我的了，”他说，“什么都拆不散我们。上帝保佑你，雷切尔！”

“再见，卢克，”随后两人便分别了。

===Original===
She had told him to go, alleging her household duties as her ground for dismissing him; but when he was gone she did not at once betake herself to her work. She sat on the seat which he had shared with her, thinking of the thing which she had done. She was now betrothed to this man as his wife, the only man towards whom her fancy had ever turned with the slightest preference. So far love for her had run very smoothly. From her first meetings with him, on those evenings in which she had hardly spoken to him, his form had filled her eye, and his words had filled her mind. She had learned to love to see him before she understood what her heart was doing for her. Gradually, but very quickly, all her vacant thoughts had been given to him, and he had become the hero of her life. Now, almost before she had had time to question herself on the matter, he was her affianced husband. It had all been so quick and so very gracious that she seemed to tremble at her own good fortune. There was that one little cloud in the sky—that frown on his mother’s brow; but now, in the first glow of her happiness, she could not bring herself to believe that this cloud would bring a storm. So she sat there dreaming of her happiness, and longing for her mother’s return that she might tell it all;—that it might be talked of hour after hour, and that Luke’s merits might receive their fitting mention. Her mother was not a woman who on such an occasion would stint the measure of her praise, or refuse her child the happiness of her sympathy.

But Rachel knew that she must not let the whole morning pass by in idle dreams, happy as those dreams were, and closely as they were allied to her waking life. After a while she jumped up with a start. “I declare there will be nothing done. Mamma will want her dinner though I’m ever so much going to be married.”

But she had not been long on foot, or done much in preparation of the cold lamb which it was intended they should eat that day, before she heard her mother’s footsteps on the gravel path. She ran out to the front door full of her own news, though hardly knowing as yet in what words she would tell it; but of her mother’s news, of any tidings which there might be to tell as to that interview which had just taken place in Baslehurst, Rachel did not think much. Nothing that Dorothea could say would now be of moment. So at least Rachel flattered herself. And as for Dorothea and all her growlings, had they not chiefly ended in this;—that the young man did not intend to present himself as a husband? But he had now done so in a manner which Rachel felt to be so satisfactory that even Dorothea’s criticism must be disarmed. So Rachel, as she met her mother, thought only of the tale which she had to tell, and nothing of that which she was to hear.
===Chinese===
她打发他走，拿家务当辞他的由头；可他人一走，她并没有立刻去做活。她坐在方才两人同坐的那张椅子上，回想自己方才做成的事。她如今同这个男人订了终身，要做他的妻子——而这个男人，是她那点芳心头一回稍稍偏爱过的人。至今为止，爱情在她这里一路走得顺顺当当。从起初同他相见的那些晚上起——那些她几乎没同他说过话的晚上——他的身形就填满了她的眼，他的言语就填满了她的心。还没等她弄明白自己的心在替她做什么，她已经爱上了见他的面。渐渐地——却又是很快地——她一切闲散的念头都交付给了他，他成了她生命里的主人公。如今，几乎没等她来得及就这事问问自己，他已经成了她的未婚夫。一切都来得这样快，这样美，好得叫她对自己的福分几乎要发抖。天上是有那么一小片云——他母亲眉间的那道蹙纹；可这会儿，幸福头一阵热气正暖着她，她怎么也不能叫自己相信，这片云当真会带来风暴。于是她坐在那儿，把幸福翻来覆去地梦想，只盼母亲快些回来，好把这一切原原本本说给她听；要一个钟头又一个钟头地讲个没完，要把卢克的种种好处说到恰如其分。这样的场合，她母亲绝不是个吝惜赞辞、拒绝拿自己的同情给孩子添喜的女人。

可雷切尔也知道，不能让整整一个上午就这么在闲梦里白白过去，尽管那些梦再甜美，同她醒着的日子贴得再近。过了一会儿，她猛地跳起来。“我敢说再这样下去，什么事也做不成了。妈妈照旧要吃午饭，哪怕我眼看就要出嫁了。”

可她下地还没多久，那顿说好这天要吃的冷羊肉还没张罗出多少名堂，就听见砾石小径上传来母亲的脚步声。她满怀自己的新闻，奔到前门口，虽然还不知道该用什么话来讲；至于母亲的新闻，至于方才在巴斯尔赫斯特那场会面可能有什么消息要带回来，雷切尔却没怎么放在心上。多萝西娅如今说什么都不相干了。至少雷切尔自己是这样美滋滋地想着的。再说多萝西娅和她那一套咕哝抱怨，到头来主要不就归结为一层：那个年轻男人并没有打算以丈夫自居？可他如今摆明了自己的身份，做得叫雷切尔觉得再满意不过，连多萝西娅的挑剔也非缴械不可。所以雷切尔迎着母亲，一心只想着自己要讲的那篇故事，全没想到自己将要听来的那一篇。

===Original===
But Mrs. Ray was so full of her tale, was so conscious of the fact that her tidings were entitled to the immediate and undivided attention of her daughter, and from their first greeting on the gravel path was so ready with her words, that Rachel, with all the story of her happiness, was for a while obliterated.

“Oh, my dear,” said Mrs. Ray, “I have such news for you!”

“So have I, mamma, news for you,” said Rachel, putting out her hand to her mother.

“I never was so warm in my life. Do let me get in; oh dear, oh dear! It’s no good looking in the basket, for when I came away from Dorothea I was too full of what I had just heard to think of buying anything.”

“What have you heard, mamma?”

“I’m sure I hope she’ll be happy; I’m sure I do. But it’s a great venture, a terribly great venture.”
===Chinese===
可雷太太满心满口都是她的故事，满心认定她的消息理应立刻独占女儿的注意，打砾石小径上头一声招呼起，话就滔滔不绝，一时间雷切尔连同她那整套幸福的故事，竟全被淹没了。

“哦，我亲爱的，”雷太太说，“我有天大的消息要告诉你！”

“我也有，妈妈，也有消息要告诉你，”雷切尔说着，向母亲伸出手去。

“我活了一辈子没这样热过。快让我进屋；哎呀，哎呀！篮子就别看了，我打多萝西娅那儿出来的时候，满脑子都是刚听见的事，把买东西忘得干干净净。”

“你听见什么了，妈妈？”

“我自然巴望她会幸福；真的巴望。可这是一场大冒险，一场大得怕人的冒险。”

===Original===
“What is it, mamma?” And Rachel, though she could not yet think that her mother’s budget could be equal in importance to her own, felt that there was that which it was necessary that she should hear.

“Your sister is going to be married to Mr. Prong.”

“Dolly?”

“Yes, my dear. It’s a great venture; but if any woman can live happy with such a man, she can do so. She’s troubled about her money;—that’s all.”

“Marry Mr. Prong! I suppose she may if she likes. Oh dear! I can’t think I shall ever like him.”

“I never spoke to him yet, so perhaps I oughtn’t to say; but he doesn’t look a nice man to my eyes. But what are looks, my dear? They’re only skin deep; we ought all of us to remember that always, Rachel; they’re only skin deep; and if, as she says, she only wants to work in the vineyard, she won’t mind his being so short. I dare say he’s honest;—at least I’m sure I hope he is.”
===Chinese===
“到底是什么呀，妈妈？”雷切尔虽然还不觉得母亲那包新闻能有她自己的那份要紧，却也感到其中有非听不可的东西。

“你姐姐要嫁给普朗先生了。”

“多莉？”

“是啊，我亲爱的。这是一场大冒险；可天下的女人要是有谁能同这样的男人过日子过得幸福，她就能。她只是在钱财的事上犯难；——不过如此。”

“嫁给普朗先生！她愿意就嫁吧，我想。哎呀！我看我这辈子也喜欢不上他。”

“我同他还没讲过话，所以这话也许不该我说；可在我眼里，他看上去不是个体面人。可相貌算什么呢，我亲爱的？相貌不过一张皮；咱们人人都该时时刻刻记住这个，雷切尔；相貌不过一张皮；再说，照她说的，她一心只要在葡萄园里做工，他个子矮不矮她不会计较的。我想他是诚实的；——至少我诚心盼着他是。”

===Original===
“I should think he’s honest, at any rate, or he wouldn’t be what he is.”

“There’s some of them are so very fond of money;—that is, if all that we hear is true. Perhaps he mayn’t care about it; let us hope that he doesn’t; but if so he’s a great exception. However, she means to have it tied up as close as possible, and I think she’s right. Where would she be if he was to go away some fine morning and leave her? You see, he’s got nobody belonging to him. I own I do like people who have got people belonging to them; you feel sure, in a sort of way, that they’ll go on living in their own houses.”

Rachel immediately reflected that Luke Rowan had people belonging to him—very nice people—and that everybody knew who he was and from whence he came.

“But she has quite made up her mind about it,” continued Mrs. Ray; “and when I saw that I didn’t say very much against it. What was the use? It isn’t as though he wasn’t quite respectable. He is a clergyman, you know, my dear, though he never was at any of the regular colleges; and he might be a bishop, just as much as if he had been; so they tell me. And I really don’t think that she would ever have come back to the cottage—not unless you had promised to have been ruled by her in everything.”

“I certainly shouldn’t have done that;” and Rachel, as she made this assurance with some little obstinacy in her voice, told herself that for the future she meant to be ruled by a very different person indeed.
===Chinese===
“我看他横竖是诚实的，不然他也就不是现在这样的人了。”

“他们那号人里头，有的把钱看得极重；——当然，这是倘若我们听来的话都属实。也许他并不在乎钱；但愿他不在乎；可若真不在乎，那他就是个天大的例外。好在她的意思是要把财产捆得越紧越好，我看她做得对。倘若哪天早上他忽然走人，把她撇下，她可怎么办？你要明白，他孤身一个，什么亲人也没有。说实在的，我就喜欢有亲有故的人；这样你多少有个底，觉得他们总会在自己家里安安稳稳住下去。”

雷切尔立刻想到，卢克·罗恩是有亲有故的人——还是顶好顶好的人——而且人人都知道他是谁、从哪儿来的。

“不过她这桩事主意已经拿定，”雷太太接着说；“我一看是这样，也就没多说什么反对的话。有什么用呢？又不能说他不够体面。他是位牧师，你知道的，我亲爱的，虽说正经的学院他一处也没进过；可他照样可能当上主教，跟进过学院的没两样；人家是这么对我说的。而且我真觉得，她本来无论如何也不会回村舍来住——除非你肯样样都答应受她的辖制。”

“这个我当然不会答应；”雷切尔这样说，话音里带着点小小的倔强，心里却暗暗对自己说，往后要来辖制她的，可是全然不同的一个人了。

===Original===
“No, I suppose not; and I’m sure I shouldn’t have asked you, because I think it isn’t the thing, dragging people away out of their own parishes, here and there, to anybody’s church. And I told her that though I would of course go and hear Mr. Prong now and then if she married him, I wouldn’t leave Mr. Comfort, not as a regular thing. But she didn’t seem to mind that now, much as she used always to be saying about it.”

“And when is it to be, mamma?”

“On Friday; that is, tomorrow.”

“Tomorrow!”
===Chinese===
“是啊，我想你不会答应；我自然也不会开口要你这样，因为把人从自己的堂区里硬拖出来，东一处西一处，赶到随便什么人的教堂去，总归不是个道理。我也对她说了，她若嫁给普朗先生，我自然偶尔也去听听普朗先生讲道，可康福特先生那边我是不会离开的，总不能拿那个当正经。如今她好像也不计较这个了，往常她可是老把这话挂在嘴上的。”

“那日子定在哪天呢，妈妈？”

“星期五；也就是说，就是明天。”

“明天！”

===Original===
“That is, she’s to go and tell him tomorrow that she means to take him—or he’s to come to her at Miss Pucker’s lodgings. It’s not to be wondered at when one sees Miss Pucker, really; and I’m not sure I’d not have done the same if I’d been living with her too; only I don’t think I ever should have begun. I think it’s living with Miss Pucker has made her do it; I do indeed, my dear. Well, now that I have told you, I suppose I may as well go and get ready for dinner.”

“I’ll come with you, mamma. The potatoes are strained, and Kitty can put the things on the table. Mamma”—and now they were on the stairs—“I’ve got something to tell also.”

We’ll leave Mrs. Ray to eat her dinner, and Rachel to tell her story, merely adding a word to say that the mother did not stint the measure of her praise, or refuse her child the happiness of her sympathy. That evening was probably the happiest of Rachel’s existence, although its full proportions of joy were marred by an unforeseen occurrence. At four o’clock a note came from Rowan to his “Dearest Rachel,” saying that he had been called away by telegraph to London about that “horrid brewery business.” He would write from there. But Rachel was almost as happy without him, talking about him, as she would have been in his presence, listening to him.
===Chinese===
“这是说，明天她要去告诉他，说她愿意要他——或者他到帕克小姐的寓所去见她。这事你见了帕克小姐本人，就真个一点儿也不奇怪了；我自己若也同她住在一处，说不定也会走上这一步；只是我想我断不会起这个头。我看就是同帕克小姐住在一起，才把她弄成这样的；真的是这样，我亲爱的。好了，话既然对你说完了，我想我不如去张罗午饭吧。”

“我陪你一起去，妈妈。土豆已经滗干了水，基蒂（Kitty）会把餐具摆上桌。妈妈”——这会儿她们正走上楼梯——“我也有件事要告诉你。”

雷太太吃她的午饭，雷切尔讲她的故事，我们就留给她们吧，只补一句话：做母亲的那份赞辞没有半点吝惜，也没有拒绝拿自己的同情给女儿添喜。那天晚上，多半是雷切尔一生中最幸福的一晚，虽说这满溢的欢喜，叫一桩没有料到的事打了折扣。四点钟，罗恩捎来一张字条，写给他“最亲爱的雷切尔”，说他接到电报，为那桩“可恶的酿酒厂事务”给叫到伦敦去了。他会从那边写信来。可是雷切尔身边没有他，嘴上谈着他，也差不多同他在跟前、听着他说话时一样幸福。

## XV Maternal Eloquence / XV 母亲的雄辩

===Original===

On the Friday morning there was a solemn conference at the brewery between Mrs. Tappitt and Mrs. Rowan. Mrs. Rowan found herself to be in some difficulty as to the line of action which she ought to take, and the alliances which she ought to form. She was passionately attached to her son, and for Mrs. Tappitt she had no strong liking. But then she was very averse to this proposed marriage with Rachel Ray, and was willing for a while to make a treaty with Mrs. Tappitt, offensive and defensive, as against her own son, if by doing so she could put a stop to so outrageous a proceeding on his part. He had seen her before he started for London, and had told her both the occurrences of the day. He had described to her how Tappitt had turned him out of the brewery, poker in hand, and how, in consequence of Tappitt’s “pigheaded obstinacy,” it was now necessary that their joint affairs should be set right by the hand of the law. He had then told her also that there was no longer any room for doubt or argument between them as regarding Rachel. He had gone out to Bragg’s End that morning, had made his offer, and had been accepted. His mother therefore would see—so he surmised—that, as any opposition on her part must now be futile, she might as well take Rachel to her heart at once. He went so far as to propose to her that she should go over to Rachel in his absence—“it would be very gracious if you could do it tomorrow, mother,” he said—and go through that little process of taking her future daughter-in-law to her heart. But in answer to this Mrs. Rowan said very little. She said very little, but she looked much. “My dear, I cannot move so quick as you do; I am older. I am afraid, however, that you have been rash.” He said something, as on such occasions young men do, as to his privilege of choosing for himself, as to his knowing what wife would suit him, as to his contempt for money, and as to the fact—“the undoubted fact,” as he declared it—and in that declaration I am prepared to go hand-in-hand with him—that Rachel Ray was a lady. But he was clearheaded enough to perceive that his mother did not intend to agree with him. “When we are married she will come round,” he said to himself, and then he took himself off by the night mail train to London.

Under these circumstances Mrs. Rowan felt that her only chance of carrying on the battle would be by means of a treaty with Mrs. Tappitt. Had the affair of the brewery stood alone, Mrs. Rowan would have ranged herself loyally on the side of her son. She would have resented the uplifting of that poker, and shown her resentment by an immediate withdrawal from the brewery. She would have said a word or two—a stately word or two—as to the justice of her son’s cause, and have carried herself and her daughter off to the inn. As things were now, her visit to the brewery must no doubt be curtailed in its duration; but in the meantime might not a blow be struck against that foolish matrimonial project—an opportune blow, and by the aid of Mrs. Tappitt? Therefore on that Friday morning, when Mr. Prong was listening with enraptured ears to Mrs. Prime’s acceptance of his suit—under certain pecuniary conditions—Mrs. Rowan and Mrs. Tappitt were sitting in conference at the brewery.

===Chinese===

礼拜五早晨，酿酒厂里举行了一场郑重其事的会谈，与会双方是罗恩太太（Mrs. Rowan）和塔皮特太太（Mrs. Tappitt）。罗恩太太发觉自己处境颇为为难：该走哪条路子，该同谁结盟，她一时拿不定主意。她对儿子爱得深切，对塔皮特太太却谈不上多大好感。可另一方面，她又一万个不愿意促成这门同雷切尔·雷（Rachel Ray）的婚事，因而愿意暂时同塔皮特太太缔结一纸攻守同盟，矛头对准自己的儿子——只要这样做能拦住他那桩骇人听闻的行径。动身去伦敦之前，他见过母亲，把那一天的两桩事都对她讲了。他向她描述了塔皮特如何手持拨火棍把他赶出酿酒厂，又如何由于塔皮特的“死脑筋犟脾气”，如今他们的共同事务非得请法律之手来拨正不可了。随后他还告诉她，关于雷切尔，他们母子之间已不容置疑、无可争辩。那天上午他去了布拉格斯恩德（Bragg’s End），求了婚，也被应允了。所以，据他揣度，他母亲自然看得明白：她再反对也是枉然，倒不如索性即刻把雷切尔搂进自己心坎。他甚至进而提议，要母亲趁他不在时到雷切尔那边走一趟——“您要是明天就去，那可太有气度了，妈妈，”他说——去履行那道小小的工序，把未来儿媳接纳进心头。对此罗恩太太却回答得极少。话说得极少，神色却表露得极多。“我亲爱的，我没法像你那样说动就动；我年岁大些。不过，我怕你行事太孟浪了。”他像这种场合的年轻人惯常那样，说了些辩白的话：他有自主择偶的权利，他知道自己配什么样的妻子，他蔑视金钱，还有那个事实——按他的说法，是“确凿无疑的事实”——在这个论断上，我乐意与他携手同心——即雷切尔·雷是位淑女。但他头脑毕竟清楚，看得出母亲并不打算赞同他。“等我们结了婚，她会回心转意的，”他心里想着，随后便搭夜班邮车去伦敦了。

在这样的情势下，罗恩太太觉得，要把这场仗打下去，唯一的指望便是同塔皮特太太结盟。倘若酿酒厂的事是孤立的，罗恩太太本会忠心耿耿地站到儿子一边。她会痛心于那记举起的拨火棍，并立即从酿酒厂抽身离去，以示愤懑。她会就儿子一方的公道说上一两句——一两句雍容得体的话——然后带着自己和女儿搬去客栈。可如今事情如此这般，她这次在酿酒厂的做客无疑得缩短时日了；不过趁着这个当口，何不朝那桩愚蠢的婚事谋划敲上一记——一记及时的打击，而且有塔皮特太太相助？于是，就在那个礼拜五早晨——普朗先生（Mr. Prong）正竖起耳朵听得心醉神迷，听普赖姆太太（Mrs. Prime）应允他的求婚——附带某些钱财上的条件——罗恩太太和塔皮特太太正坐在酿酒厂里会谈。

===Original===

They agreed together at that meeting that Rachel Ray was the head and front of the whole offence, the source of all the evil done and to be done, and the one great sinner in the matter. It was clear to Mrs. Rowan that Rachel could have no just pretensions to look for such a lover or such a husband as her son; and it was equally clear to Mrs. Tappitt that she could have had no right to seek a lover or a husband out of the brewery. If Rachel Ray had not been there all might have gone smoothly for both of them. Mrs. Tappitt did not, perhaps, argue very logically as to the brewery business, or attempt to show either to herself or to her ally that Luke Rowan would have made himself an agreeable partner if he had kept himself free from all love vagaries; but she was filled with an indefinite woman’s idea that the mischief, which she felt, had been done by Rachel Ray, and that against Rachel and Rachel’s pretensions her hand should be turned.

They resolved therefore that they would go out together and call at the cottage. Mrs. Tappitt knew, from long neighbourhood, of what stuff Mrs. Ray was made. “A very good sort of woman,” she said to Mrs. Rowan, “and not at all headstrong and perverse like her daughter. If we find the young lady there we must ask her mamma to see us alone.” To this proposition Mrs. Rowan assented, not eagerly, but with a slow, measured, dignified assent, feeling that she was derogating somewhat from her own position in allowing herself to be led by such a one as Mrs. Tappitt. It was needful that on this occasion she should act with Mrs. Tappitt and connect herself with the Tappitt interests; but all this she did with an air that distinctly claimed for herself a personal superiority. If Mrs. Tappitt did not perceive and understand this, it was her fault, and not Mrs. Rowan’s.

===Chinese===

在那次会谈中，两人一致认定：雷切尔·雷是全部罪愆的罪魁祸首，是已做和将做的一切坏事的祸源，是此事中唯一的头号罪人。罗恩太太看得很清楚：雷切尔毫无正当名分，妄图指望她儿子那样的情人、那样的丈夫；塔皮特太太看得同样清楚：她更没有道理跑到酿酒厂外面去寻情人觅丈夫。倘若没有雷切尔·雷这个人在，她们两人本可诸事顺遂。至于酿酒厂那一摊生意，塔皮特太太的议论或许不怎么合乎逻辑，也未曾向自己或向她的盟友论证：卢克·罗恩（Luke Rowan）若不沾染那些恋爱的荒唐念头，本会成为一个好相处的合伙人；但她满心充塞着一种说不清的女性成见：她感到的这场祸殃，就是雷切尔·雷闯下的，她的手就该冲着雷切尔和雷切尔的非分之想打过去。

于是两人议定，一同出门，到村舍登门拜访。塔皮特太太多年比邻而居，深知雷太太（Mrs. Ray）是哪一路人物。“人是位顶和善的女人，”她对罗恩太太说，“一点儿也不像她女儿那样又倔又拗。倘若那位小姐恰好在家，咱们务必请她妈妈单独接见。”对这个提议，罗恩太太表示了同意——并非踊跃赞同，而是缓慢、有分寸、端着架子的赞同，心里感到让自己受这样一个塔皮特太太牵着走，多少有失自己的身份。这一回她不得不与塔皮特太太携手行动，把自己同塔皮特家的利益拴在一处；但这一切她做得气度俨然，明白无误地宣示自己高人一等。塔皮特太太倘若没有觉察、没有领会这一层，那是她的不是，而不是罗恩太太的不是。

===Original===

At two o’clock they stepped into a fly at the brewery door and had themselves driven out to Bragg’s End.

“Mamma, there’s a carriage,” said Rachel.

“It can’t be coming here,” said Mrs. Ray.

“But it is; it’s the fly from the Dragon. I know it by the man’s white hat. And, oh dear, there’s Mrs. Rowan and Mrs. Tappitt! Mamma, I shall go away.” And Rachel, without another word, escaped out into the garden. She escaped, utterly heedless of her mother’s little weak prayer that she would remain. She went away quickly, so that not a skirt of her dress might be visible. She felt instantly, by instinct, that these two women had come out there especially as her enemies, as upsetters of her happiness, as opponents of her one great hope in life; and she knew that she could not fight her battle with them face to face. She could not herself maintain her love stoutly and declare her intention of keeping her lover to his word; and yet she did intend to maintain her love, not doubting that he would be true to his word without any effort on her part. Her mother would make a very poor fight—of that she was quite well aware. It would have been well if her mother could have run away also. But, as that could not be, her mother must be left to succumb, and the fight must be carried on afterwards as best it might. The two ladies remained at the cottage for about an hour, and during that time Rachel was sequestered in the garden, hardening her heart against all enemies to her love. If Luke would only stand by her, she would certainly stand by him.

===Chinese===

两点钟，两人在酿酒厂门口登上了一辆轻便出租马车，叫车夫送她们到布拉格斯恩德去。

“妈妈，来了一辆马车，”雷切尔说。

“不会是上咱们这儿来的，”雷太太说。

“可偏偏就是；是龙客栈（the Dragon）的那辆轻便马车。赶车人那顶白帽子，我一眼就认出来了。哎呀，天哪，是罗恩太太和塔皮特太太！妈妈，我要走开。”雷切尔话音未落，人就溜进了园子。她逃走了，全然不顾母亲那点软弱的小小央求——求她留下来。她走得飞快，连裙裾的一角也不让人瞧见。她凭直觉即刻感到，这两位太太是专程来跟她作对的，是来搅扰她的幸福的，是来反对她此生唯一的重大指望的；她也明白，自己没法同她们当面锣对面鼓地打这一仗。要她自己挺身捍卫爱情、宣告她决意要情人信守诺言，她做不到；然而她确实决意捍卫这份爱情，并且毫不怀疑，无需她费半分力气，他也自会言而有信。母亲会打得非常糟糕——这一点她心里清楚得很。倘若母亲也能一走了之，倒还罢了。可既然走不得，只好撇下母亲去屈服，这一仗留待日后见机再打。两位太太在村舍盘桓了约莫一个钟头，这期间雷切尔一直避在园子里，把心一横，同一切与她爱情为敌的人对抗。只要卢克站在她一边，她必定站在他一边。

===Original===

There was a good deal of ceremony between the three ladies when they first found themselves together in Mrs. Ray’s parlour. Mrs. Rowan and Mrs. Tappitt were large and stiff in their draperies, and did not fit themselves easily in among Mrs. Ray’s small belongings; and they were stately in their demeanour, conscious that they were visiting an inferior, and conscious also that they were there on no friendly mission. But the interview was commenced with a show of much civility. Mrs. Tappitt introduced Mrs. Rowan in due form, and Mrs. Rowan made her little bow, if with some self-asserting supremacy, still with fitting courtesy. Mrs. Ray hoped that Mrs. Tappitt and the young ladies were quite well, and then there was a short silence, very oppressive to Mrs. Ray, but refreshing rather than otherwise to Mrs. Rowan. It gave a proper business aspect to the visit, and paved the way for serious words.

“Miss Rachel is out, I suppose,” said Mrs. Tappitt.

“Yes, she is out,” said Mrs. Ray. “But she’s about the place somewhere, if you want to see her.” This she added in her weakness, not knowing how she was to sustain the weight of such an interview alone.

===Chinese===

三位太太头一回同处雷太太的客厅时，彼此之间客套了许多。罗恩太太和塔皮特太太衣饰宽大挺括，在雷太太那些小巧的家什中间坐得很不舒展；她们举止端庄，心里明白自己是来拜访一个低自己一头的人，也明白自己此来并非友好的差事。不过会谈开场时还是摆出了十足的客气。塔皮特太太按正式礼数引见了罗恩太太，罗恩太太微微欠身还礼，虽说带着几分自我标榜的居高临下，却也合乎礼节。雷太太问候塔皮特太太和几位小姐身体可好，随后出现了一阵短短的沉默，雷太太觉得压抑得很，罗恩太太却觉得正中下怀、神清气爽。这一阵沉默给这次登门添上了正当的公事气象，为正经话铺平了道路。

“雷切尔小姐出门了吧，我猜，”塔皮特太太说。

“是啊，出门了，”雷太太说。“不过就在这宅子附近什么地方，你们要是想见她的话。”这句添话是她在软弱中加上的，她不知道这样的场面，自己一个人怎么扛得住。

===Original===

“Perhaps it is as well that she should be away just at present,” said Mrs. Rowan, firmly but mildly.

“Quite as well,” said Mrs. Tappitt, as firmly, but less mildly.

“Because we wish to say a few words to you, Mrs. Ray,” said Mrs. Rowan.

“That is what has brought us out so early,” said Mrs. Tappitt. It was only half-past two now, and company visiting was never done at Baslehurst till after three. “We want to say a few words to you, Mrs. Ray, about a very serious matter. I’m sure you know how glad I’ve always been to see Rachel with my girls, and I had her at our party the other night, you know. It isn’t likely therefore that I should be disposed to say anything unkind about her.”

===Chinese===

“眼下她不在场，或许倒好，”罗恩太太说，语气坚定，却还温和。

“再好不过，”塔皮特太太说，同样坚定，却不那么温和。

“因为我们想同您说几句话，雷太太，”罗恩太太说。

“为的就是这个缘故，我们才这么早登门，”塔皮特太太说。这时才两点半，在巴斯尔赫斯特（Baslehurst），拜访客人向来要过三点才算合规矩。“我们想同您谈一件十分要紧的事，雷太太。您一定知道，雷切尔同我家几个姑娘来往，我素来多高兴；前几天晚上的聚会，我还请了她在场，您是知道的。所以说，我断不会存心说她什么难听的话。”

===Original===

“At any rate not to me, I hope,” said Mrs. Ray.

“Not to anybody. Indeed I’m not given to say unkind things about people. No one in Baslehurst would give me that character. But the fact is, Mrs. Ray—”

“Perhaps, Mrs. Tappitt, you’ll allow me,” said Mrs. Rowan. “He’s my son.”

===Chinese===

“至少当着我的面不说，我希望，”雷太太说。

“对谁都不说。说实在的，我这个人从不爱讲人家难听的话。巴斯尔赫斯特没有一个人会给我那样的口碑。可是实情是，雷太太——”

“塔皮特太太，恕我插一句，”罗恩太太说。“他是我的儿子。”

===Original===

“Oh, yes, certainly;—that is, if you wish it,” said Mrs. Tappitt, drawing herself up in her chair; “but I thought that perhaps, as I knew Miss Ray so well—”

“If you don’t mind, Mrs. Tappitt—” and Mrs. Rowan, as she again took the words out of her friend’s mouth, smiled upon her with a smile of great efficacy.

“Oh, dear, certainly not,” said Mrs. Tappitt, acknowledging by her concession the superiority of Mrs. Rowan’s nature.

===Chinese===

“哦，是，当然；——就是说，只要您愿意，”塔皮特太太说，在椅子里把身子坐直了；“可我原想着，也许，我跟雷切尔小姐这么熟——”

“要是您不介意的话，塔皮特太太——”罗恩太太又一次从盟友嘴里截走了话头，同时朝她嫣然一笑，那笑容效力非凡。

“哦，亲爱的，当然不介意，”塔皮特太太说，用这一番退让承认了罗恩太太气性的优越。

===Original===

“I believe you are aware, Mrs. Ray,” said Mrs. Rowan, “that Mr. Luke Rowan is my son.”

“Yes, I’m aware of that.”

“And I’m afraid you must be aware also that there have been some—some—some talkings as it were, between him and your daughter.”

“Oh, yes. The truth is, ma’am, that he has offered himself to my girl, and that she has accepted him. Whether it’s for good or for bad, the open truth is the best, Mrs. Tappitt.”

===Chinese===

“我想您是知道的，雷太太，”罗恩太太说，“卢克·罗恩先生是我的儿子。”

“是的，我知道。”

“而且我怕您一定也知道，他同您女儿之间，有过一些——一些——可以说是几番言谈吧。”

“哦，是的。实话跟您说，夫人，他向我女儿求了婚，她也应允了他。是好是歹且不论，把实情摆在明处最好，塔皮特太太。”

===Original===

“Truth is truth,” said Mrs. Tappitt; “and deception is not truth.”

“I didn’t think it had gone anything so far as that,” said Mrs. Rowan—who at the moment, perhaps, forgot that deception is not truth; “and in saying that he has actually offered himself, you may perhaps—without meaning it, of course—be attributing a more positive significance to his word than he has intended.”

“God forbid!” said Mrs. Ray very solemnly. “That would be a very sad thing for my poor girl. But I think, Mrs. Rowan, you had better ask him. If he says he didn’t intend it, of course there will be an end of it, as far as Rachel is concerned.”

“I can’t ask him just at present,” said Mrs. Rowan, “because he has gone up to London. He went away yesterday afternoon, and there’s no saying when he may be in Baslehurst again.”

===Chinese===

“实话就是实话，”塔皮特太太说；“哄骗可不是实话。”

“我没想到事情已经闹到了这般地步，”罗恩太太说——这一刻她也许忘了哄骗可不是实话；“您说他确确实实求了婚，这么说，您也许——当然是无心的——把他那句话的分量坐实过了头，超出了他本来的意思。”

“上天不容！”雷太太说得极其郑重。“那样的话，我可怜的女儿就惨了。不过我想，罗恩太太，您最好去问他。他若说他没有那个意思，那自然就此作罢，就雷切尔这边而言。”

“眼下我没法问他，”罗恩太太说，“因为他上伦敦去了。他是昨天下午走的，什么时候再回巴斯尔赫斯特，谁也说不准。”

===Original===

“If ever—,” said Mrs. Tappitt, very solemnly. “Perhaps he has not told you, Mrs. Ray, that that partnership between him and Mr. T. is all over.”

“He did tell us that there had been words between him and Mr. Tappitt.”

“Words indeed!” said Mrs. Tappitt.

“And therefore it isn’t so easy to ask him,” said Mrs. Rowan, ignoring Mrs. Tappitt and the partnership. “But of course, Mrs. Ray, our object in this matter must be the same. We both wish to see our children happy and respectable.” Mrs. Rowan, as she said this, put great emphasis on the last word.

===Chinese===

“若是有回来那一天的话——，”塔皮特太太说，神色极其庄重。“他也许还没告诉您吧，雷太太：他同 T. 先生那桩合伙买卖，已经彻底告吹了。”

“他倒是跟我们说过，他同塔皮特先生之间有过口角。”

“口角！说得倒真轻巧！”塔皮特太太说。

“所以问他就不那么容易了，”罗恩太太说，把塔皮特太太和合伙的事全然撇在一边。“不过当然，雷太太，在这件事上，我们的目标总归是一致的。我们都盼望自己的孩子又幸福又体面。”罗恩太太说到末一个词时，特意把语气压得格外重。

===Original===

“As to my girl, I’ve no fear whatever but what she’ll be respectable,” said Mrs. Ray, with more heat than Mrs. Tappitt had thought her to possess.

“No doubt; no doubt. But what I’m coming to is this, Mrs. Ray; here has this boy of mine been behaving foolishly to your daughter, as young men will do. It may be that he has really said something to her of the kind you suppose—”

“Said something to her! Why, ma’am, he came out here and asked my permission to pay his addresses to her, which I didn’t answer because just at that moment Rachel came in from Farmer Sturt’s opposite—”

“Farmer Sturt’s!” said Mrs. Tappitt to Mrs. Rowan, in an under voice and nodding her head. Whereupon Mrs. Rowan nodded her head also. One of the great accusations made against Mrs. Ray had been that she lived on the Farmer Sturt level, and not on the Tappitt level;—much less on the Rowan level.

“Yes—from Farmer Sturt’s,” continued Mrs. Ray, not at all understanding this byplay. “So I didn’t give him any answer at all.”

===Chinese===

“至于我姑娘，她横竖会规规矩矩做人，这一点我半点儿不担心，”雷太太说，那股火气大出塔皮特太太的意料。

“自然，自然。不过我要说的是这个意思，雷太太：瞧我这个儿子，对您女儿举止糊涂孟浪，年轻人免不了来这一套。也许他真对她说了一些您猜想的那一类话——”

“说了些话！哎呀，夫人，他亲自到这儿来，求我允准他向我女儿求婚，这话我还没来得及答，正赶上那一刻雷切尔从对门斯特特农场（Farmer Sturt’s）回来了——”

“斯特特农场！”塔皮特太太压低了嗓门对罗恩太太说，一面点头。罗恩太太也跟着点了点头。原来外界攻讦雷太太的一大罪名，便是她过的是斯特特农场那一档的日子，而不是塔皮特家那一档；——更不必说罗恩家那一档了。

“是啊——从斯特特农场回来，”雷太太接着说，对这一番眉眼官司全然不解。“所以我根本没给他任何答复。”

===Original===

“You wouldn’t encourage him,” said Mrs. Rowan.

“I don’t know about that; but at any rate he encouraged himself, for he came again the next morning when I was in Baslehurst.”

“I hope Miss Rachel didn’t know he was coming in your absence,” said Mrs. Rowan.

“It would look so sly;—wouldn’t it?” said Mrs. Tappitt.

“No, she didn’t, and she isn’t sly at all. If she had known anything she would have told me. I know what my girl is, Mrs. Rowan, and I can depend on her.” Mrs. Ray’s courage was up, and she was inclined to fight bravely, but she was sadly impeded by tears, which she now found it impossible to control.

===Chinese===

“您没有鼓励过他，”罗恩太太说。

“这个我说不好；可不管怎么说，他自己给自己壮了胆，因为第二天早晨趁我去了巴斯尔赫斯特，他又来了。”

“我希望雷切尔小姐并不知道他趁您不在会上门来，”罗恩太太说。

“那可显得太鬼鬼祟祟了；——可不是吗？”塔皮特太太说。

“她不知道，她也一点儿不鬼祟。她但凡知道点什么，准会告诉我。我姑娘是什么样的人我清楚，罗恩太太，我信得过她。”雷太太的勇气提了上来，一心想勇敢地打这一仗，却苦于泪水碍事，这会儿她怎么也止不住眼泪。

===Original===

“I’m sure it isn’t my wish to distress you,” said Mrs. Rowan.

“It does distress me very much, then, for anybody to say that Rachel is sly.”

“I said I hoped she wasn’t sly,” said Mrs. Tappitt.

“I heard what you said,” continued Mrs. Ray; “and I don’t see why you should be speaking against Rachel in that way. The young man isn’t your son.”

“No,” said Mrs. Tappitt, “indeed he’s not;—nor yet he ain’t Mr. Tappitt’s partner.”

===Chinese===

“我确信自己决没有让您伤心的意思，”罗恩太太说。

“那这话可真叫我难受得很了——谁说雷切尔鬼祟，我都难受。”

“我说的是我希望她不鬼祟，”塔皮特太太说。

“你说的话我听见了，”雷太太接着说；“我不明白你干吗要那样说雷切尔的坏话。那个年轻人又不是你儿子。”

“可不是，”塔皮特太太说，“他确实不是；——也不是塔皮特先生的合伙人呢。”

===Original===

“Nor wishes to be,” said Mrs. Rowan, with a toss of her head. It was a thousand pities that Mrs. Ray had not her wits enough about her to have fanned into a fire of battle the embers which glowed hot between her two enemies. Had she done so they might probably have been made to consume each other—to her great comfort. “Nor wishes to be!” Then Mrs. Rowan paused a moment, and Mrs. Tappitt assumed a smile which was intended to indicate incredulity. “But Mrs. Ray,” continued Mrs. Rowan, “that is neither here nor there. Luke Rowan is my son, and I certainly have a right to speak. Such a marriage as this would be very imprudent on his part, and very disagreeable to me. From the way in which things have turned out it’s not likely that he’ll settle himself at Baslehurst.”

“The most unlikely thing in the world,” said Mrs. Tappitt. “I don’t suppose he’ll ever show himself in Baslehurst again.”

“As for showing himself, Mrs. Tappitt, my son will never be ashamed of showing himself anywhere.”

“But he won’t have any call to come to Baslehurst, Mrs. Rowan. That’s what I mean.”

“If he’s a gentleman of his word, as I take him to be,” said Mrs. Ray, “he’ll have a great call to show himself. He never can have intended to come out here, and speak to her in that way, and ask her to marry him, and then never to come back and see her any more! I wouldn’t believe it of him, not though his own mother said it!”

===Chinese===

“他也并不想当，”罗恩太太说着，把头一扬。顶可惜的是，雷太太竟然慌得没了主意，不懂得把她两个对头之间烧得正炽的余烬扇成一片战火。她若扇了，这两位多半能互相烧个干净——她也乐得清静。“他并不想当！”接着罗恩太太顿了顿，塔皮特太太脸上挂起一副意在表示难以置信的笑。“不过雷太太，”罗恩太太接着说，“这与本题不相干。卢克·罗恩是我的儿子，我自然有权说话。这样一桩婚事，于他是极不慎重的，于我是极不痛快的。照眼下事情的走向看，他多半不会在巴斯尔赫斯特安家落户了。”

“天底下再没有比这更不可能的事了，”塔皮特太太说。“依我看，他再也不会在巴斯尔赫斯特露面了。”

“说到露面，塔皮特太太，我儿子走到哪儿露面都不会害臊。”

“可他不会再有什么缘由上巴斯尔赫斯特来了，罗恩太太。我说的是这个意思。”

“他若是个守信用的人——我看他是——”雷太太说，“那他就大有个缘由要来露面。他总不至于存心到这儿来，那样同她说话，求她嫁给他，然后从此不再回来见她！这样的事我不信是他做的，哪怕他亲娘亲口这么说，我也不信！”

===Original===

“I don’t say anything,” said Mrs. Rowan, who felt that her position was one of some difficulty. “But we all do know that in affairs of that kind young men do allow themselves to go great lengths. And the greater lengths they go, Mrs. Ray, the more particular the young ladies ought to be.”

“But what’s a young lady to do? How’s she to know whether a young man is in earnest, or whether he’s only going lengths, as you call it?” Mrs. Ray’s eyes were still moist with tears; and, I grieve to say that though, as far as immediate words are concerned, she was fighting Rachel’s battle not badly, still the blows of the enemy were taking effect upon her. She was beginning to wish that Luke Rowan had never been seen, or his name heard, at Bragg’s End.

“I think it’s quite understood in the world,” said Mrs. Rowan, “that a young lady is not to take a gentleman at his first word.”

“Oh, quite,” said Mrs. Tappitt.

“We’ve all of us daughters,” said Mrs. Rowan.

===Chinese===

“我什么也没说，”罗恩太太说，她觉得自己的处境有些为难。“不过我们大家都明白，那一类的事情上，年轻人是会放纵自己走得很远的。他们走得越远，雷太太，做小姐的就该越加检点。”

“可小姐又该怎么办呢？她怎么知道一个年轻人是真心实意，还是照您的说法，只在放任胡来呢？”雷太太眼里还噙着泪水；说来痛心，尽管单就眼下的言辞而论，她替雷切尔打的这一仗并不算差，敌人的拳脚却已在她身上见效了。她开始巴望卢克·罗恩从没在布拉格斯恩德露过面，名字也从没被人听见过。

“我想世上的规矩是明摆着的，”罗恩太太说，“小姐不该把绅士的头一句话就信以为真。”

“哦，可不是，”塔皮特太太说。

“我们人人都有女儿，”罗恩太太说。

===Original===

“Yes, all of us,” said Mrs. Tappitt. “That’s what makes it so fitting that we should discuss this matter together in a friendly feeling.”

“My son is a very good young man—a very good young man indeed.”

“But a little hasty, perhaps,” said Mrs. Tappitt.

“If you’ll allow me, Mrs. Tappitt.”

“Oh, certainly, Mrs. Rowan.”

===Chinese===

“是啊，人人都有，”塔皮特太太说。“正因为这样，咱们抱着一团和气，一道来商量这件事，才格外名正言顺。”

“我儿子是个非常好的年轻人——实实在在非常好的年轻人。”

“不过也许性子急了些，”塔皮特太太说。

“塔皮特太太，请容我接着说。”

“哦，您请便，罗恩太太。”

===Original===

“A very good young man indeed; and I don’t think it at all probable that in such a matter as this he will act in opposition to his mother’s wishes. He has his way to make in the world.”

“Which will never be in the brewery line,” said Mrs. Tappitt.

“He has his way to make in the world,” continued Mrs. Rowan, with much severity; “and if he marries in four or five years’ time, that will be quite as soon as he ought to think of doing. I’m sure you will agree with me, Mrs. Ray, that long engagements are very bad, particularly for the lady.”

“He wanted to be married next month,” said Mrs. Ray.

“Ah, yes; that shows that the whole thing couldn’t come to much. If there was an engagement at all, it must be a very long one. Years must roll by.” From the artistic manner in which Mrs. Rowan allowed her voice to dwell upon the words which signified duration of space, any hope of a marriage between Luke and Rachel seemed to be put off at any rate to some future century. “Years must roll by, and we all know what that means. The lady dies of a broken heart, while the gentleman lives in a bachelor’s rooms, and dines always at his club. Nobody can wish such a state of things as that, Mrs. Ray.”

===Chinese===

“实实在在是个非常好的年轻人；并且我以为，在这一类事情上，他绝不可能违逆他母亲的心愿行事。他还有自己的前程要去闯。”

“而他的前程，绝不会在酿酒这一行里，”塔皮特太太说。

“他还有自己的前程要去闯，”罗恩太太接着说，神色十分凛然；“倘若他四五年后成婚，那已经够早的了。我相信您一定赞同我，雷太太：订婚拖得太久是极糟糕的事，尤其对女方。”

“他原来想下个月就结婚，”雷太太说。

“啊，是啊；这恰恰表明这件事成不了什么大气候。真要订婚的话，那也得是一桩极长的婚约。岁月总得一年一年地流转过去。”罗恩太太让嗓音在那些表示时光绵延的字眼上流连不去，做派何等讲究，卢克和雷切尔结合的希望，简直被她一推推到了未来某个世纪。“岁月总得一年一年地流转过去，而我们都知道那意味着什么。小姐伤心碎骨而死，绅士却住着单身汉的寓所，顿顿上俱乐部用饭。那样的局面，雷太太，谁也不愿意见到。”

===Original===

“I knew a girl who was engaged for seven years,” said Mrs. Tappitt, “and she wore herself to a thread-paper—so she did. And then he married his housekeeper after all.”

“I’d sooner see my girl make up her mind to be an old maid than let her have a long engagement,” said Mrs. Rowan.

“And so would I, my girls, all three. If anybody comes, I say to them, ‘Let your papa see them. He’ll know what’s the meaning of it.’ It don’t do for young girls to manage those things all themselves. Not but what I think my girls have almost as much wit about them as I have. I won’t mention any names, but there’s a young man about here as well-to-do as any young man in the South Hams, but Cherry won’t as much as look at him.” Mrs. Rowan again tossed her head. She felt her misfortune in being burdened with such a colleague as Mrs. Tappitt.

===Chinese===

“我认得一个姑娘，婚订了七年，”塔皮特太太说，“把自己熬得瘦成了一根纸捻——真的，瘦成一根纸捻。到头来那人却娶了他的女管家。”

“我宁可见我女儿拿定主意当老姑娘，也不让她订那样长长的婚约，”罗恩太太说。

“我也是这么想，我家三个姑娘都是这样。有谁来提亲，我就对她们说：‘让你们爸爸去见客。他懂这里头的门道。’年轻姑娘自家张罗这些事，总归不妥。当然喽，我也并非不觉得我家几个姑娘的心眼儿差不多不输给我。名字我不点了，咱们这一带有位年轻人，论家底不输南哈姆斯（South Hams）随便哪一位年轻人，可彻丽（Cherry）连正眼也不肯瞧他一瞧。”罗恩太太又把头一扬。她深深感到，摊上塔皮特太太这样一位同道共事，实在是她的不幸。

===Original===

“What is it you want me to do, Mrs. Rowan?” asked Mrs. Ray.

“I want you and your daughter, who I am sure is a very nice young lady, and good-looking too—”

“Oh, quite so,” said Mrs. Tappitt.

“I want you both to understand that this little thing should be allowed to drop. If my boy has done anything foolish I’m here to apologize for him. He isn’t the first that has been foolish, and I’m afraid he won’t be the last. But it can’t be believed, Mrs. Ray, that marriages should be run up in this thoughtless sort of way. In the first place the young people don’t know anything of each other; absolutely nothing at all. And then—but I’m sure I don’t want to insist on any differences that there may be in their positions in life. Only you must be aware of this, Mrs. Ray, that such a marriage as that would be very injurious to a young man like my son Luke.”

===Chinese===

“您究竟要我做什么呢，罗恩太太？”雷太太问。

“我要您和您女儿——我相信令嫒是位极好的小姐，人也长得好看——”

“哦，一点不错，”塔皮特太太说。

“我要你们母女俩都明白，这件小事应当听任它就此作罢。我儿子若做了什么糊涂事，我在这里替他赔不是。做糊涂事的，他不是头一个，我怕也不会是最后一个。可是雷太太，婚姻大事怎么能这样轻率地撮合起来，这是叫人无法相信的。首先，这两个年轻人彼此毫无了解；压根儿毫无了解。再者——不过我确信，我不必执意去强调两人在身份地位上可能有的差别。只是您必须明白这一点，雷太太：那样一桩婚事，对我儿子卢克这样的年轻人是极为有害的。”

===Original===

“My child wouldn’t wish to injure anybody.”

“And therefore, of course, she won’t think any more about it. All I want from you is that you should promise me that.”

“If Rachel will only just say that,” said Mrs. Tappitt, “my daughters will be as happy to see her out walking with them as ever.”

“Rachel has had quite enough of such walking, Mrs. Tappitt; quite enough.”

“If harm has come of it, it hasn’t been the fault of my girls,” said Mrs. Tappitt.

===Chinese===

“我的孩子是不愿伤害什么人的。”

“所以，她自然不会再把这事放在心上了。我要您应允我的，也就是这一条。”

“只要雷切尔肯说一句这样的话，”塔皮特太太说，“我家几个姑娘看见她照旧同她们一道出去走走，还会像从前一样高兴。”

“雷切尔那样的走走已经受够了，塔皮特太太；受够了。”

“倘若这里头出了什么坏事，那可怪不到我家姑娘们头上，”塔皮特太太说。

===Original===

Then there was a pause among the three ladies, and it appeared that Mrs. Rowan was waiting for Mrs. Ray’s answer. But Mrs. Ray did not know what answer she should make. She was already disposed to regard the coming of Luke Rowan to Baslehurst as a curse rather than a blessing. She felt all but convinced that Fate would be against her and hers in that matter. She had ever been afraid of young men, believing them to be dangerous, bringers of trouble into families, roaring lions sometimes, and often wolves in sheep’s clothing. Since she had first heard of Luke Rowan in connection with her daughter she had been trembling. If she could have acted in accordance with her own feelings at this moment, she would have begged that Luke Rowan’s name might never again be mentioned in her presence. It would be better for them, she thought, to bear what had already come upon them, than to run further risk. But she could not give any answer to Mrs. Rowan without consulting Rachel;—she could not at least give any such answer as that contemplated without doing so. She had sanctioned Rachel’s love, and could not now undertake to oppose it. Rachel had probably been deceived, and must bear her misfortune. But, as the question stood at present between her and her daughter, she could not at once accede to Mrs. Rowan’s views in the matter. “I will talk to Rachel,” she said.

“Give her my kindest respects,” said Mrs. Rowan; “and pray make her understand that I wouldn’t interfere if I didn’t think it was for both their advantages. Goodbye, Mrs. Ray.” And Mrs. Rowan got up.

“Goodbye, Mrs. Ray,” said Mrs. Tappitt, putting out her hand. “Give my love to Rachel. I hope that we shall be good friends yet, for all that has come and gone.”

But Mrs. Ray would not accept Mrs. Tappitt’s hand, nor would she vouchsafe any answer to Mrs. Tappitt’s amenities. “Goodbye, ma’am,” she said to Mrs. Rowan. “I suppose you mean to do the best you can by your own child.”

===Chinese===

于是三位太太之间静了片刻，看来罗恩太太是在等雷太太的回答。可雷太太不知道该怎么回答才好。她本来已经倾向于把卢克·罗恩来到巴斯尔赫斯特看作一场灾祸，而非福分。她几乎深信，在这件事上，命运存心要跟她和她的一家作对。她向来怕年轻男人，认定他们危险，是往人家家里带祸殃的，有时是吼叫的狮子，更多时候是披着羊皮的狼。打头一回听说卢克·罗恩同她女儿牵连到一处，她就一直在发抖。此刻她若是能依着自己的心性行事，就会哀求从此再不许人在她面前提卢克·罗恩的名字。她想，已经落到头上的，认下来扛过去，总比再往前冒险好。可是不经雷切尔同意，她没法对罗恩太太作任何答复；——至少，她心中盘算的那一种答复，不经她同意是给不出的。她曾认可了雷切尔的爱情，如今不能翻脸出来反对。雷切尔多半是受了哄骗，那这份不幸她认了就是。可是，就眼下她同女儿之间这件事的格局而论，她也不能即刻便依了罗恩太太的主张。“我去同雷切尔谈谈，”她说。

“请代我向她致以最恳切的问候，”罗恩太太说；“并务请让她明白，我若不是认定这于他们两人都有好处，是断断不肯来干涉的。再会了，雷太太。”罗恩太太站起身来。

“再会了，雷太太，”塔皮特太太说着伸出手去。“替我问雷切尔好。经过这些风风雨雨，我还是盼望咱们往后能做好朋友。”

可雷太太不肯接塔皮特太太的手，对她那些客套也不肯赏半句回音。“再会了，夫人，”她对罗恩太太说。“我想，您是要尽力为您自己的孩子打算的。”

===Original===

“And by yours too,” said Mrs. Rowan.

“If so, I can only say that you must think very badly of your own son. Goodbye, ma’am.” Then Mrs. Ray curtseyed them out—not without a certain amount of dignity, although her eyes were red with tears, and her whole body trembling with dismay.

Very little was said in the fly between the two ladies on their way back to the brewery, nor did Mrs. Rowan remain very long as a visitor at Mrs. Tappitt’s house. She had found herself compelled by circumstances to take a part inimical to Mrs. Ray, but she felt in her heart a much stronger animosity to Mrs. Tappitt. With Mrs. Ray she could have been very friendly, only for that disastrous love affair; but with Mrs. Tappitt she could not again put herself into pleasant relations. I must point out how sadly unfortunate it was that Mrs. Ray had not known how to fan that flame of anger to her own and her daughter’s advantage.

===Chinese===

“也为您的孩子，”罗恩太太说。

“倘若如此，我只能说，您把您自己的儿子也看得忒坏了。再会了，夫人。”随后雷太太屈膝万福，把两位送出门去——那礼数自有一番气度，尽管她两眼哭得通红，浑身惊惶得直打颤。

回酿酒厂的一路上，两位太太在车中几乎没有说什么话；此后罗恩太太在塔皮特太太府上做客，也没有再久留。她发觉自己迫于情势，扮演了一个同雷太太为敌的角色，可她心底里对塔皮特太太的憎恶要强烈得多。若不是那桩倒霉的恋爱风波，她本可以同雷太太处得非常亲善；而对塔皮特太太，她是再也无法重新相处融洽了。我不能不指出：雷太太竟不知道如何把那股怒火扇向于自己和女儿有利的地方去，实在是令人痛惜的不幸。

===Original===

“Well, mamma,” said Rachel, returning to the room as soon as she heard the wheels of the fly in motion upon the road across the green. She found her mother in tears—hardly able to speak because of her sobs. “Never mind it, mamma: of course I know the kind of things they have been saying. It was what I expected. Never mind it.”

“But, my dear, you will be brokenhearted.”

“Brokenhearted! Why?”

===Chinese===

“怎么样，妈妈，”雷切尔说。她一听见车轮碾过绿地对面大路的动静，就回到了屋里。只见母亲泪流满面——哭得几乎说不出话。“别往心里去，妈妈：她们说的那一类话，我当然知道。我早料到了。别往心里去。”

“可是，我的乖乖，你会心碎的。”

“心碎！为什么？”

===Original===

“I know you will. Now that you have learned to love him, you’ll never bear to lose him.”

“And must I lose him?”

“She says so. She says that he doesn’t mean it, and that it’s all nonsense.”

“I don’t believe her. Nothing shall make me believe that, mamma.”

“She says it would be ruinous to all his prospects, especially just now when he has quarrelled about this brewery.”

“Ruinous to him!”

===Chinese===

“我知道你会。你如今已经学会了爱他，往后要失掉他，你受不住的。”

“那我非失掉他不可吗？”

“她这么说。她说他并没有那个意思，说这统统是胡闹。”

“我不信她。妈妈，说什么也不能叫我相信这个。”

“她说这会毁了他所有的前程，眼下他正为这酿酒厂的事闹翻了，尤其如此。”

“毁了他的前程！”

===Original===

“His mother says so.”

“I will never wish him to do anything that shall be ruinous to himself; never;—not though I were brokenhearted, as you call it.”

“Ah, that is it, Rachel, my darling; I wish he had not come here.”

Rachel went away across the room and looked out of the window upon the green. There she stood in silence for a few minutes while her mother was wiping her eyes and suppressing her sobs. Tears also had run down Rachel’s cheeks; but they were silent tears, few in number and very salt. “I cannot bring myself to wish that yet,” said she.

===Chinese===

“他妈妈是这么说的。”

“我永远不会巴望他去做任何毁掉自己的事；永远不会；——哪怕照你的说法，我会心碎。”

“唉，正是这样啊，雷切尔，我的心肝；我巴不得他从来没来过这里。”

雷切尔穿过屋子走到窗前，望着窗外的绿地。她在那儿默默站了几分钟，母亲在一旁擦着眼睛，压着呜咽。泪水也从雷切尔的腮上淌过；可那是无声的泪，数目不多，咸得厉害。“至少眼下，我还没法巴望那样的事，”她说。

===Original===

“But he has gone away, and what can you do if he does not come again?”

“Do! Oh, I can do nothing. I could do nothing, even though he were here in Baslehurst every day of his life. If I once thought that he didn’t wish me—to—be—his wife, I should not want to do anything. But, mamma, I can’t believe it of him. It was only yesterday that he was here.”

“They say that young men don’t care what they say in that way nowadays.”

===Chinese===

“可他已经走了，他若是不再来，你又有什么办法呢？”

“办法！唉，我什么办法也没有。纵使他天天都在巴斯尔赫斯特，我也还是没有办法。我一旦想到他并不愿意我——做——做他的妻子，我就什么也不想做了。可是，妈妈，我不能相信他会这样。昨天他才来过这儿。”

“人家说，如今的年轻男人，那种话张嘴就来，根本不当回事。”

===Original===

“I don’t believe it of him, mamma; his manner is so steadfast, and his voice sounds so true.”

“But then she is so terribly against it.”

Then again they were silent for a while, after which Rachel ended the conversation. “It is clear, at any rate, that you and I can do nothing, mamma. If she expects me to say that I will give him up, she is mistaken. Give him up! I couldn’t give him up, without being false to him. I don’t think I’ll ever be false to him. If he’s false to me, then—then, I must bear it. Mamma, don’t say anything to Dolly about this just at present.” In answer to which request Mrs. Ray promised that she would not at present say anything to Mrs. Prime about Mrs. Rowan’s visit.

The following day and the Sunday were not passed in much happiness by the two ladies at Bragg’s End. Tidings reached them that Mrs. Rowan and her daughter were going to London on the Monday, but no letter came to them from Luke. By the Monday morning Mrs. Ray had quite made up her mind that Luke Rowan was lost to them forever, and Rachel had already become worn with care. During that Saturday and Sunday nothing was seen of Mrs. Prime at Bragg’s End.

===Chinese===

“我不信他会这样，妈妈；他的神气那么坚稳，他的声音听着那么真。”

“可是她反对得那么凶啊。”

随后母女俩又静了一会儿，雷切尔收束了这场谈话。“至少有一点是明白的，妈妈：你我都是没有办法的。她若是指望我亲口说我愿意放弃他，那她看错了人。放弃他！除非背弃他，我才做得到放弃他。我不会背弃他的。他若背弃我，那——那也只好由我担着。妈妈，这件事眼下先别同多莉（Dolly）提。”对这个央求，雷太太应允了：暂时不会向普赖姆太太提罗恩太太来访的事。

第二天和礼拜日，布拉格斯恩德的母女俩过得都不怎么快活。有消息传来说，罗恩太太和她女儿礼拜一要去伦敦，卢克却一封信也没有来。到了礼拜一早晨，雷太太已经拿定了主意：卢克·罗恩是她们永远失去的人了；雷切尔也已愁损了形容。那个礼拜六和礼拜日，布拉格斯恩德始终不见普赖姆太太的踪影。

## XVI Rachel Ray’s First Love-Letter / XVI 雷切尔·雷的第一封情书

===Original===
On the Monday evening, after tea, Mrs. Prime came out to the cottage. It was that Monday on which Mrs. Rowan and her daughter had left Baslehurst and had followed Luke up to London. She came out and sat with her mother and sister for about an hour, restraining herself with much discretion from the saying of disagreeable things about her sister’s lover. She had heard that the Rowans had gone away, and she had also heard that it was probable that they would be no more seen in Baslehurst. Mr. Prong had given it as his opinion that Luke would not trouble them again by his personal appearance among them. Under these circumstances Mrs. Prime had thought that she might spare her sister. Nor had she said much about her own love affairs. She had never mentioned Mr. Prong’s offer in Rachel’s presence; nor did she do so now. As long as Rachel remained in the room the conversation was very innocent and very uninteresting. For a few minutes the two widows were alone together, and then Mrs. Prime gave her mother to understand that things were not yet quite arranged between herself and Mr. Prong.

“You see, mother,” said Mrs. Prime, “as this money has been committed to my charge, I do not think it can be right to let it go altogether out of my own hands.”

In answer to this Mrs. Ray had uttered a word or two agreeing with her daughter. She was afraid to say much against Mr. Prong;—was afraid, indeed, to express any very strong opinion about this proposed marriage; but in her heart she would have been delighted to hear that the Prong alliance was to be abandoned. There was nothing in Mr. Prong to recommend him to Mrs. Ray.

===Chinese===
星期一傍晚，喝过茶之后，普赖姆太太（Mrs. Prime）到村舍这边来了。正是那个星期一，罗恩太太（Mrs. Rowan）带着女儿离开了巴斯尔赫斯特（Baslehurst），追着卢克（Luke）上伦敦去了。她来陪母亲和妹妹坐了约莫一个钟头，处处极有分寸地克制着自己，不去说她妹妹那位情人的不好。她已听说罗恩家的人走了，还听说他们多半不会再在巴斯尔赫斯特露面了。普朗先生（Mr. Prong）发表过他的意见，说卢克不会再屈尊亲自露面，到他们中间来搅扰了。既然如此，普赖姆太太便觉得可以饶妹妹这一遭。她自己恋爱上的事，也没有多说什么。普朗先生的求婚，她从未当着雷切尔的面提起过；这回也没有提。只要雷切尔还在屋里，谈话便非常清白无邪，也非常乏味。有那么几分钟，两个寡妇单独待在一起，普赖姆太太这才让母亲明白：她同普朗先生之间的事，还没有完全说定。

“您瞧，妈妈，”普赖姆太太说，“这笔钱既然托付到了我手里，我就觉得，若让它整个儿脱出我自己的掌管，恐怕不妥。”

听了这话，雷太太（Mrs. Ray）应了一言半语，表示赞同女儿。她不敢多说普朗先生的坏话；——说实话，对这门提出来的婚事，她连一句态度鲜明的话也不敢讲；可心里头，若是听说普朗家这门亲事就此作罢，她定会满心欢喜。普朗先生身上，没有半点能让雷太太看得中的地方。

===Original===
“And is she going to marry him?” Rachel asked, as soon as her sister was gone.

“There’s nothing settled as yet. Dorothea wants to keep her money in her own hands.”

“I don’t think that can be right. If a woman is married the money should belong to the husband.”

“I suppose that’s what Mr. Prong thinks;—at any rate, there’s nothing settled. It seems to me that we know so little about him. He might go away any day to Australia, you know.”

===Chinese===
“那么，她要嫁给他吗？”姐姐前脚刚走，雷切尔（Rachel）便问。

“还什么都没定呢。多萝西娅（Dorothea）想把自己的钱攥在自己手里。”

“我看那样不合适。女人既然结了婚，钱就该归丈夫。”

“我想普朗先生准是这么想的；——反正，眼下什么都没定。照我看，我们对这个人知道得太少。他兴许哪一天就动身去澳大利亚了，你晓得的。”

===Original===
“And did she say anything about—Mr. Rowan?”

“Not a word, my dear.”

And that was all that was then said about Luke even between Rachel and her mother. How could they speak about him? Mrs. Ray also believed that he would be no more seen in Baslehurst; and Rachel was well aware that such was her mother’s belief, although it had never been expressed. What could be said between them now—or ever afterwards—unless, indeed, Rowan should take some steps to make it necessary that his doings should be discussed?

===Chinese===
“那她有没有提到——罗恩先生？”

“一个字也没提，我亲爱的。”

关于卢克，雷切尔母女之间，当时也只说了这些。她们还能怎么谈他呢？雷太太同样相信他不会再在巴斯尔赫斯特露面了；雷切尔心里也清楚母亲是这么信的，尽管这话从没说出口。眼下她们之间——乃至往后——还能有什么可说的呢？除非罗恩当真采取什么行动，叫人不能不议论起他的行止来。

===Original===
The Tuesday passed and the Wednesday, without any sign from the young man; and during these two sad days nothing was said at the cottage. On that Wednesday his name was absolutely not mentioned between them, although each of them was thinking of him throughout the day. Mrs. Ray had now become almost sure that he had obeyed his mother’s behests, and had resolved not to trouble himself about Rachel any further; and Rachel herself had become frightened if not despondent. Could it be that all this should have passed over her and that it should mean nothing?—that the man should have been standing there, only three or four days since, in that very room, with his arm round her waist, begging for her love, and calling her his wife;—and that all of it should have no meaning? Nothing amazed her so much as her mother’s firm belief in such an ending to such an affair. What must be her mother’s thoughts about men and women in general if she could expect such conduct from Luke Rowan—and yet not think of him as one whose falsehood was marvellous in its falseness!

But on the Thursday morning there came a letter from Luke addressed to Rachel. On that morning Mrs. Ray was up when the postman passed by the cottage, and though Rachel took the letter from the man’s hand herself, she did not open it till she had shown it to her mother.

“Of course it’s from him,” said Rachel.

===Chinese===
星期二过去了，星期三也过去了，年轻男人那边音信全无；愁苦的两天里，村舍中谁也没提这件事。到了那个星期三，他的名字在母女俩之间是断然不提的，尽管两个人整整一天都在想着他。雷太太如今几乎已经笃定：他是遵从了母亲的号令，决意不再为雷切尔多费心思了；雷切尔自己即便还谈不上灰心丧气，也已然害怕起来。难道这一切从她身上过去了，竟可以毫无意味？——那个人仅仅三四天之前还站在那儿，就在那间屋子里，胳膊搂着她的腰，求她的爱，唤她做自己的妻子；——难道这一切竟没有半点意味？最让她惊愕不过的，莫过于母亲笃定这样一桩事会有这样一个收场。倘若她料得到卢克·罗恩会做出这等行径——却又不把他看成一个虚伪得叹为观止的虚伪之徒——那她心目中对于世间男男女女通盘的想法，究竟该是怎样的呢！

可到了星期四早上，来了一封卢克写给雷切尔的信。那天早上邮差打村舍门前经过时，雷太太已经起身；雷切尔虽是亲手从邮差手里接过了信，却先拿去给母亲看过，这才拆开。

“当然是他写来的，”雷切尔说。

===Original===
“I suppose so,” said Mrs. Ray, taking the unopened letter in her hand and looking at it. She spoke almost in a whisper, as though there were something terrible in the coming of the letter.

“Is it not odd,” said Rachel, “but I never saw his handwriting before? I shall know it now forever and ever.” She also spoke in a whisper, and still held the letter as though she dreaded to open it.

“Well, my dear,” said Mrs. Ray.

“If you think you ought to read it first, mamma, you may.”

“No, Rachel. It is your letter. I do not wish you to imagine that I distrust you.”

Then Rachel sat herself down, and with extreme care opened the envelope. The letter, which she read to herself very slowly, was as follows:—

===Chinese===
“想必是吧，”雷太太说着，把那封没拆的信接在手里端详。她说话的声音低得近乎耳语，仿佛这封信的到来有什么可怕之处。

“你说怪不怪，”雷切尔说，“他的笔迹我从前竟从没见过？从今往后，我可要一辈子一辈子都认得它了。”她说话也是悄声细语，信仍旧捏在手里，仿佛生怕拆开它似的。

“嗯，我亲爱的，”雷太太说。

“要是您觉得该您先看，妈妈，您就看吧。”

“不，雷切尔。这是你的信。我不愿意让你以为我不信任你。”

于是雷切尔坐了下来，小心翼翼地拆开了信封。那封信她默默地读得极慢，全文如下：——

===Original===
> My own dearest Rachel,
> It seems so nice having to write to you, though it would be much nicer if I could see you and be sitting with you at this moment at the churchyard stile. That is the spot in all Baslehurst that I like the best. I ought to have written sooner, I know, and you will have been very angry with me; but I have had to go down into Northamptonshire to settle some affairs as to my father’s property, so that I have been almost living in railway carriages ever since I saw you. I am resolved about the brewery business more firmly than ever, and as it seems that “T”

—Mrs. Tappitt would occasionally so designate her lord, and her doing so had been a joke between Luke and Rachel—

===Chinese===
> 我的最最亲爱的雷切尔，
> 给你写信这件事，似乎就叫人欢喜；虽说倘能见着你，此刻正同你一起坐在教堂墓地的梯磴上，还要欢喜得多。全巴斯尔赫斯特数那个地方我最喜欢。我知道我本该早些动笔，你一定已经很生我的气了；可我不得不下北安普敦郡（Northamptonshire）去，料理我父亲产业上的几桩事务，打从见你那天起，我简直一直住在火车车厢里。酿酒厂这桩生意，我的心意比什么时候都更坚决；而看样子，“T”

——塔皮特太太（Mrs. Tappitt）偶尔便这样称呼她的夫君，这叫法在卢克和雷切尔之间曾是一桩笑谈——

===Original===
> will not come to reason without a lawsuit, I must scrape together all the capital I have, or I shall be fifty years old before I can begin. He is a pigheaded old fool, and I shall be driven to ruin him and all his family. I would have done—and still would do—anything for him in kindness; but if he drives me to go to law to get what is as much my own as his share is his own, I will build another brewery just under his nose. All this will require money, and therefore I have to run about and get my affairs settled.
> But this is a nice love-letter—is it not? However, you must take me as I am. Just now I have beer in my very soul. The grand object of my ambition is to stand and be fumigated by the smoke of my own vats. It is a fat, prosperous, moneymaking business, and one in which there is a clear line between right and wrong. No man brews bad beer without knowing it—or sells short measure. Whether the fatness and the honesty can go together;—that is the problem I want to solve.
> You see I write to you exactly as if you were a man friend, and not my own dear sweet girl. But I am a very bad hand at lovemaking. I considered that that was all done when you nodded your head over my arm in token that you consented to be my wife. It was a very little nod, but it binds you as fast as a score of oaths. And now I think I have a right to talk to you about all my affairs, and expect you at once to get up the price of malt and hops in Devonshire. I told you, you remember, that you should be my friend, and now I mean to have my own way.

===Chinese===
> 不吃一场官司是断然不肯讲理的，那我就非得把手里全部的资本搜罗拼凑起来不可，否则还没等我开张，怕就已经五十岁了。他是个又倔又蠢的老糊涂，早晚要逼得我毁掉他，连他的家人一齐毁掉。出于好意，我本来什么都肯为他做——如今也还肯；可他若逼得我对簿公堂，去取回那份产业——它之属于我，正如他那一份之属于他——那我就在他的鼻子底下另起一座酿酒厂。这一切都得花钱，因此我只得四处奔走，把各样事务料理妥当。
> 不过这可是一封顶呱呱的情书——是不是？不管怎样，你只能原原本本地接受我这个人。这会儿我连灵魂最深处都是啤酒。我雄心壮志的头号目标，就是站在那儿，让自己酒桶的烟气熏着。这是一门肥实、兴旺、来钱的营生，而且在这一行里，正与邪界线分明。没有人酿坏了啤酒自己却不知道——也没有人短斤缺两地卖酒。肥实与诚实究竟能不能并行；——这正是我想要解答的难题。
> 你瞧，我给你写信，简直把你当作一位男朋友，而不是我那亲爱的甜蜜姑娘。可论谈情说爱，我实在笨拙得很。我原以为，等你伏在我的胳膊上点了头，表示应允做我的妻子，这一套就算全都办完了。那一点头很小很小，可它把你拴得牢牢的，不亚于二十遍海誓山盟。如今我想，我既有权同你谈论我的一切事务，便指望你立刻去摸熟德文郡（Devonshire）麦芽和酒花的行情。你还记得，我对你说过，你要做我的朋友；如今我打算要照我自己的意思办了。

===Original===
> You must tell me exactly what my mother has been doing and saying at the cottage. I cannot quite make it out from what she says, but I fear that she has been interfering where she had no business, and making a goose of herself. She has got an idea into her head that I ought to make a good bargain in matrimony, and sell myself at the highest price going in the market;—that I ought to get money, or if not money, family connection. I’m very fond of money—as is everybody, only people are such liars—but then I like it to be my own; and as to what people call connection, I have no words to tell you how I despise it. If I know myself I should never have chosen a woman as my companion for life who was not a lady; but I have not the remotest wish to become second cousin by marriage to a baronet’s grandmother. I have told my mother all this, and that you and I have settled the matter together; but I see that she trusts to something that she has said or done herself to upset our settling. Of course, what she has said can have no effect on you. She has a right to speak to me, but she has none to speak to you;—not as yet. But she is the best woman in the world, and as soon as ever we are married you will find that she will receive you with open arms.
> You know I spoke of our being married in August. I wish it could have been so. If we could have settled it when I was at Bragg’s End, it might have been done. I don’t, however, mean to scold you, though it was your fault. But as it is, it must now be put off till after Christmas. I won’t name a day yet for seeing you, because I couldn’t well go to Baslehurst without putting myself into Tappitt’s way. My lawyer says I had better not go to Baslehurst just at present. Of course you will write to me constantly—to my address here; say, twice a week at least. And I shall expect you to tell me everything that goes on. Give my kind love to your mother.
> Yours, dearest Rachel, 

 Most affectionately, 

 **Luke Rowan**.

===Chinese===
> 你务必原原本本地告诉我，我母亲在村舍那边都做了什么、说了什么。听她自己讲的那些，我总归弄不明白，只怕她插手了她压根儿管不着的事，把自己弄成了一个呆鹅。她脑子里存了一个念头，以为我在婚姻上应当做一笔好买卖，把自己按市面上顶高的价钱卖出去；——以为我该捞到钱，捞不到钱，至少也该攀上好亲家门第。我很爱钱——人人都是如此，只不过人人都爱撒谎罢了——可我爱的是这钱归我自己；至于人们嘴里的什么门第亲缘，我对它的鄙夷，言语都没法向你形容。倘若我还有自知之明，那我挑选终身伴侣，就绝不会选一个不是淑女的女人；可我连一丝一毫的念头也没有，要去给某位从男爵的祖母做姻亲的远房表亲。这些话我都对我母亲说过了，也说了你我已经把这件事一同定了下来；可我看得出，她指望靠她自己说过的什么话、做过的什么事，来搅翻我们的定局。自然，她说的话对你起不了作用。她有权同我讲，却无权同你讲；——至少眼下还没有。不过她是世上顶好的女人，等我们一成婚，你就会发现，她会张开双臂迎接你。
> 你知道，我说过我们八月里成婚的话。我巴不得当真能够如此。倘若我人在布拉格斯恩德（Bragg’s End）那时节就把事情定下，本是办得到的。不过我并不想责怪你，尽管那原是你的不是。事到如今，只好推迟到圣诞节以后了。见面的日子我暂时不定，因为眼下我要进巴斯尔赫斯特，就免不了自己送到塔皮特的眼皮子底下。我的律师说，目前我最好别去巴斯尔赫斯特。你当然要不断地给我写信——寄到我这边的地址；就说，一星期至少两封吧。这里的一切动静，我都要你一一讲给我听。替我向你母亲致以亲切的问候。
> 你最亲爱的雷切尔，

 最深情地爱你的，

 **卢克·罗恩**。

===Original===
The letter was not quite what Rachel had expected, but, nevertheless, she thought it very nice. She had never received a love-letter before, and probably had never read one—even in print; so that she was in possession of no strong preconceived notions as to the nature or requisite contents of such a document. She was a little shocked when Luke called his mother a goose;—she was a little startled when he said that people were “liars,” having an idea that the word was one not to be lightly used;—she was amused by the allusion to the baronet’s grandmother, feeling, however, that the manner and language of his letter was less pretty and love-laden than she had expected;—and she was frightened when he so confidently called upon her to write to him twice a week. But, nevertheless, the letter was a genial one, joyous, and, upon the whole, comforting. She read it very slowly, going back over much of it twice and thrice, so that her mother became impatient before the perusal was finished.

“It seems to be very long,” said Mrs. Ray.

“Yes, mamma, it is long. It’s nearly four sides.”

“What can he have to say so much?”

“There’s a good deal of it is about his own private affairs.”

“I suppose, then, I mustn’t see it.”

===Chinese===
这封信跟雷切尔原先想的不大一样，可她还是觉得它很好。她从前从没收到过情书，多半也从来没读过一封——连印出来的都没读过；所以对于这样一纸文书该是什么性质、必得有些什么内容，她心里并无任何根深蒂固的成见。卢克把自己的母亲叫作呆鹅，她小小地吃了一惊；他说世人都是“撒谎的人”，她也小小地吃了一惊，觉得这个字眼不是可以随便用的；从男爵祖母那句打趣让她觉得好笑，可她又觉得，这封信的做派和言辞，不似她预期的那么旖旎、那么满载情意；而他那样信心十足地要她一星期给他写两封信，又让她心里发怵。然而不管怎样，这封信是亲切的、欢快的，总的说来令人宽慰。她读得极慢，许多段落来回读了两三遍，以致母亲在还未读完之前就已经等得不耐烦了。

“好像很长呢，”雷太太说。

“是啊，妈妈，是长。快有四面信纸了。”

“他能有这么多话好说？”

“里头有好些都是讲他自己的私事。”

“那么，想必我是不能看的了。”

===Original===
“Oh yes, mamma!” And Rachel handed her the letter. “I shouldn’t think of having a letter from him and not showing it to you;—not as things are now.” Then Mrs. Ray took the letter and spent quite as much time in reading it as Rachel had done. “He writes as though he meant to have everything quite his own way,” said Mrs. Ray.

“That’s what he does mean. I think he will do that always. He’s what people call imperious; but that isn’t bad in a man, is it?”

Mrs. Ray did not quite know whether it was bad in a man or no. But she mistrusted the letter, not construing it closely so as to discover what might really be its full meaning, but perceiving that the young man took, or intended to take, very much into his own hands; that he demanded that everything should be surrendered to his will and pleasure, without any guarantee on his part that such surrendering should be properly acknowledged. Mrs. Ray was disposed to doubt people and things that were at a distance from her. Some check could be kept over a lover at Baslehurst; or, if perchance the lover had removed himself only to Exeter, with which city Mrs. Ray was personally acquainted, she could have believed in his return. He would not, in that case, have gone utterly beyond her ken. But she could put no confidence in a lover up in London. Who could say that he might not marry someone else tomorrow—that he might not be promising to marry half a dozen? It was with her the same sort of feeling which made her think it possible that Mr. Prong might go to Australia. She would have liked as a lover for her daughter a young man fixed in business—if not at Baslehurst, then at Totnes, Dartmouth, or Brixham—under her own eye as it were;—a young man so fixed that all the world of South Devonshire would know of all his doings. Such a young man, when he asked a girl to marry him, must mean what he said. If he did not there would be no escape for him from the punishment of his neighbours’ eyes and tongues. But a young man up in London—a young man who had quarrelled with his natural friends in Baslehurst—a young man who was confessedly masterful and impetuous—a young man who called his own mother a goose, and all the rest of the world liars, in his first letter to his ladylove;—was that a young man in whom Mrs. Ray could place confidence as a lover for her pet lamb? She read the letter very slowly, and then, as she gave it back to Rachel, she groaned.

===Chinese===
“哦，当然给你看，妈妈！”雷切尔把信递了过去。“我决不会想着收了他的信却不给你看；——照现在这样的情形，决不会。”于是雷太太接过信来，读它所花的时间，同雷切尔方才读的差不多一样多。“他这信写得，好像事事都要完全依着他自己的意思来似的，”雷太太说。

“他就是这个意思。我看他往后也会一直这样。他就是人家所说的专横；不过男人专横并不坏，是不是？”

雷太太不很清楚男人专横究竟坏不坏。可她信不过这封信——倒不是细加推究、要弄清它究竟包藏着怎样的全部用意，而是看出这个年轻人把许多事情抓在了自己手里，或者打算抓在自己手里；看出他要求一切都交由他的意志和喜好摆布，而他这一方却不给任何保证，确保这种交出会得到应有的承认。离她远的人、离她远的事，雷太太素来疑心。对一位在巴斯尔赫斯特的情人，总还有办法加以管束；倘若情人不过挪去了埃克塞特（Exeter）——那座城雷太太是亲身熟识的——她还能相信他会回来。果真那样，他总不至于跑得完全出了她的目力。可对一位远在伦敦的情人，她就万难放心了。谁说得准他明天不会另娶别人——说得准他不是同时向半打人许过要娶？这同她那种觉得普朗先生没准儿会去澳大利亚的心思，是同一类感受。她巴望女儿的情人是这样一个年轻人：营生有定所——不在巴斯尔赫斯特，就在托特尼斯（Totnes）、达特茅斯（Dartmouth）或布里克斯姆（Brixham）——好歹在她的眼皮子底下；——营生定得这样牢，以致南德文郡的整个天地都知道他的一举一动。这样的年轻人开口向姑娘求婚，说出来的话必定作数。若不作数，街坊四邻的眼睛和舌头便是惩罚，他逃不脱。可一个远在伦敦的年轻人——一个同他在巴斯尔赫斯特的自家亲友吵翻了的年轻人——一个公认专横急躁的年轻人——一个在给他意中人的头一封信里，就把自己的母亲叫作呆鹅、把世上其余的人统统叫作撒谎的人的年轻人；——这样一个人做她宝贝羔羊的情郎，雷太太能把信心放在他身上吗？她把信读得极慢，读罢把信还给雷切尔时，发了一声愁叹。

===Original===
For nearly half an hour after that nothing was said in the cottage about the letter. Rachel had perceived that it had not been thought satisfactory by her mother; but then she was inclined to believe that her mother would have regarded no letter as satisfactory until arguments had been used to prove to her that it was so. This, at any rate, was clear—must be clear to Mrs. Ray as it was clear to Rachel—that Luke had no intention of shirking the fulfilment of his engagement. And after all, was not that the one thing as to which it was essentially necessary that they should be confident? Had she not accepted Luke, telling him that she loved him? and was it not acknowledged by all around her that such a marriage would be good for her? The danger which they feared was the expectation of such a marriage without its accomplishment. Even the forebodings of Mrs. Prime had shown that this was the evil to which they pointed. Under these circumstances what better could be wished for than a ready, quick, warm assurance on Luke’s part, that he did intend all that he had said?

With Rachel now, as with all girls under such circumstances, the chief immediate consideration was as to the answer which should be given. Was she to write to him, to write what she pleased; and might she write at once? She felt that she longed to have the pen in her hand, and that yet, when holding it, she would have to think for hours before writing the first word. “Mamma,” she said at last, “don’t you think it’s a good letter?”

“I don’t know what to think, my dear. I doubt whether any letters of that sort are good for much.”

===Chinese===
那之后将近半个钟头，村舍里再没人提这封信。雷切尔看得出，母亲并不认为这封信令人满意；不过她倾向于认为，不拿出道理来向母亲证明哪一封信令人满意，母亲便不会认为哪一封信令人满意。至少有一点是明白的——雷太太应当同雷切尔一样明白——卢克并没有躲避履行婚约的意思。说到底，他们真正必须确信的，难道不正是这一件事么？她岂不是已经接受了卢克，告诉过他她爱他么？她身边的人岂不是也都承认，这门婚事于她是有好处的么？他们所惧怕的危险，是盼着这样一桩婚事，它却终无成果。连普赖姆太太的种种不祥预感也表明，他们所指的祸殃正是这个。既然如此，卢克这边爽爽快快、热热乎乎地保证他当真有意践行自己说过的一切——还能盼到什么比这更好的呢？

这时，同一切处于这种境地的姑娘一样，雷切尔眼下的头一桩要紧考虑，便是回信该怎么写。她要不要给他写信，写她想写的话；能不能立刻就写？她觉得自己巴不得笔已到手，可又觉得，笔一到手，落第一字之前，怕也得思量上几个钟头。“妈妈，”她终于开口道，“您不觉得这是一封好信吗？”

“我不知道该怎么想，我亲爱的。那一类信究竟能顶多大用，我怀疑。”

===Original===
“Of what sort, mamma?”

“Letters from men who call themselves lovers to young girls. It would be safer, I think, that there shouldn’t be any;—very much safer.”

“But if he hadn’t written we should have thought that he had forgotten all about us. That would not have been good. You said yourself that if he did not write soon, there would be an end of everything.”

“A hundred years ago there wasn’t all this writing between young people, and these things were managed better then than they are now, as far as I can understand.”

“People couldn’t write so much then,” said Rachel, “because there were no railways and no postage stamps. I suppose I must answer it, mamma?” To this proposition Mrs. Ray made no immediate answer. “Don’t you think I ought to answer it, mamma?”

“You can’t want to write at once.”

===Chinese===
“哪一类，妈妈？”

“自称是情郎的男人写给年轻姑娘的信。我想，干脆没有这种信，倒更稳妥些；——稳妥得多。”

“可他若不来信，我们就该当他把我们忘得一干二净了。那样可不妙。您自己也说过，他若不快来信，一切就都完了。”

“一百年前，年轻人之间没有这么多信来信往，依我所能明白的来看，那时的这些事情办得比如今得体。”

“那时的人没法写这么多信，”雷切尔说，“因为没有铁路，也没有邮票。我想这信我总得回吧，妈妈？”对这个提议，雷太太没有立刻作答。“您不觉得我应该回它一封吗，妈妈？”

“你总不至于想立刻就写吧。”

===Original===
“In the afternoon would do.”

“In the afternoon! Why should you be in so much hurry, Rachel? It took him four or five days to write to you.”

“Yes; but he was down in Northamptonshire on business. Besides he hadn’t any letter from me to answer. I shouldn’t like him to think—”

“To think what, Rachel?”

“That I had forgotten him.”

“Psha!”

===Chinese===
“下午写也来得及。”

“下午！你急什么呢，雷切尔？他给你写信还用了四五天呢。”

“是啊；可他在北安普敦郡有事务在身。再说，他也没有我的信要回呀。我不愿意叫他以为——”

“以为什么，雷切尔？”

“以为我把他忘了。”

“呸！”

===Original===
“Or that I didn’t treat his letter with respect.”

“He won’t think that. But I must turn it over in my mind; and I believe I ought to ask somebody.”

“Not Dolly,” said Rachel, eagerly.

“No, not your sister. I will not ask her. But if you don’t mind, my dear, I’ll take the young man’s letter out to Mr. Comfort, and consult him. I never felt myself so much in need of somebody to advise me. Mr. Comfort is an old man, and you won’t mind his seeing the letter.”

Rachel did mind it very much, but she had no means of saving herself from her fate. She did not like the idea of having her love-letter submitted to the clergyman of the parish. I do not know any young lady who would have liked it. But bad as that was, it was preferable to having the letter submitted to Mrs. Prime. And then she remembered that Mr. Comfort had advised that she might go to the ball, and that he was father to her friend Mrs. Butler Cornbury.

===Chinese===
“或者以为我对他这封信不够敬重。”

“他不会那么想的。可这事我得在心里好好转一转；我想我该找个人商量商量。”

“别找多莉（Dolly），”雷切尔急忙说。

“不，不找你姐姐。我不会去问她。不过你要是不介意，我亲爱的，我就把这个年轻人的信带出去给康福特先生（Mr. Comfort），向他请教。我从没觉得自己这样需要有人给我拿个主意。康福特先生是位上了年纪的人，他看这封信，你不会介意的。”

雷切尔其实介意得很，可她全无办法把自己从命运里搭救出来。自己那封情书要呈给堂区牧师过目，她想到这个就老大不情愿。我不知道有哪位年轻小姐会喜欢这样的事。可这事虽糟，比起把信交到普赖姆太太手里，还是要好一些。何况她又记起，康福特先生当初曾发话许她去参加舞会，再说，他还是她的朋友巴特勒·康伯里太太（Mrs. Butler Cornbury）的父亲。

## XVII Electioneering / XVII 竞选活动

===Original===

And now, in these days—the days immediately following the departure of Luke Rowan from Baslehurst—the Tappitt family were constrained to work very hard at the task of defaming the young man who had lately been living with them in their house. They were constrained to do this by the necessities of their position; and in doing so by no means showed themselves to be such monsters of iniquity as the readers of the story will feel themselves inclined to call them. As for Tappitt himself, he certainly believed that Rowan was so base a scoundrel that no evil words against him could be considered as malicious or even unnecessary. Is it not good to denounce a scoundrel? And if the rascality of any rascal be specially directed against oneself and one’s own wife and children, is it not a duty to denounce that rascal, so that his rascality may be known and thus made of no effect? When Tappitt declared in the reading-room at the Dragon, and afterwards in the little room inside the bar at the King’s Head, and again to a circle of respectable farmers and tradesmen in the Corn Market, that young Rowan had come down to the brewery and made his way into the brewery-house with a ready prepared plan for ruining him—him, the head of the firm—he thought that he was telling the truth. And again, when he spoke with horror of Rowan’s intention of setting up an opposition brewery, his horror was conscientious. He believed that it would be very wicked in a man to oppose the Bungall establishment with money left by Bungall—that it would be a wickedness than which no commercial rascality could be more iniquitous. His very soul was struck with awe at the idea. That anything was due in the matter to the consumer of beer, never occurred to him. And it may also be said in Tappitt’s favour that his opinion—as a general opinion—was backed by those around him. His neighbours could not be made to hate Rowan as he hated him. They would not declare the young man to be the very Mischief, as he did. But that idea of a rival brewery was distasteful to them all. Most of them knew that the beer was almost too bad to be swallowed; but they thought that Tappitt had a vested interest in the manufacture of bad beer;—that as a manufacturer of bad beer he was a fairly honest and useful man;—and they looked upon any change as the work, or rather the suggestion, of a charlatan.

“This isn’t Staffordshire,” they said. “If you want beer like that you can buy it in bottles at Griggs’.”

“He’ll soon find where he’ll be if he tries to undersell me,” said young Griggs. “All the same, I hope he’ll come back, because he has left a little bill at our place.”

And then to other evil reports was added that special evil report—that Rowan had gone away without paying his debts. I am inclined to think that Mr. Tappitt can be almost justified in his evil thoughts and his evil words.

===Chinese===

如今，在这些日子里——也就是卢克·罗恩前脚离开巴斯尔赫斯特、后脚紧跟着的这些日子里——塔皮特一家不得不奋力操持起一桩活计：糟践那个前不久还同他们住在同一座宅子里的年轻人。他们不得不这样做，是处境使然；而这样做，也绝不表明他们就是本书读者心里忍不住要骂的那种罪大恶极的魔头。至于塔皮特本人，他确乎真心相信罗恩是个下作透顶的无赖，说他多少坏话都算不得恶毒，甚至算不得多余。痛斥无赖难道不是好事吗？倘若某个无赖的无赖行径偏偏冲着自己、冲着自己的老婆孩子而来，把那无赖痛斥一番，让他的无赖行径广为人知、从而再无效力，难道不是分内之责吗？塔皮特在龙客栈的阅览室里宣告，随后又在王首客栈（the King’s Head）酒吧里面的小客屋里宣告，再后来又对谷物市场（Corn Market）上一圈体面的农场主和商贩宣告：小罗恩下到酿酒厂来，钻进厂里那所住宅，怀揣的就是一套要整垮他的现成盘算——整垮他，商号的当家人——他说这些话的时候，自认为讲的是实话。再者，他带着惊恐讲到罗恩想另立一家竞争酿酒厂的图谋时，那份惊恐也是出于良心的。他相信，一个人若拿邦格尔留下的钱财来跟邦格尔的字号作对，那是大大的恶行——天下再没有哪种商业无赖行径比这更不义的了。这念头叫他打心底里悚然。至于啤酒的消费者在这桩事情上也该有份什么权利，他从来没有想到过。为塔皮特说句公道话，他的看法——作为一种普遍看法——也有周围的人给他撑腰。他的街坊们没法被教得像他那样恨罗恩。他们不肯像他那样，把这个年轻人说成魔王本尊。可“另立一家酿酒厂”这个念头，他们人人听着都硌硬。他们大多知道那啤酒几乎难以下咽；但他们认为，塔皮特在造坏啤酒这营生里握有一份既得的利益——作为一个造坏啤酒的厂家，他总算是个相当本分、有用的人；而任何变革，在他们看来都是江湖骗子耍的手腕，或者说得更准些，是江湖骗子出的馊主意。

“这儿又不是斯塔福德郡（Staffordshire），”他们说，“要喝那样的啤酒，上格里格斯家铺子里买瓶装的去。”

“他要是想压我的价，很快就会知道自己有几斤几两，”小格里格斯说，“话虽如此，我还是盼着他回来，因为他在我们铺子里还挂着一笔小账呢。”

这种种恶言之外，又添上了一条特别的恶谤——说罗恩欠着一身债，一走了之。我想，塔皮特先生的恶念和恶语，差不多是可以开脱的。

===Original===

I cannot make out quite so good a case for Mrs. Tappitt and her two elder daughters;—for even Martha, Martha the just, shook her head in these days when Rowan’s name was mentioned;—but something may be said even for them. It must not be supposed that Mrs. Tappitt’s single grievance was her disappointment as regarded Augusta. Had there been no Augusta on whose behalf a hope had been possible, the predilection of the young moneyed stranger for such a girl as Rachel Ray would have been a grievance to such a woman as Mrs. Tappitt. Had she not been looking down on Rachel Ray and despising her for the last ten years? Had she not been wondering among her friends, with charitable volubility, as to what that poor woman at Bragg’s End was to do with her daughter? Had she not been regretting that the young girl should be growing up so big, and promising to look so coarse? Was it not natural that she should be miserable when she saw her taken in hand by Mrs. Butler Cornbury, and made the heroine at her own party, to the detriment of her own daughters, by the fashionable lady in catching whom she had displayed so much unfortunate ingenuity? Under such circumstances how could she do other than hate Luke Rowan—than believe him to be the very Mischief—than prophesying all manner of bad things for Rachel—and assist her husband tooth and nail in his animosity against the sinner?

Augusta was less strong in her feelings than her parents, but of course she disliked the man who could admire Rachel Ray. As regards Martha, her dislike to him—or rather, her judicial disapproval—was founded on his social and commercial improprieties. She understood that he had threatened her father about the business—and she had been scandalized in that matter of the champagne. Cherry was very brave, and still stood up for him before her mother and sisters;—but even Cherry did not dare to say a word in his favour before her father. Mr. Tappitt had been driven to forget himself, and to take a poker in his hand as a weapon of violence! After that let no one speak a word on the offender’s behalf in Tappitt’s house and within Tappitt’s hearing!

In that affair of the champagne Rowan was most bitterly injured. He had ordered it, if not at the request, at least at the instigation of Mrs. Tappitt;—and he had paid for it. When he left Baslehurst he owed no shilling to any man in it; and, indeed, he was a man by no means given to owing money to anyone. He was of a spirit masterful, self-confident, and perhaps self-glorious;—but he was at the same time honest and independent. That wine had been ordered in some unusual way—not at the regular counter, and in the same way the bill for it had been paid. Griggs, when he made his assertion in the barroom at the King’s Head, had stated what he believed to be the truth. The next morning he chanced to hear that the account had been settled, but not, at the moment, duly marked off the books. As far as Griggs went that was the end of it. He did not again say that Rowan owed money to him; but he never contradicted his former assertion, and allowed the general report to go on—that report which had been founded on his own first statement. Thus before Rowan had been a week out of the place it was believed all over the town that he had left unpaid bills behind him.

===Chinese===

塔皮特太太和她两个大女儿的情形，我就没法替她们说得这么圆了——因为这些日子里，连玛莎，连公正的玛莎，一听到罗恩的名字也要摇头——不过，即便替她们，也总有话可说。切不可以为，塔皮特太太唯一的心病只是在奥古斯塔身上落了空。就算没有奥古斯塔、没有那份可以寄托的希望，这位手头阔绰的年轻外乡人偏偏看上雷切尔·雷这样的姑娘，单凭这一条，对塔皮特太太这样的女人来说也已是桩心病了。这十年来，她难道不是一直小看雷切尔·雷、瞧她不起？在亲友中间，她难道不是口口声声一片善心，纳闷布拉格斯恩德那个可怜女人拿她这个女儿可怎么办？她难道不是一直惋惜这姑娘长得这么高大，眼看着一天比一天粗气？如今又眼见她被巴特勒·康伯里太太接在手里照管，在她自家的聚会上被捧成女主角，教自己的女儿们黯然失色——而这位时髦阔太太，当初为把她攀附到手，塔皮特太太的好些心机施展得实在不是地方——事已至此，她除了恨卢克·罗恩，除了认定他是魔王本尊，除了给雷切尔预言种种恶果，除了同丈夫一道对那个罪人恨之入骨、全力相助，还能有别的样子吗？

奥古斯塔的心思不如父母那样激烈，但那个居然看得上雷切尔·雷的男人，她自然也是厌恶的。至于玛莎，她对他的反感——毋宁说，她那法官式的否定——依据的是他社交和商务两方面的失体。她得知他曾在生意上拿话威胁过父亲；香槟那桩事，更叫她大为骇然。彻丽胆子大，在母亲和姐姐们跟前依旧替他说话；可就连彻丽，也不敢在父亲面前替他吭一声。塔皮特先生是被逼得忘了身份，抄起一根拨火棍当凶器的！自那以后，在这所宅子里、在塔皮特耳朵听得见的地方，谁还敢替那个冒犯者说半个字！

香槟那桩事里，横遭冤屈最深的其实是罗恩。那酒是他订的——即便不是应塔皮特太太之请，至少也是受她的撺掇——而且钱是他付的。他离开巴斯尔赫斯特的时候，镇上没有一个人他欠着一先令；说实在的，他这人压根儿不爱欠任何人的钱。他性子专断，自信，或许还颇为自负；但同时他为人诚实，自立。那批酒订得不同寻常——没走平日的柜台；账，也是照同样不寻常的路子付清的。格里格斯在王首客栈酒吧间里放话的时候，说的是他自己信以为实的话。第二天早上，他碰巧听说那笔账已经结了，只是账簿上当时还没照规矩销掉。就格里格斯而言，到此为止。他没有再说罗恩欠他的钱；可他也从不出来更正自己先前的话，任由那通流言继续传——那流言的根子，正是他自己头一句造出来的。于是，罗恩离镇还不满一个星期，全镇都信了：他留下一堆没付的账跑了。

“I am told that young man is dreadfully in debt,” said Mr. Prong to Mrs. Prime. At this time Mr. Prong and Mrs. Prime saw each other daily, and were affectionate in their intercourse—with a serious, solemn affection; but affairs were by no means settled between them. That affection was, however, strong enough to induce Mr. Prong to take a decided part in opposing the Rowan alliance. “They say he owes money all over the town.”

“So Miss Pucker tells me,” said Mrs. Prime.

“Does your mother know it?”

“Mother never knows anything that other people know. But he has gone now, and I don’t suppose we shall hear of him or see him again.”

“听说那个年轻人债台高筑呢，”普朗先生对普赖姆太太说。这时候，普朗先生和普赖姆太太天天见面，来往之间颇有情意——一种一本正经、庄重肃穆的情意；不过两人的事情还远没有定下来。这份情意却也足够热乎，热乎得让普朗先生旗帜鲜明地出面反对这桩罗恩姻缘。“人家说他满镇的债。”

“帕克小姐也这么跟我说。”普赖姆太太说。

“你母亲知道吗？”

“母亲从来不知道别人都知道的事。不过他这已经走了，我想我们不会再听到他的消息，也不会再见到他了。”

===Original===

“He has not written to her, Dorothea?”

“Not that I know of.”

“You should find out. You should not leave them in this danger. Your mother is weak, and you should give her the aid of your strength. The girl is your sister, and you should not leave her to grope in darkness. You should remember, Dorothea, that you have a duty in this matter.”

Dorothea did not like being told of her duty in so pastoral a manner, and resolved to be more than ever particular in the protection of her own pecuniary rights before she submitted herself to Mr. Prong’s marital authority once and forever. By Miss Pucker she was at any rate treated with great respect, and was allowed perhaps some display of pastoral manner on her own part. It began to be with her a matter of doubt whether she might not be of more use in that free vineyard which she was about to leave, than in that vineyard with closed doors and a pastoral overseer, which she was preparing herself to enter. At any rate she would be careful about the money. But, in the meantime, she did agree with Mr. Prong that Rowan’s proper character should be made known to her mother, and with this view she went out to the cottage and whispered into Mrs. Ray’s astonished ears the fact that Luke was terribly in debt.

===Chinese===

“他没给她写信吧，多萝西娅？”

“据我所知没有。”

“你应当打听清楚。你不该把他们母子撇在这种危险里不管。你母亲软弱，你应当把你的力量借给她。那姑娘是你妹妹，你不该任由她在黑暗里摸索。你应当记住，多萝西娅，在这件事情上，你有一份责任。”

多萝西娅不喜欢人家用这样一副牧者口吻来教训她守责，便打定主意：在把自己永久交到普朗先生的夫权之下以前，对保护自己的钱财权利，要比以往更加分毫必较。至少帕克小姐待她是极恭敬的，兴许还容得她自己摆一摆牧者架子。她心里开始犯嘀咕：自己快要离开的那片自由葡萄园，同那扇门常闭、上有牧者监工、自己正预备跨进去的葡萄园相比，自己在前一处说不定还更有用处些。无论如何，钱上头她是要仔细的。不过眼下，普朗先生说的有一点她倒也同意：罗恩的真实为人，应当让她母亲知道。抱着这个想法，她去了村舍，把卢克欠了一身骇人听闻的债这个事实，悄悄说进雷太太惊愕的耳朵里。

“You don’t say so!”

“It was an honest letter enough—very honest to my thinking; and speaking as though everything between them was quite settled.”

“That’s nonsense, mother.”

===Chinese===

“不会吧！”

“那封信倒是一封老实的信——依我看老实得很；口气就像两人之间的事已经全然定了局似的。”

And I must say this for him, that he has always spoken of her as though he loved her very dearly; and I believe he has been a most excellent son. He shouldn’t have said goose;—at any rate in a letter;—not to my way of thinking. But perhaps they don’t mind those things up in London.”

“I never knew a young man so badly spoken of at a place he’d left as he is in Baslehurst. I think it right to tell you; but if you have made up your mind to ask Mr. Comfort—”

===Chinese===

“兴许是胡说吧，多萝西娅；可我只是把信上的话学给你听。他管他母亲叫呆鹅；这是信里头最不像话的一处。”

“一个年轻人走了以后，名声给糟践得这么厉害的，我还从来没见过，比他在巴斯尔赫斯特这儿的下场更糟的了。我认为应当告诉你；可你既然拿定主意要去请教康福特先生——”
