===Original===
In the morning she took down the letter in her hand and gave it to her mother. Mrs. Ray read it very slowly and demurred over it at sundry places. She especially demurred at that word about the omen, and even declared that it ought to be expunged. But Rachel was very stern and held her ground. She had put into the letter, she said, all that she had been bidden to say. Such a word from herself to one who had been so dear to her must be allowed to her.
The letter was not altered and was taken away by the postman that evening.

===Chinese===
早晨，她把信拿在手里带下楼，交给母亲。雷太太读得极慢，好几处都踌躇不依，尤其是那个说到预兆的字眼，她最不以为然，甚至声明应当把它删掉。可雷切尔非常坚决，寸步不让。她说，吩咐她要写的话，她都已经写进信里了；至于这样一句话——对一个曾经同她这样亲的人，由她自己说出这样一句话——总该容许她吧。
信一个字也没有改动，当天傍晚便由邮差取走了。

## XXI Mrs. Ray Goes to Exeter, and Meets a Friend / XXI 雷太太去埃克塞特，遇见一位朋友

===Original===

Six weeks passed over them at Bragg’s End, and nothing was heard of Luke Rowan. Rachel’s letter, a copy of which was given in our last chapter, was duly sent away by the postman, but no answer to it came to Bragg’s End. It must, however, be acknowledged that it not only required no answer, but that it even refused to be answered. Rachel had told her lover that he was not to correspond with her, and that she certainly would not write to him again. Having so said, she had no right to expect an answer; and she protested over and over again that she did expect none. But still she would watch, as she thought unseen, for the postman’s coming; and her heart would sink within her as the man would pass the gate without calling. “He has taken me at my word,” she said to herself very bitterly. “I deserve nothing else from him; but—but—but—” In those days she was ever silent and stern. She did all that her mother bade her, but she did little or nothing from love. There were no more banquets, with clotted cream brought over from Mrs. Sturt’s. She would speak a word or two now and then to Mrs. Sturt, who understood the whole case perfectly; but such words were spoken on chance occasions, for Rachel now never went over to the farm. Farmer Sturt’s assistance had been offered to her; but what could the farmer do for her in such trouble as hers?

During the whole of these six weeks she did her household duties; but gradually she became slower in them and still more slow, and her mother knew that her disappointment was becoming the source of permanent misery. Rachel never said that she was ill; nor, indeed, of any special malady did she show signs: but gradually she became thin and wan, her cheeks assumed a haggard look, and that aspect of the brow which her mother feared had become habitual to her. Mrs. Ray observed her closely in all that she did. She knew well of those watchings for the postman. She was always thinking of her child, and, after a while, longing that Luke Rowan might come back to them, with a heart almost as sore with longing as was that of Rachel herself. But what could she do? She could not bring him back. In all that she had done—in giving her sanction to this lover, and again in withdrawing it, she had been guided by the advice of her clergyman. Should she go again to him and beg him to restore that young man to them? Ah! no; great as was her trust in her clergyman she knew that even he could not do that for her.

During all these weeks hardly a word was spoken openly between the mother and daughter about the matter that chiefly occupied the thoughts of them both. Luke Rowan’s name was hardly mentioned between them. Once or twice some allusion was made to the subject of the brewery, for it was becoming generally known that the lawyers were already at work on behalf of Rowan’s claim; but even on such occasions as these Mrs. Ray found that her speech was stopped by the expression of Rachel’s eyes, and by those two lines which on such occasions would mark her forehead. In those days Mrs. Ray became afraid of her younger daughter—almost more so than she had ever been afraid of the elder one. Rachel, indeed, never spoke as Mrs. Prime would sometimes speak. No word of scolding ever passed her mouth; and in all that she did she was gentle and observant. But there was ever on her countenance that look of reproach which by degrees was becoming almost unendurable. And then her words during the day were so few! She was so anxious to sit alone in her own room! She would still read to her mother for some hours in the evening; but this reading was to her so manifestly a task, difficult and distasteful!

===Chinese===

六个星期过去了，布拉格斯恩德（Bragg’s End）再没有听到卢克·罗恩（Luke Rowan）的一丝音信。雷切尔（Rachel）的那封信——上一章我们抄录了它的原文——由邮差按期送走了，可回信始终没有到布拉格斯恩德来。然而必须承认，这封信不但用不着回答，甚至还摆出一副拒绝回答的架势。雷切尔对她的情人说过，他不许同她通信，她自己也断然不会再给他写信。话既如此说，她便没有权利指望回音；而且她一遍又一遍地申明，自己确实什么都不指望。可她仍旧守望着邮差的到来，还自以为守得神不知鬼不觉；那人一走过院门、并不进来，她的心便直往下沉。“他把我这句话认起真来了，”她辛酸地对自己说。“受他这样的对待也是我应得的；可是——可是——可是——”那些日子里，她一贯沉默而冷峻。母亲吩咐的事她样样都做，可她做起事来，几乎再没有一样是出于爱心。再没有摆过那样的欢宴，有从斯特特太太（Mrs. Sturt）家送来的凝脂奶油了。她偶尔还同斯特特太太说上一两句，斯特特太太对这事的前前后后看得再透不过；可这样的话都是碰巧遇上的场合才说的，雷切尔如今从不往农场那边去。斯特特先生（Farmer Sturt）主动提出过要帮她忙；可她这等烦恼，一个农场主又能帮她什么呢？

这六个星期里，她照旧操持家务；可她渐渐地慢了下来，愈来愈慢，她母亲也看出，她的失望正在变成一种长住的悲苦。雷切尔从没说过自己有病；她也的确没有显出什么特别病症的迹象：只是渐渐地瘦了、白了，两颊有了憔悴之色，而她母亲害怕的那种眉头神情，已经成了她的常态。雷太太（Mrs. Ray）对她的一举一动都看在眼里。她对女儿守望邮差的事知道得清清楚楚。她心里时时想着自己的孩子，过了一阵，竟也盼起卢克·罗恩会回到她们身边来，那颗心给盼得作痛，几乎同雷切尔自己的心一样。可她又能怎样呢？她没法叫他回来。她所做的一切——先是允准了这个情人，继而又收回允准——都是听了她牧师的指教。她该不该再去求他，请他把那个年轻人还给她们母女？唉！不行；她对牧师信得再深，也知道就连他也替她办不到这一层。

这许多个星期里，母女俩对那件占着两人心思的头等大事，几乎从不曾明言半句。卢克·罗恩的名字在她们中间几乎绝口不提。有一两回，话头沾到酿酒厂的事，因为罗恩一方请的律师已在替他的权利主张出力，此事渐渐尽人皆知；可就连这样的场合，雷太太也发觉自己的话头被雷切尔的眼色截住了，被她额上逢这种时候便会显出来的两道纹截住了。那些日子里，雷太太怕起她的小女儿来——几乎比她素来怕大女儿怕得还厉害。说实在的，雷切尔从不像普赖姆太太（Mrs. Prime）有时那样说话。她嘴里从没出过一句责骂；做什么事都温婉而循礼。可她脸上总挂着那副含着责备的神情，一点一点地，变得几乎叫人受不了。再说，她白天的话是多么少啊！她又是多么巴不得独自坐在自己屋里！晚上她照旧给母亲念上几个钟头的书；可这念书于她分明是一件苦差，又费力，又不堪消受！

===Original===

It may be remembered that Mrs. Prime, with her lover, Mr. Prong, and her friend Miss Pucker, had promised to call at Bragg’s End on the evening after Rachel’s walk into Baslehurst. They did come as they had promised, about half an hour after Rachel’s letter to Luke had been carried away by the postman. They had come, and had remained at Bragg’s End for an hour, eating cake and drinking currant wine, but not having, on the whole, what our American friends call a good time of it. That visit had been terrible to Mrs. Ray. Rachel had sat there cold, hard, and speechless. Not only had she not asked Miss Pucker to take off her bonnet, but she had absolutely declined to speak to that lady. It was wonderful to her mother that she should thus, in so short a time, have become wilful, masterful, and resolved in following out her own purposes. Not one word on that occasion did she speak to Miss Pucker; and Mrs. Prime, observing this, had grown black and still blacker, till the horror of the visit had become terrible to Mrs. Ray. Miss Pucker had grinned and smiled, and striven gallantly, poor woman, to make the best of it. She had declared how glad she had been to see Miss Rachel on the previous evening, and how well Miss Rachel had looked, and had expressed quite voluminous hopes that Miss Rachel would come to their Dorcas meetings. But to all this Rachel answered not a syllable. Now and then she addressed a word or two to her sister. Now and then she spoke to her mother. When Mr. Prong specially turned himself to her, asking her some question, she would answer him with one or two monosyllables, always calling him Sir; but to Miss Pucker she never once opened her mouth. Mrs. Prime became very angry—very black and very angry; and the time of the visit was a terrible time to Mrs. Ray.

But this visit is to be noticed in our story chiefly on account of a few words which Mr. Prong found an opportunity of saying to Mrs. Ray respecting his proposed marriage. Mrs. Ray knew that there were difficulties about the money, and was disposed to believe, and perhaps to hope, that the match would be broken off. But on this occasion Mr. Prong was very marked in his way of speaking to Mrs. Ray, as though everything were settled. Mrs. Ray was thoroughly convinced by this that it was so, and her former beliefs and possible hopes were all dispersed. But then Mrs. Ray was easily convinced by any assertion. In thus speaking to his future mother-in-law he had contrived to turn his back round upon the other three ladies, so as to throw them together for the time, and thus make their position the more painful. It must be acknowledged that Rachel was capable of something great, after her determined resistance to Miss Pucker’s blandishments under such circumstances as these.

“Mrs. Ray,” Mr. Prong had said—and as he spoke his voice was soft with mingled love and sanctity—“I cannot let this moment pass without expressing one word of what I feel at the prospect of connecting myself with your amiable family.”

===Chinese===

读者也许还记得，普赖姆太太曾带着她的情人普朗先生（Mr. Prong）和她的朋友帕克小姐（Miss Pucker），应许在雷切尔步行进城去巴斯尔赫斯特之后的那个晚上，到布拉格斯恩德来拜访。他们果然如约而来，就在雷切尔写给卢克的信被邮差送走之后约莫半个钟头。他们来了，在布拉格斯恩德坐了一个钟头，吃蛋糕，喝醋栗酒，可是总的说来，过得并不像我们美国朋友所说的那样“快活”。那一晚的拜访，于雷太太是一场煎熬。雷切尔坐在那儿，冷淡、僵硬、一言不发。她不但没请帕克小姐解下帽子来小坐，简直干脆拒绝同那位小姐说话。她竟在这样短的时日里，变得这般任性、这般有主见、这般执意按自己的心思行事，做母亲的简直不能不惊叹。那一晚她对帕克小姐没说过一个字；普赖姆太太瞧在眼里，脸色一阵黑似一阵，直熬得这场拜访的阴森可怖，全压到了雷太太头上。帕克小姐咧着嘴、堆着笑，竭力撑持——可怜的女人——想把局面敷衍得体面些。她一口一声地说，前一晚见到雷切尔小姐多么高兴，雷切尔小姐气色多么好，又絮絮地表示了长长的盼望，巴望雷切尔小姐赏光到她们的多卡斯缝纫会（Dorcas meetings）来。可对这一切，雷切尔半个字也不答。偶尔她同姐姐说上一两句。偶尔她同母亲说上一两句。普朗先生特意转过身来问她一句什么话的时候，她也只用一两个单音节的字打发，口口声声称他“先生”；可对帕克小姐，她自始至终没有开过一次口。普赖姆太太大为恼怒——脸色黑沉沉的，怒气大得很；那段做客的时光，对雷太太真是一段可怕的时光。

不过，我们这个故事要把这场拜访记上一笔，主要还是因为普朗先生寻着机会，就他那桩拟议中的婚事，同雷太太说了几句话。雷太太本知道钱上头还有难处，也倾向于相信，或许还暗自盼望，这头亲事会散。可这一回，普朗先生同她说话的口气十分郑重其事，仿佛万事已定局。雷太太由此深信果真如此，她原先的信念和那点可能的指望，就此烟消云散。不过话说回来，雷太太这个人，人家断言什么她都容易信。他这样同未来岳母说话的时候，还设法把身子转了过去，背朝着另外三位女士，把她们一时撇作一堆，教她们的处境愈发难堪。必须承认，雷切尔在这般处境之下，还能坚决顶住帕克小姐的甜言蜜语，是有些了不起的气性的。

“雷太太，”普朗先生说——他说话的声音又软又柔，透着爱与神圣交织的味道——“这样的时刻不容它白白过去，我总得说出一句话来，表白表白：想到自己即将同您贤淑的一家人结成亲眷，我心里是什么滋味。”

===Original===

“I’m sure I’m much obliged,” Mrs. Ray had answered.

“Of course I am aware that Dorothea has mentioned the matter to you.”

“Oh yes; she has mentioned it, certainly.”

“And therefore I should be remiss, both as regards duty and manners, if I did not take this opportunity of assuring you how much gratification I feel in becoming thus bound up in family affection with you and Miss Rachel. Family ties are sweet bonds of sanctified love; and as I have none of my own—nearer, that is, than Geelong, the colony of Victoria, where my mother and brother and sisters have located themselves—I shall feel the more pleasure in taking you and Miss Rachel to my heart.”

This was complimentary to Mrs. Ray; but with her peculiar feelings as to the expediency of people having their own belongings, she almost thought that it would have been better for all parties if Mr. Prong had gone to Geelong with the rest of the Prong family: this opinion, however, she did not express. As to taking Mr. Prong to her heart, she felt some doubts of her own capacity for such a performance. It would be natural for her to love a son-in-law. She had loved Mr. Prime very dearly, and trusted him thoroughly. She would have been prepared to love Luke Rowan, had fate been propitious in that quarter. But she could not feel secure as to loving Mr. Prong. Such love, moreover, should come naturally, of its own growth, and not be demanded categorically as a right. It certainly was a pity that Mr. Prong had not made himself happy, with that happiness for which he sighed, in the bosom of his family at Geelong. “I’m sure you’re very kind,” Mrs. Ray had said.

“And when we are thus united in the bonds of this world,” continued Mr. Prong, “I do hope that other bonds, more holy in their nature even than those of family, more needful even than them, may join us together. Dorothea has for some months past been a constant attendant at my church—”

===Chinese===

“我真是不胜感激，”雷太太答道。

“当然，我知道多萝西娅（Dorothea）已经同您提过这件事了。”

“哦，是的；她提过，确实提过。”

“因此，我若不趁今天这个机会向您保证——想到自己就这样同您和雷切尔小姐结成亲情，我心中何等快慰——那么无论论本分还是论礼数，我都有亏欠。骨肉之亲，是神圣之爱甜美的纽带；我自己可说是一无骨肉——我的亲人，最近的也在吉朗（Geelong）了，那是维多利亚殖民地（the colony of Victoria），我母亲和弟弟妹妹们都迁到那里安了家——这样，把您和雷切尔小姐收进我的心坎，我倒要越发欢喜了。”

这番话对雷太太算是恭维；可她心里对人们同自家亲人相守相宜这一点，自有一套特别的讲究，她几乎觉得，倘若普朗先生索性同普朗家其余的人一道去了吉朗，倒对各方都好些；不过这个想法，她没有说出口。至于把普朗先生收进自己心坎这件事，她对自己可有没有这份能耐，心里不免打鼓。爱一个女婿，于她本是顺理成章的事。她从前疼爱普赖姆先生爱得极深，也把他全然信得过。倘若命运在那头肯行个方便，她也早就预备好了要去爱卢克·罗恩。可要她爱普朗先生，她心里实在没底。况且这样的爱，应当自然而然、由自家心里长出来，不该像讨一笔债那样，板起脸来当作权利讨要。普朗先生没能在他吉朗的家宅里、在他自己叹息渴求的那种幸福里自得其乐，这实在是桩憾事。“您真是客气，”雷太太说。

“等到我们在这尘世的纽带里这样连成一体，”普朗先生接着说，“我就着实盼望，还有另一种纽带——论性质比骨肉之亲更神圣，论必要也比骨肉之亲更要紧——能把我们连在一起。多萝西娅这几个月来，一直回回不落地到我教堂里来做礼拜——”

===Original===

“Oh, I couldn’t leave Mr. Comfort; indeed I couldn’t,” said Mrs. Ray in alarm. “I couldn’t go away from my own parish church was it ever so.”

“No, no; not altogether, perhaps. I am not sure that it would be desirable. But will it not be sweet, Mrs. Ray, when we are bound together as one family, to pour forth our prayers in holy communion together?”

“I think so much of my own parish church, Mr. Prong,” Mrs. Ray replied. After that Mr. Prong did not, on that occasion, press the matter further, and soon turned round his chair so as to relieve the three ladies behind him.

“I think we had better be going, Mr. Prong,” said Mrs. Prime, rising from her seat with a display of anger in the very motion of her limbs. “Good evening, mother: good evening to you, Rachel. I’m afraid our visit has put you out. Had I guessed as much, we would not have come.”

“You know, Dolly, that I am always glad to see you—only you come to us so seldom,” said Rachel. Then with a very cold bow to Miss Pucker, with a very warm pressure of the hand from Mr. Prong, and with a sisterly embrace for Dorothea, that was not cordial as it should have been, she bade them goodbye. It was felt by all of them that the visit had been a failure;—it was felt so, at least, by all the Ray family. Mr. Prong had achieved a certain object in discussing his marriage as a thing settled; and as regarded Miss Pucker, she also had achieved a certain object in eating cake and drinking wine in Mrs. Ray’s parlour.

For some weeks after that but little had been seen of Mrs. Prime at the cottage; and nothing had been said of her matrimonial prospects. Rachel did not once go to her sister’s lodgings; and, on the few occasions of their meeting, asked no questions as to Mr. Prong. Indeed, as the days and weeks went on, her heart became too heavy to admit of her asking any questions about the love affairs of others. She still went about her work, as I have before said. She was not ill—not ill so as to demand the care due to an invalid. But she moved about the house slowly, as though her limbs were too heavy for her. She spoke little, unless when her mother addressed her. She would sit for hours on the sofa doing nothing, reading nothing, and looking at nothing. But still, at the postman’s morning hours, she would keep her eye upon the road over which he came, and that dull look of despair would come across her face when he passed on without calling at the cottage.

===Chinese===

“哦，我可不能离开康福特先生（Mr. Comfort）；真真不能，”雷太太慌了，说。“自家的堂区教堂，说什么我也不能撇下。”

“不，不；也许不必全然如此。我也不敢说那样就一定可取。可是雷太太，等到我们结作一家人，同心合意、在圣洁的相通里一同倾吐祷告，那岂不是一桩美事？”

“普朗先生，我对自己堂区的教堂，是看得极重的，”雷太太答道。打那以后，那一晚普朗先生没有再逼这桩事，不多时便把椅子转了回去，好教身后那三位女士松快松快。

“我看我们该走了，普朗先生，”普赖姆太太说，站起身来，一举一动都摆明了在动气。“母亲，晚上好：雷切尔，也祝你晚上好。只怕我们这趟拜访搅得你们不安生。早料到是这样，我们就不会来了。”

“多莉（Dolly），你知道我一向高兴见你——只是你上我们这儿来得太少了，”雷切尔说。随后，她朝帕克小姐极冷地一躬身，让普朗先生热切地握了握手，又同多萝西娅行了姐妹的拥抱礼——那拥抱却远不如应有的那般亲热——把客人送走了。他们全都觉出这趟拜访砸了；——至少雷家上下全都这么觉得。普朗先生达成了他的一项目的：把他的婚事当着定局来谈论；至于帕克小姐，她也达成了自己的一项目的：在雷太太的客厅里吃到了蛋糕，喝到了酒。

打那以后有几个星期，普赖姆太太在村舍难得露面；她的婚事前景，也再没人提起。雷切尔一回也没去姐姐的住处；偶尔碰见，也绝口不问普朗先生的事。说实在的，日子和星期一天天过去，她心里沉得装不下任何打听别人情爱的问话了。她还照常做她的活计，像我前头说过的。她没有病——没有病到该当病人照料的份上。只是她在屋里走动得慢，仿佛四肢重得抬不动似的。她话很少，除非母亲先开口同她说话。她会在沙发上一坐几个钟头，什么都不做，什么都不读，什么都不看。可每天早上邮差该到的时辰，她仍守望他去的那条路；他一走过去、不进村舍的门，她脸上便掠过那副木然绝望的神情。

===Original===

But on a certain morning towards the end of the six weeks the postman did call—as indeed he had called on other days, though bringing with him no letter from Luke Rowan. Neither now, on this occasion, did he bring a letter from Luke Rowan. The letter was addressed to Mrs. Ray; and, as Rachel well knew from the handwriting, it was from the gentleman who managed her mother’s little money matters—the gentleman who had succeeded to the business left by Mr. Ray when he died. So Rachel took the letter up to her mother and left it, saying that it was from Mr. Goodall.

Mrs. Ray’s small income arose partly from certain cottages in Baslehurst, which had been let in lump to a Baslehurst tradesman, and partly from shares in a gas company at Exeter. Now the gas company at Exeter was the better investment of the two, and was considered to be subject to less uncertainty than the cottages. The lease under which the cottages had been let was out, and Mrs. Ray had been advised to sell the property. Building ground near the town was rising in value; and she had been advised by Mr. Goodall to part with her little estate. Both Mrs. Ray and Rachel were aware that this business, to them very important, was imminent; and now had come a letter from Mr. Goodall, saying that Mrs. Ray must go to Exeter to conclude the sale. “We should only bungle matters,” Mr. Goodall had said, “if I were to send the deeds down to you; and as it is absolutely necessary that you should understand all about it, I think you had better come up on Tuesday; you can get back to Baslehurst easily on the same day.”

“My dear,” said Mrs. Ray, coming into the parlour, “I must go to Exeter.”

===Chinese===

可是六个星期将尽的某个早晨，邮差当真上门来了——不错，别的日子他也来过，只是从没带来卢克·罗恩的信。这一回，他仍旧没带来卢克·罗恩的信。信是写给雷太太的；雷切尔从笔迹上一眼认得，这是替她母亲打理那点钱财事务的先生——雷先生过世时留下的那摊事务，便是他接的手。于是雷切尔把信拿上楼交给母亲，留下话说是古德尔先生（Mr. Goodall）来的，便走了。

雷太太那一小笔进项，一半出自巴斯尔赫斯特（Baslehurst）的几所村舍——那些房子整批租给了一个巴斯尔赫斯特的买卖人——一半出自埃克塞特（Exeter）一家煤气公司的股份。这两样里头，埃克塞特煤气公司是更稳靠的一注，人们认为它比那几所村舍少些变数。村舍的租约已经到期，有人劝雷太太把产业出手。镇子近旁的屋基行情正在看涨；古德尔先生也劝她把那点小产业让掉。雷太太和雷切尔都明白，这桩于她们干系极大的买卖已迫在眉睫；如今古德尔先生的信来了，说雷太太必须上埃克塞特去把卖契办结。“倘若我把契据寄下来给你们，”古德尔先生信里说，“事情只会办得七颠八倒；这桩事您非得一清二楚不可，所以我看您顶好礼拜二上来；当天赶回巴斯尔赫斯特，一点不费难。”

“亲爱的，”雷太太走进客厅来说，“我得上一趟埃克塞特。”

===Original===

“Today, mamma?”

“No, not today, but on Tuesday. Mr. Goodall says I must understand all about the sale. It is a dreadful trouble.”

But, dreadful as the trouble was, it seemed that Mrs. Ray was not made unhappy by the prospect of the little expedition. She fussed and fretted as ladies do on such occasions, but—as is also common with ladies—the excitement of the journey was, upon the whole, a gratification to her. She asked Rachel to accompany her, and at first pressed her to do so strongly; but such work at the present moment was not in accord with Rachel’s mood, and at last she escaped from it under the plea of expense.

“I think it would be foolish, mamma,” she said. “Now that Dolly has gone you will be run very close; and when Mr. Goodall first spoke of selling the cottages, he said that perhaps you might be without anything from them for a quarter.”

“But he has sold them now, my dear; and there will be the money at once.”

“I don’t see why you should throw away ten and sixpence, mamma,” said Rachel.

===Chinese===

“今天就去吗，妈妈？”

“不，不是今天，是礼拜二。古德尔先生说，这桩买卖的底细我都必须弄明白。真是一桩愁死人的麻烦事。”

可是这麻烦虽然愁人，眼见这一趟小小出门的前景，雷太太倒并不显得愁苦。她忙乱、烦躁，像太太小姐们遇着这等场合的光景；不过——这也是太太小姐们的通例——旅途的兴奋，总的说来于她反倒是一种受用。她邀雷切尔同去，起初还死拉硬拽地劝；可这样的差事，此刻同雷切尔的心境全然不合，末了她拿破费做托词，躲了过去。

“我看那可是犯傻，妈妈，”她说。“多莉既然走了，你手头会很紧；古德尔先生头一回提起卖村舍的时候就说，兴许有一个季度，你从那上头什么也收不着。”

“可他如今已经把它们卖掉了，亲爱的；钱马上就到手。”

“我不明白您为什么要把十先令六便士白白扔掉，妈妈，”雷切尔说。

===Original===

And as she spoke in that resolved and masterful tone, her mother, of course, gave up the point. So when the Tuesday morning came, she went with her mother only as far as the station.

“Don’t mind meeting me, because I can’t be sure about the train,” said Mrs. Ray. “But I shall be back tonight, certainly.”

“And I’ll wait tea for you,” said Rachel. Then, when her mother was gone, she walked back to the cottage by herself.

She walked back at once, but took a most devious course. She was determined to avoid the length of the High Street, and she was determined also to avoid Brewery Lane; but she was equally determined to pass through the churchyard. So she walked down from the railway station to the hamlet at the bottom of the hill below the church, and from thence went up by the field-path to the stile. In order to accomplish this she went fully two miles out of her way, and now the sun over her head was very hot. But what was the distance or the heat of the sun to her when her object was to stand for a few moments in that place? Her visit, however, to the spot which was so constantly in her thoughts did her no good. Why had she been so injured? Why had this sacrifice of herself been demanded from her? As she sat for a moment on the stile this was the matter that filled her breast. She had been exalted to the heavens when she first heard her mother speak of Mr. Rowan as an acceptable suitor. She had been filled with joy as though Paradise had been opened to her, when she found herself to be the promised bride of Luke Rowan. Then had come her lover’s letter, and the clergyman’s counsel, and her own reply; and after that the gates of her Paradise had been closed against her! “I wonder whether it’s the same thing to him,” she said to herself. “But I suppose not. I don’t think it can be the same thing or he would come. Wouldn’t I go to him if I were free as he is!” She barely rested in the churchyard, and then walked on between the elms at a quick pace, with a heart sore—sore almost to breaking. She would never have been brought to this condition had not her mother told her that she might love him! Thence came her vexation of spirit. There was the cruelty. All the world knew that this man had been her lover;—all her world knew it. Cherry Tappitt had sung her little witless song about it. Mrs. Tappitt had called at the cottage about it. Mr. Comfort had given his advice about it. Mrs. Cornbury had whispered to her about it out of her pony carriage. Mrs. Sturt had counselled her about it. Mr. Prong had thought it very wrong on her part to love the man. Mr. Sturt had thought it very right, and had offered his assistance. All this would have been as nothing had her lover remained to her. Cherry might have sung till her little throat was tired, and Mr. Prong might have expressed his awe with outspread hands, and have looked as though he expected the skies to fall. Had her Paradise not been closed to her, all this talking would have been a thing of course. But such talking—such widespread knowledge of her condition, with the gates of her Paradise closed against her, was very hard to bear! And who had closed the gates? Her own hands had done it. He, her lover, had not deserted her. He had done for her all that truth and earnestness demanded, and perhaps as much as love required. Men were not so soft as girls, she argued within her own breast. Let a man be ever so true it could not be expected that he should stand by his love after he had been treated with such cold indifference as had been shown in her letter! She would have stood by her love, let his letter have been as cold as it might. But then she was a woman, and her love, once encouraged, had become a necessity to her. A man, she said to herself, would be more proud but less stanch. Of course she would hear no more from him. Of course the gates of her Paradise were shut. Such were her thoughts as she walked home, and such the thoughts over which she sat brooding alone throughout the entire day.

===Chinese===

她说这话的时候，口气又决绝又专断，她母亲自然只好让步。于是礼拜二早晨到了，她只送母亲到火车站，便止了步。

“不必来接我，火车几时到我说不准，”雷太太说。“不过我今儿晚上一定回来。”

“我烧好茶等你，”雷切尔说。母亲走了之后，她便独自走回村舍去。

她当即往回走，却绕了一条七拐八绕的远路。她打定主意不走大街（High Street）那长长的一段，也打定主意绕开酿酒厂巷（Brewery Lane）；可她同样打定主意，要从教堂墓地里穿过去。于是她从火车站一路下坡，走到教堂下方山脚的那片小村落，再从那里顺着田间小径，往那座梯磴上去。为了走这一遭，她足足多绕了两英里的路，头顶上的太阳也正毒。可她的心愿不过是到那个地方站上一小会儿，路远也罢，日头毒也罢，于她算得了什么？然而，她这一趟去那个日夜萦怀的地方，并未得着半点安慰。她为什么受这样的委屈？为什么偏要她作出这样的自我牺牲？她在梯磴上坐了一小会儿，胸中塞满了的就是这桩事。头一回听母亲说罗恩先生是个可以应允的求婚人，她给捧得高高地升上了天。等到发现自己已是卢克·罗恩许了亲的新娘，她满心欢喜，仿佛乐园已向她敞开了门。随后来了情人的信，来了牧师的指教，来了她自己的回信；再往后，她那乐园的门，便对着她关上了！“不知这在他心里是不是一样滋味，”她自言自语说。“我想不会的吧。我想总不会是一样滋味，不然他就该来了。倘若我同他一样自由自在，我难道不会奔他而去！”她在教堂墓地里几乎没歇脚，便顺着两行榆树中间的小径快步走去，心里痛——痛得几乎要碎。倘若母亲不曾说她可以爱他，她断断不会落到这步田地！她的烦恼苦闷便由此而来。残忍也正在这里。普天之下都知道这个人做过她的情人；——她那个小天地里的人也全都知道。彻丽·塔皮特（Cherry Tappitt）为这个唱过她那支傻里傻气的小调。塔皮特太太（Mrs. Tappitt）为这个上过村舍的门。康福特先生为这个出过他的主意。康伯里太太（Mrs. Cornbury）为这个坐在自己的小马马车里附耳同她嘀咕过。斯特特太太为这个劝过她。普朗先生认定她爱这个人大错特错。斯特特先生认定这事大对特对，还主动要来帮忙。这一切，倘若她的情人还留在她身边，原本都算不得什么。彻丽尽可以唱下去，唱到她那小嗓子发哑为止；普朗先生尽可以摊开双手表示他的惊骇，摆出一副只怕天要塌下来的架势。她的乐园只要不曾对她关门，这些闲话就全是理所当然的事。可这样的话头——这样人人尽知的她的处境——偏偏又赶上乐园的门对她关死了，可就叫人怎么受得住！门是谁关的呢？是她自己的手关的。他，她的情人，并没有负她。凡是真诚和郑重要求于他的，他都为她做到了，或许连爱所要求的也都做到了。男人的心不像姑娘家的那样软，她在自己胸中细细分辩。一个男人纵然再真心实意，受了像她信里那样一副冷冰冰的淡漠待遇之后，还能指望他守着他的爱情不成！倘若他那封信写得再冷，她也照样会守着自己的爱情。可她是个女人，她的爱情一经鼓励，就成了她的必需。男人嘛，她对自己说，会更高傲，却更守不住。她自然再听不到他的音信。她那乐园的门自然是关上了。她一路往家走，想的是这些；独自枯坐、把这一整天都坐过去，翻来覆去地盘算的也是这些。

===Original===

At half-past seven in the evening Mrs. Ray came back home, wearily trudging across the green. She was very weary, for she had now walked above two miles from the station. She had also been on her feet half the day, and, which was probably worse than all the rest had she known it, she had travelled nearly eighty miles by railway. She was very tired, and would under ordinary circumstances have been disposed to reckon up her grievances in the evening quite as accurately as Rachel had reckoned hers in the morning. But something had occurred in Exeter, the recollection of which still overcame the sense of weariness which Mrs. Ray felt;—overcame it, or rather overtopped it; so that when Rachel came out to her at the cottage door she did not speak at once of her own weariness, but looked lovingly into her daughter’s face—lovingly and anxiously, and said some little word intended to denote affection.

“You must be very tired,” said Rachel, who, with many self-reproaches and much communing within her own bosom, had for the time vanquished her own hard humour.

“Yes, I am tired, my dear; very. I thought the train never would have got to the Baslehurst station. It stopped at all the little stations, and really I think I could have walked as fast.” A dozen years had not as yet gone by since the velocity of these trains had been so terrible to Mrs. Ray that she had hardly dared to get into one of them!

“And whom have you seen?” said Rachel.

“Seen!” said Mrs. Ray. “Who told you that I had seen anybody?”

“I suppose you saw Mr. Goodall.”

===Chinese===

晚上七点半，雷太太回到了家，拖着乏透的步子走过村头的草地。她乏得很，因为单从车站走到家，就已走了两英里还多。她还有半天没沾过椅子；而且——她倘若知道的话，这恐怕比其余一切都更伤人——她坐火车走了差不多八十英里。她累极了；若在平常的日子里，到了晚上，她本会像雷切尔早上清点自己的委屈那样，把自己的苦处也细细清点一遍。可是在埃克塞特出了一件事，那件事的追忆压过了雷太太身上的乏；——压过了，或者毋宁说，盖过了；因此雷切尔到村舍门口迎她出来的时候，她没有立刻诉说自己的劳累，而是满怀爱怜地端详女儿的脸——又爱怜又担忧——说了一句两句表示疼爱的小话。

“您一定乏极了，”雷切尔说；她这一番不知自责了多少回、心里翻腾了多少场，总算一时把她那股硬心肠压了下去。

“是啊，乏了，亲爱的；乏得很。我还当那火车再也不会到巴斯尔赫斯特车站了。一站一站的小站它都停，说真的，我看我走都能走得跟它一样快。”满打满算，十二年的光阴还没过去呢：那时候这些火车的速度在雷太太看来可怕极了，她几乎不敢往车厢里迈腿！

“那您都见着谁了？”雷切尔说。

“见着谁！”雷太太说。“谁告诉你我见着人了？”

“想必您见着古德尔先生了吧。”

===Original===

“Oh yes, I saw him of course. I saw him, and the cottages are all sold. We shall have seven pounds ten a year more than before. I’m sure it will be a very great comfort. Seven pounds ten will buy so many things.”

“But ten pounds would buy more.”

“Of course it would, my dear. And I told Mr. Goodall I wished he could make it ten, as it would make it sound so much more regular like; but he said he couldn’t do it because the gas has gone up so much. He could have done it if I had sixty pounds, but of course I hadn’t.”

“But, mamma, whom did you see except Mr. Goodall? I know you saw somebody, and you must tell me.”

“That’s nonsense, Rachel. You can’t know that I saw anybody.” It may, however, be well to explain at once the cause of Mrs. Ray’s hesitation, and that this may be done in the proper course, we will go back to her journey to Exeter. All the incidents of her day may be told very shortly; but there was one incident in her day which filled her with so much anxiety, and almost dismay, that it must be narrated.

===Chinese===

“哦，是的，他我自然见到了。我见着他了，村舍也都卖掉了。往后一年比先前多七镑十先令。我确信这可是顶大的宽慰。七镑十先令能买多少东西啊。”

“可十镑能买得更多。”

“那当然，亲爱的。我还同古德尔先生说，要是能凑成十镑就好了，那样说起来多么整整齐齐像回事；可他说办不到，因为煤气的行情涨得太高。我要是有六十镑，他就能给我办成，可我当然没有。”

“可是，妈妈，除了古德尔先生，您还见着谁了？我知道您见着人了，您非告诉我不可。”

“胡说，雷切尔。你不可能知道我见着了人。”不过，雷太太为什么这样支吾，眼下就把缘故说明白也好；为把这缘故按着正当的顺序讲清，我们且回到她那趟埃克塞特之行。她那一天的种种事情，三言两语就能交代完；可那一天有一桩事，叫她满心焦灼，几乎张皇失措，不能不细细道来。

===Original===

On arriving at Exeter she got into an omnibus which would have taken her direct to Mr. Goodall’s office in the Close; but she was minded to call at a shop in the High Street, and had herself put down at the corner of one of those passages which lead from the High Street to the Close. She got down from the step of the vehicle, very carefully, as is the wont with middle-aged ladies from the country, and turned round to walk directly into the shop; but before her, on the pavement, she saw Luke Rowan. He was standing close to her, so that it was impossible that they should have pretended to miss seeing each other, even had they been so minded. Any such pretence would have been impossible to Mrs. Ray, and would have been altogether contrary to Luke Rowan’s nature. He had been coming out of the shop, and had been arrested at once by Mrs. Ray’s figure as he saw it emerging from the door of the omnibus.

“How d’you do?” said he, coming forward with outstretched hand, and speaking as though there was nothing between him and Mrs. Ray which required any peculiar word or tone.

“Oh, Mr. Rowan! is this you?” said she. “Dear, dear! I’m sure I didn’t expect to see you in Exeter.”

===Chinese===

到了埃克塞特，她上了一辆公共马车（omnibus），那车本可以一直把她送到古德尔先生设在教堂围地（the Close）的账房；可她有意要去大街上一家铺子里买东西，便叫人在一条小巷口停了车——那样的窄巷，从大街通到教堂围地的还有好几条。她扶着踏板小心下车——乡下来的中年太太们向来如此——转过身便要径直进那家铺子；可就在她眼前，人行道上，她看见了卢克·罗恩。他就站在她近旁，哪怕两人存心装作没瞧见彼此，也是装不成的。这样的装腔，雷太太断然做不出来，也全然有悖卢克·罗恩的性情。他本是从那家铺子里出来的，一眼望见雷太太的身影从公共马车的车门里冒出来，登时定在了原地。

“您好啊？”他说着迎上前来，伸出手，那口气就仿佛他和雷太太之间平平常常，用不着任何特别的字眼或特别的腔调似的。

“哦，罗恩先生！这不是您吗？”她说。“哎哟，哎哟！我担保我万万没料到会在埃克塞特见着您。”

===Original===

“I dare say not, Mrs. Ray; and I didn’t expect to see you. But the odd thing is I’ve come here about the same business as you, though I didn’t know anything about it till yesterday.”

“What business, Mr. Rowan?”

“I’ve bought your cottages in Baslehurst.”

“No!”

“But I have, and I’ve paid for them too, and you’re going this very minute to Mr. Goodall to sign the deed of sale. Isn’t that true? So you see I know all about it.”

“Well, that is strange! Isn’t it, now?”

===Chinese===

“多半没料到吧，雷太太；我也没料到会见着您。可巧就巧在，我上这儿来办的，同您是同一桩事，尽管直到昨天我还一无所知。”

“什么事呀，罗恩先生？”

“我把你们在巴斯尔赫斯特的那几所村舍买下了。”

“不会吧！”

“可我买了，钱也付清了，您这一会儿正是要到古德尔先生那儿去签卖契。是不是这样？您瞧，这事的底细我全知道。”

“哎呀，这可真奇了！可不是吗？”

===Original===

“The fact is I must have a bit of land at Baslehurst for building. Tappitt will go on fighting; and as I don’t mean to be beaten, I’ll have a place of my own there.”

“And you’ll pull down the cottages?”

“If I don’t pull him down first, so as to get the old brewery. I was obliged to buy your bit of ground now, as I might not have been able to get any just when I wanted it. You’ve sold it a deal too cheap. You tell Mr. Goodall I say so.”

“But he says I’m to gain something by selling it.”

“Does he? If it is so, I’m very glad of it. I only came down from London yesterday to finish this piece of business, and I’m going back today.”

During all this time not a word had been said about Rachel. He had not even asked after her in the ordinary way in which men ask after their ordinary acquaintance. He had not looked as though he were in the least embarrassed in speaking to Rachel’s mother, and now it seemed as though he were going away, as though all had been said between them that he cared to say. Mrs. Ray at the first moment had dreaded any special word; but now, as he was about to leave her, she felt disappointed that no special word had been spoken. But he was not as yet gone.

===Chinese===

“实话是这么回事：我在巴斯尔赫斯特必须有一块地皮盖房子。塔皮特还要斗下去；我可不打算输，我非得在那儿有一处自己的立足之地不可。”

“那您要把村舍拆掉？”

“除非我先把塔皮特撂倒，把那座老酿酒厂拿到手。你们那块地，我如今是非买不可，不然等到我要用的时候，兴许就弄不着地了。这地你们卖得太贱、太贱了。您就替我捎话给古德尔先生，说这是我讲的。”

“可他说我卖了能多得些好处。”

“是吗？果真如此，我很高兴。我昨天才从伦敦下来办结这桩事，今天就回去。”

这么半天，一句关于雷切尔的话也没有说出口。他甚至没有像男人寻常问候寻常相识那样，顺口问一声她的好。他同雷切尔的母亲说话，神色间没有半点窘迫；此刻眼看要走开了，仿佛两人之间他乐意说的话，已经统统说尽。方才头一阵，雷太太原是怕他说出什么出格的话来；可这会儿他就要撒手走了，她反倒因为一句出格的话也没听着，心里空落落的。可他还没有走。

===Original===

“I literally haven’t a minute to spare,” he said, offering her his hand for a second time; “for I’ve two or three people to see before I get to the train.”

“Goodbye,” said Mrs. Ray.

“Goodbye, Mrs. Ray. I don’t think I’ve been very well treated among you. I don’t indeed. But I won’t say any more about that at present. Is she quite well?”

“Pretty well, thank you,” said she, all of a tremble.

“I won’t send her any message. As things are at present, no message would be of any service. Goodbye.” And so saying he went from her.

Mrs. Ray at that moment had no time for making up her mind as to what she would do or say in consequence of this meeting—or whether she would do or say anything. She looked forward to all the leisure time of her journey home for thinking of that; so she finished her shopping and hurried on to Mr. Goodall’s office without resolving whether or no she would tell Rachel of the encounter. At Mr. Goodall’s she remained some little time, dining at that gentleman’s house as well as signing the deed, and asking questions about the gas company. He had grateful recollections of kindnesses received from Mr. Ray, and always exercised his hospitality on those rare occasions which brought Mrs. Ray up to Exeter. As they sat at table he asked questions about the young purchaser of the property which somewhat perplexed Mrs. Ray. Yes, she said, she did know him. She had just met him in the street and heard his news. Young Rowan, she told her friend, had been at the cottage more than once, but no mention had been made of his desire to buy these cottages. Was he well spoken of in Baslehurst? Well;—she was so little in Baslehurst that she hardly knew. She had heard that he had quarrelled with Mr. Tappitt, and she believed that many people had said that he was wrong in his quarrel. She knew nothing of his property; but certainly had heard somebody say that he had gone away without paying his debts. It may easily be conceived how miserable and ineffective she would be under this cross-examination, although it was made by Mr. Goodall without any allusion to Rachel.

===Chinese===

“我真真是分秒都没有了，”他说着，第二次向她伸出手去，“我还得见两三个人，然后才赶得上火车。”

“再会，”雷太太说。

“再会，雷太太。我在你们那儿受的待遇，可算不得好。实在算不得好。不过这话眼下我不多说。她好吗？”

“挺好的，谢谢您，”她说，浑身直打颤。

“我不给她捎什么口信。照眼下这样，捎什么口信也无济于事。再会。”说完，他便从她跟前走了。

这当口，雷太太哪里还有工夫拿定主意：经过这场相遇，她该做什么、说什么——还是干脆什么都不做、什么都不说。这层心思，她预备留到回家路上所有的闲工夫里去想；于是她买完了东西，便匆匆往古德尔先生的账房去，心里还没拿定要不要把这场相遇告诉雷切尔。她在古德尔先生家盘桓了一阵，不但签了契，还在那位先生府上用了饭，又问起煤气公司的种种。雷先生生前待他的种种好处，他记在心里，怀着感激；每逢雷太太难得上埃克塞特来，他总要尽一尽东道之谊。席间他问起那位买产业的年轻买主，问得雷太太颇为狼狈。是的，她说，她认得他。她刚刚还在街上遇见他，听了他的一番新闻。她对这位朋友说，小罗恩到村舍来过不止一次，可从没提过他想买这几所村舍。他在巴斯尔赫斯特名声可好？这个嘛；——她不大在巴斯尔赫斯特走动，实在说不上来。她听说他同塔皮特先生闹翻了，而且她相信，许多人都说这场争吵错在他。他的家底她一概不知；不过的确听人说过，他欠着债，一走了之。不难想见，在这番盘问之下，她有多么凄惶、多么语无伦次——虽然古德尔先生问这些话时，对雷切尔半个字也没有提。

===Original===

“At any rate we have got our money,” said Mr. Goodall; “and I suppose that’s all we care about. But I should say he’s rather a harum-scarum sort of fellow. Why he should leave his debts behind him I can’t understand, as he seems to have plenty of money.”

All this made Mrs. Ray’s task the more difficult. During the last two or three weeks she had been wishing that she had not gone to Mr. Comfort—wishing that she had allowed Rachel to answer Rowan’s letter in any terms of warmest love that she might have chosen—wishing, in fact, that she had permitted the engagement to go on. But now she began again to think that she had been right. If this man were in truth a harum-scarum fellow was it not well that Rachel should be quit of him—even with any amount of present sorrow? Thinking of this on her way back to Baslehurst she again made up her mind that Rowan was a wolf. But she had not made up her mind as to what she would, or what she would not tell Rachel about the meeting, even when she reached her own door. “I will send her no message,” he had said. “As things are at present no message would be of service.” What had he meant by this? What purpose on his part did these words indicate? These questions Mrs. Ray had asked herself, but had failed to answer them.

But no resolution on Mrs. Ray’s part to keep the meeting secret would have been of avail, even had she made such resolution. The fact would have fallen from her as easily as water falls from a sieve. Rachel would have extracted from her the information, had she been ever so determined not to impart it. As things had turned out she had at once given Rachel to understand that she had met someone in Exeter whom she had not expected to meet.

===Chinese===

“无论如何，钱是到手了，”古德尔先生说；“我想咱们操心的也就这一点。可依我看，那家伙是个相当冒失浮躁的性子。他似乎有的是钱，为什么欠着债一走了之，我可弄不懂。”

这一切，都叫雷太太的难处又深了一层。最近两三个星期，她一直在巴不得自己没去过康福特先生家——巴不得自己容让雷切尔随她挑什么最热烈的情话去回罗恩的信——说实在的，就是巴望自己当初容让这桩婚事继续下去。可如今，她又开始觉得自己是做对了。倘若这人当真是个冒失浮躁的性子，雷切尔趁早甩脱了他，岂不是好——哪怕眼下有多少悲伤也在所不惜？回巴斯尔赫斯特的路上想着这些，她又拿定主意：罗恩是头狼。可是，这场相遇该不该同雷切尔讲、讲到什么分寸，直到自家门口，她还没拿定主意。“我不给她捎什么口信，”他说过。“照眼下这样，捎什么口信也无济于事。”他这话是什么意思？这些话表明他存着什么心思？这些问题雷太太问过自己，却答不上来。

可是雷太太纵然拿定主意要守口如瓶，也断然守不住，哪怕她真拿了这个主意。那桩事也会从她嘴里漏出来，就像水从筛子里漏出来一样容易。哪怕她横下一条心一个字不吐，雷切尔也能从她嘴里把消息掏出来。而事情的结局是，她已经立刻让雷切尔明白了：她在埃克塞特遇见了一个她万万想不到会遇见的人。

===Original===

“But, mamma, whom did you see except Mr. Goodall?” Rachel asked. “I know you saw somebody, and you must tell me.”

“That’s nonsense, Rachel; you can’t know that I saw anybody.”

After that there was a pause for some moments, and then Rachel persisted in her inquiry. “But, mamma, I do know that you met somebody.”—Then there was another pause.—“Mamma, was it Mr. Rowan?”

Mrs. Ray stood convicted at once. Had she not spoken a word, the form of her countenance when the question was asked would have answered it with sufficient clearness. But she did speak a word. “Well; yes, it was Mr. Rowan. He had come down to Exeter on business.”

“And what did he say, mamma?”

“He didn’t say anything—at least, nothing particular. It is he that has bought the cottages, and he had come down from London about that. He told me that he wanted some ground near Baslehurst, because he couldn’t get the brewery.”

===Chinese===

“可是，妈妈，除了古德尔先生，您还见着谁了？”雷切尔问。“我知道您见着人了，您非告诉我不可。”

“胡说，雷切尔；你不可能知道我见着了人。”

打这以后，静了好一会儿，雷切尔却不肯罢休。“可是，妈妈，我知道您是遇见人了。”——又静了一会儿。——“妈妈，是不是罗恩先生？”

雷太太登时像个被当场定罪的犯人。哪怕她一个字不吐，问出这句话时她脸上的神色，也足以把答案清清楚楚地供出来。可她到底吐了字。“唉；是啊，是罗恩先生。他到埃克塞特来办事。”

“他说了什么呀，妈妈？”

“他什么也没说——至少没什么特别的。村舍就是他买的，他就是为这个从伦敦下来的。他跟我说，他要在巴斯尔赫斯特近旁弄一块地，因为酿酒厂他弄不到手。”

===Original===

“And what else did he say, mamma?”

“I tell you that he said nothing else.”

“He didn’t—didn’t mention me then?”

Mrs. Ray had been looking away from Rachel during this conversation—had been purposely looking away from her. But now there was a tone of agony in her child’s voice which forced her to glance round. Ah me! She beheld so piteous an expression of woe in Rachel’s face that her whole heart was melted within her, and she began to wish instantly that they might have Rowan back again with all his faults.

“Tell me the truth, mamma; I may as well know it.”

“Well, my dear, he didn’t mention your name, but he did say a word about you.”

===Chinese===

“他还说了什么呀，妈妈？”

“我告诉你，他别的什么也没说。”

“他没——没提到我吗？”

这场对话里，雷太太一直把眼光躲着雷切尔——存心把眼光躲着她。可这会儿，孩子话音里那股痛楚的调子，逼得她不得不回过头去。天可怜见！雷切尔脸上那副悲容凄惶得叫她整颗心都化了，她登时转了念头：但愿罗恩回来吧，带着他一身的毛病回来吧。

“跟我说实话吧，妈妈；我横竖是要知道的。”

“唉，亲爱的，他没提你的名字，可他的确说了你一句。”

===Original===

“What word, mamma?”

“He said he would send no message because it would be no good.”

“He said that, did he?”

“Yes, he said that. And so I suppose he meant it would be no good sending anything till he came himself.”

“No, mamma; he didn’t mean quite that. I understand what he meant. As it is to be so, he was quite right. No message could be of any use. It has been my own doing, and I have no right to blame him. Mamma, if you don’t mind, I think I’ll go to bed.”

“My dear, you’re wrong. I’m sure you’re wrong. He didn’t mean that.”

===Chinese===

“说了什么呀，妈妈？”

“他说他不捎什么口信，因为捎了也没用。”

“他这么说的，是吗？”

“是啊，他这么说的。所以我猜他的意思是：在他自己回来之前，捎什么去都是白搭。”

“不，妈妈；他的意思不完全是这个。我懂他的意思。事情既然要这样，他做得全对。捎什么口信都不会有用。这都是我自己造成的，我没有权利怪他。妈妈，您要不介意，我想我去睡了。”

“亲爱的，你错了。我担保你错了。他的意思不是这个。”

===Original===

“Didn’t he, mamma?” And as she spoke a sad, weary, wobegone smile came over her face—a smile so sad and piteous that it went to her mother’s heart more keenly than would have done any sound of sorrow, any sobs, or wail of grief. “But I think he did mean that, mamma. It’s no good doubting or fearing any longer. It’s all over now.”

“And it has been my fault!”

“No, dearest. It has not been your fault, nor do I think that it has been mine. I think we’d better not talk of faults. Ah dear;—I do wish he had never come here!”

“Perhaps it may be all well yet, Rachel.”

“Perhaps it may—in another world. It will never be well again for me in this. Good night, mamma. You must never think that I am angry with you.”

Then she went upstairs, leaving Mrs. Ray alone with her sorrow.

===Chinese===

“不是吗，妈妈？”说话间，她脸上浮起一个凄凉、疲惫、愁惨的微笑——那微笑又悲又楚，扎进母亲的心，比任何哀声、任何啜泣、任何恸哭都扎得更深。“可我看他的意思就是这个，妈妈。疑心也罢，害怕也罢，如今都不中用了。全都完了。”

“这都怪我不好！”

“不，我最亲爱的。这不是你的错，我也不觉得是我的错。依我说，咱们最好别再谈谁的错。唉，天哪；——但愿他压根儿就没来过这儿！”

“兴许到头来还会好起来的，雷切尔。”

“兴许会好——在另一个世界里。在这个世界里，我永远好不了了。晚安，妈妈。您千万不能当作我在生您的气。”

说罢她上楼去了，撇下雷太太独自一人守着自己的悲哀。

## XXII Domestic Politics at the Brewery / XXII 酿酒厂里的家政政治

===Original===
In the meantime things were not going on very pleasantly at the brewery, and Mr. Tappitt was making himself unpleasant in the bosom of his family. A lawsuit will sometimes make a man extremely pleasant company to his wife and children. Even a losing lawsuit will sometimes do so, if he be well backed up in his pugnacity by his lawyer, and if the matter of the battle be one in which he can take a delight to fight. “Ah,” a man will say, “though I spend a thousand pounds over it, I’ll stick to him like a burr. He shan’t shake me off.” And at such times he is almost sure to be in a good humour, and in a generous mood. Then let his wife ask him for money for a dinner-party, and his daughters for new dresses. He has taught himself for the moment to disregard money, and to think that he can sow five-pound notes broadcast without any inward pangs. But such was by no means the case with Mr. Tappitt. His lawyer Honyman was not backing him up; and as cool reflection came upon him he was afraid of trusting his interests to those other men, Sharpit and Longfite. And Mrs. Tappitt, when cool reflection came on her, had begun to dread the ruin which it seemed possible that terrible young man might inflict upon them. She had learned already, though Mrs. Ray had not, how false had been that report which had declared Luke Rowan to be frivolous, idle, and in debt. To her it was very manifest that Honyman was afraid of the young man; and Honyman, though he might not be as keen as some others, was at any rate honest. Honyman also thought that if the brewery were given up to Rowan that thousand a year which had been promised would be paid regularly; and to this solution of the difficulty Mrs. Tappitt was gradually bending herself to submit as the best which an untoward fate offered to them. Honyman himself had declared to her that Mr. Tappitt, if he were well advised, would admit Rowan in as a partner, on equal terms as regarded power and ultimate possession, but with that lion’s share of the immediate concern for himself which Rowan offered. But this she knew that Tappitt would not endure; and she knew, also, that if he were brought to endure it for a while, it would ultimately lead to terrible sorrows. “They would be knocking each other about with the pokers, Mr. Honyman,” she had said; “and where would the custom be when that got into the newspapers?” “If I were Mr. Tappitt, I would just let him have his own way,” Honyman had replied. “That shows that you don’t know Tappitt,” had been Mrs. Tappitt’s rejoinder. No;—the thousand a year and dignified retirement in a villa had recommended itself to Mrs. Tappitt’s mind. She would use all her influence to attain that position—if only she could bring herself to feel assured that the thousand a year would be forthcoming.

As to Tappitt himself, he was by no means so anxious to prolong the battle as he had been at the time of Rowan’s departure. His courage for fighting was not maintained by good backing. Had Honyman clapped him on the shoulder and bade him put ready money in his purse, telling him that all would come out right eventually, and that Rowan would be crushed, he would have gone about Baslehurst boasting loudly, and would have been happy. Then Mrs. T. and the girls would have had a merry time of it; and the Tappitts would have come out of the contest with four or five hundred a year for life instead of the thousand now offered to them, and nobody would have blamed anybody for such a result. But Honyman had not spirit for such backing. In his dull, slow, droning way he had shaken his head and said that things were looking badly. Then Tappitt had cursed and had sworn, and had half resolved to go to Sharpit and Longfite. Sharpit and Longfite would have clapped him on the back readily enough, and have bade him put plenty of money in his purse. But we may suppose that Fate did not intend the ruin of Tappitt, seeing that she did not make him mad enough to seek the counsels of Sharpit and Longfite. Fate only made him very cross and unpleasant in the bosom of his family. Looking out himself for some mode of escape from this terrible enemy that had come upon him, he preferred the raising of the sum of money which would be necessary to buy off Rowan altogether. Rowan had demanded ten thousand pounds, but Tappitt still thought that seven, or, at any rate, eight thousand would do it.

===Chinese===
与此同时，酿酒厂里的事情进行得很不痛快，塔皮特先生正把自己弄得在一家人当中惹人生厌。一场官司，有时倒能把一个男人变成老婆儿女跟前极其可亲可爱的伴侣。就算是一场必输的官司，有时也能有此奇效——只要律师在他的好斗性子上给他撑足了腰，只要这一仗争的事，正是他打得津津有味的事。“啊，”这样的人会说，“就算为这桩事花上一千镑，我也要像颗牛蒡子似的粘住他不放。他休想把我甩脱。”这种时候，他几乎必定和颜悦色，出手也慷慨大方。这当口，任凭妻子为办宴席向他要钱，任凭女儿们为做新衣裳向他要钱。他一时之间已教会自己不把钱当回事，自认为可以把五镑钞票当种子四下里撒，心里不见半点疼惜。可塔皮特先生的情形，却远不是这么回事。他的律师霍尼曼不肯给他撑腰；而冷静的思量一旦袭来，他又不敢把自己的利益托付给另外那两个人——夏皮特和朗费特。塔皮特太太这边，冷静的思量一旦袭来，也已经开始惧怕那个可怕的年轻人兴许会加给他们一家的倾覆。她已经得知——雷太太却还蒙在鼓里——那通说卢克·罗恩轻浮、游惰、负债的流言，原是何等的子虚乌有。在她看来，霍尼曼怕那个年轻人，这是再明白不过的；而霍尼曼纵然不似有些人那样犀利，至少是诚实的。霍尼曼还认为，倘若把酿酒厂让给罗恩，那许下的一年一千镑便会按期照付；对这道难题的这样一个解法，塔皮特太太正渐渐弯下身子去俯就，把它看作乖戾的命运肯赏给他们的最好出路。霍尼曼本人已对她言明：塔皮特先生若肯纳忠言，就该让罗恩入伙做合伙人，权力与最终产权两家均等，而眼前操持这份营生的大头，则照罗恩开出的条件归他自己。可这一条她知道塔皮特忍受不了；她同样知道，纵然一时逼他受了，到头来也必酿成大悲大痛。“那他们爷儿俩就要拿拨火棍你敲我、我敲你了，霍尼曼先生，”她说过，“这种事一上了报纸，买卖还往哪儿去？”“我若是塔皮特先生，我就索性随他自己的便，”霍尼曼答过。“这话可见您不认得塔皮特，”塔皮特太太顶了这么一句。不；——一年一千镑、退居别墅、安享体面——这一条才是说进了塔皮特太太心坎的。她要使出浑身的解数去谋到那个地位——只消她能叫自己确信，那一千镑年终是拿得到的。

至于塔皮特本人，他续战下去的心气，已远不如罗恩出走那阵子足了。他的斗志没人好生接济，撑持不住。霍尼曼倘若拍拍他的肩膀，叫他只管把现钱捂紧在钱袋里，告诉他事情到头来定然不差，罗恩必被压垮，他便会满巴斯尔赫斯特大声夸口，快快活活。那样一来，塔皮特太太和小姐们也有一场热闹好过；塔皮特一家打完这一仗，也能终身落得一年四五百镑——而不是如今许给他们的那一千镑——而这样的结果，也不会有谁去怪罪谁。可霍尼曼没有这份替人撑腰的豪气。他拿他那副沉闷、迟缓、嗡嗡念经的腔调摇了摇头，说事情看着不妙。塔皮特于是咒天骂地，有一半心思要去投夏皮特和朗费特。夏皮特和朗费特拍他的后背原是极爽快的，还会叫他往钱袋里多多地装现钱。不过我们不妨猜想，命运并不存心要塔皮特倾家荡产，否则断不会没把他逼疯到去求教夏皮特和朗费特的地步。命运只是叫他脾气坏透，在自家人的怀里惹人生厌。他自家也在寻思逃离这个临头的可怕仇敌的路数，比来比去，看中了筹一笔款子、把罗恩整个儿买断这条道。罗恩开口要一万镑，塔皮特却仍旧觉得七千，退一万步八千，总能办得下来。

===Original===
“I don’t think he’ll take less than ten,” said Honyman, “because his share is really worth as much as that.”

This was very provoking; and who can wonder that Tappitt was not pleasant company in his own house?

On the day after Mrs. Ray’s visit to Exeter, Tappitt, as was now his almost daily practice, made his way into Mr. Honyman’s little back room, and sat there with his hat on, discussing his affairs.

“I find that Mr. Rowan has bought those cottages of the widow Ray’s,” said Honyman.

===Chinese===
“我看他一万镑以下是不肯松口的，”霍尼曼说，“因为他那份产业实实在在就值那么多。”

这话实在叫人冒火；塔皮特在自己家里成了个不讨人喜欢的伴儿，这又有什么可奇怪的呢？

雷太太去埃克塞特走了一遭的次日，塔皮特照着他如今几乎每日一趟的老例，踱进霍尼曼先生那间小小的后屋，戴着帽子坐在那里，商量他的事务。

“我发现，罗恩先生把寡妇雷家的那几所小屋买了下来，”霍尼曼说。

===Original===
“Nonsense!” shouted Tappitt, as though such a purchase on Rowan’s part was a new injury done to himself.

“Oh, but he has,” said Honyman. “There’s not a doubt in life about it. If he does mean to build a new brewery, it wouldn’t be a bad place. You see it’s out of the thoroughfare of the town, and yet, as one may say, within a stone’s throw of the High Street.”

I will not repeat Mr. Tappitt’s exclamation as he listened to these suggestions of his lawyer, but it was of a nature to show that he had not heard the news with indifference.

“You see he’s such a fellow that you don’t know where to have him,” continued Honyman. “It’s not only that he don’t mind ruining you, but he don’t mind ruining himself either.”

“I don’t believe he’s got anything to lose.”

===Chinese===
“胡说！”塔皮特嚷道，仿佛罗恩买下这份产业，又是加在他自己身上的一桩新伤害。

“哦，可他买下了，”霍尼曼说，“这事儿再没有半点可疑。他若当真要另起一座酿酒厂，那地方还不坏。您看，它不在镇上通衢大道上，可又可以说，离大街不过一石之遥。”

塔皮特先生听律师说出这些话头时喊了些什么，我不在此复述了；只说那一声的性质足以表明，这消息他听在耳里，绝非无动于衷。

“您瞧，他就是这么一个叫你摸不着深浅的人，”霍尼曼接着说，“他不光不在乎把你毁了，连把自己毁了也不在乎。”

“我不信他有什么可输的东西。”

===Original===
“Ah! that’s where you’re wrong. He has paid ready money for this bit of land to begin with, or Goodall would never have let him have it. Goodall knows what he’s about as well as any man.”

“And do you mean to tell me that he’s going to put up buildings there at once?” And Tappitt’s face as he asked the question would have softened the heart of any ordinary lawyer. But Honyman was one whom nothing could harden and nothing soften.

“I don’t know what he’s going to put up, Mr. Tappitt, and I don’t know when. But I know this well enough; that when a man buys little bits of property about a place it shows that he means to do something there.”

“If he had twenty thousand pounds, he’d lose it all.”

“That’s very likely; but the question is, how would you fare in the meantime? If he hadn’t this claim upon you, of course you’d let him build what he liked, and only laugh at him.” Then Mr. Tappitt uttered another exclamation, and pulling his hat tighter on to his head, walked out of the lawyer’s office and returned to the brewery.

===Chinese===
“啊！您这可就错了。单说这块地，他付的就是现钱，不然古德尔先生决计不肯撒手给他。古德尔那个人，做什么事心里都有数，不比谁差。”

“您是想告诉我，他马上就要在那儿动工起房了吧？”塔皮特问这话时的那副脸色，寻常的律师见了，心肠都要软下来。可霍尼曼这个人，什么也硬不了他，什么也软不了他。

“他要起什么，塔皮特先生，我不知道；几时动工，我也不知道。可有一层我看得清清楚楚：一个人在一处地方零零碎碎地置产业，就说明他打算在那儿干点什么。”

“他就是有两万镑，也会输个精光。”

“那很可能；可问题在于，这当口您自己怎么过？他若不是捏着您这样一笔债权，您自然随他爱盖什么盖什么，只拿他当笑话看。”塔皮特先生又喊了一声什么，把帽子往头上勒紧，出了律师事务所，回酿酒厂去了。

===Original===
They dined at three o’clock at the brewery, and during dinner on this day the father of the family made himself very disagreeable. He scolded the maidservant till the poor girl didn’t know the spoons from the forks. He abused the cook’s performances till that valuable old retainer declared that if “master got so rampageous he might suit hisself, the sooner the better; she didn’t care how soon; she’d cooked victuals for his betters and would again.” He snarled at his daughters till they perked up their faces and came silently to a mutual agreement that they would not condescend to notice him further while he held on in his present mood. And he replied to his wife’s questions—questions intended to be soothing and kindly conjugal—in such a tone that she determined to have it out with him before she allowed him to go to bed. “She knew her duty,” she said to herself, “and she could stand a good deal. But there were some things she couldn’t stand and some things that weren’t her duty.” After dinner Tappitt took himself out at once to his office in the brewery, and then, for the first time, saw the *Baslehurst Gazette and Totnes Chronicle* for that week. The *Baslehurst Gazette and Totnes Chronicle* was an enterprising weekly newspaper, which had been originally intended to convey on Sunday mornings to the inhabitants of South Devonshire the news of the past week, and the paper still bore the dates of successive Sundays. But it had gradually pushed itself out into the light of its own world before its own date, gaining first a night and then a day, till now, at the period of which I am speaking, it was published on the Friday morning.

===Chinese===
酿酒厂里三点开正餐；这一天吃饭的工夫，一家之主把自己弄得惹人生厌极了。他把女仆骂得那可怜姑娘连勺子叉子都分不清。他把厨娘的手艺数落个没完，直数落得那位可贵的老家仆放出话来：“老爷要是发起横来，尽可以自己将就伺候自己，越快越好；多快她都不在乎；她给比他体面的人做过饭菜，往后还要再做。”他又冲女儿们龇牙咧嘴地吼，直吼得她们把脸一绷，无声无息地暗暗订下攻守同盟：他这副脾气不改，她们再不肯屈尊搭理他。他回答妻子问话——那原是些意在抚慰、满含夫妻情分的问话——的那副腔调，叫她打定了主意：不跟他把话说个明白，休想放他上床睡觉。“她知道自己的本分，”她对自己说，“她受得住许多事。可有几件事她受不住，还有几件事，算不得她的本分。”饭后塔皮特立刻躲进酿酒厂里他的账房，这才头一回看到那一期的《巴斯尔赫斯特公报暨托特尼斯纪事报》（*Baslehurst Gazette and Totnes Chronicle*）。《巴斯尔赫斯特公报暨托特尼斯纪事报》是一份雄心勃勃的周报，当初的本意是在礼拜日早晨把过去一星期的新闻送到南德文郡居民手里，报头至今仍标着接连各礼拜日的日期。可它一步一步抢在自己日期的前头挤进了世人眼前，先提前一夜，又提前一天，到我所讲的这个时期，已经改在礼拜五早晨出报了。

===Original===
“You ought just to look at this,” a burly old foreman had said, handing him the paper in question, with his broad thumb placed upon a certain column. This foreman had known Bungall, and though he respected Tappitt, he did not fear him. “You should just look at this. Of course it don’t amount to nothing; but it’s as well to see what folks say.” And he handed the paper to his master, almost making a hole in it by screwing his thumb on to the spot he wished to indicate.

Tappitt read the article, and his spirit was very bitter within him. It was a criticism on his own beer written in no friendly tone. “There is no reason,” said the article, “why Baslehurst should be flooded with a liquor which no Christian ought to be asked to drink. Baslehurst is as capable of judging good beer from bad as any town in the British empire. Let Mr. Tappitt look to it, or some young rival will spring up beneath his feet and seize from his brow the hop-leaf wreath which Bungall won and wore.” This attack was the more cruel because the paper had originally been established by Bungall’s money, and had, in old days, been altogether devoted to the Bungall interest. That this paper should turn against him was very hard. But what else had he a right to expect? It was known that he had promised his vote to the Jew candidate, and the paper in question supported the Cornbury interest. A man that lives in a glass house should throw no stones. The brewer who brews bad beer should vote for nobody.

===Chinese===
“这个您真该瞧瞧，”一个粗壮的老工头说过，把那份报纸递到他手里，宽阔的大拇指按定某一栏。这工头是认得邦格尔的，他敬重塔皮特，却不怕他。“您真该瞧瞧这个。当然喽，这里头什么名堂也没有；可人家说了些什么，看看总没坏处。”他把报纸递给东家，大拇指拧在他要指的那一处，几乎要在报上拧出个窟窿来。

塔皮特把那篇文章读了，心里的苦水直往上翻。那是就他自酿的啤酒写的一篇评论，笔调全无善意。“巴斯尔赫斯特没有道理，”文章说，“要叫一种连基督徒都不该被请求下咽的液体灌满街市。论判别啤酒的好坏，巴斯尔赫斯特不比不列颠帝国哪座镇子差。塔皮特先生好自为之，不然他脚下就会蹦出个年轻的对头，把邦格尔赢得又戴过的那顶啤酒花叶冠，从他额头上一把夺去。”这一击所以分外刻毒，还因为这家报纸当初本是拿邦格尔的钱办起来的，早年间一心一意只向着邦格尔家的利益。这家报纸如今倒戈相向，于他实在难堪。可他又有权利指望别的什么？人人知道他已把票许给了那位犹太候选人，而这家报纸偏偏拥护康伯里家的利益。住玻璃房子的人，不该朝人扔石头。酿坏啤酒的酿酒商，谁的票也不该投。

===Original===
But Tappitt would not regard this attack upon him in its proper political light. Every evil at present falling upon him was supposed to come from his present enemy. “It’s that dirty underhand blackguard,” he said to the foreman.

“I don’t think so, Mr. Tappitt,” said the foreman. “I don’t think so indeed.”

“But I tell you it is,” said Tappitt, “and I don’t care what you think.”

“Just as you please, Mr. Tappitt,” said the foreman, who thereupon retired from the office, leaving his master to meditate over the newspaper in solitude.

可塔皮特不肯把这一击放到它应有的政治光线下看待。眼下落到他头上的每一桩祸事，他一概记到眼前这个仇敌的账上。“就是那个下流阴损的恶棍干的，”他对工头说。

“我不这么看，塔皮特先生，”工头说。“我实在不这么看。”

“可我告诉你，就是他，”塔皮特说，“你怎么看我，我毫不在意。”

“您请便，塔皮特先生，”工头说，说罢便退出账房，留东家一个人对着报纸独自思量。

===Original===
It was a very bitter time for the poor brewer. He was one of those men whose spirit is not wanting to them while the noise and tumult of contest are around them, but who cannot hold on by their own convictions in the quiet hours. He could storm, and talk loud, and insist on his own way while men stood around him listening and perhaps admiring; but he was cowed when left by himself to think of things which seemed to be adverse. What could he do, if those around him, who had known him all his life as those newspaper people had known him—what could he do if they turned against him, and talked of bad beer as Rowan had talked? He was not man enough to stand up and face this new enemy unless he were backed by his old friends. Honyman had told him that he would be beaten. How would it fare with him and his family if he were beaten? As he sat in his little office, with his hat low down over his eyes, balancing himself on the hind legs of his chair, he abused Honyman roundly. Had Honyman been possessed of wit, of skill, of professional craft—had he been the master of any invention, all might have been well. But the attorney was a fool, an ass, a coward. Might it not be that he was a knave? But luckily for Honyman, and luckily also for Mr. Tappitt himself, this abuse did not pass beyond the precincts of Tappitt’s own breast. We all know how delightful is the privilege of abusing our nearest friends after this fashion; but we generally satisfy ourselves with that limited audience to which Mr. Tappitt addressed himself on the present occasion.

===Chinese===
可怜的酿酒商，这一晌过得真苦。世上有一种人，只要争斗的喧嚣纷扰在四围响着，他们的胆气并不短少；可一到清静的时辰，便撑不住自己认定的主意了。塔皮特便是这种人。身边围着一圈听着、说不定还带着几分钦佩的人时，他尽可以咆哮，大声嚷嚷，一意坚持自己的路数；可一旦撇下他独自去想那些看着不妙的事，他就蔫了。倘若他周围那些人——正像报馆那些人一样打小认得他的那些人——倘若他们翻过脸来，也像罗恩那样把坏啤酒挂在嘴上，他可怎么办？除非有老朋友们给他撑腰，他就没有那份男子汉的胆量站起来，迎面挡住这个新敌人。霍尼曼已经对他说过，他这一仗要输。倘若输了，他和他一家人往后怎么过？他坐在那间小账房里，帽子低低压到眼皮上，身子靠着椅子后两条腿摇摇晃晃地平衡着，把霍尼曼骂了个狗血淋头。霍尼曼倘若有点机智，有点本领，有点律师的看家手艺——倘若他肚里有一点发明创见，事情本可以全然两样。可这位律师是个蠢货，一头驴，一个懦夫。保不齐还是个无赖？不过霍尼曼福大，塔皮特先生自己也福大，这通咒骂没有走出塔皮特自己胸膛的疆界。我们大家都知道，照这个样子咒骂我们顶亲近的朋友，是天底下多么惬意的特权；不过我们一般也就满足于塔皮特先生这会儿给自己限定的那一小圈听众罢了。

In the meantime Mrs. Tappitt was sitting upstairs in the brewery drawing-room with her daughters, and she also was not happy in her mind. She had been snubbed, and almost browbeaten, at dinner time, and she also had had a little conversation in private with Mr. Honyman. She had been snubbed, and, if she did not look well about her, she was going to be ruined. “You mustn’t let him go on with this lawsuit,” Mr. Honyman had said. “He’ll certainly get the worst of it if he does, and then he’ll have to pay double.” She disliked Rowan quite as keenly as did her husband, but she was fully alive to the folly of spiting Rowan by doing an injury to her own face. She would speak to Tappitt that night very seriously, and in the meantime she turned the Rowan controversy over in her own mind, endeavouring to look at it from all sides. It had never been her custom to make critical remarks on their father’s conduct to any of the girls except Martha; but on the present great occasion she waived that rule, and discussed the family affairs in full female family conclave. “I don’t know what’s come over your papa,” she began by saying. “He seems quite beside himself today.”

这时候，塔皮特太太正同女儿们坐在楼上的酿酒厂客厅里，她心里也不痛快。吃饭的时候她挨了抢白，差点儿没叫气势压倒；她同霍尼曼先生也私下谈过一小番话。她挨了抢白，倘若她再不把眼睛放亮些，眼看着就要倾家荡产。“这桩官司您可不能由他打下去了，”霍尼曼先生说过。“再打下去他准得吃大亏，到那时就得双倍地掏钱。”她厌恶罗恩，恶得同她丈夫一样厉害；可她把一件事看得再透不过：为着怄罗恩而伤了自己的脸面，是天底下傻不过的事。当晚她要同塔皮特正正经经谈一谈；这当儿，她先把罗恩这场争端在心里翻来覆去掂量，想法子从四面八方看个周全。女儿们当中，除了玛莎，她从来不惯对谁议论她们父亲的行事；可眼下这个非常关口，她把这规矩搁下了，把家事拿到一堂女眷的枢密会议上摊开来议。“我不知道你们爸爸今儿是中了什么邪，”她开口说。“他今天简直魂不守舍。”

===Original===
“He’ll never do that,” said Mrs. Tappitt with energy.

“Never; never!” said Augusta—with more energy.

In this way the large and influential feminine majority of the family at the brewery was brought round to look at one of the propositions made by Rowan without disfavour. It was not that that young man’s sins had been in any degree forgiven, but that they all perceived, with female prudence, that it would be injudicious to ruin themselves because they hated him. And then to what lady living in a dingy brick house, close adjoining to the smoke and smells of beer-brewing, would not the idea of a marine villa at Torquay be delicious? None of the family, not even Mrs. Tappitt herself, had ever known what annual profit had accrued to Mr. T. as the reward of his life’s work. But they had been required to live in a modest, homely way—as though that annual profit had not been great. Under the altered circumstances, as now proposed, they would all know that papa had a thousand a year to spend;—and what might not be done at Torquay with a thousand a year? Before Mr. Tappitt came home for the evening—which he did not do on that day till past ten, having been detained, by business, in the bar of the Dragon Inn—they had all resolved that the combined ease and dignity of a thousand a year should be accepted.

===Chinese===
“他断不敢，”塔皮特太太斩钉截铁地说。

“不敢，万万不敢！”奥古斯塔说——口气更足。

就这样，酿酒厂这一家里人数众多、举足轻重的女性多数，被引得转过头来，对罗恩所提条件中的一条不加嫌恶地正视起来。倒不是那个年轻人的罪过得到几分宽宥，而是她们凭着女人的精明，人人看得分明：因为恨他，就连自己一并毁掉，这打算实在欠高明。再说，住着一所暗沉沉的砖房、紧挨着酿酒的烟气和气味的太太，托基一处海滨别墅的念头，谁能听了不心向往之？这一家人里，连塔皮特太太本人在内，谁也不知道T.先生操劳一生的酬报，究竟给他带来多少年收益。可他们一直被要求过着谦抑朴素的日子——仿佛那份年收益并不怎么可观似的。情形一变，照如今的提议，他们人人都将知道爸爸一年有一千镑好花；——在托基，一年一千镑，还有什么办不成的？塔皮特先生晚上到家之前——那天他给生意耽搁在龙客栈的酒吧间里，过了十点才回来——她们全体已经拿定主意：一年一千镑，又安逸又体面，这个提议应该接下来。
