“Then,” said Cherry, “he’ll marry Rachel Ray, and she’ll be mistress of the brewery house.”

“Never!” said Mrs. Tappitt, very solemnly. “Never! He’ll never be such a fool as that.”

“Never!” said Augusta. “Never!”

===Chinese===
“那么，”彻丽说，“他就要娶雷切尔·雷了，她就要做酿酒厂宅子的女主人了。”

“断乎不会！”塔皮特太太庄重之极地说。“断乎不会！他还不至于蠢到那步田地。”

“断乎不会！”奥古斯塔说。“断乎不会！”

===Original===
In the meantime the meeting went on at the Dragon. I can’t say that Mr. Tappitt was on this occasion called upon to preside over the petition. He was simply invited to take the chair at a meeting of a dozen men at Baslehurst who were brought together by Mr. Sharpit in order that they might be induced by him to recommend Mr. Hart to employ him, Mr. Sharpit, in getting up the petition in question; and in order that there might be some sufficient temptation to these twelve men to gather themselves together, the dinner at the Dragon was added to the meeting. Mr. Tappitt took the chair in the big, uncarpeted, fusty room upstairs, in which masonic meetings were held once a month, and in which the farmers of the neighbourhood dined once a week, on market days. He took the chair and some seven or eight of his townsmen clustered round him. The others had sent word that they would manage to come in time for the dinner. Mr. Sharpit, before he put the brewer in his place of authority, prompted him as to what he was to do, and in the course of a quarter of an hour two resolutions, already prepared by Mr. Sharpit, had been passed unanimously. Mr. Hart was to be told by the assembled people of Baslehurst that he would certainly be seated by a scrutiny, and he was to be advised to commence his proceedings at once. These resolutions were duly committed to paper by one of Mr. Sharpit’s clerks, and Mr. Tappitt, before he sat down to dinner, signed a letter to Mr. Hart on behalf of the electors of Baslehurst. When the work of the meeting was completed it still wanted half an hour to dinner, during which the nine electors of Baslehurst sauntered about the yard of the inn, looked into the stables, talked to the landlady at the bar, indulged themselves with gin and bitters, and found the time very heavy on their hands. They were nine decent-looking, middle-aged men, dressed in black not of the newest, in swallow-tailed coats and black trousers, with chimney-pot hats, and red faces; and as they pottered about the premises of the Dragon they seemed to be very little at their ease.

“What’s up, Jim?” said one of the postboys to the ostler.

“Sharpit’s got ’em all here to get some more money out of that ere Jew gent;—that’s about the ticket,” said the ostler.

“He’s a clever un,” said the postboy.

===Chinese===
与此同时，集会在龙客栈里进行着。要说塔皮特先生这一回是受请来主持那桩选举申诉，这话我可说不出口。其实不过是请他在巴斯尔赫斯特十来个人的一个集会上坐主席位；这十来个人是夏皮特先生纠集起来的，好叫他们受他的撺掇，去荐举哈特先生聘他夏皮特先生办理那桩选举申诉；而为了让这十二个人有足够的香饵肯聚拢来，集会之外又添了一顿龙客栈的正餐。塔皮特在楼上那间没有铺地毯、霉气扑鼻的大间里坐了主席——那屋子每月开一次共济会的会，每礼拜逢集市日，左近的农场主又在那儿聚一回餐。他坐了主席位，七八个镇上人围拢在他身边。其余的人捎话说，赶得上正餐时再来。夏皮特把这位酿酒商安放进他那份权威的座位之前，先提词教他该做什么；一刻钟的工夫，两桩由夏皮特先生预先拟好的决议，已经全场一致通过了。要由聚拢一堂的巴斯尔赫斯特士民告诉哈特先生：一经逐票复查，他必定坐上议席；并劝他从速着手申诉。这些决议由夏皮特先生手下的一个书记照章誊录成文；塔皮特先生在入席之前，以巴斯尔赫斯特选民的名义在致哈特先生的一封信上签了字。集会的正事办完，离开饭还有半个钟头；这半个钟头里，那九位巴斯尔赫斯特选民在客栈院子里溜达，往马厩里张望，在酒吧柜台边同老板娘搭话，拿杜松子酒加苦精滋润自己，都觉得这时间沉甸甸地压手。这九位都是模样齐整的中年人，穿一身不见得顶时新的黑衣裳：燕尾服、黑裤子，头顶高筒礼帽，一张张红脸膛；他们在龙客栈的地界里磨磨蹭蹭转来转去，看上去极不自在。

“出什么事了，吉姆（Jim）？”一个马童问马夫说。

“夏皮特把他们全弄到这儿来，好再从那个犹太老爷身上刮一笔钱；——就是这么一档子事儿，”马夫说。

“他是个机灵鬼儿，”马童说。

===Original===
At last the dinner was ready; and the total number of the party having now completed itself, the liberal electors of Baslehurst prepared to enjoy themselves. No bargain had been made on the subject, but it was understood by them all that they would not be asked to pay for their dinner. Sharpit would see to that. He would probably know how to put it into his little bill; and if he failed in that the risk was his own.

But while the body of the liberal electors was peeping into the stables and drinking gin and bitters, Mr. Sharpit and Mr. Tappitt were engaged in a private conference.

“If you come to me,” said Sharpit, “of course I must take it up. The etiquette of the profession don’t allow me to decline.”

“But why should you wish to decline?” said Tappitt, not altogether pleased by Mr. Sharpit’s manner.

“Oh, by no means; no. It’s just the sort of work I like;—not much to be made by it, but there’s injury to be redressed and justice to be done. Only you see poor Honyman hasn’t got much of a practice left to him, and I don’t want to take his bread out of his mouth.”

===Chinese===
正餐到底备好了；人马一齐到齐，巴斯尔赫斯特的自由党选民们便准备快活一番了。这上头并没有讲定什么条件，但他们人人心里有数：这顿饭不会要他们掏钱。夏皮特自会料理。他多半知道怎么把它塞进他那本小账单里去；塞不进去，风险也是他自家的。

可趁着自由党选民大队人马往马厩里张望、喝杜松子酒加苦精的当儿，夏皮特先生同塔皮特先生正在进行一场私谈。

“你既来找我，”夏皮特说，“我自然非接手不可。这一行的规矩不容我推辞。”

“可你为什么要推辞呢？”塔皮特说，对夏皮特先生那副做派不很受用。

“哦，绝不是；不。这恰是我就喜欢的那类活儿；——油水不大，可里有冤屈要昭雪，有公道要伸张。只是你看，可怜的霍尼曼手里剩不下多少业务了，我不愿意砸他的饭碗。”

===Original===
“But I’m not to be ruined because of that!”

“As I said before, if you bring the business to me I must take it up. I can’t help myself, if I would. And if I do take it up I’ll see you through it. Everybody who knows me knows that of me.”

“I suppose I shall find you at home about ten tomorrow?”

“Yes; I’ll be in my office at ten;—only you should think it well over, you know, Mr. Tappitt. I’ve nothing to say against Mr. Honyman—not a word. You’ll remember that, if you please, if there should be anything about it afterwards. Ah! you’re wanted for the chair, Mr. Tappitt. I’ll come and sit alongside of you, if you’ll allow me.”

===Chinese===
“可总不能为了那个就叫我毁掉！”

“方才我已经说过，你把事务送到我手里，我就非接不可。我愿意也罢不愿意也罢，由不得我自己。我既接了，就保你办到底。认得我的人，都知道我这个人是这样的。”

“我想明天十点来钟，府上能寻着你吧？”

“不错；十点钟我在账房里；——只是你知道，塔皮特先生，这事你该好好想透。我对霍尼曼先生毫无异议——半个字也没有。往后这桩事若有什么风言风语，这一层请你记着。啊！有人请你回主席位上去呢，塔皮特先生。你若容许，我就来挨着你坐。”

===Original===
The dinner itself was decidedly bad, and the company undoubtedly dull. I am inclined to think that every individual there would have dined more comfortably at home. A horrid mess concocted of old gravy, catsup, and bad wine was distributed under the name of soup. Then there came upon the table half a huge hake—the very worst fish that swims, a fish with which Devonshire is peculiarly invested. Some hard dark brown mysterious balls were handed round, which on being opened with a knife were found to contain sausage-meat, very greasy and by no means cooked through. Even the *dura ilia* of the liberal electors of Baslehurst declined to make acquaintance with these dainties. After that came the dinner, consisting of a piece of roast beef very raw, and a leg of parboiled mutton, absolutely blue in its state of rawness. When the gory mess was seen which displayed itself on the first incision made into these lumps of meat, the vice-president and one or two of his friends spoke out aloud. That hard and greasy sausage-meat might have been all right for anything they knew to the contrary, and the soup they had swallowed without complaint. But they did know what should be the state of a joint of meat when brought to the table, and therefore they spoke out in their anger. Tappitt himself said nothing that was intended to be carried beyond the waiter, seeing that beer from his own brewery was consumed in the tap of the Dragon; but the vice-president was a hardware dealer with whom the Dragon had but small connection of trade, and he sent terrible messages down to the landlady, threatening her with the Blue Boar, the Mitre, and even with that nasty little pothouse the Chequers. “What is it they expects for their three-and-sixpence?” said the landlady, in her wrath; for it must be understood that Sharpit knew well that he was dealing with one who understood the value of money, and that he did not feel quite sure of passing the dinner in Mr. Hart’s bill. Then came a pie with crust an inch thick, which nobody could eat, and a cabinet pudding, so called, full of lumps of suet. I venture to assert that each liberal elector there would have got a better dinner at home, and would have been served with greater comfort; but a public dinner at an inn is the recognized relaxation of a middle-class Englishman in the provinces. Did he not attend such banquets his neighbours would conceive him to be constrained by domestic tyranny. Others go to them, and therefore he goes also. He is bored frightfully by every speech to which he listens. He is driven to the lowest depths of dismay by every speech which he is called upon to make. He is thoroughly disgusted when he is called on to make no speech. He has no point of sympathy with the neighbours between whom he sits. The wine is bad. The hot water is brought to him cold. His seat is hard and crowded. No attempt is made at the pleasures of conversation. He is continually called upon to stand up that he may pretend to drink a toast in honour of some person or institution for which he cares nothing; for the hero of the evening, as to whom he is probably indifferent; for the church, which perhaps he never enters; the army, which he regards as a hotbed of aristocratic insolence; or for the Queen, whom he reveres and loves by reason of his nature as an Englishman, but against whose fulsome praises as repeated to him *ad nauseam* in the chairman’s speech his very soul unconsciously revolts. It is all a bore, trouble, ennui, nastiness, and discomfort. But yet he goes again and again—because it is the relaxation natural to an Englishman. The Frenchman who sits for three hours tilted on the hind legs of a little chair with his back against the windowsill of the café, with first a cup of coffee before him and then a glass of sugar and water, is perhaps as much to be pitied as regards his immediate misery; but the liquids which he imbibes are not so injurious to him.

===Chinese===
这顿饭本身是断然坏的，在座诸公也无疑闷得慌。我颇疑心，在场的每一个人若在家里吃，都会吃得舒服些。先端上来一样可怕的糊糊，拿隔宿的肉汁、番茄酱和坏酒调制品成，冒名为汤。随后桌上摆上半条好大的狗鳕——游在水里的鱼中顶坏的一种，又是德文郡独多的一种。又有几团硬邦邦、深棕色、来历不明的圆子传递上来，用刀切开一看，里头是香肠肉馅，油腻之极，远没有煮透。就连巴斯尔赫斯特自由党选民们的 *dura ilia*——铁打的肚肠——也不肯同这些美味相交。再往后才是正经的大菜：一块生得透生透生的烤牛肉，一条焯得半熟、生得简直发蓝的羊腿。头一刀切进这两大块肉、露出里头血糊糊的一摊时，副主席和他一两位朋友便高声开了腔。那又硬又腻的香肠馅，兴许原是没有毛病的——他们说不出个所以然来；那汤他们也吞下去了，不曾抱怨。可大块肉端上桌来该是什么成色，这个他们却是懂的，于是便怒气冲冲地说了出来。塔皮特本人一句也没说让话头传到侍者耳后头去的话，因为龙客栈的吧台上卖着的，正是他自己酿酒厂的啤酒；可那位副主席是个五金商，龙客栈同他的买卖来往无多，他便往下边给老板娘捎去了可怕的话，扬言往后要去光顾蓝野猪客栈（the Blue Boar）、主教冠客栈（the Mitre），甚至还要去那家寒碜的小酒馆棋盘客栈（the Chequers）。“他们那三先令六便士，还想吃出个什么名堂来？”老板娘怒冲冲地说；须知夏皮特心里清楚，他打交道的是一位识得金钱斤两的人物，这顿饭能不能记进哈特先生的账，他原没多大把握。随后上来一张馅饼，面皮足有一英寸厚，谁也吃不下去；又是一道号称“内阁布丁”的甜点，满口尽是板油疙瘩。我敢断言，在场的每一位自由党选民若在家里吃，都会吃得更好，受用得更自在；然而客栈里的公众晚餐，是外省中不溜儿英国人公认的一种消遣。他若不去赴这类宴会，邻人便要疑心他是叫家里的雌威拘束住了。旁人都去，所以他也就去。听人家演说，每一篇都叫他厌烦得要死；轮到他演说，每一篇都把他驱赶到丧胆的最深处；不请他演说，他又浑身不痛快。同他坐在一条板凳上的近邻，他找不到一丝共鸣之处。酒是坏的。热水端到他面前已经凉了。座位又硬又挤。谁也不打算从谈话里找乐趣。人家又不断地请他起立，装模作样地为这个人那个人、这个机构那个机构举杯祝酒，其实他一个也不放在心上：为今晚的主角——那主角他多半根本无动于衷；为教会——那教会他只怕从未跨进去过；为军队——在他眼里那不外乎贵族傲慢的温床；或者为女王——女王他本着英格兰人的天性是敬爱有加的，可主席演说里那套谀词翻来覆去（*ad nauseam*）地灌到他耳朵里，他的灵魂深处却在不知不觉地起反感。这一切统统是无聊、受罪、倦怠、腌臜和不自在。可他还是要一趟一趟地去——因为这是英格兰人天生的消遣。那位法国人，在小咖啡馆里把一把小椅子翘起后腿、背靠窗台坐着，一坐三个钟头，面前先是一杯咖啡，后来是一杯糖水，就眼前受的罪而论，或许同样值得怜悯；只是他灌下肚去的那些液体，害处没有那么大罢了。

===Original===
Mr. Tappitt with the eleven other liberal electors of Baslehurst went through the ceremony of their dinner in the usual way. They drank the health of the Queen, and of the volunteers of the county because there was present a podgy little grocer who had enrolled himself in the corps and who was thus enabled to make a speech; and then they drank the health of Mr. Hart, whose ultimate return for the borough they pledged themselves to effect. Having done so much for business, and having thus brought to a conclusion the political work of the evening, they adjourned their meeting to a cosy little parlour near the bar, and then they began to be happy. Some few of the number, including the angry vice-president, who sold hardware, took themselves home to their wives. “Mrs. Tongs keeps him sharp enough by the ears,” said Sharpit, winking to Tappitt. “Come along, old fellow, and we’ll get a drop of something really hot.” Tappitt winked back again and shook his head with an affected laugh; but as he did so he thought of Mrs. T. at home, and the terrible words she had spoken to him;—and at the same moment an idea came across him that Mr. Sharpit was a very dangerous companion.

About half a dozen entered the cosy little parlour, and there they remained for a couple of hours. While sitting in that cosy little parlour they really did enjoy themselves. About nine o’clock they had a bit of the raw beef broiled, and in that guise it was pleasant enough; and the water was hot, and the tobacco was grateful and the stiffness of the evening was gone. The men chatted together and made no more speeches, and they talked of matters which bore a true interest to them. Sharpit explained to them how each man might be assisted in his own business if this rich London tailor could be brought in for the borough. And by degrees they came round to the affairs of the brewery, and Tappitt, as the brandy warmed him, spoke loudly against Rowan.

“By George!” said the podgy grocer, “if anybody would offer me a thousand a year to give up, I’d take it hopping.”

===Chinese===
塔皮特同巴斯尔赫斯特另外十一位自由党选民，照老例把吃饭的仪式一场一场演完了。他们祝女王康健，又祝郡里志愿军的康健——因为席上有一位矮墩墩的小杂货商，自己报了名加入那一团，借这个由头得以演说一场；随后他们祝哈特先生康健，并且赌下誓愿，务使哈特先生到底为这个选邑坐上议席。正经事做到这一步，今晚的政治工作便算告成，他们把集会挪到酒吧间近旁一间暖融融的小客堂里，这才开始快活起来。人丛里有几位——包括那位动了怒的五金副主席——各自回家找老婆去了。“通斯太太（Mrs. Tongs）揪住他的耳朵，管得他够紧的呢，”夏皮特朝塔皮特挤挤眼说。“来吧，老伙计，咱们去弄一盅真正够劲儿的滚热的东西。”塔皮特也回挤了挤眼，假笑着一摇头；可就在这时，他想起了家里的T.太太，想起她对他说过的那些可怕的话；——而且就在这一刻，一个念头掠过他的心头：夏皮特先生是个很危险的伴当。

进到那间暖融融的小客堂里的约有五六个人，他们在那里待了两个钟头。坐在那间暖融融的小客堂里，他们倒是真的快活起来了。九点钟光景，他们把方才那生牛肉烤了几角来吃，换了这个做法倒也十分受用；水是热的，烟斗是香的，一晚上的拘谨劲儿也散了。众人闲谈起来，不再演说，谈的都是于自己有真切利害的事。夏皮特对他们讲解：只要能把这位阔绰的伦敦衣商弄进议会来代表这个选邑，各人的营生都能得到怎样的好处。渐渐地，话头转到酿酒厂的事务上，白兰地一暖到身上，塔皮特便放开了嗓子数落罗恩。

“老天爷！”矮墩墩的杂货商说，“谁要是肯给我一年一千镑叫我撒手，我蹦着跳着就接下来。”

===Original===
“Then I wouldn’t,” said Tappitt, “and what’s more, I won’t. But brewing ain’t like other businesses;—there’s more in it than in most others.”

“Of course there is,” said Sharpit; “it isn’t like any common trade.”

“That’s true too,” said the podgy grocer.

A man usually receives some compensation for having gone through the penance of the chairman’s duties. For the remainder of the evening he is entitled to the flattery of his companions, and generally receives it till they become tipsy and insubordinate. Tappitt had not the character of an intemperate man, but on this occasion he did exceed the bounds of a becoming moderation. The room was hot and the tobacco smoke was thick. The wine had been bad and the brandy was strong. Sharpit, too, urged him to new mixtures and stronger denunciations against Rowan, till at last, at eleven o’clock, when he took himself to the brewery, he was not in a condition proper for the father of such daughters or for the husband of such a wife.

===Chinese===
“那我就不接，”塔皮特说，“而且我把话说死，我不接。不过酿造这一行不同于别的买卖；——这里头的名堂，比大多数行当都多。”

“名堂自然多，”夏皮特说；“这可不是寻常的行当。”

“这话也是真的，”矮墩墩的杂货商说。

一个人熬过了主席职分的那番苦修，照例总要领一点酬报。这一晚剩下的时光，他有资格领受同伴们的奉承，一般也真能领受到手，直到他们喝得醉醺醺、不守规矩起来为止。塔皮特素来算不得贪杯的人，可这一回，他的确越过了得体的节制所许的界线。屋里闷热，烟气浓重。饭上的酒原是坏的，白兰地又冲。夏皮特还一个劲儿撺掇他换新式的掺法，对罗恩放出更狠的咒骂，到末了十一点钟他动身回酿酒厂的时候，他那副情形，做这样几位女儿的爸爸固已失体，做这样一位太太的丈夫更是不像样了。

===Original===
“Shall I see him home?” said the podgy grocer to Mr. Sharpit.

Tappitt, with the suspicious quickness of a drunken man, turned sharply upon the podgy and abashed grocer, and abused him for his insolence. He then made his way out of the innyard, and along the High Street, and down Brewery Lane to his own door, knowing the way as well as though he had been sober, and passing over it as quickly. Nor did he fall or even stumble, though now and again he reeled slightly. And as he went the idea came strongly upon him that Sharpit was a dangerous man, and that perhaps at this very moment he, Tappitt, was standing on the brink of a precipice. Then he remembered that his wife would surely be watching for him, and as he made his first attempt to insert the latchkey into the door his heart became forgetful of the brandy, and sank low within his breast.

How affairs went between him and Mrs. Tappitt on that night I will not attempt to describe. That she used her power with generosity I do not doubt. That she used it with discretion I am quite convinced. On the following morning at ten o’clock Tappitt was still in bed; but a note had been written by Mrs. T. to Messrs. Sharpit and Longfite, saying that the projected visit had, under altered circumstances, become unnecessary. That Tappitt’s head was racked with pain, and his stomach disturbed with sickness, there can be no doubt, and as little that Mrs. T. used the consequent weakness of her husband for purposes of feminine dominion; but this she did with discretion and even with kindness. Only a word or two was said as to the state in which he had returned home—a word or two with the simple object of putting that dominion on a firm basis. After that Mrs. Tappitt took his condition as an established fact, administered to him the comforts of her medicine-chest and teapot, excused his illness to the girls as having been produced by the fish, and never left his bedside till she had achieved her purpose. If ever a man got tipsy to his own advantage, Mr. Tappitt did so on that occasion. And if ever a man in that condition was treated with forbearing kindness by his wife, Mr. Tappitt was so treated then.

===Chinese===
“要我送他回去么？”矮墩墩的杂货商问夏皮特先生说。

塔皮特带着醉汉那种叫人生疑的敏捷，猛地转身对着那个矮墩墩、满面窘色的杂货商，骂他放肆。随后他出了客栈的院子，沿着大街走下去，再拐进酿酒厂巷，到了自家门口；那段路他认得同清醒时一般无二，走得也同清醒时一般快。他既没有跌倒，连踉跄也不曾踉跄一下，只是时不时身子微微一晃。走着走着，一个念头重重地压上他的心头：夏皮特是个危险人物；说不定就在这一刻，他塔皮特正站在悬崖的边上。跟着他记起，妻子准在守着他；他头一回把门锁钥匙往门上插的时候，那颗心把白兰地忘得一干二净，在胸膛里头沉沉地坠了下去。

那一夜他同塔皮特太太之间怎样收场，我不打算去描写了。她行使她的权柄时是宽宏的，这我不怀疑；她行使得有分寸，这我深信无疑。第二天上午十点钟，塔皮特还躺在床上；但T.太太已经给夏皮特和朗费特二位先生写了一张短简，说是情形既有变更，原拟的造访已无必要。塔皮特头痛如裂、肠胃翻搅欲呕，这是毫无疑问的；T.太太就借丈夫这一时的虚弱，达成闺阃治权的目的，这也同样毫无疑问；不过她做得有分寸，甚至还带着几分温存。至于他昨夜到家时那副情形，只点了一两句话——点这一两句，用意单纯，不过要把这份治权安放在坚实的根基上。这之后，塔皮特太太便把他的情形当作既成事实看待，拿她药箱和茶壶里的种种安慰来调理他，对姑娘们只说他病是鱼闹出来的，并且守在他的床边寸步不离，直到目的达成。世上若有哪个男人喝醉反醉得于己有利，塔皮特先生那一回便是；世上若有哪个男人在那副情形里得妻子隐忍善待，塔皮特先生那一回受的便是。

===Original===
“Don’t disturb yourself, T.,” she said; “there’s nothing wants doing in the brewery, and if it did what would it signify in comparison with your health? The brewery won’t be much to you now, thank goodness; and I’m sure you’ve had enough of it. Thirty years of such work as that would make any man sick and weak. I’m sure I don’t wonder at your being ill;—not the least. The wonder is that you’ve ever stood up against it so long as you have. If you’ll take my advice you’ll just turn round and try to sleep for an hour or so.”

Tappitt took her advice at any rate, so far that he turned round and closed his eyes. Up to this time he had not given way about the brewery. He had uttered no word of assent. But he was gradually becoming aware that he would have to yield before he would be allowed to put on his clothes. And now, in the base and weak condition of his head and stomach, yielding did not seem to him to be so very bad a thing. After all, the brewery was troublesome, the fight was harassing. Rowan was young and strong, and Mr. Sharpit was very dangerous. Rowan, too, had risen in his estimation as in that of others, and he could not longer argue, even to himself, that the stipulated income would not be paid. He did not sleep, but got into that half-drowsy state in which men think of their existing affairs, but without any power of active thought. He knew that he ought to be in his countinghouse and at work. He half feared that the world was falling away from him because he was not there. He was ashamed of himself, and sometimes almost entertained a thought of rising up and shaking off his lethargy. But his stomach was bad, and he could not bring himself to move. His head was tormented, and his pillow was soft; and therefore there he lay. He wondered what was the time of day, but did not think of looking at his watch which was under his head. He heard his wife’s steps about the room as she shaded some window from his eyes, or crept to the door to give some household order to one of her girls outside; but he did not speak to her, nor she to him. She did not speak to him as long as he lay there motionless, and when he moved with a small low groan she merely offered him some beef tea.

It was nearly six o’clock, and the hour of dinner at the brewery was long passed, when Mrs. Tappitt sat herself down by the bedside determined to reap the fruit of her victory. He had just raised himself in his bed and announced his intention of getting up—declaring, as he did so, that he would never again eat any of that accursed fish. The moment of his renovation had come upon him, and Mrs. Tappitt perceived that if he escaped from her now, there might even yet be more trouble.

===Chinese===
“你别动弹，T.，”她说，“酿酒厂里没有什么要办的，就算有，跟你身子骨一比，又算得了什么？谢天谢地，酿酒厂往后跟你没多大相干了；你受够了它，这我拿得准。三十年这样的活计，谁做谁也要做病做垮。你病倒，我一点儿也不奇怪；——一点儿也不。奇怪的是你竟硬撑了这么久。你听我的，就翻个身，睡上个把钟头。”

这一回塔皮特好歹听了她的劝，翻了个身，闭上了眼睛。到这时为止，酿酒厂的事他还没有松口，半个应承的字也没吐。可他渐渐明白，不先服软，人家是不许他穿衣裳起来的。而眼下，脑瓜和肠胃都虚软委顿到这般地步，服软在他看来也就不算怎么坏的事了。说到底，酿酒厂是桩麻烦事，这一仗又磨人。罗恩年轻力壮，夏皮特先生又危险得很。罗恩在他心里的分量，也同在别人心里一样涨上去了；那笔讲定的进项到时不会照付，这话他连对自己也再辩不下去了。他没有睡着，只是进到那种半昏半醒的状态里：现下的事务桩桩件件从心头过，却使不上一分劲去想。他知道自己这会儿该在账房里做事。他隐隐害怕，只因自己不在那里，世界正从他身边溜走。他愧对自己，有时几乎起了一个念头：撑起身来，把这一身懒骨头抖落掉。可他肠胃难受，怎么也挪不动身子。脑瓜受着煎熬，枕头又软；于是他就那么躺着。他纳闷现在几点了，却没想到看表——表正枕在他脑袋底下。他听得见妻子在屋里走动的脚步：一会儿替哪扇窗遮光，免得晃他的眼；一会儿蹑手蹑脚到门口，隔着门吩咐外头的哪个女儿一句家务。可他不同她说话，她也不同他说话。他一动不动躺着的时候，她一言不发；待他低低呻吟着动了一动，她也只递过来一点牛肉汤。

快六点钟了，酿酒厂里开正餐的时辰早过了，塔皮特太太在床边坐下，打定主意要收她这场胜仗的果实。他刚撑起身子，宣布要起来了——一面宣布，一面赌咒说，那该咒的鱼他往后再也不碰一口。他回过神来的这一刻到了，塔皮特太太看出：这会儿若让他从手里溜脱了，往后兴许还有麻烦。

===Original===
“It wasn’t only the fish, T.,” she said, with somewhat of sternness in her eye.

“I hardly drank anything,” said Tappitt.

“Of course I wasn’t there to see what you took,” said she; “but you were very bad when you came home last night;—very bad indeed. You couldn’t have got in at the door only for me.”

“That’s nonsense.”

“But it is quite true. It’s a mercy, T., that neither of the girls saw you. Only think! But there’ll be nothing more of that kind, I’m sure, when we are out of this horrid place; and it wouldn’t have happened now, only for all this trouble.”

To this Tappitt made no answer, but he grunted, and again said that he thought he would get up.

===Chinese===
“不光是鱼的事，T.。”她说，眼里的神色有几分厉。

“我几乎什么也没喝，”塔皮特说。

“我自然不在场，你吃了什么我没瞧见，”她说，“可你昨儿夜里到家的时候糟得很；——糟得不得了。没有我，你连门都进不来。”

“胡说。”

“可这是千真万确的。T.，多亏两个姑娘谁也没瞧见你。想想吧！不过等我们离开这个鬼地方，我拿准不会再有这种事了；也就是这一摊子麻烦，才闹出今儿这一场来。”

对这话塔皮特没有答腔，只哼了一声，又说他想起来了。

===Original===
“Of course it’s settled now, T., that we’re to leave this place.”

“I don’t know that at all.”

“Then, T., you ought to know it. Come now; just look at the common sense of the thing. If we don’t give up the brewery what are we to do? There isn’t a decent respectable person in the town in favour of our staying here, only that rascal Sharpit. You desired me this morning to write and tell him you’d have nothing more to do with him; and so I did.” Tappitt had not seen his wife’s letter to the lawyer—had not asked to see it, and now became aware that his only possible supporter might probably have been driven away from him. Sharpit too, though dangerous as an enemy, was ten times more dangerous as a friend!

“Of course you’ll take that young man’s offer. Shall I sit down and write a line to Honyman, and tell him to come in the morning?”

===Chinese===
“T.，咱们要离开这儿，这如今自然是定了的喽。”

“我才不知道呢。”

“那你就该知道，T.。来，你只看看这事情的常理。咱们若不撒手酿酒厂，还怎么办？镇上可有一个正正经经、体体面面的人赞成咱们留下？只有那个无赖夏皮特。今儿早上是你吩咐我写信告诉他，说你再不跟他来往；我就照办了。”塔皮特没有看见他妻子给律师写的那封信——也没有要求看；此刻他醒悟过来：他唯一可能的帮手，八成已经给撵走了。而夏皮特这个人，做仇敌已够危险，做朋友更危险十倍！

“那个年轻人的提议，你自然是要应下的。我坐下来给霍尼曼写一行字，叫他明儿早上过来，好不好？”

===Original===
Tappitt groaned again and again, said that he would get up, but Mrs. T. would not let him out of bed till he had assented to her proposition that Honyman should be again invited to the brewery. He knew well that the battle was gone from him—had in truth known it through all those half-comatose hours of his bedridden day. But a man, or a nation, when yielding must still resist even in yielding. Tappitt fumed and fussed under the clothes, protesting that his sending for Honyman would be useless. But the letter was written in his name and sent with his knowledge; and it was perfectly understood that that invitation to Honyman signified an unconditional surrender on the part of Mr. Tappitt. One word Mrs. T. said as she allowed her husband to escape from his prison amidst the blankets, one word by which to mark that the thing was done, and one word only. “I suppose we needn’t leave the house for about a month or so—because it would be inconvenient about the furniture.”

“Who’s to turn you out if you stay for six months?” said Tappitt.

The thing was marked enough then, and Mrs. Tappitt retired in muffled triumph—retired when she had made all things easy for the simplest ceremony of dressing.

===Chinese===
塔皮特呻吟了又呻吟，说要起来；可T.太太不放他下床，直到他应承了她的提议——再请霍尼曼到酿酒厂来。他心里明白，这一仗他已经输了——说实在的，卧床这一整天那些半昏迷的时辰里，他心里一直明白。可一个人——一个国家也一样——让步的时候，纵然在让步，也得撑着抵抗。塔皮特在被窝里冒火、折腾，一口咬定他去请霍尼曼也是白请。可那封信到底以他的名义写了出去，送出去他也是知情的；而这份给霍尼曼的邀请意味着塔皮特先生无条件投降，这一点彼此心里都再明白不过。T.太太放她丈夫从被窝的牢狱里脱身的时候，说了一句话——一句标明事情已成的话，而且只有一句。“我看咱们总还得有一个月上下不必搬——为着家具，搬早了不方便。”

“住上六个月，谁又撵得动你们？”塔皮特说。

这话已经标记得再明白不过，塔皮特太太便按捺着胜利的得意退了出去——退出去时，连穿衣裳这桩顶简单的仪式，她都替他张罗得样样顺手。

===Original===
“Just sponge your face, my dear,” she said, “and put on your dressing-gown, and come down for half an hour or so.”

“I’m all right now,” said Tappitt.

“Oh! quite so;—but I wouldn’t go to the trouble of much dressing.” Then she left him, descended the stairs, and entered the parlour among her daughters. When there she could not abstain from one blast of the trumpet of triumph. “Well, girls,” she said, “it’s all settled, and we shall be in Torquay now before the winter.”

“No!” said Augusta.

===Chinese===
“拿海绵擦把脸，我亲爱的，”她说，“换上晨衣，下楼来待上个把钟头。”

“我如今全好了，”塔皮特说。

“哦！那是自然；——不过我也犯不着费事多穿戴。”说罢她丢下他，下了楼梯，进客厅来到女儿们中间。到了那里，她憋不住把得胜的号角吹了一声。“好啦，姑娘们，”她说，“事情全定了，入冬之前咱们就在托基了。”

“不会吧！”奥古斯塔说。

===Original===
“That’ll be a great change,” said Martha.

“In Torquay before the winter!” said Cherry. “Oh, mamma, how clever you have been!”

“And now your papa is coming down, and you should thank him for what he’s doing for you. It’s all for your sake that he’s doing it.”

===Chinese===
“那可是个大变动，”玛莎说。

“入冬之前就到托基！”彻丽说。“哦，妈妈，您真能干极了！”

“如今你们爸爸就要下来了，他这样为你们办事，你们该谢谢他。他这么做，全是出于你们。”

===Original===
Mr. Tappitt crept into the room, and when he had taken his seat in his accustomed armchair, the girls went up to him and kissed him. Then they thanked him for his proposed kindness in taking them out of the brewery.

“Oh, papa, it is so jolly!” said Cherry.

Mr. Tappitt did not say much in answer to this;—but luckily there was no necessity that he should say anything. It was an occasion on which silence was understood as giving a perfect consent.

===Chinese===
塔皮特先生蹭进屋里，在他惯坐的扶手椅上落了座，姑娘们便围上去吻他。随后她们谢他应下了这番善心，肯把她们带出酿酒厂去。

“哦，爸爸，这可太美了！”彻丽说。

对这些话塔皮特先生没有多说什么；——所幸也用不着他说什么。这样的场合，沉默就被领会作十足的应允。

## XXVIII What Took Place at Bragg’s End Farm / XXVIII 布拉格斯恩德农场上发生的事

===Original===
When Mrs. Tappitt had settled within her own mind that the brewery should be abandoned to Rowan, she was by no means, therefore, ready to assent that Rachel Ray should become the mistress of the brewery house. “Never,” she had exclaimed when Cherry had suggested such a result; “never!” And Augusta had echoed the protestation, “Never, never!” I will not say that she would have allowed her husband to remain in his business in order that she might thus exclude Rachel from such promotion, but she could not bring herself to believe that Luke Rowan would be so fatuous, so ignorant of his own interests, so deluded, as to marry that girl from Bragg’s End! It is thus that the Mrs. Tappitts of the world regard other women’s daughters when they have undergone any disappointment as to their own. She had no reason for wishing well to Rowan, and would not have cared if he had taken to his bosom a harpy in marriage; but she could not endure to hear of the success of the girl whose attractions had foiled her own little plan. “I don’t believe that the man can ever be such a fool as that!” she said again to Augusta, when on the evening of the day following Tappitt’s abdication, a rumour reached the brewery that Luke Rowan had been seen walking out upon the Cawston road.

===Chinese===
塔皮特太太心里虽已拿定主意，把酿酒厂让给罗恩，却断没有因此就肯应承，让雷切尔·雷来做酿酒厂宅子的女主人。彻丽提出这样一个结局的时候，她曾失声叫道：“决不！”奥古斯塔也跟着应声抗议：“决不，决不！”我不敢说，她是为了把雷切尔挡在这步高升之外，才肯让丈夫继续守住他的营生；可她怎么也不能叫自己相信，卢克·罗恩会糊涂到那种地步，会那样不识自家的利害、那样受人哄骗，竟去娶布拉格斯恩德的那个姑娘！世上的塔皮特太太们，凡在自己的事上受过挫失的，看待别人家的女儿便都是这样。她本没有理由盼着罗恩好，任他娶个鹰身女妖进门她也懒得管；可那个姑娘——她的迷人处搅黄了她自己那点小算盘——要听说她得了好结果，她可万难忍受。“我不信那人能糊涂到那步田地！”塔皮特让位的次日晚上，酿酒厂里传来风声，说有人瞧见卢克·罗恩出门走在考斯顿路上，她又对奥古斯塔念叨了一遍。

===Original===
Mr. Honyman, in accordance with his instructions, called at the brewery on that morning, and was received by Mr. Tappitt with a sullen and almost savage submission. Mrs. T. had endeavoured to catch him first, but in that she had failed; she did, however, manage to see the attorney as he came out from her husband.

“It’s all settled,” said Honyman; “and I’ll see Rowan myself before half an hour is over.”

“I’m sure it’s a great blessing, Mr. Honyman,” said the lady—not on that occasion assuming any of the glory to herself.

“It was the only thing for him,” said Mr. Honyman;—“that is if he didn’t like to take the young man in as acting partner.”

“That wouldn’t have done at all,” said Mrs. T. And then the lawyer went his way.

===Chinese===
那天早晨，霍尼曼先生遵照指示来到酿酒厂，塔皮特先生接待他时，一副怏怏的、近乎蛮野的俯首听命。T. 太太本想抢在前头把他截住，可这一着落了空；不过律师从她丈夫屋里出来时，她还是设法见到了他。

“事情全都谈定了，”霍尼曼说，“不出半个钟头，我自己还要去见罗恩。”

“我信这是天大的福气，霍尼曼先生，”这位太太说——这一回，她倒没把功劳往自己身上揽。

“那是他唯一的出路，”霍尼曼先生说，“——我是说，除非他情愿让那个年轻男人进来做管事的合伙人。”

“那可万万使不得，”T. 太太说。律师随即自去了。

===Original===
In the meantime Tappitt sat sullen and wretched in the countinghouse. Such moments occur in the lives of most of us—moments in which the real work of life is brought to an end—and they cannot but be sad. It is very well to talk of ease and dignity; but ease of spirit comes from action only, and the world’s dignity is given to those who do the world’s work. Let no man put his neck from out of the collar till in truth he can no longer draw the weight attached to it. Tappitt had now got rid of his collar, and he sat very wretched in his brewery countinghouse.

“Be I to go, sir?”

Tappitt in his meditation was interrupted by these words, spoken not in a rough voice, and looking up he saw Worts standing in the countinghouse before him. Worts had voted for Butler Cornbury, whereas, had he voted for Mr. Hart, Mr. Hart would have been returned; and, upon that, Worts, as a rebellious subject, had received notice to quit the premises. Now his time was out, and he came to ask whether he was to leave the scene of his forty years of work. But what would be the use of sending Worts away even if the wish to punish his contumacy still remained? In another week Worts would be brought back again in triumph, and would tread those brewery floors with the step almost of a master, while he, Tappitt, could tread them only as a stranger, if he were allowed to tread them at all.

“You can stay if you like,” said Tappitt, hardly looking up at the man.

===Chinese===
这当口，塔皮特阴沉着脸，凄凄惶惶地坐在账房里。我们大多数人的一生里，都有这样的时刻——人生真正的营生就此告终的时刻——叫人不能不黯然神伤。清闲和体面，说起来自然轻巧；可心境的清闲只能从劳作中来，世上的体面也只给予替世上做活计的人。不到实在拉不动套在轭上的重载之时，谁也别把脖颈从轭圈里退出来。塔皮特如今算是把轭圈褪了，于是在他酿酒厂的账房里坐着，凄惶得很。

“先生，可是要我走？”

塔皮特正自出神，被这句话打断了，话音并不粗鲁；他抬起头来，看见沃茨站在账房里他跟前。沃茨投了巴特勒·康伯里的票，而他若投哈特先生一票，哈特先生本可当选；就为这个，沃茨算是做了忤逆的臣仆，收到了叫他迁出厂地的通知。如今期限已满，他来问一声，是不是该离开他做了四十年活计的地方。可即便惩治他那点倔强的念头还没消，把沃茨撵走又有什么用？再过一个星期，沃茨就要得胜还乡似的被请回来，踏上那些酿酒厂的地面时，脚步几乎像个东家；而他塔皮特，就算还容他踏上去，也只能以陌生人的身份踏了。

“你要愿意，就留下吧，”塔皮特说，眼睛难得朝那人抬一下。

===Original===
“I know you be a going, Mr. Tappitt,” said the man; “and I hear you be a going very handsome like. Gentlefolk such as yeu needn’t go on working allays like uz. If so be yeu be a going, Mr. Tappitt, I hope yeu and me’ll part friendly. We’ve been together a sight o’ years;—too great a sight for uz to part unfriendly.”

Mr. Tappitt admitted the argument, shook hands with the man, and then of course took him into his immediate confidence with more warmth than he would have done had there been no quarrel between them. And I think he found some comfort in this. He walked about the premises with Worts, telling him much that was true, and some few things that were not strictly accurate. For instance, he said that he had made up his mind to leave the place, whereas that action of decisive resolution which we call making up our minds had perhaps been done by Mrs. Tappitt rather than by him. But Worts took all these assertions with an air of absolute belief which comforted the brewer. Worts was very wise in his discretion on that day, and threw much oil on the troubled waters; so that Tappitt when he left him bade God bless him, and expressed a hope that the old place might still thrive for his sake.

“And for your’n too, master,” said Worts, “for yeu’ll allays have the best egg still. The young master, he’ll only be a working for yeu.”

There was comfort in this thought; and Tappitt, when he went into his dinner, was able to carry himself like a man.

===Chinese===
“我知道您要走了，塔皮特先生，”那人说；“还听说您走得挺体面哪。像您这样的上等人，用不着像我们这号人一直做活做到底。您既要走了，塔皮特先生，但愿您我分手和和气气。咱们搭伙的年头可不算少；——年头这么长，我们可不能不欢而散。”

塔皮特认了这番道理，同那人握了手，随后自然便把他引为心腹，比两人没有翻过脸时还要热络几分。我想他从中也得了些安慰。他带着沃茨在厂里各处走，跟他说了许多实话，也有那么几件说得不大确切。比方他说，他已打定主意要离开这地方，可那种叫作“拿定主意”的下定决心的举动，或许出自塔皮特太太，而不是出自他。不过这一番话，沃茨桩桩件件都带着深信不疑的神气听受了，这叫酿酒匠心里熨帖。那一天，沃茨的分寸拿捏得极是聪明，往翻腾的水面上浇了不少油；于是塔皮特别他的时候，求上帝保佑他，还说盼着看在他的分上，老地方照旧兴旺。

“也为您的好处，东家，”沃茨说，“顶好的那只蛋，横竖永远是您的。少东家，他只管给您卖力气。”

这个念头里自有安慰；塔皮特进去吃午饭的时候，居然拿得出个男子汉的气派了。

===Original===
The tidings which had reached Mrs. Tappitt as to Rowan having been seen on that evening walking on the Cawston road with his face towards Bragg’s End were true. On that morning Mr. Honyman had come to him, and his career in life was at once settled for him.

“Mr. Tappitt is quite in time, Mr. Honyman,” he had said. “But he would not have been in time this day week unless he had consented to pay for what work had been already done; for I had determined to begin at once.”

“The truth is, Mr. Rowan, you step into an uncommon good thing; but Mr. Tappitt is tired of the work, and glad to give it up.”

Thus the matter was arranged between them, and before nightfall everybody in Baslehurst knew that Tappitt and Rowan had come to terms, and that Tappitt was to retire upon a pension. There was some little discrepancy as to the amount of Tappitt’s annuity, the liberal faction asserting that he was to receive two thousand a year, and those of the other side cutting him down to two hundred.

===Chinese===
塔皮特太太听来的那桩消息——说那天晚上有人瞧见罗恩走在考斯顿路上，脸朝着布拉格斯恩德那头——是真的。那天早晨霍尼曼先生来过他那里，他的人生道路就此一下子定了下来。

“塔皮特先生来得正是时候，霍尼曼先生，”他当时这样说。“不过要搁到下个礼拜的今天，他若不肯出钱偿付已经做下的活儿，就赶不及了；因为我已打定主意，马上动手。”

“实话对您说，罗恩先生，您接手的是一桩少有的好买卖；只是塔皮特先生做厌了这行当，巴不得撒手呢。”

事情就这样在他们之间议定了；天还没黑，巴斯尔赫斯特已是人人皆知：塔皮特和罗恩讲好了条件，塔皮特要领一笔年金退养。塔皮特这份年金的数目，传言略有出入——自由党那一口咬定他一年要领两千镑，对面那派的人把他砍到两百镑。

===Original===
On the evening of that day—in the cool of the evening—Luke Rowan sauntered down the High Street of Baslehurst, and crossed over Cawston bridge. On the bridge he was all alone, and he stood there for a moment or two leaning upon the parapet looking down upon the little stream beneath the arch. During the day many things had occupied him, and he had hardly as yet made up his mind definitely as to what he would do and what he would say during the hours of the evening. From the moment in which Honyman had announced to him Tappitt’s intended resignation he became aware that he certainly should go out to Bragg’s End before that day was over. It had been with him a settled thing, a thing settled almost without thought ever since the receipt of Rachel’s letter, that he would take this walk to Bragg’s End when he should have put his affairs at Baslehurst on some stable footing; but that he would not take that walk before he had so done.

“They say,” Rachel had written in her letter, “they say that as the business here about the brewery is so very unsettled, they think it probable that you will not have to come back to Baslehurst any more.”

In that had been the offence. They had doubted his stability, and, beyond that, had almost doubted his honesty. He would punish them by taking them at their word till both should be put beyond all question. He knew well that the punishment would fall on Rachel, whereas none of the sin would have been Rachel’s sin; but he would not allow himself to be deterred by that consideration.

“It is her letter,” he said to himself, “and in that way will I answer her. When I do go there again they will all understand me better.”

It had been, too, a matter of pride to him that Mr. Comfort and Mrs. Butler Cornbury should thus be made to understand him. He would say nothing of himself and his own purposes to any of them. He would speak neither of his own means nor his own steadfastness. But he would prove to them that he was steadfast, and that he had boasted of nothing which he did not possess. When Mrs. Butler Cornbury had spoken to him down by the Cleeves, asking him of his purpose, and struggling to do a kind thing by Rachel, he had resolved at once that he would tell her nothing. She should find him out. He liked her for loving Rachel; but neither to her, nor even to Rachel herself, would he say more till he could show them that the business about the brewery was no longer unsettled.

===Chinese===
那天晚上——晚间凉爽的时辰——卢克·罗恩信步走下巴斯尔赫斯特的大街，过了考斯顿桥。桥上只他一个人。他在那儿站了一两分钟，倚着桥栏，俯望桥洞下面那道细细的流水。这一天许多事占着他的心，至于这天晚上的时辰里他要做什么、说什么，他还没拿定十分的主意。自打霍尼曼向他宣布塔皮特有意退让的那一刻起，他就明白，这一天过完之前，他一定要到布拉格斯恩德去。自收到雷切尔那封信起，这在他已成定局——几乎不假思量的定局：等他把巴斯尔赫斯特的事务安顿到立得住脚的地步，他就要走这趟布拉格斯恩德；而在安顿妥当之前，这趟路他决计不走。

“他们说，”雷切尔在信里写道，“他们说，这边酿酒厂的事这样没个定准，他们想着，多半你往后不必再回巴斯尔赫斯特来了。”

过错就出在这一句里。他们疑他立不住脚，还不止如此，几乎疑到他不老实。他就要把他们的话当真照办，借此罚一罚他们，直到把这两层疑心一并扫除得再无可疑。他心里明白，这惩罚要落在雷切尔身上，而罪过却一丝一毫也不是雷切尔的罪过；可他不肯叫这层顾虑拴住自己。

“这是她的信，”他对自己说，“我就用这个法子回她。等我再去那边，他们会更明白我是个什么样的人。”

还有一层，叫康福特先生和巴特勒·康伯里太太也因此看明白他，这在他是一桩关乎志气的事。对他们中间随便哪一个，他都不肯说自己，不说自己的打算。自己的进项他不讲，自己的坚执他也不讲。可他要拿凭据向他们证明：他是坚执的，他自夸的没有一样是他没有的。巴特勒·康伯里太太在崖壁下同他说话，问他的打算，一心想替雷切尔做件好事的那一回，他当下便打定主意，什么都不告诉她。她该自己去把他看出来。他喜欢她，因为她疼雷切尔；可无论对她，还是对雷切尔本人，在能拿出凭据、叫他们看到酿酒厂的事再不是没个定准之前，他决计不多说一个字。

===Original===
But up to this moment—this moment in which he was standing on the bridge, he had not determined what he would say to Rachel or to Rachel’s mother. He had never relaxed in his purpose of making Rachel his wife since his first visit to the cottage. He was one who, having a fixed resolve, feels certain of their ultimate success in achieving it. He was now going to Bragg’s End to claim that which he regarded as his own; but he had not as yet told himself in what terms he would put forward his claim. So he stood upon the bridge thinking.

He stood upon the bridge thinking, but his thoughts would only go backwards, and would do nothing for him as to his future conduct. He remembered his first walk with her, and the churchyard elms with the setting sun, and the hot dances in Mrs. Tappitt’s house; and he remembered them without much of the triumph of a successful lover. It had been very sweet, but very easy. In so saying to himself he by no means threw blame upon Rachel. Things were easy, he thought, and it was almost a pity that they should be so. As for Rachel, nothing could have been more honest or more to his taste, than her mode of learning to love him. A girl who, while intending to accept him, could yet have feigned indifference, would have disgusted him at once. Nevertheless he could not but wish that there had been some castles for him to storm in his career. Tappitt had made but poor pretence of fighting before he surrendered; and as to Rachel, it had not been in Rachel’s nature to make any pretence. He passed from the bridge at last without determining what he would say when he reached the cottage, but he did not pass on till he had been seen by the scrutinizing eyes of Miss Pucker.

“If there ain’t young Rowan going out to Bragg’s End again!” she said to herself, comforting herself, I fear, or striving to comfort herself, with an inward assertion that he was not going there for any good. Striving to comfort herself, but not effectually; for though the assertion was made by herself to herself, yet it was not believed. Though she declared, with well-pronounced mental words, that Luke Rowan was going on that path for no good purpose, she felt a wretched conviction at her heart’s core that Rachel Ray would be made to triumph over her and her early suspicions by a happy marriage. Nevertheless she carried the tidings up into Baslehurst, and as she repeated it to the grocer’s daughters and the baker’s wife she shook her head with as much apparent satisfaction as though she really believed that Rachel oscillated between a ruined name and a broken heart.

可直到此刻——他站在桥上的此刻——他要同雷切尔说什么、同雷切尔的母亲说什么，还没有定下来。自头一回到村舍去，他要雷切尔做他妻子的主意，从未松过劲。他是这样一种人：主意一经拿定，便笃信最终定能如愿。他如今到布拉格斯恩德去，是去认领他看作自己分内的东西；至于拿什么话头去认领，他还没对自己交代过。于是他站在桥上想。

他站在桥上想，可心思偏只往后跑，对他往后的行止一点忙也帮不上。他想起头一回同她散步，想起教堂墓地的榆树和落日，想起塔皮特太太家里那些热腾腾的舞会；想起来，却不大带一个得风情郎的凯旋味道。一切都是甜的，可也都是容易的。这样对自己说，他丝毫没有怪雷切尔的意思。事情容易，他想，容易得几乎叫人惋惜。至于雷切尔，她学着爱他的那个路数，再诚实不过，也再对他的脾气不过。一个姑娘，心里打算接受他，面上却还能装冷淡——那样的姑娘，他会立刻倒了胃口。话虽如此，他不能不巴望自己这条路上也有几座城堡，好让他去攻打。塔皮特投降之前，抵抗的那点架势撑得可怜巴巴；至于雷切尔，装假本不是雷切尔的性子。他末了走下桥去，到了村舍要说什么仍未拿定；不过他是在叫帕克小姐那双侦伺的眼睛看了去之后，方才走开的。

“这不是小罗恩又要上布拉格斯恩德去了吗！”她自个儿对自己说。我怕，她是拿心里一句断语给自己解宽心，或者说竭力想给自己解宽心：他上那边去，绝没安好心。竭力想解宽心，却解不成；这话虽是她对自己说的，她自己却不信。她心里把字句咬得清清楚楚，宣称卢克·罗恩走上那条路，去意不善；可她心底最深处偏偏沉着一个叫她苦楚的确信：雷切尔·雷终要借一门美满的婚事，胜过她，也胜过她早先那些疑心。然而她照样把消息捎上巴斯尔赫斯特，对着杂货店家的女儿们、面包师的老婆一遍遍学舌，一面摇头摇得那样一副心满意足的样子，仿佛她真信了雷切尔正在身败名裂与心碎肠断之间摇摆。

He walked on very slowly towards Bragg’s End, as though he almost dreaded the interview, swinging his stick as was his custom, and keeping his feet on the grassy edges of the road till he came to the turn which brought him on to the green. When on the green he did not take the highway, but skirted along under Farmer Sturt’s hedge, so that he had to pass by the entrance of the farmyard before he crossed over to the cottage. Here, just inside her own gate, he encountered Mrs. Sturt standing alone. She had been intent on the cares of her poultry-yard till she had espied Luke Rowan; but then she had forgotten chickens and ducks and all, and had given herself up to thoughts of Rachel’s happiness in having her lover back again.

“It’s he as sure as eggs,” she had said to herself when she first saw him; “how mortal slow he do walk, to be sure! If he was coming as joe to me I’d soon shake him into quicker steps than them.”

“Oh, Mrs. Sturt!” said he, “I hope you’re quite well,” and he stopped short at her gate.

“Pretty bobbish, thankee, Mr. Rowan; and how’s yourself? Are you going over to the cottage this evening?”

“错不了，是他，鸡蛋是鸡蛋一样错不了，”她头一眼望见他时就自个儿说；“瞧他那个走法，慢得要死，可不是嘛！他要是来会我这心上人，看我三晃两晃，不叫他迈得比这快些。”

“托您的福，还算过得去，罗恩先生；您自己可好？今晚是上村舍那边去吗？”

Mrs. Sturt walked quickly across the road to the cottage door, and went at once to the open window of the sitting-room. Mrs. Ray was there with a book in her hand—a serious book, the perusal of which I fear was in some degree due to the presence of her elder daughter; and Mrs. Prime was there with another book, evidently very serious; and Rachel was there too, seated on the sofa, deeply buried in the manipulation of a dress belonging to her mother. Mrs. Sturt was sure at once that they had not seen Luke Rowan as he passed inside the farmyard gate, and that they did not suspect that he was near them.

“Oh, Mrs. Sturt, is that you?” said the widow, looking up. “You’ll just come in for a minute, won’t you?” and Mrs. Ray showed by a suppressed yawn that her attention had not been deeply fixed by that serious book. Rachel looked up, and bade the visitor welcome with a little nod; but it was not a cheery nod as it would have been in old days, before her sorrow had come upon her.

“I’ll have the cherries back in her cheeks before the evening’s over,” said Mrs. Sturt to herself, as she looked at the pale-faced girl. Mrs. Prime also made some little salutation to their neighbour; but she did so with the very smallest expenditure of thoughts or moments. Mrs. Sturt was all very well, but Mrs. Prime had greater work on hand than gossiping with Mrs. Sturt.

“I’ll not just come in, thankee, Mrs. Ray; but if it ain’t troubling you I want to speak a word to you outside; and a word to Rachel too, if she don’t mind coming.”

“A word to me!” said Rachel getting up and putting down her dress. Her thoughts nowadays were always fixed on the same subject, and it seemed that any special word to her must have reference to that. Mrs. Ray also got up, leaving her mark in her book. Mrs. Prime went on reading, harder than ever. There was to be some conference of importance from which she could not but feel herself to be excluded in a very special way. Something wicked was surely to be proposed, or she would have been allowed to hear it. She said nothing, but her head was almost shaken by the vehemence with which she read the book in her lap.

“不等今晚过完，我就叫她脸颊上的樱桃回来，”斯特特太太望着那张苍白的小脸，心里说。普赖姆太太也向邻居略微招呼了一声；可那一点儿心思、那一会儿工夫，她破费得真是少到不能再少。斯特特太太原也算过得去，可普赖姆太太手头有更大的功课，顾不上同斯特特太太闲磕牙。

Mrs. Sturt retired beyond the precincts of the widow’s front garden before she said a word. Rachel had followed her first through the gate, and Mrs. Ray came after with her apron turned over her head. “What is it, Mrs. Sturt?” said Rachel. “Have you heard anything?”

“Heard anything? Well; I’m always a hearing of something. Do you slip across the green while I speak just one word to your mother. And Rachel, wait for me at the gate. Mrs. Ray, he’s in my little parlour.”

“Who? not Luke Rowan?”

“But he is though; that very young man! He’s come over to make it up with her. He’s told me so with his own mouth. You may be as sure of it as—as—as anything. You leave ’em to me, Mrs. Ray; I wouldn’t bring them together if it wasn’t for good. It’s my belief our pet would a’ died if he hadn’t come back to her—it is then.” And Mrs. Sturt put her apron up to her eyes.

Rachel having paused for a moment, as she looked first at her mother and then at Mrs. Sturt, had done as she was bidden, and had walked quickly across the green. Mrs. Ray, when she heard her neighbour’s tidings, stood fixed by dismay and dread, mingled with joy. She had longed for his coming back; but now that he was there, close upon them, intending to do all that she had wished him to do, she was half afraid of him! After all was he not a young man; and might he not, even yet, be a wolf? She was horrorstricken at the idea of sending Rachel over to see a lover, and looked back at the cottage window, towards Mrs. Prime, as though to see whether she was being watched in her iniquity. “Oh, Mrs. Sturt!” she said, “why didn’t you give us time to think about it?”

“Give you time! How could I give you time, and he here on the spot? There’s been too much time to my thinking. When young folk are agreeable and the old folk are agreeable too, there can’t be too little time. Come along over and we’ll talk of it in the kitchen while they talks in the parlour. He’d a’ been in there among you all only for Mrs. Prime. She is so dour like for a young man to have to say anything before her, of the likes of that. That’s why I took him into our place.”

“听着什么了？哦，我这耳朵向来不断听见点什么。你趁我同你妈说一句话的工夫，先溜过绿地去。还有，雷切尔，你在院门口等我。雷太太，他在我家小客厅里。”

“可就是他呀；就是那个年轻男人！他是来同她和好的。这是他亲口对我说的。您可以放一百二十个心，跟——跟——跟什么都一样。您把他们交给我，雷太太；要不是为了好事，我才不把他们往一块儿领呢。我信得着，咱们的宝贝儿，他若不回来，命都要没了——真是这样呢。”斯特特太太说着，把围裙掩到了眼睛上。

“给你们工夫！他人就杵在眼面前，我怎么给你们工夫？依我看，工夫已经太多了。小辈们愿意，长辈们也愿意，这样的工夫再短也不嫌短。快跟我过来，他们在客厅里谈，咱们在厨房里也说它一说。要不是普赖姆太太在，他这会儿早进屋同你们大伙儿坐在一处了。她在跟前，那样的事，年轻人怎么好开口？她那副样子太板啦。就为这个，我才把他安置到我们家。”

“And that’s just the truth,” said Mrs. Sturt, triumphantly. “He’s through there in the little parlour, and you must just go to him, my dear, and hear what he’s got to say to you.”

“I suppose you must do what she tells you,” said Mrs. Ray.

===Original===
“Mamma, you must go to him,” said Rachel.

“That won’t do at all,” said Mrs. Sturt.

“And why has he come here?” said Rachel.

“Ah! I wonder why,” said Mrs. Sturt. “I wonder why any young man should come on such an errand! But it won’t do to leave him there standing in my parlour by himself, so do you come along with me.”

So saying Mrs. Sturt took Rachel by the arm to lead her away. Mrs. Ray in this great emergency was perfectly helpless. She could simply look at her daughter with imploring, loving eyes, and stand quivering in doubt against the dresser. Mrs. Sturt had very decided views on the matter. She had put Luke Rowan into the parlour with a promise that she would bring Rachel to him there, and she was not going to break her word through any mock delicacy. The two young people liked one another, and they should have this opportunity of saying so in each other’s hearing. So she took Rachel by the arm, and opening the door of the parlour led her into the room. “Mr. Rowan,” she said, “when you and Miss Rachel have had your say out, you’ll find me and her mamma in the kitchen.” Then she closed the door and left them alone.

===Original===
Rachel, when first summoned out of the cottage, had felt at once that Mrs. Sturt’s visit must have reference to Luke Rowan. Indeed everything with her in her present moods had some reference to him—some reference though it might be ever so remote. But now before she had time to form a thought, she was told that he was there in the same house with her, and that she was taken to him in order that she might hear his words and speak her own. It was very sudden; and for the space of a few moments she would have fled away from Mrs. Sturt’s kitchen had such flight been possible. Since Rowan had gone from her there had been times in which she would have fled to him, in which she would have journeyed alone any distance so that she might tell him of her love, and ask whether she had got any right to hope for his. But all that seemed to be changed. Though her mother was there with her and her friend, she feared that this seeking of her lover was hardly maidenly. Should he not have come to her—every foot of the way to her feet, and there have spoken if he had aught to say, before she had been called on to make any sign? Would he like her for thus going to him? But then she had no chance of escape. She found herself in Mrs. Sturt’s kitchen under her mother’s sanction, before she had been able to form any purpose; and then an idea did come to her, even at that moment, that poor Luke would have had a hard task of it in her sister’s presence. When she was first told that he was there in the farmhouse parlour, her courage left her and she dreaded the encounter; but she was able to collect her thoughts as she passed out of the kitchen, and across the passage, and when she followed Mrs. Sturt into the room she had again acquired the power to carry herself as a woman having a soul of her own.

“Rachel!” Rowan said, stepping up to her and tendering his hand to her. “I have come to answer your letter in person.”

“I knew,” she said, “when I wrote it, that my letter did not deserve any answer. I did not expect an answer.”

“But am I wrong now to bring you one in person? I have thought so much of seeing you again! Will you not say a word of welcome to me?”

===Chinese===
雷切尔方才头一个被唤出村舍时，心里立时明白，斯特特太太这趟来，必是同卢克·罗恩有干系。说实在的，她如今这种心境，样样事都免不了牵到他——纵然牵得再远，也是牵到他。可这一回，还没容她转出一个念头，人家已经告诉她，他就在同一所房子里，就要把她领到他跟前，叫她听他的话，也说自己的话。这太突然了；有那么几息的工夫，若逃得脱，她真要从斯特特太太的厨房里逃出去。罗恩走后，她也有过想逃到他身边去的时候，想过独自一人赶多远的路都甘愿，好去告诉他她的情意，问一问她有没有权利指望他的情意。可如今一切似乎都变了样。虽说有母亲在身边，有这位朋友在场，她还是怕，这样去寻情郎，不大合乎少女的身份。难道不该他来找她么——一步一步都走到她脚边来，有话就在那儿说，哪能先叫她表态？这样自己送上门去，他会喜欢她吗？可她已经没有退路了。主意还没拿起来，她已发觉自己身在斯特特太太的厨房里，有她母亲点头应承着；就在那一刻，她心里倒闪过一个念头：可怜的卢克，若当着她姐姐的面开口，只怕难得够呛。头一回听说他在农舍客厅里的时候，她的勇气跑了个精光，直怕这场会面；可穿过厨房、走过过道的一路，她把心神收拾齐整了，跟着斯特特太太进屋的时候，她已经重新拿得住自己，撑得起一个有自家魂灵的女人的样子了。

“雷切尔！”罗恩说着迎上前来，向她伸出手。“我是亲自来给你回信的。”

“我写信的时候就明白，”她说，“我那封信不配讨一个回音。我也没指望有回音。”

“可如今我把回音亲手送来了，难道错了？能再见你一面，我想了多少时候！你不肯对我说一句欢迎的话吗？”

===Original===
“I am glad to see you, Mr. Rowan.”

“Mr. Rowan! Nay; if it is to be Mr. Rowan I may as well go back to Baslehurst. It has come to that, that it must be Luke now, or there must be no naming of names between us. You chided me once when I called you Rachel.”

“You called me so once, sir, when I should have chided you and did not. I remember it well. You were very wrong, and I was very foolish.”

“But I may call you Rachel now?” Then, when she did not answer him at the moment, he asked the question again in that imperious way which was common with him. “May I not call you now as I please? If it be not so my coming here is useless. Come, Rachel, say one word to me boldly. Do you love me well enough to be my wife?”

She was standing at the open window, looking away from him, while he remained at a little distance from her as though he would not come close to her till he had exacted from her some positive assurance of her love as a penance for the fault committed by her letter. He certainly was not a soft lover, nor by any means inclined to abate his own privileges. He paused a moment as though he thought that his last question must elicit a plain reply. But no reply to it came. She still looked away from him through the window, as though resolved that she would not speak till his mood should have become more tender.

===Chinese===
“见着您我很高兴，罗恩先生。”

“罗恩先生！不行；要还叫罗恩先生，我不如就回巴斯尔赫斯特去。事情已经到了这一步：如今非叫卢克不可，不然咱们之间就谁也别提谁的名字。当初我叫你雷切尔，你还责备过我呢。”

“你倒是叫过我一回，先生，那一回我本该责备你，却没有。我记得清清楚楚。你很不对，我很糊涂。”

“那我现在可以叫你雷切尔了吧？”她一时不答，他便拿他那副惯常的专断口气又问了一遍。“如今我叫你，还由不得我自己称心吗？若是不然，我这趟来就是白来。来，雷切尔，大胆对我说一句话。你爱我，爱到肯做我妻子的地步了吗？”

她站在敞开的窗前，脸朝着别处，不理会他；他离她远远地站着，仿佛不先从她那里讨来一句明明白白爱的保证——就当是罚她那封信的过错——便不肯挨近她。他断然不是个软绵绵的情郎，也绝无意削减自己分内的特权。他顿了一顿，只当末了这一问总会逼出一个明白的回答。回答却没有来。她照旧隔着窗子望着外头，不理他，像是打定了主意，非等他的性子变得温存些，决不开口。

===Original===
“You said something in your letter,” he continued, “about my affairs here in Baslehurst being unsettled. I would not show myself here again till that matter was arranged.”

“It was not I,” she said, turning sharply round upon him. “It was not I who thought that.”

“It was in your letter, Rachel.”

“Do you know so little of a girl like me as to suppose that what was written there came from me, myself? Did I not tell you that I said what I was told to say? Did I not explain to you that mamma had gone to Mr. Comfort? Did you not know that all that had come from him?”

“I only know that I read it in your letter to me—the only letter you had ever written to me.”

===Chinese===
“你信里说到，”他接着讲，“我在巴斯尔赫斯特这边的买卖没个定准。那件事没安排妥当，我就不肯再在这里露面。”

“那不是我，”她说，猛地转过身来冲着他。“那样想的不是我。”

“话是写在你信里的，雷切尔。”

“你对我这样的姑娘就这么不了情吗？竟当那些话一字一句都是出自我自己？我不是告诉过你，那些话是人家教我说的，我才说的？我不是同你讲明白，妈妈去求教过康福特先生？那些话都打他那儿来，你不知道？”

“我只知道，那些话是你写给我的信上的——你写给我的唯一的一封信。”

===Original===
“You are unfair to me, Mr. Rowan. You know that you are unfair.”

“Call me Luke,” he said. “Call me by my own name.”

“Luke,” she said, “you are unfair to me.”

“Then by heavens it shall be for the last time. May things in this world and the next go well with me as I am fair to you for the future!” So saying he came up close to her, and took her at once in his arms.

“Luke, Luke; don’t. You frighten me; indeed you do.”

===Chinese===
“您待我不公道，罗恩先生。您自己知道您不公道。”

“叫我卢克，”他说。“叫我自己名字。”

“卢克，”她说，“你待我不公道。”

“那好，我指天为誓，这是最后一回。往后我若待你有一分不公道，就叫这世上和来世的事，都跟我不顺遂！”说着他挨到她跟前，一把将她搂进怀里。

“卢克，卢克；别这样。你吓着我了；真的吓着了。”

===Original===
“You shall give me a fair open kiss, honestly, before I leave you—in truth you shall. If you love me, and wish to be my wife, and intend me to understand that you and I are now pledged to each other beyond the power of any person to separate us by his advice, or any mother by her fears, give me a bold, honest kiss, and I will understand that it means all that.”

Still she hesitated for a moment, turning her face away from him while he held her by the waist. She hesitated while she was weighing the meaning of his words, and taking them home to herself as her own. Then she turned her neck towards him, still holding back her head till her face was immediately under his own, and after another moment’s pause she gave him her pledge as he had asked it. Mrs. Sturt’s words had come true, and the cherries had returned to her cheek.

“My own Rachel! And now tell me one thing: are you happy?”

“So happy!”

“My own one!”

===Chinese===
“我走之前，你定要给我一个光明正大的吻，实心实意的——真的，你一定得给。你若爱我，愿意做我的妻子，又要叫我明白：你我如今已彼此订了终身，任凭什么人凭他的劝说、哪个母亲凭她的惊慌，都拆不散我们——那就给我一个大胆的、诚实的吻，我便明白，这一个吻就是这个意思。”

她仍旧迟疑了一忽儿，脸偏着躲开他，他搂着她的腰。她迟疑着，掂量他这番话的分量，把它们一点一点收进心里，当作自己的东西领受。随后她把颈子朝他转过去，头还往后仰着收，直到自己的脸正正对着他的脸，又停了一停，便照他讨要的那样，把她的信誓给了他。斯特特太太的话应验了，她脸颊上的樱桃回来了。

“我的雷切尔！这会儿告诉我一件事：你幸福吗？”

“幸福极了！”

“我的人儿！”

===Original===
“But, Luke—I have been wretched;—so wretched! I thought you would never come back to me.”

“And did that make you wretched?”

“Ah!—did it? What do you think yourself? When I wrote that letter to you I knew I had no right to expect that you would think of me again.”

“But how could I help thinking of you when I loved you?”

===Chinese===
“可是，卢克——我一直苦透了；——苦透了！我以为你再也不会回到我跟前来了。”

“这个叫你苦了？”

“哎！——叫不叫人苦？你自己想呢？写那封信给你的时候，我就知道，我没有权利指望你还会想起我来。”

“我既然爱你，叫我怎么不想你？”

===Original===
“And then when mamma saw you in Exeter, and you sent me no word of message!”

“I was determined to send none till this business was finished.”

“Ah! that was cruel. But you did not understand. I suppose no man can understand. I couldn’t have believed it myself till—till after you had gone away. It seemed as though all the sun had deserted us, and that everything was cold and dark.”

They stood at the open window looking out upon the roses and cabbages till the patience of Mrs. Sturt and of Mrs. Ray was exhausted. What they said, beyond so much of their words as I have repeated, need not be told. But when a low half-abashed knock at the door interrupted them, Luke thought that they had hardly been there long enough to settle the preliminaries of the affair which had brought him to Bragg’s End.

===Chinese===
“还有妈妈在埃克塞特撞见你那回，你连一句口信也不捎给我！”
